title: Lawsuit alleging guards fatally beat inmate prompts calls for state review of prison deaths
description: More than eight months after 24-year-old Malik Avila died in custody at High Desert State Prison his family is still left with questions around the circumstances that lead to his death.  James Urrutia, an attorney at LJU law firm, which is representing Avila’s family, filed a wrongful death lawsuit Monday seeking answers and alleging prison […]
text:
Attorney James Urrutia and the family of Malik Avila, who died with incarcerated in Nevada, announced a wrongful death lawsuit.
(Photo: Michael Lyle/ Nevada Current)More than eight months after 24-year-old Malik Avila died in custody at High Desert State Prison his family is still left with questions around the circumstances that lead to his death. 
James Urrutia, an attorney at LJU law firm, which is representing Avila’s family, filed a wrongful death lawsuit Monday seeking answers and alleging prison guards fatally beat Avila.
“Malik Avila’s case is extremely disturbing,” Urrutia said Monday during a press conference on the steps of the Regional Justice Center in downtown Las Vegas. “We have again a case of an underlying beating of an inmate by guards.”
The Clark County Coroner’s Office classified Avila’s death as “natural” caused from a lack of oxygen and brain damage. The road to finding answers, and justice, has been plagued by obstacles from state and local officials. 
The Nevada Department of Corrections declined to respond to questions from Nevada Current, saying it does not comment on pending litigation.
NV prison system mortality report ‘sounds like a lot of unexplained deaths,’ legislator says

The litigation comes weeks after state lawmakers questioned corrections officials about the number of deaths in Nevada prisons. 
At the time of its July 16 presentation to the Interim Judiciary Committee, 166 people had died since 2024 while in NDOC custody, officials said. 
Two additional deaths have been reported since then, including another death Monday at High Desert State Prison, bringing this year’s death toll to 38 so far. 
Of the 166 deaths corrections officials presented to state lawmakers in July, 98 were classified as natural – just like Avila. 
State Sen. Melanie Scheible, who chairs the committee, said at the time the 166 figure  “sounds like a lot of unexplained deaths to me.”
When an incarcerated person dies in custody, it should be considered a “red flag,” Urrutia said. 
“There are so few inmates who have life sentences,” he said. “One of the challenges is that a prison controls the evidence. They are the ones telling the story to a coroner. And yes, the body tells a story. But it needs context. If the only context you’re getting is from the prison, they are not getting the proper context. It’s a huge problem.”
In an interview, Urrutia said the Nevada Attorney General’s Office should consider pursuing an independent investigation into all those who died in custody and review the manner and cause of death determined by a county’s coroner’s office. 
Alcinia Whiters, a spokesperson for the AG’s office, said the Nevada Office of the Inspector General is tasked with handling “investigations into suspicious deaths” at state prisons.
“Our office may become involved when a case is referred to us, including when an inmate’s death involves an alleged use of force by a correctional officer,” Whiters said in a statement. 
When asked under what circumstance would Attorney General Aaron Ford consider a broader holistic review of inmate deaths, the office said “prosecutorial decisions are made on a case-by-case basis.”
“We also regularly review and discuss broader issues that may affect inmate safety and deaths within Nevada’s correctional system,” Whiters wrote in an email. “Our focus is ensuring accountability where the evidence supports it while remaining attentive to systemic issues that may emerge through the cases we handle.”
The Current also asked Gov. Joe Lombardo’s office under what circumstances should the state review in-custody deaths. 
“To strengthen safety and support the Department’s mission of maintaining secure, humane facilities while preparing offenders for successful reentry, NDOC is evaluating additional measures to curb the flow of illegal substances while increasing surveillance, adjusting staff operations, and reviewing standard procedures regarding classification of offenders and housing practices,” Drew Galang, a spokesperson for the for the governor, said in a statement.
  ‘I will never understand’ 

Avila’s family joined Urrutia at the press conference Monday ahead of the lawsuit being filed. 
“I miss him so much,” Lucy Avila, Malik’s grandmother, said as she fought back tears. “Every single day I think of him. He had a beautiful smile.”
In 2019, a then-17-year-old Avila was convicted of second degree murder and began serving a 10-year sentence.




Quotation







“There are so few inmates who have life sentences. One of the challenges is that a prison controls the evidence. They are the ones telling the story to a coroner. And yes, the body tells a story. But it needs context. If the only context you’re getting is from the prison, they are not getting the proper context. It’s a huge problem.” 


– James Urrutia, attorney for the family of Malik Avila



Lucy Avila described her only grandson’s efforts to better himself in prison by taking classes and working as a porter serving meals to other inmates. The family mourns the person he could have become if he hadn’t died.
“For over a week, Malik had been requesting medical assistance,” the lawsuit reads. “Prison guards mocked him. Malik’s mom started calling the prison to seek assistance. Prison guards mocked Malik even more.”
A summary of the investigation included in the autopsy report says that a Correctional Emergency Response Team was dispatched to Avila’s cell at 4 a.m. Nov. 4 after a family member called the prison to inform staff he was having a seizure.The investigation alleges that Avila had access to an unauthorized cellphone. 
The report alleges Avila became “combative” and the CERT unit went “hands-on” and “took him down.”
Urrutia said the firm obtained a voice recording from a whistleblower within the prison system who captured the incident. 
“We know what his last words were,” Urrutia said. “‘Please stop. Please stop.'”
The autopsy report says Avila refused medical treatment and only began to have a seizure needing medical assistance nearly three hours later. The lawsuit alleges he was rushed to the infirmary immediately after the CERT unit entered his cell. 
“By 7:53 am, still in the infirmary, Malik began convulsing unconsciously; his brain damaged,” according to the lawsuit. 
A prison nurse called 911 seeking for Avila to be transported to the hospital after he began convulsing. During the call, the nurse described Avila as a “stupid young idiot.”
Though he arrived at Mountain View Hospital on Nov. 4, Avila’s family didn’t know where he was at the time, according to the lawsuit.  
“The family shouldn’t have to be searching all over the state of Nevada for where their son is.” Urrutia said. “And while they are searching, they don’t even know his status. They don’t even know why he is missing.”
Corrections officials “never told his next of kin that he’s on life support,” Urrutia said during the press conference. “It takes eight days for the family to finally find where Malik is laying unconscious on life support. How that is OK I will never understand.”
The lawsuit also alleges that the prison lied multiple times, telling the family officials “suspect he ingested a substance” and that “he wasn’t involved in any altercation.”
“How can we expect our medical staff to provide proper care when they are being told lies from the prison?” Urrutia asked. “It causes confusion with medical treatment. It causes confusion for the family?”
Avila died Nov. 22 according to the autopsy report. Urrutia questioned the determination as a “natural” death.
“If people have head trauma, they are not dying naturally,” Urrutia said in an interview, adding the family has waited eight months to receive a final autopsy report. “Families should not have to wait eight months to find out why their son died.”
Clark County didn’t respond to requests for comment. 
In conversations with the coroner’s office, “they just keep saying they are still investigating and that they sent Malik’s brain to a neuropathologist … and they are waiting to get that result back,” Urrutia said. “My understanding is they have gotten the results back but still aren’t letting us have access to the brain yet so we can do our own analysis.”
Following the 10 a.m. press conference, the Current emailed Clark County to confirm it hadn’t released the autopsy report to the family and explain the timeframe for releasing reports.
Urrutia said the family was sent the final autopsy report that night.
  ‘Justice has to be done’ 

In addition to a lawsuit on behalf of Avila’s family, Urruita also filed a separate lawsuit July 30 in the deaths of three other inmates in 2024. 
“It hurts my heart that we keep having to show up and talk about this,” Urrutia said. “We hope at some point our government officials will put more work into solving this problem.”
A deadly fight took place at Ely State Prison in 2024 and three people who were incarcerated died.
“The prison officials working that day watched as multiple men bled out and took no action to save their lives,” Urrutia said at the press conference. “It doesn’t make sense for a group of prison guards to watch men or women bleed to death.”
Monday isn’t the first time Urruita stood on the steps of the Regional Justice Center surrounded by grieving families searching for answers after loved ones died under unexplained circumstances while in NDOC custody. 
The attorney also represented the family Christian Walker, another inmate who died in 2023.
At the time the lawsuit was filed – April 2024 – Urruita said corrections staff “beat him and left him to die in a cell all by himself.”  
Walker’s family was awarded a $4.6 million settlement in October 2025 for his wrongful death.
His death – like Avila’s – was also determined to be natural, Alyssa Piraino, an attorney at LJU Law Firm, said.
In the Walker’s case, the Nevada Office of the Inspector General recommended criminal charges. 
“Up at the next level, at the attorney general’s office, the criminal prosecution division chose not to press charges,” Urrutia said. 
The Attorney General’s Office, which was defending NDOC in the wrongful death lawsuit, argued last summer there wasn’t enough evidence to bring criminal charges. 
The LJU attorneys said that three independent medical experts disagreed with that determination. But “the coroner’s office filed a motion for summary judgement,” said Piraino, ending the case.
All these incidents together should show a need for reform to Nevada corrections institutions, the attorneys said. 
“We need the camera system regularly inspected, unannounced,” Urrutia said. “The prison should not be the only one responsible for saving the footage. We need somebody independent to be monitoring the cameras and the footage.” 
In the meantime, the families still wait for answers. 
“We are just looking for justice,” Lucy Avila said. “Justice has to be done for the inmates who have lost their lives.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: IG report ignored the critical role of over-prosecution in straining the indigent defense system
description: Massachusetts cannot ignore the realities of how over-prosecution and overcharging are part of the reason for the price tag on indigent defense.
text:
THE OFFICE OF THE INSPECTOR GENERAL recently released its long-awaited report on indigent defense in Massachusetts, accompanied by grand announcements about a broken system for fulfilling the state’s obligations to uphold the right to counsel when accused of a crime.  
The report was conducted pursuant to legislation enacted to identify flaws in the current indigent defense system after a record number of court-appointed lawyers declined to accept new cases during the summer of 2025, citing inadequate payment rates, leaving thousands of individuals facing criminal charges without a lawyer. 
Despite taking a year to investigate the complex and nuanced issues involved in providing indigent defense, the 150-page report contains a glaring omission. The report places blame at the feet of the Committee for Public Counsel Services, the state agency which is responsible for ensuring that people too poor to afford their own lawyers have representation when they are accused of crimes as well as the courts, the Probation Department, and the lawyers who provide this constitutionally required representation at a fraction of what they could be making in any other type of legal work.  
In its 42 findings, the report blames CPCS for not having full-time salaried staff attorneys take enough cases during the crisis as well as before and after. It proposes that CPCS conduct more audits of the work of court-appointed lawyers and cap the number of hours they can work on a case.  
The report blames the Probation Department for failing to adequately evaluate indigency when assigning lawyers and blames the courts for waiving fees charged to people so poor that they can’t afford a lawyer. What the report makes no mention of is the role over-prosecution and over-criminalization play in the state’s counsel crisis. 
The right to counsel is not universal. In fact, the right to counsel in Massachusetts is only guaranteed if the charge that the defendant is facing carries the possibility of incarceration.  
Every day, courtrooms across the Commonwealth are packed with people charged with low-level offenses, nearly all carrying the possibility of incarceration, and persons overcharged by overly aggressive prosecution. Charges that do not carry the possibility of incarceration are few. 
Individuals whose cases are so minor that they will never be incarcerated sit in the courtrooms waiting to be appointed a lawyer. Prosecutors across the Commonwealth regularly charge people as aggressively as possible to gain the upper hand in forcing a plea, creating in the process more work for the lawyers assigned to the cases. These charging decisions do not exist in a vacuum, and there has been much discussion in recent years about the racial disparities in the criminal justice system.  
A 2020 study conducted by The Criminal Justice Program at Harvard Law School found that racial and ethnic differences in the type and severity of initial charges account for over 70 percent of the disparities in sentence length.  Bringing both more serious charges than the facts warrant and charges in situations where criminalization is unnecessary adds to the financial burden on indigent defense. 
Prosecutors in Massachusetts wield broad authority. They decide whether to charge, what to charge, and how aggressively to pursue a case. When discretion is used to maximize exposure rather than to calibrate charges to culpability, it can not only distort outcomes but also add to the Commonwealth’s need for appointed counsel.  
Overcharging has become an accepted practice, and attention is rarely paid to charging decisions. A prosecutor can overcharge by adding multiple counts to a single incident or charging a more serious charge than the facts warrant.  
Both methods help prosecutors gain the upper hand in plea negotiations, but this very tactic requires the defense lawyer to spend more hours on the case. While charging decisions are complex, the fact that a report on indigent defense fails to address this variable in the system’s cost is a critical oversight. 
Any observer of the district and municipal courts, where most of the expense of indigent defense is incurred, knows that a large percentage of cases involve minor offenses that are unlikely to result in incarceration.  
For example, in 2025, there were 21,683 cases brought in the Commonwealth under laws that criminalize driving with a suspended or revoked license or registration and provide for imprisonment. In each of these cases, if the defendant was found to be indigent, a lawyer was assigned, and that lawyer was constitutionally required to spend time defending against the allegations. 
These hours and cases add up, and they can’t be discounted in any sort of accurate analysis of the indigent defense system. Decriminalizing lower-level offenses for which there is almost never an incarceration sentence would significantly reduce the number of people in need of appointed counsel. 
Future conversations about the indigent defense system in Massachusetts cannot ignore the realities of how over-prosecution and overcharging are part of the reason for the price tag on indigent defense. 
Shira Diner is a lecturer and clinical instructor at the Criminal Defense Clinic at Boston University School of Law.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: As forests burn across the state, a cluster of residential fires also takes a toll
description: Utah’s raging wildfires have burned fast and big in the backcountry, but cities and suburbs are also dealing with destructive fires.
text:
The North Union Apartments in Midvale are pictured on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, after a large fire days earlier displaced residents from all 220 occupied units. (McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)Utah’s raging wildfires have burned enough land in the backcountry to match the size of Salt Lake County this year. And along northern Utah’s urban corridor, a number of recent structure fires have also proved destructive, torching homes, displacing hundreds of people and forcing still more to evacuate. 
“Collectively, it’s been a very, very busy season,” Sandy Fire Chief Ryan McConaghie said Tuesday. 
The spate of house and apartment fires taking place from Cache County’s small city of Nibley to more densely populated West Jordan has kept firefighters hard at work as their departments focus on keeping them safe in this summer’s punishing heat.

And even if they sound like a broken record, city officials are urging Utahns to stay vigilant and on their best behavior, calling attention to this summer’s tinder-dry conditions. 
“We try to tell people, again: If you’re pulling trailers, try not to be dragging chains,” said Nate Cochran, spokesperson for Unified Fire Authority. “If you are smoking, try not to flick your cigarette butts out the window. If you are doing any type of barbecuing or outdoor fires — anything like that — making sure you have a water source with you.”
He noted firefighting agencies help each other out when backup is needed, but said if they get spread too thin, response times may stretch out a somewhat longer. 
McConaghie and Cochran said their agencies have been stocking up on electrolyte supplements and keeping a close eye on crews to help ensure they do not overheat as they battle blazes in scorching temperatures.
“We try to cycle guys into what we call ‘rehab,’ let them take their gear off, cool down, hydrate up, and then just really watching those work cycles,” Cochran said. 
The North Union Apartments in Midvale are pictured on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, after a large fire days earlier displaced residents from all 220 occupied units. (McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)The North Union Apartments in Midvale are pictured on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, after a large fire days earlier displaced residents from all 220 occupied units. (McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)The North Union Apartments in Midvale are pictured on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, after a large fire days earlier displaced residents from all 220 occupied units. (McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)
But the high temperatures can still take a toll. Cochran said a Unified firefighter was treated for heat exhaustion last week after attacking an aggressive apartment fire in Midvale that tore through the building’s roof and top floor, displacing residents of more than 200 apartments. 
Thankfully, the agency serving unincorporated areas of Salt Lake County and the city of Eagle Mountain hasn’t recorded any major injuries this summer, Cochran added. 
But some residents have been severely affected by the fires. Two people in Sandy were hospitalized and a cat was killed in a house fire this week that was sparked by a candle, McConaghie said.  
He and Cochran agreed that while blazing outside temperatures don’t seem to intensify house fires, gusty winds will carry them quickly to other properties. And in an indirect result of hotter weather, overworked air conditioning units can also place stress on mechanical equipment that can lead to fires, they said. As for the cause of the Midvale fire, officials cited a mechanical issue but haven’t released further details. 
McConaghie said it’s fortunate his community is not experiencing the level of devastation seen in the Pacific Northwest. In Spokane, Washington, and its surrounding areas this week, hundreds of homes and other buildings were leveled and more than 65,000 people were told to evacuate because of wildfires. Officials there said Monday they arrested a man suspected of arson.  
With a focus on the potential for devastating wildfires where Utah neighborhoods meet rugged terrain, state lawmakers created a program to assess fees on homeowners in those zones and allow them to trim down that expense by taking steps to mitigate fire risk. Inspectors are expected to start visiting properties in coming weeks.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: National Dems to target GOP congressional leader in NC
description: North Carolina’s 9th district has long been considered a safe Republican seat.
text:
U.S. Rep. Richard Hudson (left), a North Carolina Republican, talks with state Sen. Bobby Hanig (right), a Republican running for North Carolina's 1st Congressional District, in Raleigh on Dec. 1, 2025. (Photo: Galen Bacharier/NC Newsline)The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is adding North Carolina’s 9th Congressional District to its “Districts in Play” program, targeting longtime Republican incumbent Rep. Richard Hudson. 
This program focuses on competitive districts held by vulnerable Republicans across the country as Democrats seek to regain a majority in the House, according to a Wednesday announcement. Other targets include Reps. Greg Murphy in NC-03 and Chuck Edwards in NC-11. 
It’s a bold move. Hudson has served as chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee for three years, raising money for the U.S. House Republican Caucus and deciding where it needs to spend that money to pick up or defend seats. 
North Carolina’s 9th district has long been considered a safe Republican seat. In 2024, Hudson defeated Democrat Nigel William Bristow by 18 percent of the vote. President Donald Trump carried the district that year by a similar margin. 
The GOP isn’t worried about the seat. Members view the addition as Democrats baiting them to spend more money in the district, diverting resources away from tighter races. 
“National Democrats know they can’t beat Chairman Hudson on his record, so they’re trying to buy what they can’t earn,” NRCC spokesperson Will Kiley said. “This is what desperation looks like with a checkbook.”
But Democrats are hopeful about Alamance and Guilford counties, which first became a part of Hudson’s district for the 2024 cycle. Democrat Josh Stein won both in the gubernatorial contest that same year. 
NC Congressman Chuck Edwards to face censure in US House for inappropriate conduct

DCCC spokesperson Madison Andrus said North Carolina voters aren’t happy with Hudson’s record of attacking affordable health care and hurting working families. Democrats are also inspired by members of the party overperforming in special elections this cycle, although she said the DCCC has not conducted recent polling in the district.
“Voters know Richard Hudson is responsible for House Republicans’ disastrous anti-working family platform crushing North Carolinians,” DCCC chair Suzan DelBene said in a statement. “A protector of corruption, and self-interested Republicans at the expense of North Carolina’s working families, Hudson does not work for this community.”
At the moment, Republicans hold a 218-212 majority in the House, with four vacancies. One independent, Rep. Kevin Kiley of California, caucuses with the Republicans. 
Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former Army major and West Virginia state senator, is facing Hudson in November. 
Ojeda spent about 15 years at Fort Bragg near Fayetteville during his military career. Upon moving to West Virginia, he won election to the state Senate in 2016.
He’s no stranger to running in Republican areas. Ojeda briefly ran for president in 2020, before dropping out and challenging U.S. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito. He did not win the Democratic nomination in the primary election. 
After that, he returned to North Carolina. Ojeda has raised $2.2 million since he launched his campaign, according to reports filed with the Federal Election Commission. 
“This race is winnable, and people are seeing that our hard work is paying off,” Ojeda said in a statement. “This district has been shifting, because people here are tired of having a member of Congress beholden to the MAGA machine in Washington.”
Hudson has been in office since 2013, with his district previously numbered as the 8th. He serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
New poll shows Whatley within striking distance of Cooper as GOP support coalesces

As NRCC chair, Hudson is the fifth-ranking member in Republican leadership and the highest-ranking Republican member of Congress from North Carolina in history, according to the committee.  
Hudson has raised $3.2 million so far during this election cycle, according to reports filed with the Federal Election Commission. 
The Hudson campaign did not respond to requests for comment. 
Both parties are funding candidates across the Tar Heel State. 
The DCCC previously added Jamie Ager, a fourth-generation farmer from a political family, to its “Red to Blue” program, supporting his bid to oust Edwards in Western North Carolina. They’re also investing in Rep. Don Davis, an incumbent in the 1st Congressional District, the most competitive of the state. 
Republicans aren’t backing down. They’re aiming for NC-01 as well, adding Army Veteran Laurie Buckhout to the NRCC’s “MAGA Majority” program. U.S. House Majority Leader Mike Johnson, R-La., campaigned with Buckhout in the district this week.
Over in the Senate, Democrats view North Carolina’s open seat as one of their best pick-up opportunities in 2026. Recent polls show Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper leading former Republican National Committee chair Michael Whatley, with Cooper also well ahead of Whatley in fundraising. 
The general election takes place Nov. 3.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Paid Leave is helping workers — and businesses like mine
description: More than half of Minnesota Paid Leave applicants earn less than $78,000 a year, according to state data. These are the workers who staff our restaurants, clinics, retail counters and construction crews. These workers historically had the least access to employer-paid leave and the least cushion to fall back on when life happened anyway.  Before […]
text:
More than 38,000 approved applications for Paid Leave so far have been for new parents. (Photo by John Moore/Getty Images)More than half of Minnesota Paid Leave applicants earn less than $78,000 a year, according to state data. These are the workers who staff our restaurants, clinics, retail counters and construction crews. These workers historically had the least access to employer-paid leave and the least cushion to fall back on when life happened anyway. 
Before this program, an hourly employee facing a serious illness or a new baby often had two options: quit or return to work before they were ready. Unless they worked for my small business, which has paid out of pocket for loyal employees to get the care they need or to support those in need. These options are less than ideal for the employee and for the employer. 
For small businesses like mine, the Paid Leave program saves me money while providing a safety net that my employees deserve. To do some back-of-the-napkin math, an employee earning $78,000 would have a premium of less than $700 a year. And that $700 is the total; businesses can decide whether to split the premium equally or take on a bit more. In return, the employee can receive partial wage replacement while away. For a worker earning $78,000 a year, estimated weekly payments from Paid Leave exceed $1,000. The math is clear. This is a good deal. 
The geographic data reinforces why this matters beyond the Twin Cities. The Department of Employment and Economic Development, which runs the program, reports that 44% of applicants live outside the 7-county metro area. Greater Minnesota’s small businesses often operate with limited staff and fewer nearby job candidates to draw on than their metro counterparts; losing even one employee who has to care for an aging relative can mean weeks of scrambling. Without a return-to-work date, a small business owner might hesitate to hire a replacement, leaving them understaffed. Or they spend time, effort and money finding and training a new employee only to have them leave a few months later. A program that helps a rural clinic or hardware store retain the employee they already trained —  rather than searching a shallow labor pool for a replacement — is doing real economic work in exactly the communities that can least afford instability.
The gender breakdown deserves attention, too. Nearly two-thirds of applicants are women. This is unsurprising given that more than 38,000 approved applications so far have been for new parents. Much of the retail and hospitality industries are disproportionately staffed by women. Not to mention child care centers, home health and personal care aides, cleaning companies and educators. Small employers in these women-dominated sectors have long struggled to retain talent through pregnancy and early parenthood — not for lack of will but for lack of resources to hold a position open unpaid for months. Paid Leave gives them a tool they never had before: a state-administered benefit that lets them keep experienced staff on the books through one of the most common reasons people leave the workforce altogether — in exactly the industries that can least afford to lose them.
None of this is free, and small business owners are right to have asked hard questions about the premiums when the law passed. But the program was built with that concern in mind. Employers with 30 or fewer employees pay a reduced premium rate, and because the benefit itself is paid by the state — not the employer’s payroll — a small business no longer has to choose between funding a worker’s leave out of its own cash flow and letting that worker go. Grant assistance is also available to help smaller employers offset early administrative costs.
Six months of data is not proof of a program’s long-term success, and Minnesota should keep watching how Paid Leave performs as it matures. But the early numbers point in a clear direction: The workers using Paid Leave are disproportionately the ones small businesses most need to retain and who previously could least afford to hold on to. 
That is not a case against small business. It is a case for how far a modest, shared investment can go toward keeping Minnesota’s small employers competitive with the large ones down the street.

name: Mississippi Today
title: FEMA cut staff without planning for future work, watchdog says
description: The Federal Emergency Management Agency headquarters is photographed in Washington, May 5, 2025.
text:
The Trump administration cut the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s workforce without a plan, Congress’ watchdog found.
The disaster-response agency is at risk of being unprepared and without the necessary staff to respond to future emergencies, the Government Accountability Office said in a report released Tuesday.
As of May, FEMA has pushed out over 6,400 employees since President Donald Trump took office last year, according to data maintained by the Office of Personnel Management. FEMA is now trying to hire nearly 350 employees deemed a priority by the agency, according to the GAO, although the watchdog says that as of last month, FEMA still hasn’t done the analysis and planning related to its workforce necessary to make sure that it’s prepared for future disasters.
“FEMA did not base its workforce reduction decisions or proposed future workforce actions on an analysis of the current state of its workforce or a forecast of future requirements,” the report says. “As a result, FEMA does not know the impact of these changes on its capacity to meet mission needs now or in the future.”
After scrapping its strategic plan in May of last year, the agency waited to develop a new one until a FEMA Review Council established by Trump issued its report, which didn’t happen for another year due to several delays in its release. Typically, FEMA’s strategic plan would be used to guide workforce planning. The panel ultimately recommended in May of this year that much of the responsibility for disaster response be shifted to state and local government.
In the meantime, FEMA is still without goalposts to guide its actions. Because of this, FEMA hasn’t conducted workforce planning for future incidents — including the 2026 hurricane season, the GAO says.
The office said that it found “no evidence” that DHS or FEMA leadership assessed the impact of the agency’s move earlier this year to reduce the number of on-call employees who help with disaster recovery. In May, the agency began offering employees new appointments after previously not renewing their contracts.
Since Trump took office, FEMA did submit a staffing plan to DHS late last year that proposed cutting FEMA’s workforce in half. But there isn’t any evidence that that was based on a workforce analysis, either, the GAO says. That proposed reduction to 11,383 employees was made despite staffing analysis from program and regional offices that recommended the agency have 23,000 employees.
“With the start of the 2026 hurricane season and the increasing cost and complexity of federal support as natural disasters become more frequent and intense, FEMA is facing similar or greater risk of disaster workforce capacity and competency limitations than the agency faced in 2024 following Hurricanes Helene and Milton,” the watchdog agency said in the report.
Long-standing workforce challenges hampered FEMA’s response to those back-to-back disasters in 2024, the GAO has previously reported.
As part of its latest report, the GAO recommended that lawmakers consider providing “additional accountability” by mandating that future workforce changes at FEMA are informed by workforce planning at the agency and requiring that FEMA report to Congress on its workforce planning process before every hurricane season.
The report comes after a tumultuous year and a half for the agency, which has had four acting administrators since January 2025. This is both the longest it hasn’t had a confirmed administrator and the highest turnover in at least 15 years, according to the GAO.
Trump nominated one of those previous acting administrators, Cameron Hamilton, to lead the agency in May after ousting him just a year prior over Hamilton publicly breaking with the administration’s efforts to dismantle the agency. He’s yet to be confirmed by the Senate.
FEMA is also in the midst of an ongoing lawsuit arguing that separating the agency’s on-call response and recovery employees by refusing to renew their terms was unlawful.
DHS said in a response included in the GAO report that it “remains committed to continuing to help people before, during, and after disasters, as we seek to bring real reform to FEMA to meet the challenges of mission delivery and enhance how we assist survivors.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: What Tuesday’s primary results say about Amendment 5 and the next Missouri Senate
description: Missourians went to the polls Tuesday, and the results resist a single storyline. Here’s what’s worth noticing. Amendment 5 is the clearest verdict of the night. It lost 83-16. Not close, not regional — a rout. The governor’s top priority, backed by $17.2 million from donors who never had to identify themselves and it couldn’t […]
text:
The Missouri Capitol Building in Jefferson City on May 12 (Jason Hancock/Missouri Independent). Missourians went to the polls Tuesday, and the results resist a single storyline. Here’s what’s worth noticing.
Amendment 5 is the clearest verdict of the night. It lost 83-16. Not close, not regional — a rout. The governor’s top priority, backed by $17.2 million from donors who never had to identify themselves and it couldn’t even clear 20%.
Watch what that did downballot. State Rep. Greg Sharpe voted against it every time it came up, drew more than $91,000 in attack spending for it, and won going away. In the 6th District, the two candidates who ran hardest against it — Rudy Veit and Ike Skelton — together drew 47.3% of the vote, nearly twice the winner’s share. Jake Vogel won that race with 26.6% while offering the least enthusiastic endorsement in Missouri politics: “It is a plan.”
The theory in June was that Amendment 5 would be a loyalty test with consequences. It turned out to be a liability most Republicans had already sensed and run from. Gov. Mike Kehoe says the work isn’t over. The arithmetic suggests otherwise, at least in this form.
The anti-establishment wave didn’t arrive. Dusty Blue lost in northeast Missouri, finishing 18 points behind Sharpe. Dan Stacy lost by 25 in Lee’s Summit to House Speaker Jon Patterson, who helped shepherd Amendment 5 through the legislature. Tricia Byrnes, who built her campaign on data centers in a district where Amazon and Google are actually building them, lost by 12.
Running against Jefferson City was not, by itself, enough. Several candidates spent the summer promising to go to the Capitol and blow things up, and voters mostly declined the offer.
Except in the 20th District.
Lori Rook did exactly that — ran against Jefferson City, its lobbyists and its power structure — and knocked off state Sen. Curtis Trent.
That one matters beyond southwest Missouri. Trent wasn’t just an incumbent. He was running to become Senate majority floor leader, the person who controls what legislation reaches the floor. He had the backing of much of the Republican establishment and an allied PAC that spent $838,000, more than $500,000 of it attacking Rook.
She won anyway.
Which brings us to money.
A national school-choice group spent nearly $90,000 trying to defeat state Sen. Jill Carter, almost $150,000 opposing Bill Hardwick and $36,000 against Rook. It went 0-for-3.
But Patterson’s roughly $2.9 million war chest certainly didn’t hurt him against Stacy, who had $43,000. And Hardwick won after an Illinois gambling company seeking to legalize video lottery terminals poured $422,000 into a PAC attacking Hannah Kelly while giving another $95,000 to a PAC aligned with him.
So Tuesday wasn’t a rejection of money any more than it was a rejection of the establishment.
Maybe the better way to understand the results is that Republican voters were selective about what they were angry about — and whom they blamed.
They overwhelmingly rejected the tax plan Jefferson City handed them. They punished Trent, who had accumulated power in the Capitol, but rewarded Patterson, who had accumulated far more. They chose Sharpe over the candidate endorsed by the outgoing Senate president. But they rejected insurgents elsewhere who made essentially the same argument about a broken political system.
Tuesday didn’t produce a revolution.
It produced something potentially more interesting: a Republican Senate with no obvious mandate about what voters want it to become.

title: ‘I’m the awakener’: Evangelist Tommie Zito plans to transform Poultney’s Green Mountain College campus into a Christian university
description:
Some are skeptical of the preacher’s Z University proposal given his past business ventures, but Zito says he has learned from his mistakes. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘I’m the awakener’: Evangelist Tommie Zito plans to transform Poultney’s Green Mountain College campus into a Christian university.
text:
Evangelical preacher Tommie Zito is planning to covert Green Mountain College in Poultney into Z University.  Seen on Friday, July 31, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
POULTNEY — Tommie Zito was visiting Vermont to preach for congregations in Rutland and Burlington earlier this year when he learned of a call for the “third great awakening” from the owner of the defunct Green Mountain College.
The whiskey merchant and former media personality Raj Bhakta, who bought the campus for over $4 million in 2020, put it up for donation to a Catholic organization seeking to revive “Western Civilization” in late February. 
Zito, a Florida evangelist, said Bhakta’s pitch caught his attention as he had been looking for a place to land and open up a Christian university in recent years. 
“‘If it’s an awakening you’re looking for,’ I said, ‘I’m the awakener,’” Zito said in an interview on July 31, referring to his work evangelizing internationally. “I run the American awakening, Canadian awakening, Italian awakening, Japanese awakening, Dubai awakening.”
Zito sat down for an interview with VTDigger on a muggy Friday afternoon in one of Bhakta’s lounge areas in Withey Hall.
He ran late to the meeting as he said he was baptising around 20 people in the Poultney River just prior. Later that night, Zito held a banquet seeking donations to his nonprofit educational venture, which saw 200 attendees, he said after the event. 
Zito will not be acquiring the campus through donation. The deal is yet to be disclosed, but it is a “fair price,” Zito said. The transfer is planned for the fall, as Zito is waiting for Bhakta to move out of the campus.
“It’s a big operation, so we’re just taking a slow road,” Zito said.
Green Mountain College in Poultney on Friday, July 31, 2026. Evangelical preacher Tommie Zito is planning to covert the college into Z University. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Bhakta had several large-scale plans for the former college — including a sustainable agriculture initiative or a hotel with some residential development — but that never came to fruition after clashes with the town over a tax stabilization agreement and failing to complete Act 250 requirements. The state also alleged Bhakta violated Act 250 by modifying the buildings and operating a school and whiskey business on campus in March while searching for a new owner of the college. Bhakta — also known for his appearance on President Donald Trump’s reality TV show “The Apprentice” and a political stunt involving an elephant and a mariachi band — planned to donate the college by late April, but the spring came and went with no announcement. 
Suddenly, as the country was celebrating its 250th anniversary last month, Vermonters caught wind of a Florida preacher posting on social media that he would be taking over the Poultney campus for a Christian school called ‘Z University.’ Bhakta’s team previously confirmed with VTDigger that Zito was indeed the planned recipient of the nearly 200-year-old college campus. 
He plans to name the college ‘Z University’ after his father, who he said was a lay preacher while Zito was growing up and inspired his preaching. 
Zito plans to enroll the first batch of Z University students in August of 2027, and wants to offer an AI-driven curriculum for Christians to study government, digital media, music and creative arts and evangelism and global missions, among other possible classes. He eventually wants to open similar schools around the world, but he said “the Lord told me America first…we had to create a model here first.”
Who is Tommie Zito? 
Zito, 52, has served as an evangelical preacher for nearly 30 years, since dropping out of college where he studied sociology and psychology. Though he spends approximately 200 days a year preaching around the world, Zito said his family is rooted in South Florida. 
Zito said his father was an orphan in the Brooklyn Boys Home in New York, and witnessed abuse from the leaders of the orphanage who had “a cross around their neck and a Bible in their hand,” driving him away from Christianity. Later in life but before Zito’s birth, Zito’s father “met Jesus in a radical way.” His father separated his experience of the church with his belief in Jesus, which influenced Zito’s own preaching. 
“I’m not a huge believer in the building of a church,” Zito said. “We’re supposed to take Christ out, you know, to the people.”
Pamela Bolton, hailing from Whitehall, New York who preaches at a church nearby, organized Zito’s preaching visits to Vermont and showed him Bhakta’s donation plans. Bolton said she and Zito share an interest in regional religious revivals and think a fully accredited Christian university on the New York border in Vermont will benefit New England. 
Vermont used to be a very religious state, evident in the many church steeples in municipalities around the state, Zito said. Now it consistently ranks among the least religious states in the country, so Zito said he can make a larger impact by spreading his message in Vermont.
Evangelical preacher Tommie Zito is planning to covert Green Mountain College in Poultney into Z University.  Seen on Friday, July 31, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
“I just think it would be a wonderful thing for this area, and I believe that there would be many people who would be very supportive of this,” Bolton said. 
Early on in his preaching career, Zito said he helped Dr. Rodney Howard-Browne with the River Bible Institute, a school in Tampa, Florida in 1997. Browne, Zito’s mentor, made headlines in 2020 when he was arrested for holding church services during the COVID-19 pandemic, and subsequently prompted Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis to exempt church gatherings from the state’s stay-at-home order. Zito was holding in-person church services as well, just with a lower profile, and he said he supports Browne despite not being affiliated with the preacher currently.
Zito also started a religious school called Zoe Bible College in Florida in the 2010s, which is no longer in operation. Zito said he has learned that running a school requires more hands-on leadership and higher tuition to cover costs. 
He filed for bankruptcy for his organization Tommie Zito Ministries in 2010, and the Internal Revenue Services revoked the 501(c) 3 status of Zito’s nonprofit the American Awakening Inc. in 2025, according to a federal database.
‘Really big dreams’
Some are skeptical of the scale of Zito’s plans though, as he leaves a trail of failed ventures in his wake in Florida. 
Given his past track record, James Johnson, Poultney business owner of Analog Cycles, said he doubts that Zito has the finances or fundraising ability to get the university off the ground. 
“It’s hard to start a school from scratch, much less an evangelical school in the middle of nowhere,” Johnson said. “I think it’s just going to collapse under its own weight very rapidly.”
Rebecca Cook, the Poultney Public Library’s director, said that there has been a lot of build up for what appears to be premature plans, but she’s waiting to see how things unfold. Cook and Johnson both said that Poultney has invested in recreation to bolster the local economy despite the empty college at the end of its downtown corridor. 
“It seems like a lot of really big dreams without necessarily having the building blocks in place,” Cook said. “I think at this point, I’m just not sure anybody’s going to do anything down there because nothing ever seems to quite materialize.”
Zito said that these financial concerns are “all being worked out for good” with lawyers, and he will answer further press questions when he returns to Vermont in November after he plans to acquire the campus. 
“Leadership is learned, right, learned through a lot of trials and errors and mistakes, and having the right people involved is an important part of any organization,” Zito said. “Normally, you know, there’s a lot of failure before there’s success.” 
Now he recognizes that he is not trained to run a university and said he is working on recruiting qualified people and delegating leadership roles. He said he is early on in soliciting donations, but acknowledges that the necessary improvements and renovations will require significant funding. Bhakta’s donation website stated the college would require $1 million to operate annually on top of the estimated $500 million in deferred maintenance. 
Zito said he offered the first donation to his project. Zito said he previously received a salary of $100,000 per year for the next 10 years from an undisclosed benefactor for his preaching, and decided to put that toward the college. 
“Leaders have to lead, and it allows me to stand in front of people that have millions of dollars and say, you know what? I had nothing. Somebody gave me this, and I’m putting it into the gospel,” Zito said.
Where does Zito go from here?
Zito has to jump through many hoops before his dream for Z University can become a reality.
He said he is working through the process for zoning and addressing the previous alleged Act 250 violations. 
“We’re planning on doing everything proper,” Zito said. “We are team players. There’s rules for a reason.”
Zito’s team has reached out to discuss permitting obligations, Peter Gill, executive director of the state’s Land Use Review Board, wrote in a Monday email. 
“Responsibility to resolve or remediate an alleged violation of an Act 250 permit runs with the land and passes to the current owner,” Gill wrote.

READ MORE

Zito also is looking into accreditation, either with the New England Commission of Higher Education or with a Christian school accreditation entity.
While Zito plans for an August 2027 opening of Z University, an “application for accreditation is a long process, extending over many years, with no guarantee of success,” the New England Commission of Higher Education President Lawrence Schall wrote in an email to VTDigger Monday. 
Zito said has met with the town of Poultney to cultivate a better relationship going forward, and hopes to bring foot traffic to town businesses and open the campus up to residents as well. “Our university is Poultney’s University,” he added. “I’m an evangelist. I want people on this campus.” 
Poultney Town Manager Paul Donaldson wrote in a Tuesday email that he urged Zito to seek Vermont-based counsel with knowledge of the “legal and permitting climate of the State” at the meeting last week. 
“He has very ambitious plans for the campus, and the Town looks forward to supporting his efforts to have a successful launch of his endeavors,” Donaldson wrote in the email.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: National Democrats put NE-01 in its ‘districts in play’ program
description: DCCC's program is a different tier from its “Red-to-Blue” program, which the Nebraska 2nd Congressional District is in.
text:
Chris Backemeyer at a Nebraska Democratic Party fundraiser at the Omaha Hilton on Nov. 8, 2025. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — National Democrats are putting Nebraska’s 1st Congressional District in their “districts in play,” a program for districts seen as competitive in the eyes of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee this cycle. 
The DCCC, the campaign arm for U.S. House Democrats, announced the move Wednesday; the program is a different tier from its “Red-to-Blue” program, which the Nebraska 2nd Congressional District Democratic nominee, Denise Powell, is in.
Unlike the 2nd District, this is the first time the 1st District has been put in this program. The DCCC said the addition of the incumbent Republican Rep. Mike Flood’s district sends “the clear message that Democrats know Nebraska voters are souring on Flood’s wildly unpopular record of raising costs, attacking affordable health care, and hurting working families.” 
“This November, Nebraskans are going to fire Flood and elect a representative who is going to put them and their concerns over D.C. party bosses,” said DCCC Chair Suzan DelBene.
Flood is in a race with Democratic nominee Chris Backemeyer and Libertarian Nik Sandman. Austin Ahlman was mounting a nonpartisan campaign but dropped out over concerns about his father’s health. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Backemeyer might benefit from the race being part of the program, as it will likely help with fundraising. According to the FEC, Backemeyer has $290,610 cash on hand while Flood has $1.5 million to spend. 
Brentin Ungar, Flood’s campaign manager, said, “It’s no surprise DC Democrats are rallying behind 20-year DC resident Chris Backemeyer, even as he struggles to win over Democrats back home in Nebraska.”
“Partisan noise has never mattered to Congressman Flood, which is why he will keep listening to his district and delivering results like the bipartisan housing bill to make life more affordable for Nebraskans,” Ungar said in a statement. 
Backemeyer said Flood “has spent years in elected office, but what do we have to show for it?”
“Families are struggling with rising costs for groceries, gas, healthcare, and housing. Farmers are facing higher expenses and uncertainty in the markets they rely on,” Backemyer said. “Our neighbors deserve a leader who will put people first, show up every day, and fight for lower costs and real opportunities for hardworking Nebraskans to get ahead.”
National Democrats are hoping to take over Republicans’ slim majority in the closely divided U.S. House, as the party that controls the White House typically doesn’t do well in the midterms. 
The 1st District comprises 12 counties, including Lancaster County, which is home to heavily Democratic Lincoln, a city whose blue voters are often drowned out by the region’s more conservative smaller cities and rural areas. 
Flood has won his past two U.S. House elections by 20 and 16 percentage points, respectively. Analysts, including the nonpartisan Center for Politics, The Cook Political Report and Inside Elections, consider the 1st District seat safely Republican.
With the 1st District added to the DCCC’s districts in play, the total is now 47 races included in the program. 
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland wants better readers. Have we asked children what they need?
description: There's lots of talk about the importance of keeping kids reading over the summer to prevent the dreaded summer slide, but one thing may be missing from those discussions,  writes Melissa Bellamy: Is anyone is asking the kids what they want to read?
text:
One way to make sure kids are reading over the summer, or anytime, is as simple as asking them what they want to read, writes Melissa Bellamy.Each summer, Maryland families are encouraged to keep children reading. Schools send home book lists, libraries launch reading initiatives, and educators remind parents about the “summer slide” — the decline in reading skills that can occur when students stop reading during summer break.
These efforts are important. Strong literacy skills are linked to academic achievement, lifelong learning, workforce readiness and civic participation. Maryland has made literacy a priority, and communities across the state continue investing in programs that help children become confident readers.
But amid the conversations about improving literacy, one question often goes unanswered: Have we asked children what makes them want to read?
As homeschool parents, we know firsthand that every child learns differently. We also know that children are more likely to embrace reading when they have ownership over it. Instead of assuming we knew the answers, we decided to ask our four children what they thought.
Our first question was simple: “What don’t you like about reading?”
Their answers were remarkably similar.
Sometimes the books they’re expected to read don’t match their interests. Sometimes reading feels like another assignment instead of an opportunity to explore. Sometimes they’re told what to read without ever being asked what they would like to read.
Then we asked a second question: “What would make you read more?”
Again, the answers were consistent.




Your opinion matters

They wanted books about topics they genuinely enjoy. Sports. Animals. Music. History. Adventure. Graphic novels. Science. They also wanted reading to be fun — not because someone told them it should be, but because they had a reason to keep turning the pages.
This summer, our family joined the Summer Break Baltimore program at the Enoch Pratt Free Library. While checking out books was exciting, what immediately captured our children’s attention was the Summer Break Bingo Board.
Rather than measuring success only by the number of books completed, the bingo board encourages children to experience literacy in different ways. Families can read outside, attend library programs, visit different library branches, write stories, create artwork inspired by books, recommend books to friends, explore nature and participate in community events. Reading becomes part of discovery rather than another task to complete.
For our children, that made all the difference.
Zaiden: “When I can pick books about things I like, I actually want to finish them.”
Zaine: “The bingo board makes reading feel like a challenge instead of homework.”
Zuri: “I like stories that let me draw something after I read.”
Zainuri: “I like earning bingo squares so we can be entered into the drawing for cool prizes.”
Their responses reminded us that children often know exactly what motivates them — we simply have to take the time to listen.
Our family conversation continued with their dad, Paul, who reflected on one of his favorite childhood memories: participating in Pizza Hut’s BOOK IT! program. Reading enough books earned him a personal pan pizza, but what stayed with him wasn’t the reward itself. It was the excitement of reaching a goal and feeling proud of becoming a reader.
That memory highlights something educators and parents have known for years: positive reinforcement matters. Whether it’s a library bingo board, a reading competition, a bookmark filled with stickers, or a free pizza, these incentives don’t replace a love of reading — they can help spark it.
Libraries like the Enoch Pratt Free Library are demonstrating what literacy can look like when it is interactive, community-centered and joyful. Their summer programming reminds us that reading doesn’t have to compete with summer fun. It can be part of it.
As Maryland continues investing in literacy, we hope educators, librarians, policymakers and families will add one more strategy to the conversation.
Ask children what they enjoy reading.
Ask them what discourages them.
Ask what would make them pick up another book tomorrow.
The answers may be different for every child, but one thing is certain: Children deserve a voice in shaping the reading experiences designed for them.
If Maryland wants to raise lifelong readers, the next chapter shouldn’t be written only by adults.
It should be written with children, too.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma school leaders, state lawmakers at odds over State Question 844
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — A nonpartisan state question appearing on Aug. 25 runoff ballots, which has vocal support from the state Capitol, has raised concerns that it could come at a cost to public schools. State Question 844 would give the Oklahoma Legislature the authority to recalculate how much it should pay to local government entities, […]
text:
Voters mark their ballots in the Oklahoma County Election Board on June 11 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Courtney Bell/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A nonpartisan state question appearing on Aug. 25 runoff ballots, which has vocal support from the state Capitol, has raised concerns that it could come at a cost to public schools.
State Question 844 would give the Oklahoma Legislature the authority to recalculate how much it should pay to local government entities, including school districts and counties, in reimbursements for a manufacturing tax incentive.
The incentive offers a five-year property tax exemption to manufacturers who set up new operations in the state. Under the law, the state must reimburse local entities for the property tax revenue a company is exempted from paying. 
Public school leaders said these state reimbursements have added millions in funding that transformed their districts for the better. They contend that allowing lawmakers to reduce the repayments could negatively impact districts statewide, not only in their select areas.
Legislators say the reimbursement rates have become overly expensive and disproportionately benefit a few counties. 
Last year, Oklahoma paid $88.6 million for manufacturing exemption reimbursements. About 40% alone went to entities in Mayes County.
The county, located northeast of Tulsa, contains the state’s largest industrial park and earns the biggest share of the repayments. 
Much of the park’s developed areas sit within the borders of Pryor Public Schools. The school system received $24 million this year in reimbursements from the manufacturing exemption, likely the most of any Oklahoma district, Superintendent Lisa Muller said.
That money contributes significantly to her district’s operations and payroll, its budget for facilities and its capacity to pay school bond debt.
“It’s revolutionized what we’re able to do within Pryor Public Schools,” Muller said.
The manufacturing exemption reimbursements help generate enough local revenue that some districts, like Pryor, don’t receive any money from the state aid formula, the chief driver of state funding for public schools. Losing the reimbursement revenue could make Pryor and other districts once again reliant on state funding formula dollars, Muller said.
Increasing the number of schools that rely on a finite amount of formula funds would proportionally decrease the dollars available to each district statewide, Muller and other local superintendents told Oklahoma Voice.
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, said the claim is simply a “scare tactic.” Rather than paying higher reimbursements to a few districts, he said lawmakers could redistribute some of those funds to schools statewide.
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, speaks in the House chamber of the state Capitol in Oklahoma City on April 28. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
He said it’s not the Legislature’s intent to change any reimbursement rates that are already established. Rather, he pledged lawmakers only would try to negotiate new deals that arise in the future.
Hilbert said lawmakers should be given input in the reimbursement amounts, particularly if state officials believe a new manufacturer has received too high of a property value assessment.
“As it stands right now, a county assessor assesses one of these properties, and whatever the assessed value is, the state of Oklahoma has to pick up the tab,” Hilbert said. “It’s a blank check. The state of Oklahoma doesn’t have the ability to contest this. So, one county assessor gets to determine what the check is going to be, and the other 76 counties have to write the check.”
If lawmakers wanted to eliminate all current and future reimbursements, they could by deeming every industry ineligible for the program, he said. SQ 844 doesn’t introduce that possibility. 
The Legislature attempted to do so in 2020, but Gov. Kevin Stitt vetoed it. 
“Much of the fearmongering about (SQ) 844 hurting schools and the fear of what the Legislature would potentially do if this state question passed, the Legislature has already had the authority to do,” Hilbert said. “Those are things that the Legislature could already do if it desired to.”
In 1985, the Legislature put the manufacturing tax exemption program on the ballot, and Oklahoma voters agreed to enshrine it in the state Constitution. One percent of the state’s personal income tax and corporate income tax revenue is dedicated to paying reimbursements to local governments, according to the Oklahoma Policy Institute. 
Over time, criteria to qualify for the exemption has expanded and changed. The program’s cost has grown far beyond the fund dedicated to support it, requiring state lawmakers to add tens of millions in supplemental appropriations, Hilbert said. 
Public schools alone needed a $64.8 million supplement in the 2025 fiscal year to cover all reimbursement obligations.
Minco Public Schools Superintendent Kevin Sims said if the program is too expensive, the Legislature over the years should have put more limits on who could qualify for the tax exemption.
Lawmakers already have whittled certain industries out of the program. They disqualified wind energy farms in 2015, data centers in 2021 and will phase out solar farms in 2028.
Sims said his district, about 30 miles southwest of Oklahoma City, received a “huge” benefit from past manufacturing reimbursements for a nearby wind farm. 
The repayments enabled Minco to pay teachers $5,000 above state minimum salaries, make improvements to the district’s football field and build a new high school, middle school and auditorium, he said. A new solar farm is expected to generate more reimbursement revenue for Minco in the coming year.
Sims said he understands “there’s only so many dollars” the state can spend, but SQ 844 presents “a pretty costly situation.”
“The Legislature created this, and they’re trying to create a solution,” he said. “Schools and counties are pretty negatively impacted, in my opinion, from that solution.”

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming property tax cuts ripple down to childcare
description:
To make up for a drop in tax revenues, Western Wyoming Community College charged students more for the subsidized childcare that’s long been considered an enrollment incentive. 
The post Wyoming property tax cuts ripple down to childcare appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
ROCK SPRINGS—College took a back seat when Melody Nathan’s son was born. 
She had already earned her associate’s degree, but without family help nearby, she stopped attending school to care for her newborn while her husband worked. A daughter followed, and pretty soon Nathan had been home raising her babies for five years. 
When her son started kindergarten, she began considering reentering the workforce. The thought of earning a bachelor’s degree was appealing. But it felt complicated, she said. The idea of handing off her toddler daughter to strangers at a childcare facility was daunting. There was also the cost of higher education, which would be compounded by the expense of childcare at a time when she wouldn’t be earning an income.
Then she found the Western Wyoming Community College Children’s Center. 
“Having this place was the push I needed to feel comfortable going back to school to get my bachelor’s degree,” Nathan said. 
The center has been providing subsidized on-campus preschool to the children of college students since 1975. The idea is that affordable, convenient childcare could help remove one higher-learning hurdle for student-parents in southwest Wyoming. 
For people like Nathan, it did just that. Once she saw the quality care her daughter received and the center’s proximity to her classes, Nathan said, she felt confident committing. 
Mother and daughter both recently graduated. Nathan with her bachelor’s degree in business organizational management, and her daughter, Maren, as a kindergarten-ready preschool alum. 
While the college-run preschool has long kept prices rock-bottom for students, it’s had to increase fees over the last year as statewide property tax reductions have left it with a smaller budget. The center used to charge student-parents just $23 per credit, which totalled around $275 per semester for a full-time college student. Now, it charges student-parents $200 per month, or about $800 a semester. (Faculty and members of the public pay more).
That is still a bargain compared to market rates, said Center Director Susie Young, but she worries it’s another chink in the robust student support services that have enticed many students to Western. 
“These students don’t have jobs; they are trying to get an education,” she said. A cost increase of even a couple hundred dollars could be enough to make college untenable, she worries.
Children’s Center Director Susie Young in a classroom at the center, which is located on the campus of Western Wyoming Community College. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
“It’s just getting harder and harder to support the students,” Young said. 
Around Wyoming, subsidized childcare is feeling the pinch of declining tax revenues. It’s among the downstream victims of recent state laws that reduced residential property taxes. Reductions have diminished the revenue pools that fund municipalities and special districts. 
Impacts have touched everything from library budgets to park maintenance and hospitals around the state. They are also affecting subsidized childcare meant to soften the blow for parents already struggling with high costs of living or, in the case of Western, hoping to gain an education that can ensure better long-term job prospects. 
These tax revenues could take a further slashing. A citizen-initiated ballot measure will ask voters this fall to create a new 50% homeowner’s tax exemption. If it passes, revenues that fund fire departments, community colleges and county municipalities will dwindle further.  
“If the tax cut passes, our revenue will go down. That’s just an absolute,” said Mark Rembacz, Western Wyoming Community College interim vice president of student services. “We’ll have to make a decision as an institution where that reduction falls, whether it be the children’s center or the swimming pool or our athletic programs.”
Not just daycare
Hot days occasionally force the center to hold summer recess indoors, but a cloudy sky kept temperatures down on a Wednesday afternoon in July. A group of preschoolers bounded around the playground equipment, shrieking and taking laps on the slide. 
The center accepts children ages 2-5, and had about 65 enrolled during the spring semester. They are divided into classrooms based on age: “bunnies,” “bears” and “turtles.” Young, the center’s sole full-time staffer, employs lead teachers for each classroom along with several aides. 
The center aims to create kindergarten-ready students. The young pupils learn the basics of phonics and numbers; they practice motor skills and work on independence and sharing; and they learn colors and shapes. Miniature tables, bright rugs, bookshelves and alphabet charts occupy its rooms.
Students store their belongings in cubbies at Western Wyoming Community College Children’s Center in Rock Springs in July 2026. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
For most of its history, the center only served college students and faculty. It opened spots to the public last year as part of its effort to raise extra revenue. The public rate is $800 per month. 
Karen Dickson, who the students call “Miss Karen,” first encountered the center decades ago as a parent. She had moved to Rock Springs, where her husband’s employer allowed him to earn his associate’s degree at Western. After hearing about the childcare benefit, she enrolled her kids and was impressed. Dickson took an aide position in 1989, worked for 35 years as a bunnies teacher and now fills in.   
When her she came aboard, the center was free for college students. “So many moms got to go to college, and we got so many nurses through our nursing school, because we took their kids,” Dickson said. “This is a really special place.”
Rembacz and Young agreed that the center makes programs like nursing — which is very time intensive — possible for many student-parents.  
“If this service was not here,” he said, “we would have people who would not be able to attend school.” 
Revenue sources
Western Wyoming gets funding from three buckets, Rembacz explained. The first is student tuition, which the school strives to keep as low as possible. The second is Legislature-appropriated state revenue, and the third is local tax funded by the mill levy. 
“The mill levy for us is the largest portion of our funding,” he said. 
Western administrators realized funding declines would follow a 2025 tax exemption law, and made some “really hard financial decisions,” Rembacz said. That included a reduction in force and an assessment of ancillary programs. Administrators eliminated the volleyball program and reworked the children’s center, raising student fees and opening to the public.  
To alleviate the burden, Young obtained grant funding to help students with tuition costs for their kids. The added support was fantastic, she said, but grants aren’t a guaranteed permanent solution. 
Currently, Rembacz said, the college is working to understand how the ballot initiative could further impact the bottom line: “How much revenue do we stand to lose, and what are the things that we’re going to have to eliminate in order to make up that shortfall?”
It’s a tricky balance, he said. Administrators want to make the community college as affordable as possible. Higher enrollment means a more educated population and creates a highly coveted workforce of nurses and industrial manufacturers, he said. But when tax revenues ebb, something has to give. 
“And so we want to be mindful of every dollar that we ask for from students,” he said. 
Filling a desperate need
Part of the grant funding Young secured came from the Wyoming Women’s Foundation, which works to expand opportunities for women and girls. The organization is keeping close tabs on the way tax policy is impacting services like subsidized childcare, said Associate Director of Policy Micah Richardson. 
“I don’t know if everyone’s understanding the ripple effects to businesses and families,” she said. If future tax-reduction measures pass, she added, services like subsidized childcare are likely to be among “one of the first things on the chopping block.”
The Children’s Center isn’t the only place feeling the squeeze. 
Sublette BOCES Early Education Program, commonly known as BEEP, is an early education and childcare center in Pinedale. The program started years ago as part of a program to train educators, Executive Director Robin Schamber said, but “it was also filling a desperate [childcare] need in our community,” particularly for infants.  
It’s a race down the slide at Western Wyoming Community College Children’s Center in Rock Springs in July 2026. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
Today, BEEP cares for infants through preschool-aged children, with a capacity of about 50. It’s popular, but in recent years a double whammy of plunging oil-and-gas mineral revenues and decreasing property tax collections has shrunk its budget. 
“It has been a drastic impact for us, and we’re rethinking the way we’re doing things now,” Schamber told WyoFile in June. “We’ve raised prices on parents, which was not popular at all.” 
The situation is a double-edged sword, she said. High property taxes also strain residents’ budgets and contribute to the region’s high cost of living, so she understands the intent behind lowering them. She also understands that in tough times, tough decisions have to be made. 
Back at Western Wyoming, nursing school student and mother of three Madisen Danzl reflected on the value of the Children’s Center. She enrolled her youngest in the preschool after the death of her own mother, who had long helped care for her grandchildren. That freed her up to focus on classes without the burden of market-rate childcare. 
“I don’t think I could be able to go to school, honestly, without it,” Danzl said.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Judge blocks bid to end oversight of bank accused of discrimination in Newark
description: Federal oversight of Lakeland Bank will continue after allegations it avoided giving mortgages to people of color and opening branches in Newark.
text:
A federal judge has rejected the Trump administration’s effort to end federal oversight of a bank that avoided giving mortgages to people of color and opening bank branches in Black and Hispanic communities in the Newark area. (Photo by New Jersey Monitor)A judge has rejected the Trump administration’s effort to end federal oversight of a bank that avoided giving mortgages to people of color and opening bank branches in Black and Hispanic communities in the Newark area.
U.S. District Judge Claire C. Cecchi refused Friday to terminate the five-year consent decree Lakeland Bank agreed to follow in 2022 to resolve allegations it engaged in systematic, intentional discriminatory practices known as redlining.
The ruling means the bank will remain under court oversight until September 2027, as the consent decree requires.
Bank officials and Trump administration officials had argued in court filings that Lakeland had “substantially complied with” court-ordered reforms.
But Cecchi noted that the bank has unfinished obligations, including some that are “sizeable.” She pointed to a requirement that Lakeland establish a $12 million subsidy fund for customers seeking home mortgage, improvement, and refinance loans, noting that the bank has yet to disburse more than $4 million of that fund.
“A promise to reach substantial compliance in the future is not substantial compliance,” Cecchi wrote.
Lakeland merged with Provident Financial Services in 2024. Provident spokesman Keith A. Buscio said the company is “committed to fulfilling the terms of the original consent order with the Department of Justice.”
The department secured the consent decree in 2022 when Philip Sellinger, a Democratic appointee, was U.S. attorney in New Jersey but backpedaled after President Donald Trump took office last year and ordered federal agencies to reevaluate consent orders stemming from “disparate impact.” That drove Justice Department officials to try to terminate oversight of banks accused of redlining, including Lakeland and ESSA Bank & Trust in Philadelphia.
A different federal judge last summer ordered oversight of ESSA to continue, and the feds did not appeal that decision, so advocates for low- and middle-income residents don’t expect the feds to appeal Cecchi’s ruling either.
Department spokespeople did not respond to a request for comment.
Advocates had demanded Lakeland’s consent decree to remain in place, saying that ending it would threaten progress since 2022 and leave them with no remedy if the bank’s compliance falters.
Dan Urevick-Ackelsberg, senior attorney at the Public Interest Law Center, represented advocates in court. He called the effort to end oversight early “part and parcel of … an administration that is trying to tear down every vestige of the pillars of our nation’s civil rights legislation.”
“The people of Newark and its surrounding areas are entitled to a lending market free from discrimination, period,” Urevick-Ackelsberg said. “This ruling will help them have it.”
