name: Maine Morning Star
title: Maine legal groups back state’s refusal to issue covert license plates to federal agents
description: A coalition of Maine-based attorneys and legal nonprofits are arguing that the state had the right to deny federal immigration agents covert license plates and that the lawsuit filed by President Donald Trump’s administration should be dismissed. In a friend of the court brief filed in U.S. District Court on Tuesday, the coalition argues that […]
text:
A U.S. Department of Homeland Security vehicle parked outside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement field office in Scarborough on Jan. 15, 2026. (By Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)A coalition of Maine-based attorneys and legal nonprofits are arguing that the state had the right to deny federal immigration agents covert license plates and that the lawsuit filed by President Donald Trump’s administration should be dismissed.
In a friend of the court brief filed in U.S. District Court on Tuesday, the coalition argues that under the anticommandeering doctrine established by the U.S. Supreme Court, the federal government cannot “commandeer” state regulatory processes by ordering states to enact or administer a federal regulatory program, citing the 1992 ruling that expanded the power of the states established in the Tenth Amendment. 
“As a dual sovereign with the federal government, the State of Maine has authority to allocate its resources according to its own priorities and cannot be forced to issue undercover Maine license plates to immigration officials,” reads the brief. 
Emma Bond, a staff attorney with the American Civil Liberties Union of Maine, which is among the groups included in the brief, said in a statement, “The federal government cannot force Maine officials to support immigration operations that many Mainers view as tyranny and abuse.”
“The U.S. Constitution incorporates principles of dual sovereignty that prevent the federal government from conscripting states to assist in the enforcement of federal programs, including immigration enforcement,” Bond continued. “These constitutional protections ensure that the State of Maine can remain responsive to its residents and voters in their outcry against abusive, violent, and deadly immigration operations.” 
In addition to the ACLU, the group includes the Immigrant Legal Advocacy Project and Pine Tree Legal Assistance, along with Anna Welch, University of Maine School of Law professor and founding director of the school’s Refugee and Human Rights Clinic, and Erica Schair-Cardona, an adjunct professor who also serves as outreach and advocacy attorney for the clinic.
Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, who is named in the lawsuit along with Gov. Janet Mills, received a request from federal authorities for undercover license plates a week before the large-scale U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operation began in January, amid a major surge in Minnesota where federal agents shot and killed U.S citizens. 
Citing the need for assurance that Maine plates wouldn’t be used for lawless purposes, Bellows denied the agents covert plates, a decision that’s up to her discretion under state law that was defended by Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey.
Bellows then updated the state’s policy to require that applications include assurances that covert plates wouldn’t be used for civil immigration enforcement. 
The Trump administration subsequently sued in May, arguing that the state had discriminated against federal immigration agencies, following similar lawsuits against Massachusetts, Oregon and Washington.
Last month, a federal immigration officer shot and killed 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero of Biddeford, ramping up calls for state officials to do more to protect Maine residents from federal immigration operations. Federal authorities confirmed that Guerrero, a Colombian national, was not the target of a July 13 ICE operation that had brought agents to the area.
Several new laws that prevent local resources and agencies from being used to support mass deportation efforts took effect last week.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Louisville mayor calls for a data center moratorium as city considers regulations
description: The mayor of Kentucky’s largest city is calling on city council members to pass a temporary ban or moratorium on data center construction within the city while the local government mulls over potential regulations restricting the siting and impacts of large data centers.  In a Tuesday afternoon press conference, Louisville Mayor Craig Greenberg said that […]
text:
Louisville Mayor Craig Greenberg called on city council members to pass a temporary ban on data center construction to ensure no future data centers can be constructed under "outdated" existing regulations. (Screenshot/YouTube, MetroTV)The mayor of Kentucky’s largest city is calling on city council members to pass a temporary ban or moratorium on data center construction within the city while the local government mulls over potential regulations restricting the siting and impacts of large data centers. 
In a Tuesday afternoon press conference, Louisville Mayor Craig Greenberg said that by enacting a temporary ban on data center construction, it would ensure any new requests to build data centers in the city would be reviewed under data center regulations the city is considering. 
The city is continuing to hold public hearings this week seeking feedback on a regulatory framework on siting data centers that would ban any data center larger than 500,000 square feet from being built. 
Local leaders began to consider such regulations following backlash from residents after the city’s planning and zoning commission approved in March the siting of a 1.6-million-square-foot data center in West Louisville.
“I believe it’s critical that once we get through this public hearing process, which is continuing, that we approve these proposed data center regulations,” Greenberg said. “We must ensure that no additional actions related to data centers are taken while these outdated regulations are still on the books.” 
 In June, city council members on a planning and zoning committee voted to table an ordinance to enact a data center moratorium after the chair of the committee argued such a moratorium should be used as a last resort. 
Council member Shameka Parrish-Wright, who is challenging Greenberg in the mayoral general election this fall, questioned the timing of the mayor’s announcement with a Monday email she had sent to city council members urging them to un-table the moratorium ordinance. 
“It is interesting that after months of this ordinance languishing in committee after being tabled, and after weeks of poor publicity, the mayor suddenly chose to take a position on data centers only after I called for this item to be returned to the table,” Parrish-Wright said, accusing Greenberg of “using his weekly address to appear as though he has been on the side of his constituents the whole time.”
In recent months, counties and smaller cities across the state have passed temporary moratoriums on local data center construction after hearing strong concerns from residents about the potential impacts of such projects, including on local water usage, potential increases to electricity bills and more.
Louisville’s remaining public hearings seeking commentary on its proposed data center regulations will be held in person and online on August 5, August 6 and August 10.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Elliott Pritt withdraws from House ballot; law prohibits GOP to fill vacancy for November election
description: Elliott Pritt, disgraced former Republican House member arrested last month, withdrew his name from the ballot for the November election. He was seeking reelection to the House of Delegates in Fayette County.
text:
Elliott Pritt, a Republican, withdrew his name from the ballot for the House of Delegates District 50 race. Pritt recently resigned from the House after being charged with enticement of a minor in Fayette County. (Perry Bennett | West Virginia Legislative Photography)Elliott Pritt, disgraced former Republican House member arrested last month, withdrew his name from the ballot for the November election. He was seeking reelection to the House of Delegates in Fayette County.
“The Office of the Secretary of State received formal notice of the withdrawal this afternoon,” West Virginia Secretary of State Kris Warner’s office said in a news release on Tuesday.
Pritt, a public school teacher, was arrested July 22 and charged with enticement of a minor as a federal crime. He has not yet entered a plea and is currently held in a Kentucky correctional facility. 
A 2024 state election law does not permit the Republican Party to fill the vacancy on the general election ballot created by Pritt’s withdrawal.
Matthew Anderson, a special education teacher and Democrat candidate for the House of Delegates. (Photo by Amelia Ferrell Knisely/West Virginia Watch)
Matt Anderson, a special education teacher, is the Democratic challenger in the race. 
“I feel that my job is to instill the trust back into District 50,” said Anderson, 37. “It’s under unfortunate circumstances that this race has taken this turn, but we’re going forward.”
A criminal complaint said the family of a 15-year-old female reported that their child had been sexually abused by Pritt, leading to the charges. 
Pritt, 36, allegedly communicated with the girl online online games and apps before asking her to meet him in his classroom at Oak Hill High School to engage in sexual activity, which occurred on five to 10 occasions, according to the complaint.
Pritt was first elected as a Democrat to the House in 2022. He switched to the Republican party in 2023. He resigned from the House last week in a one-sentence letter to House Speaker Roger Hanshaw. 
Withdrawing from the ballot is a separate process, and West Virginia code permits a candidate for the general election to withdraw by filing a notarized statement of withdrawal with the Secretary of State no later than the close of business on Aug 11, 2026.
A Republican-sponsored bill prohibits political parties from replacing a nominee late in the election process, thus restricting how the party can deal with Pritt’s seat. It went into effect last year.
Josh Holstein, chair of the West Virginia Republican Party, declined to comment for this story. 
Warner said the Secretary of State’s office “has very little authority to exercise discretion in candidacy matters.”
“The law in this instance is clear. Because the Legislature removed the opportunity for political parties to select replacement candidates on the ballot when a vacancy is created by withdrawal, there is no alternative option to replace the candidate on the ballot,” Warner said. 
The West Virginia State Election Commission is scheduled to meet Aug. 7 to consider eligibility challenges for candidates currently on the 2026 General Election ballot. The commission had planned to discuss Pritt’s candidacy but that specific issue is no longer on the agenda due to Pritt’s voluntary withdrawal.
Pritt ran unopposed in the May primary. Anderson received more votes in that race. 
Anderson plans to continue knocking doors in the area and talking with residents about his campaign.
“My approach hasn’t changed,” he said. “I’m just going forward talking to everybody … trying to have those hard conversations that we have to have with each other to kind of bring a sense of, I guess, normalcy back.”
The West Virginia Republican Party disavowed Pritt from the party and support of his candidacy in a unanimous vote last week.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas judge says decision to strike abortion restrictions not ‘even a close call’
description: TOPEKA — A Kansas judge took a sledgehammer to a slate of abortion restrictions dating back to 1997, ruling the state came up short in arguing the Kansas Legislature should be able to impose waiting periods, mandate abortion reversal disclosures and require doctors to obtain patients’ reasons for seeking an abortion. Christopher Jayaram’s 260-page decision,[...]
text:
Traci Lynn Nauser, a Kansas OB-GYN, and Alice Wang, an attorney for the Center for Reproductive Rights, speak with a reporter on Sept. 26, 2025, outside of the Johnson County Courthouse, where a trial weighing state abortion restrictions is underway. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A Kansas judge took a sledgehammer to a slate of abortion restrictions dating back to 1997, ruling the state came up short in arguing the Kansas Legislature should be able to impose waiting periods, mandate abortion reversal disclosures and require doctors to obtain patients’ reasons for seeking an abortion.
Christopher Jayaram’s 260-page decision, written while he was still serving as a Johnson County District Court judge, came at a canny moment. He was sworn in as a Kansas Supreme Court justice hours after issuing the opinion Monday and voters across the state were set to answer a ballot question Tuesday that could change the way Supreme Court justices are selected.
The resolution in the abortion restriction case followed three years of litigation. Jayaram took nine months to author his decision after a two-part, seven-day bench trial wrapped up in October in Johnson County. He ruled the state’s abortion restrictions violated Kansans’ right to bodily autonomy and “infringe upon a woman’s fundamental rights.” 
It’s an affirmation of the right to an abortion in Kansas following a 2022 vote in which voters rejected a constitutional amendment that could’ve led to further restrictions and a 2024 state Supreme Court decision that cemented Kansans’ right to bodily autonomy.
Kansas abortion providers and clinics sued the state in June 2023, and Jayaram temporarily blocked restrictions that were passed by the Legislature over the course of more than two decades.
Among the laws Jayaram struck down by making his injunction permanent were requirements for abortion providers to give government-scripted information to patients; supply patient paperwork in specific fonts, sizes and colors; tell patients at least five times that medication abortions can be reversed, which isn’t regarded by scientists and medical organizations as safe; and obtain reasons from patients for their decision to seek an abortion. 
“Today’s ruling allows me to do my job the way I was trained to and focus on what’s most important: my patients,” said Traci Lynn Nauser, an OB-GYN in Kansas and lead plaintiff in the case. “I have been caring for patients for nearly 30 years, but these laws have interfered with my ability to provide high-quality, evidence-based health care. I have been forced to lie to my patients and delay, or even deny, people care for no medical reason. This is not how health care should work.”
Attorneys representing the state had the obligation of meeting the strict scrutiny standard to justify retention of abortion mandates, but Jayaram said in the decision the state “simply failed to clear that high bar.” 
It wasn’t “even a close call,” he wrote. 
“Invariably, some will likely disagree or take issue with the court’s ultimate conclusions and findings, whether based upon specific moral, ethical or spiritual concerns,” Jayaram wrote.
However, he said those considerations are separate from the court’s role in evaluating the state’s potential constitutional encroachments imposed under the guise of authority.
“Those constitutional guarantees include the people’s rights to make their own decisions regarding their bodies, health, family formation and family life-decisions that can include whether to continue a pregnancy — all of which are necessary corollaries to the right of bodily autonomy,” he said.
Brittany Jones, president of anti-abortion organization Kansas Family Voice, slammed Jayaram’s decision and the timing of its publication, characterizing both as controversial.
“All of these things simply give women information, give them more time and make sure we know why women are seeking abortions so that we can actually help them,” Jones said in a social media post Tuesday.
Jayaram was sworn in as a justice of the Supreme Court at a private ceremony. He was Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly’s pick to replace retired Chief Justice Marla Luckert. A nominating commission interviewed applicants and recommended three finalists for the vacancy. The governor made the final selection.
Jones alerted her organization’s social media followers to Jayaram’s decision in the abortion case. 
“If you think the Supreme Court is not political in Kansas, then wait ’til you hear what just happened,” Jones said.
Jayaram released the decision at 4:50 p.m. Monday, Jones said, which appears on the decision’s filing stamp. The Supreme Court announced Jayaram’s swearing in at 6:55 p.m. Monday. Because of the proximity to a vote on a proposed constitutional amendment, Jones encouraged viewers to vote “yes” in favor of the proposed constitutional amendment that would require the statewide election of justices to the state Supreme Court.
“Kansans should be outraged with the political machinations of their current Supreme Court,” Jones told Kansas Reflector.
She accused Jayaram of not wanting Kansans to know about his decision before voting in Tuesday’s primary.
Proponents and opponents of the amendment have acknowledged abortion as central to the placement of the question on Aug. 4 ballots. Republicans who support the question’s passage have said the Supreme Court erred in its rulings to affirm abortion as a fundamental right under the Kansas Constitution. Democrats have advocated for rejection of the ballot question, arguing the court has protected abortion rights and maintaining a merit-based appointment system for justices continues that protection. 
Alice Wang, senior staff attorney at the Center for Reproductive Rights who represented plaintiffs in the case, said the decision is a reflection of the will of Kansans.
“Restrictions like these only exist to push abortion care out of reach. And as we’ve seen across the country, people are dying because of delays in accessing essential health care,” she said. “Still, politicians have repeatedly ignored this reality and their voters as they continue to push for harmful laws”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Ethics Commission to appeal decision that allowed former Speaker to seek Supreme Court seat
description: The Rhode Island Ethics Commission will appeal a recent Superior Court ruling that cleared the way for former House Speaker K. Joseph Shekarchi to seek a vacancy on the state’s Supreme Court. Following an hour behind closed doors Tuesday, commissioners voted 4-1 to authorize its executive director and attorneys to seek a declaratory judgment from […]
text:
After meeting behind closed doors for about an hour Tuesday, the Rhode Island Ethics Commission voted 4-1 to authorize its executive director and attorneys to seek a declaratory judgment from the Rhode Island Supreme Court on whether former House Speaker K. Joseph Shekarchi's appointment to the judiciary would violate the state's ethics laws. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current) The Rhode Island Ethics Commission will appeal a recent Superior Court ruling that cleared the way for former House Speaker K. Joseph Shekarchi to seek a vacancy on the state’s Supreme Court.
Following an hour behind closed doors Tuesday, commissioners voted 4-1 to authorize its executive director and attorneys to seek a declaratory judgment from the state’s highest court on whether Shekarchi’s jump from the legislature to the judiciary violates the state’s ethics laws.
Commissioner Frank Cenerini, who voted against the initial investigation in June, was the lone opponent of the decision to appeal. Chairman Lauren Jones and commissioner Michael N. Browner were not present. 
Executive Director Jason Gramitt told reporters after the meeting that a filing will be made before Aug. 18, the deadline to appeal the Superior Court’s July 27 judgment.
Shekarchi, a Warwick Democrat, stepped down as House speaker May 7 having applied to the Judicial Nominating Commission three days prior to fill the opening created by the March retirement of Justice Maureen McKenna Goldberg. That same day, Roger Williams University School of Law Professor Michael Yelnosky filed a complaint to the state Ethics Commission arguing that a lawmaker leaping directly from one branch of government to another would violate the state’s revolving door rule,which was written into state law in 1992.
The Ethics Commission voted to authorize a full investigation on June 2. After the Ethics Commission twice rejected petitions to end its investigation, Shekarchi’s legal team filed a Superior Court lawsuit seeking to halt the probe and have a judge declare that Shekarchi did not violate the state ethics rules.
The law prohibits sitting legislators from seeking or accepting employment with any state government agency for at least one year after leaving elected office. But it exempts lawmakers who seek or accept election to a constitutional office.
Shekarchi and his attorneys have argued the Supreme Court is a constitutional office, which Superior Court Judge Richard Licht agreed with in his July 27 decision to allow the former speaker’s application to move forward.
But Licht’s ruling did not formally toss the Ethics Commission’s investigation, instead tasking both parties to work with the court to prepare the final order and judgment. The probe remains paused following a July 2 consent order.
“And it likely will be stayed for a while,” Gramitt told reporters Tuesday.
Shekarchi and his attorneys were not present at Tuesday’s hearing. Thomas Dickinson, one of his lawyers, said in an email to Rhode Island Current the appeal was not a surprise.
“We’re prepared to move forward with the appeal process, and we are confident that Judge Licht’s decision is correct based on the facts, the law, and precedent,” Dickinson wrote.
The Ethics Commission’s move comes one week after the state Judicial Nominating Commission forwarded Shekarchi’s name and four others to Gov. Dan McKee for consideration. Four members of the panel who voted for his nomination were criticized after GoLocal Providence reported they had donated to Shekarchi’s campaign, including earlier this year.
A review of Shekarchi’s second quarter campaign forms showed no donations from any of the nine members of the Judicial Nominating Commission.
John Marion, executive director of Common Cause Rhode Island who has been an outspoken opponent of Shekarchi’s judicial application, supported the Ethics Commission’s decision to appeal.
“Judge Licht’s decision left some ambiguity about the state of the law,” he told reporters after the meeting.
But he acknowledged the Rhode Island Supreme Court is now in a tricky position as it must decide whether someone is allowed to join its bench, along with whether one of its justices should recuse after taking a similar path to judicial branch.
In 2020, then-Sen. Erin Lynch Prata sought an advisory opinion from the Ethics Commission before submitting her application for the Supreme Court seat she now occupies. Ethics Commission staff concluded Lynch Prata could not join the judiciary under the rule, but commission members voted 5-2 to reject the recommendation and opened the door for then-Gov. Gina Raimondo to appoint her to the bench.
“The same set of facts were in question six years ago,” Marion said. “She should recuse.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Black Hills highway project pits safety against scenery as public comments pour in
description: Paul Horsted calls himself a “re-photographer.” He takes new photos at historic places to show what has and hasn’t changed. His projects have included photography books retracing the 1874 Custer expedition into the Black Hills, and pairing historic photos of Yellowstone National Park with modern ones.  “There’s a joy to that for me,” he said. […]
text:
A vehicle drives down U.S. Highway 85 with the Spearfish Canyon cliffs on its right and Spearfish Creek on its left. (Courtesy of Paul Horsted)Paul Horsted calls himself a “re-photographer.” He takes new photos at historic places to show what has and hasn’t changed.
His projects have included photography books retracing the 1874 Custer expedition into the Black Hills, and pairing historic photos of Yellowstone National Park with modern ones. 
“There’s a joy to that for me,” he said.
Horsted, of Custer, and dozens of other people who appreciate the beauty of the Black Hills are worried about changes that could be wrought by a state highway project. The South Dakota Department of Transportation plans to reconstruct a 16-mile stretch of U.S. Highway 85 from the Wyoming border to the intersection with U.S. Highway 14A at Cheyenne Crossing, which includes picturesque stretches through a canyon cut by Spearfish Creek. 

Travelers drive on the “Black and Yellow Trail,” or what is now U.S. Highway 85 in the northern Black Hills in 1913. (Photo by W.B. Perkins, courtesy of Paul Horsted)

The department says the $47 million project will make the road safer for locals, commuters and visitors. But a surge in public concern about the project’s potential impact on the scenic character of the area led the department to extend the public comment deadline from June 19 to Sept. 4. The department has received more than 200 comments so far regarding the latest version of the proposal.
Horsted walked near the highway earlier this summer. He saw snails and butterflies, and trout swimming in the creek.

Submit public comments for the U.S. Highway 85 reconstruction project by Sept. 4 by emailing Project Manager Mark Malone at mark.malone@state.sd.us.

“We can’t stand in the way of all development and progress, but something is always lost along the way,” Horsted said. “That’s what some of us are longing for and aiming to preserve as much as we can when it comes to this project and the incremental development that comes with it.”
The organizer of opposition to the project is David Miller, who grew up in Deadwood and lives in Rapid City. He chooses not to live within the Black Hills, he said, hoping to leave as little impact on the forest as possible. 
“We would sacrifice a lot of what makes this place what it is for speed and convenience,” Miller said of the highway project.
State says balance needed between beauty and safety
U.S. 85 has been regraded, resurfaced or repaired 10 times since 1950, but hasn’t been touched since 2010. The department says the roadway is in poor condition, and the project would also widen lanes, add paved shoulders and extend “clear zones” — buffer areas just beyond the road’s edge — to increase safety in case of run-off-the-road crashes. 
The goal is to find a balance between traffic safety and preserving the Black Hills, said Mark Malone, department project manager.
“Having a safer highway and an aesthetically pleasing highway do not have to be mutually exclusive,” Malone said in an email.

Black Hills residents listen to a presentation from the Department of Transportation about the proposed U.S. Highway 85 reconstruction on June 4, 2026. (Courtesy of Paul Horsted)

Engineers have been refining the proposal since a June open house. In an email to Miller, Malone said the team plans to “take a closer look” at a segment of the project to “identify areas where centerline shifts may not be necessary.” As of June, the proposal had eight locations where the road would be realigned.
In Spearfish Canyon, there’s little room to maneuver. Any shift toward the canyon walls risks disturbing rock faces and vegetation, project critics say, and any shift toward the creek risks encroaching on the waterway and its banks.
Malone said that as the department “develops alternatives or refines current options” it will seek to minimize work near the creek and “strive to reduce impacts” to landowners along the road.
About 600 vehicles traverse the highway each weekday, and 850 per day on weekends. The speed limit is 55 mph in most stretches, though curves have slower advisory speed limits.
The June proposal calls for roadway adjustments to provide a “consistent design speed,” Malone said.
“This inconsistency on the existing roadway creates issues for driver expectations for unfamiliar drivers as well as leads drivers either speeding up or slowing down,” Malone said. “The variations in their speed, especially the large differential between vehicles, create safety concerns and lead to crashes.” 
Between 2020 and 2024, 77 crashes resulted in one fatality and 31 injuries, a crash rate more than six times higher than the statewide average for “similar facilities” — roads of comparable type and traffic volume — over that time period. The roadway’s crash rate is 9.07 crashes per million vehicle miles traveled. A comparable roadway is U.S. Highway 14A, which has a crash rate of 1.27.
About a third of the crashes involved motorcycles and more than one-fourth involved wild animals. Vehicles left the roadway in about 60% of crashes.
Most of the crashes happened in optimal driving conditions, during daylight hours when the road was dry. More than half occurred between June and September — a period that includes the annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally — and about one-third involved turning or lane changing.
Concerns about ‘incremental development’
Horsted, Miller and others opposed to the project are sensitive to the potential impacts on the environment after witnessing other recent road construction in the Black Hills — particularly on U.S. 385, a $72 million project from Deadwood to Hill City that widened lanes, extended shoulders, straightened curves and required clearing trees and blasting rock.

Spearfish Creek flows alongside U.S. 85 in the Black Hills. (Courtesy of Paul Horsted)

Such reconstruction favors convenience over land stewardship, Horsted said, potentially turning U.S. 85 into “just another strip of pavement through the Black Hills.”
Horsted wonders if widening the road and shoulders is the only way to make the highway safe, or if reduced speed limits or other traffic-calming measures could work.
Not everyone opposes the project. Robin Nichols Miller, a local who drives on U.S. 85 daily, said the road is a hazard.
“There are no shoulders on this road, so if someone slides or runs off it, they will more than likely incur a rollover crash,” Nichols Miller wrote in response to a social media post by Horsted.
She added that some crashes have blocked traffic for hours and that existing pullouts are often too short for large trucks or campers to pull over and let other traffic pass.
“Progress and growth, whether in population or visitors, requires making things safe for everyone,” Nichols Miller said. “Many of us who drive or ride this road on an almost daily basis recognize the road needs to be made safer and can’t wait for them to get started.”
Horsted hopes the department will host another public meeting given the public interest and the potential changes being considered. The department has said it does not plan to do so.
“We’re on guard,” Horsted said. “I hope the Department of Transportation will listen carefully.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Company claims Iowa workers conspired to take over highly classified government work
description: A group of western Iowa businessmen are being sued over an alleged “brazen and coordinated scheme” to take over highly classified work for the federal government by poaching employees and stealing trade secrets from their employer. Oaklea Simpson Security, a Westminster, Maryland, company, is suing several former employees of its Iowa office in Mills County,[...]
text:
Oaklea Simpson Security, a Maryland company, is suing several former employees of its Iowa office in Mills County, alleging a “brazen and coordinated scheme” to take over highly classified work for the federal government by poaching employees and stealing trade secrets. (Photo by David Talukdar/Getty Images)A group of western Iowa businessmen are being sued over an alleged “brazen and coordinated scheme” to take over highly classified work for the federal government by poaching employees and stealing trade secrets from their employer.
Oaklea Simpson Security, a Westminster, Maryland, company, is suing several former employees of its Iowa office in Mills County, including Douglas Grave of Glenwood; Rex Thomas of Treynor; Wesley Carter of Malvern; Steven Douglas of Omaha, and Timothy Sullivan of Chesapeake, Virginia. Corporate co-defendants include the newly formed CODA Data Sciences Inc. of Omaha and Intuitive Research and Technology Corporation, or IRTC, of Texas.
Oaklea is alleging the defendants, while still employed by Oaklea, participated in a “brazen and coordinated scheme” to secretly form CODA Data Sciences as a competing business. The defendants are accused of systematically misappropriating “vast amounts” of Oaklea’s confidential information and trade secrets while orchestrating a mass resignation of 24 Oaklea employees and diverting to CODA a multimillion-dollar government contract once held by Oaklea.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
According to the lawsuit, the individual defendants held high-level government security clearances and occupied positions of “extraordinary trust and responsibility.” The defendants were allegedly responsible for managing and overseeing Oaklea’s classified work under a subcontract with IRTC. According to the lawsuit, that work includes “critical geospatial intelligence and data analytics capabilities” used by U.S. Navy ships.
The lawsuit claims the defendants routed hundreds of confidential and trade secret Oaklea materials, including some documents classified as “top secret,” to personal email accounts, recruited their co-workers to join their new venture, and positioned themselves to replace Oaklea on IRTC’s subcontract.
The lawsuit alleges that on April 30, 2026, one day before the subcontract was set to renew, the defendants “executed their scheme” when the 24 Oaklea employees resigned in a coordinated mass departure, and the defendants immediately assumed performance of the same work through their newly formed competing business, CODA.
Grave, who according to the lawsuit leased office space to Oaklea on the second floor of a rural Mills County building located at 60397 Kidd Road in Glenwood, is accused in the lawsuit of misusing his landlord position to lock Oaklea out of the facility. Oaklea claims that when it was finally able to recover company-issued laptops, it discovered that several employees had wiped the devices clean of all data.
The lawsuit alleges IRTC participated in this scheme by coordinating with the individual defendants to divert the subcontract from Oaklea to CODA.



Quotation







This was not ordinary employee turnover or lawful competition. It was the calculated exploitation of positions of trust to gut a company from the inside.


– Lawsuit filed on behalf of Oaklea Simpson Security 


Court records indicate IRTC serves as the prime contractor on a project called the Geospatial Intelligence Unified Naval Streaming System, or GUNSS, under which it subcontracted work to Oaklea.
Oaklea says it provides services and support to clients across the defense, homeland security, intelligence, and law enforcement sectors of the federal government, including the United States Strategic Command.
Founded in 2009, Oaklea says it is largely comprised of former military service members specializing in intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance sensors. The lawsuit alleges that some of the work it has performed over the years is classified at the “top secret” level, requiring many Oaklea employees to hold top-level government security clearances.
The lawsuit alleges Grave was hired by Oaklea in September 2017 and that by February 2026, he held the title of vice president for data science and had “access to virtually all” of Oaklea’s trade secrets and confidential information for the relevant programs.
Beginning in late 2025, the lawsuit alleges, the individual defendants exchanged numerous emails concerning their development of CODA and also used Oaklea resources to build what the lawsuit calls a “comprehensive trove” of sensitive information so they’d be “able to stand up CODA as a turnkey replacement” for Oaklea.
“This was not ordinary employee turnover or lawful competition,” the lawsuit alleges. “It was the calculated exploitation of positions of trust to gut a company from the inside.”
The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa, alleges misappropriation of trade secrets, breach of fiduciary duty, unjust enrichment and civil conspiracy. It seeks a preliminary and permanent injunction enjoining the defendants from performing any of the work previously performed by Oaklea under its contract and using or disclosing any of Oaklea’s trade secrets and confidential information.
It also seeks compensatory damages for lost profits and business opportunities, as well as punitive damages for willful, wanton, and malicious conduct.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach officials at CODA, or the lead attorney representing the defendants, for comment. The lead attorney’s co-counsel declined to comment on the case.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: What the end of K-12 ‘disparate impact’ rule means for CT
description: For decades, schools that disproportionately disciplined or suspended students of color risked federal investigation. Not anymore.
text:
When Connecticut Education Association President Kate Dias began her teaching career, the school she worked for had a strict attendance policy: Ten absences and you fail the class.
“You had mono, we don’t care, right? It was literally that insane,” Dias said.
The problem with such a harsh policy, Dias said, was that it ignored one key fact: Students don’t always miss class by choice. Some had to help younger siblings on and off the bus; others had insecure housing. None of that mattered. These more vulnerable students — often students of color — received no support and lost credit.
“Some of the things we know kids experience, they were screwed,” Dias said.
Eventually, Dias said, schools realized such policies disproportionately affected nonwhite students, even though on their face they were race-neutral. That realization — along with a little pressure from the federal government — compelled educators to think critically about how they manage a range of disciplinary issues.
The official term for this pattern — a neutral-seeming rule causing very non-neutral outcomes — is “disparate impact.” For decades, the U.S. Department of Education considered it a potential violation of Title VI, which prohibits race-based discrimination. Schools that disproportionately disciplined or suspended students of color risked a federal investigation by the Office of Civil Rights.
Not anymore. 
In late July, the department announced it was rescinding the disparate impact provisions of its Title VI enforcement. As a result, schools will no longer be investigated for disproportionately disciplining students of color as long as their policies are not explicitly discriminatory.
In a July 23 press release, the department said disparate impact had become “a tool for the radical left” to punish schools “for even-handedly applying race-neutral policies — with no discriminatory intent — solely because data indicated the school disciplined more minority students.” Ending those provisions, the department said, “advances President Trump’s promise to restore equality of opportunity and meritocracy.”
That’s not how Dias sees it. Thinking about disparate impact, she said, forced schools to think about implicit bias and take a hard look at whether they were inadvertently setting some groups of students up to fail.
“Oftentimes what we discovered … is that we either had policies or practices that unintentionally favored white students and put students of color at a disadvantage,” Dias said.
“Which I think has caused us as educators and as leaders to really pause and think about, what are we doing, why are we doing it, and do we have unintended consequences in these choices? And I think that that has been very healthy,” she added.
The issue remains highly relevant in Connecticut. Even today, schools in the Nutmeg State suspend and expel Black students at three times the rate of white students.
“My concern, honestly, is with these rules rolling back, there will be districts that go, ‘Great. Now I don’t have to worry about this,’” Dias said.
In the July 23 press release, Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights Kimberly Richey said the Trump Administration would continue holding schools accountable for discrimination. 
Anghy Idrovo of the Connecticut Black & Brown Student Union said the administration’s decision was “the wrong move” and “dangerous.”
“A policy can be written in neutral language and still fall almost entirely on Black and brown students,” Idrovo said. “And that’s what we see in Connecticut with suspensions and expulsions.” 
Idrovo was one of several advocates who spoke at the Capitol in the spring in favor of legislation to end suspensions for nonviolent behavior. (The bill didn’t pass.) She questioned the Trump administration’s underlying assumption that disparate impact had forced schools to under-discipline minority students.
“If that were to be true, then my work wouldn’t exist, right? Then I wouldn’t be fighting for closing the gap on racial disparities,” Idrovo said.
Kathryn Meyer, an attorney with the Center for Children’s Advocacy, said the disparate impact decision was the latest move by the Trump administration to effectively render the Education Department’s Office of Civil Rights “defunct,” taking away an important tool advocates used to keep schools accountable. She recalled a case some years ago in which CCA helped take a district to task for not providing basic access to interpretation for multilingual learners.
The threat of federal investigation was “really our legal hook for anything from a local policy or practice to a lot of our state legislation,” Meyer said. The fact that the federal government itself used disparate impact gave the concept an added weight.
Her colleague Zoe Masters questioned the legality of the move itself.
“The Trump administration just jumped to publishing a final rule, instead of publishing a draft rule and getting comments, which violates the Administrative Procedure Act,” Masters said.
In theory, someone could sue to stop the new rule, though Masters said she doesn’t know whether anyone has done so.
Department of Education spokesperson Amelia Joy responded to these concerns in an email to The Connecticut Mirror. She reiterated the Trump administration’s view that disparate impact had been weaponized to impose a “radical idea of ‘equity’” on schools.
“Removing these provisions from our regulations puts a stop to this exploitation of federal law and ensures teachers retain the utmost control over their classroom,” Joy wrote.
Joy did not address the legality of the new rule.
With the federal provisions now gone, the question shifts to whether Connecticut’s state laws can fill the void. Patrice McCarthy, executive director of the Connecticut Association of Boards of Education, said there are mechanisms at the state and local level to hold schools accountable for disparate impact.
“Parents … can go talk to the building principal. If they’re not satisfied with the outcome of that discussion, they can talk to the superintendent,” McCarthy said. From there, parents can escalate to the local school board, and in extreme cases, they can file a 10-4B complaint with the State Board of Education.
“I think we have appropriate protections in place in Connecticut,” McCarthy said.
There are explicit state-level rules about disparate impact, as well. The State Department of Education is required by law to report on the disproportionate use of discipline by schools across the state. (The latest report, which covers the 2024-2025 school year, is available here.) If schools show two consecutive years of disproportionate enforcement, CSDE will step in and recommend corrective actions.
But Meyer said despite Connecticut’s relatively strong civil rights laws, there are still significant gaps in how those laws are overseen and enforced. Filling those gaps would require legislative action, including the proposed ban on suspensions for nonviolent behavior, which she supports.
Right now, Meyer said, many state-level civil rights complaints find their way to Connecticut’s Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities. The commission has authority to ensure schools are complying with civil rights laws, but Meyer said she’d like to see the state invest in more staffing for the office — especially if it ends up taking on more of the enforcement burden around issues like disparate impact.
And she said the state should implement additional options for parents that are “even more accessible … and timely than the CHRO process can offer.”
Fran Rabinowitz, executive director of the Connecticut Association of Public School Superintendents, said reducing the racial disparity in student discipline requires a fundamental change in school culture. She said she’d like to see the state make that a top priority.
“You’ve got to look at your leadership at the school level, and you’ve got to be committed to a school culture that is honoring of every child in that school,” Rabinowitz said.
Rabinowitz said she went through that process herself when she was superintendent in Bridgeport.
“It’s not just by osmosis that this happens. There is real training that needs to be done of administration, teachers and parents,” Rabinowitz said.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Uthmeier says he’ll push to increase criminal penalties for poaching next legislative session
description: The penalties for illegal hunting or taking of wildlife in Florida could be about to get more punitive. Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Tuesday that his office will advocate for the Florida Legislature to pass a bill next year to enhance criminal penalties for individuals convicted of poaching of animals. “Over the last year and […]
text:
Photo from Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission Facebook page.The penalties for illegal hunting or taking of wildlife in Florida could be about to get more punitive.
Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Tuesday that his office will advocate for the Florida Legislature to pass a bill next year to enhance criminal penalties for individuals convicted of poaching of animals.
“Over the last year and a half since I’ve been in office as attorney general, we’ve received quite a few complaints where poaching is very prevalent here in the state of Florida,” Uthmeier said during a press conference in Panama City Beach.
“We don’t have a lot of prosecutions when people are caught. Right now, most poaching offenses are mere misdemeanors. It’s a slap on the wrist and it has not been enough to deter bad actors who are out there breaking the law.”
Poaching in Florida is defined as the illegal hunting, capturing, killing, or trafficking of fish and wildlife.
The penalty for the unlawful taking of an animal on private land would increase from a misdemeanor to a third-degree felony with potential for prison time, Uthmeier said. If an individual is convicted of poaching on private land near people, a dwelling, or infrastructure, the penalty would be elevated to a second-degree felony.
Repeated poaching could become a first-degree felony, “where you are looking at several years, many years behind bars,” he said.
Florida Land Council Chair Joshua Kellem led the constitutional amendment campaign establishing a right to hunt and fish in Florida in 2024. He said he hears frequently from Land Council members that poachers have been repeat offenders.
“Even some of the same poachers have been busted on the same property three, four, five times. That somebody committed a crime three, four, five times and not be prosecuted is insane and has to be fixed.”
Uthmeier said he’d like the statewide prosecutor to assume jurisdiction to prosecute poaching to ensure that those arrested are held accountable.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Governor grants Rapid City $1 million for industrial park, following $7.5 million state loan
description: South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden issued $1 million Tuesday from an economic development fund under his control to support an industrial and business park in Rapid City. The money comes from the Future Fund, which is built up through fees submitted by employers when they pay taxes to support unemployment benefits. The governor awards the […]
text:
South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden speaks to the media on Feb. 5, 2026, at the state Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden issued $1 million Tuesday from an economic development fund under his control to support an industrial and business park in Rapid City.
The money comes from the Future Fund, which is built up through fees submitted by employers when they pay taxes to support unemployment benefits.
The governor awards the dollars at his discretion, although a state law that took effect July 1 places new restrictions on the fund, including a more detailed description of acceptable uses and a requirement that awards must be recommended by the Governor’s Office of Economic Development.
Governor grants Mitchell $1 million for industrial park

The grant to benefit Rapid City comes atop a $7.5 million loan approved by a governor-appointed board in May from the state’s Revolving Economic Development and Initiative Fund, known as the REDI Fund. It offers low-interest loans to startup firms, businesses that are expanding or relocating, and local economic development corporations. Of that, $2 million is allocated for purchasing land and $5.5 million is for infrastructure.
Another $1 million is coming from the city’s economic development partnership, Elevate Rapid City, which is overseeing the project and was awarded the state funds. The project is part of Rapid City’s Catalyst Tax Increment Financing District. TIF districts capture new and higher property tax revenue to pay off initial financing needed to develop a site.
Elevate Rapid City will use the money to help prepare 128 acres of land near Haines Avenue and Mall Drive in the northern part of the city. That infrastructure is meant as an incentive for businesses considering expanding or locating in Rapid City, according to Jack Valentine, president and CEO of Elevate.
“This investment in Northline Business Park will give local businesses room to grow and help Rapid City compete for new employers,” Valentine said. 
Elevate hopes to have sites ready to build on in 2027. 
In a press release on the Future Fund award, Rhoden said the money will help “ensure Rapid City can compete for tomorrow’s jobs, businesses, and investments.” 
Rhoden has awarded Future Fund dollars to several projects this year, including a $1 million grant last week for Mitchell to develop a business and industrial park.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: University of Oklahoma president wades into turnpike interchange fight
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – The University of Oklahoma’s president on Tuesday said he supports adding two interchanges along a planned turnpike route despite environmental concerns and local opposition. OU President Joseph Harroz Jr. told the Oklahoma Turnpike Authority that his university supports adding two interchanges in Norman because they are “essential” and “desp[...]
text:
University of Oklahoma President Joseph Harroz, Jr., speaks Tuesday to the Oklahoma Turnpike Authority as OTA Executive Director Joe Echelle, standing right, looks on. (Photo courtesy of the Oklahoma Turnpike Authority.)OKLAHOMA CITY – The University of Oklahoma’s president on Tuesday said he supports adding two interchanges along a planned turnpike route despite environmental concerns and local opposition.
OU President Joseph Harroz Jr. told the Oklahoma Turnpike Authority that his university supports adding two interchanges in Norman because they are “essential” and “desperately needed” for “economic prosperity.”
“Having these two gateways to Norman will absolutely magnify the prosperity of the city,” Harroz said.
The Oklahoma Turnpike Authority is proposing building interchanges at Alameda Drive and Tecumseh Road as part of its South Extension Turnpike, which will carry traffic from Interstate 40 south and west to Interstate 35.
The proposed interchanges are part of a 15-year, $8.2 billion statewide turnpike improvement project, dubbed ACCESS. 
Harroz’s support comes despite a prior Norman City Council vote opposing frontage roads and interchanges at other locations on another Norman-area turnpike, called the Toby Keith Expressway, and other local opposition. The expressway will serve as an east-west connector.
Harroz said millions of visitors each year come to Norman, not just for football games, but to visit other attractions.
He said waiting to install the interchanges will drive up the cost.
Trey Kirby, who represents Ward 5 on the Norman City Council, said some members of the council are discussing the proposed interchanges.
“OU sticks its nose in a lot of places it doesn’t belong,” he said of Harroz’s comments.
Sen. Mary Boren, D-Norman, said the proposed interchanges are in areas where wildlife, water and flood management are the most sensitive.
“I can understand the use of the credibility of the president of the University of Oklahoma to justify access roads to Tecumseh and Alameda,” Boren said. “What is aggravating to me is the selectiveness of the Turnpike Authority to only hear from those that validate their preconceived ideas.”
OTA has asked the City of Norman what their requests are for the infrastructure on the South Extension, said Lisa Shearer-Salim, a spokesperson for the state agency.
“Yes, it would require them to pass a resolution and then ultimately enter a project agreement with us for those requests,” she said.
She said she could not speculate on what would happen if the city council voted against the proposed interchanges.
OTA has heard from lots of stakeholders who have expressed a variety of opinions, including those critical of the project, she said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Trump administration mounts second attempt to relax offshore Arctic drilling rules
description: The Trump administration is proposing to loosen the regulation of offshore Arctic oil drilling by revoking several safety regulations put in place during the Obama administration. The U.S. Department of the Interior announced on Monday that it will propose a new rule to change what it called “a burdensome regulatory framework” imposed a decade ago […]
text:
Cloud patterns and the midnight sun reflect over the Chukchi Sea, where the summer sea ice floats in large slabs. The Trump administration wants to conduct several lease sales in the Chukchi and other offshore Arctic areas, and it is now proposing to relax safety rules put in place by the Obama administration. (Photo by Lisa Hupp/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)The Trump administration is proposing to loosen the regulation of offshore Arctic oil drilling by revoking several safety regulations put in place during the Obama administration.
The U.S. Department of the Interior announced on Monday that it will propose a new rule to change what it called “a burdensome regulatory framework” imposed a decade ago on oil development in federal Arctic waters.
In a statement, Interior officials said the move would encourage oil development in the region.
“President Trump has made clear that America must fully avail itself of Alaska’s extraordinary resource potential for the benefit and security of the Nation and the citizens who call Alaska home,” Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum said in the statement. “This proposed rule reflects a disciplined, mission-focused approach that strengthens regulatory efficiency, reduces unnecessary barriers and ensures that Arctic energy exploration proceeds safely, responsibly and under strong federal oversight.”  
“The Alaskan Outer Continental Shelf contains some of America’s most promising offshore resources,” Matt Giacona, Interior’s acting marine mineral administration director, said in the statement. “These targeted updates would provide clear, practical compliance options for Arctic Outer Continental Shelf exploration while preserving safeguards to protect workers, the environment and Alaska’s precious natural resources.”
The proposal drew immediate criticism from one environmental group.
“There’s no such thing as safe drilling in the Arctic Ocean, and that’s why it should never, never happen,” said Cooper Freeman, Alaska director for the Center for Biological Diversity. “Having these very stringent rules and regulations to protect the Arctic and avoid catastrophe is the bare minimum.”
Arctic conditions, that feature shifting sea ice, harsh weather and remoteness, make oil spill response virtually impossible – and they make oil exploration impractical, Freeman said.

A polar bear is spotted on a multiyear ice floe in the Beaufort Sea on Aug. 13, 2023, where the U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Healy crew and researchers conducted an on-ice equipment installation. (Photo by Petty Officer 1st Class Scott Bice/U.S. Coast Guard)

“It’s incredibly expensive, risky, dangerous, uncertain,” he said. Alternatively, leaders could be developing renewable energy infrastructure now, but “that’s not what our federal or state leadership are focusing on, and it’s just hurting our environment, hurting the climate and hurting the pocketbooks of Alaskans.”
Details of the newly proposed rule were not available on Monday. The proposal will be published in the Federal Register in future days and subject to a 90-day public comment period after that, the Department of the Interior said in its statement.
There has been only sporadic oil exploration drilling in federal waters of the Arctic in past decades, and there has never been any oil produced from there or any part of the federally managed outer continental shelf off Alaska except for a small part of the Hilcorp-operated Northstar field, which is located mostly on state territory.
There has been no oil production in Canadian Arctic waters, either. Canada has long maintained a two-rig requirement, and oil development in Canadian Arctic waters has been barred under a  moratorium imposed in 2019.
Arctic oil policy changes
Monday’s Department of the Interior announcement is the latest episode in a back-and-forth pattern of Arctic oil policy.
The Obama-era rule standardized some requirements that had been applied to Shell’s multibillion-dollar exploration program in the early 2010s in the Chukchi and Beaufort seas.
That rule included a requirement that each operator have a designated backup drill rig to be available to respond to a well blowout and an integrated operating plan with steps to be taken and equipment to be used in the event of emergencies such as oil spills and extreme weather events.
The Obama-era rule went into effect in 2016, after Shell abandoned its offshore Arctic program.
The first Trump administration tried to loosen those Obama-era requirements. In a proposed rule released in 2020, the administration said it intended to relax the relief-well requirement and eliminate the requirement for an integrated operating plan among other changes.
That first Trump administration rule never went into effect. The Biden administration in 2021 rescinded the proposal, keeping the Obama-era rules in place.
The Trump administration’s proposed lease sales in federal waters off Alaska are shown on a map included in the draft five-year leasing plan. (Map provided by the U.S. Bureau of Ocean Energy Management)
The new Trump proposal, like the proposal in the first Trump term, seeks to relax the relief-well requirement and eliminate the requirement for an integrated operating plan, according to the Department of the Interior statement.
The attempt to loosen Arctic drilling rules comes as the Trump administration is pushing to expand oil development in that remote region.
The administration’s draft five-year outer continental shelf oil and gas leasing plan calls for numerous lease sales in federal Arctic waters, along with several lease sales in the Bering Sea and Bering Strait region.
That is despite President Barack Obama’s actions that withdrew the entire Chukchi Sea and much of the Beaufort Sea from the leasing program.
A previous federal court ruling struck down an earlier attempt, during the first Trump administration, to allow oil drilling in Arctic waters that Obama had withdrawn from leasing. Under the Outer Continental Shelf Leasing Act, U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason ruled in 2019, presidents may withdraw territory from the leasing program but they may not add territory.
Despite Gleason’s ruling, and despite a new lawsuit filed last year over the same issue, the Trump Department of the Interior is proposing to sell oil and gas leases not only in the Chukchi and Beaufort seas but in a newly designated, farther-north offshore region it calls the “High Arctic.” U.S. rights to that High Arctic territory have yet to be internationally recognized.
One Department of the Interior agency warned in December that it lacks the resources to properly regulate an expanded Alaska offshore leasing program. In comments on the Trump administration’s draft leasing plan, the Alaska director of the U.S. Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement said the staff in the state was down to only four and the draft leasing plan “does not address the appropriations or staff required for any amount of additional leasing, exploration, or development activity” that the administration proposed for waters off Alaska.
The Trump administration in November reinstated expired Hilcorp offshore leases at the long-languishing Liberty project. The Biden administration in late 2024 denied Hilcorp’s request for extended time to develop the leases; it was the 12th such request made since oil was discovered there in the 1990s.
Plans for the Liberty development stretch back decades. BP, the original operator, had two general proposals, one for an artificial island to be the drill site and the second for drilling from an existing onshore area using ultra-extended-reach wells. Hilcorp, after it acquired Liberty and the operator position from BP, reverted to the artificial island concept but, as of 2024, switched to the ultra-extended-reach-drilling concept that BP had tried but rejected as unfeasible.
The Center for Biological Diversity and a Native organization, Sovereign Iñupiat for a Living Arctic, have notified the Department of the Interior and its officials that they intend to sue over the reinstatement of Liberty leases. That lawsuit has not yet been filed, Freeman said.

title: NC House delays vote on hemp ban until November as advocates pack hallways
description: The North Carolina House of Representatives will not vote on a bill that would ban intoxicating hemp products in the state until November. That’s after hundreds of hemp advocates filled the halls of the legislative building on Tuesday — and despite strong support for the bill by law enforcement leaders. Last month, the Senate passed […]
text:
N.C. Rep. Reece Pyrtle, R-Rockingham, brought THC gummies to show the bright packaging during Tuesday's press conference on August 4, 2026. (Photo: Claire Michal/NC Newsline.) The North Carolina House of Representatives will not vote on a bill that would ban intoxicating hemp products in the state until November. That’s after hundreds of hemp advocates filled the halls of the legislative building on Tuesday — and despite strong support for the bill by law enforcement leaders.
Last month, the Senate passed House Bill 328, which would ban the sale of intoxicating hemp products with more than 0.4 milligrams of THC in North Carolina. The bill would also prohibit the sale of any hemp products, like CBD, or natural kratom consumables to anyone under 21, and would outlaw the sale of xylazine and synthetic kratom.
THC is the psychoactive compound in cannabis. Hemp business owners say that the low threshold allowed by the bill would amount to a ban on nearly all hemp products, crippling what advocates say has become a $4 billion industry that employs some 16,000 people in North Carolina. 
The House did not vote on the measure during its Tuesday session, and House Speaker Destin Hall, R-Caldwell, said it won’t get a vote until after the election in November.
House members “want to make sure they’re solving the problem and not making the problem worse, or doing something with unintended consequences,” Hall said. “What I plan to do is put together a group of our members to take a look at this issue and figure out the right path forward.”
Marijuana itself is currently illegal in North Carolina. It’s defined as cannabis with more than 0.3% delta-9 THC. But there are presently no restrictions, including age limits, on other hemp products that include other types of THC compounds. 
In 2015, the legislature allowed the cultivation of “industrial hemp,” and then in 2018, following federal law changes, it allowed the cultivation and sale of hemp products with less than 0.3% delta-9 THC. This created a loophole that allowed the sale of products that contain delta-8 and delta-10, two other intoxicating THC compounds, as well as THCA, a compound that turns into delta-9 THC when burned. 
Law enforcement leaders say the lack of regulation has turned the state into the “Wild West” for cannabis products. They’re largely in favor of an outright ban for adults as well as children. On Tuesday, dozens of police chiefs, sheriffs, and prosecutors gathered with Republican lawmakers supporting the bill. 
During the press conference, lawmakers and public safety officials said because North Carolina has no age limit, intoxicating hemp products are currently accessible to children. Certain products, they argue, are being marketed towards children, with brightly-colored packaging. Some even mimic popular brands of candy. 
“Some will say this bill will put stores out of business,” said Craven County Sheriff Chip Hughes.“I say if a business depends primarily on selling these dangerous products to our children, then that will indeed be the result.”
Rep. Jimmy Dixon, R-Duplin, said lawmakers made mistakes in the past when they agreed to legalize most hemp products. He said it’s time for a reset on the issue. 
“We’re here today because there were several misguided Republicans in the House,” he said. “Misguided, good people, but deceived.”
Meantime, hundreds of employees, owners and lobbyists for hemp stores gathered in the legislative building to urge lawmakers to vote no on H328 and consider some “common sense regulations” instead of full prohibition. 
Protestors wait to meet with lawmakers to express their opposition to a hemp ban on August 4, 2026. (Photo: Claire Michal/NC Newsline)
Eric Stahli owns Modern Apotheca in Raleigh. His wife has Crohn’s disease and uses hemp products to manage her chronic pain. He agreed that stricter regulations are needed to keep these products out of the hands of children. But he says an outright ban isn’t the answer.
“We’ve been spending the last eight years serving adults, not children, and so we’re here to make sure that our House members and the public know that there are really good actors in this industry that are doing right, and we’re here to get rid of the bad actors,” Stahli said.
“There are bills like SB265 that is a regulatory framework which would establish twenty-one plus requirements, marketing restrictions towards children, and a bunch of other things including testing regulations.” Chris Karis, the owner of Carolindica said “But unfortunately, that’s not what we’re here discussing.”
The bill was spurred on by a looming federal ban on intoxicating hemp products enacted in last year’s farm bill. It’s scheduled to  go into effect in November. However in June, after hemp industry lobbyists rallied to oppose the prohibition, the Trump administration sent a letter to Congress urging them to reverse the ban.
After Tuesday’s session, Hall said there’s broad agreement among House lawmakers that something needs to be done about the lack of regulation of hemp, especially when it comes to people under 21. 
“Folks recognize that the current state of our law is not tenable. There are basically no rules. Things being sold shouldn’t be. Things being sold to kids that shouldn’t be sold,” Hall told reporters. “The question is what to do about it.”

title: Alabama Public Service Commission approves solar project supporting data center
description: The Alabama Public Service Commission Tuesday approved a solar project aimed at supporting a Montgomery data center. Members unanimously approved a certificate of convenience and necessity for Alabama Power’s  “Clearview Ranch Project,” allowing the investor-owned utility to construct a 1,400 acre, 200-megawatt solar photovoltaic generating facility and a 20[...]
text:
The logo for Alabama Power, as seen on January 24, 2023. The Alabama Public Service Commission Tuesday approved a solar facility proposal from Alabama Power that will support a data center in Montgomery. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama Public Service Commission Tuesday approved a solar project aimed at supporting a Montgomery data center.
Members unanimously approved a certificate of convenience and necessity for Alabama Power’s  “Clearview Ranch Project,” allowing the investor-owned utility to construct a 1,400 acre, 200-megawatt solar photovoltaic generating facility and a 200-megawatt, two-hour duration battery energy storage system in Macon and Bullock counties.
The commission also approved an agreement that allows Alabama Power to pass the costs of the solar project to Dotier, a subsidiary of Meta, for a 20-year term.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“After reviewing the project’s economics and supporting information, staff concluded that the project meets those requirements and will not negatively impact customers,” said Cynthia Almond, the president of the Public Service Commission. “In fact, because Dotier is bearing all the project costs, Alabama Power’s customers are expected to benefit over time rather than having to pay for the project.”
Alabama Power says that Meta is supporting the cost of the project and that the social media company will then receive renewable energy credits in exchange for supporting the project.
However, Alabama Power will develop, own and operate the solar facility. It is another proposed solar project from Alabama Power that will support the $1.5 billion data center that Meta plans to construct in Montgomery along with the solar project planned for Baldwin County, according to reporting from al.com.
A message was sent to Alabama Power on Tuesday seeking comment.
Energy Alabama, an organization that advocates for more renewable energy use in the state, was listed within the docket but was not notified that staff had recommended that it be approved.
“Even as a clean energy advocate, it is very problematic when this type of information is being filed supposedly in a docket, but there is no information there,” said Daniel Tait, executive director of Energy Alabama. “And we didn’t receive any copy of it. The first we are learning of it is when it gets approved at the Public Service Commission.”
Half of the project will be in Macon County, and half in Barbour.
“It will provide power to the power grid, and it is not going to cost us any money,” said Louis Maxwell, chair of the Macon County Commission. “Now, we have not seen a data center yet, that is a different thing.”
Maxwell said he asked Alabama Power about the customers that the solar farm will serve, but the company did not provide that information. However, Alabama Power will compensate the county to build the project within its jurisdiction, according to Maxwell.
Maxwell did not say the amount but directed the Alabama Reflector to contact county staff to answer the question. The Alabama Reflector reached out to Macon County officials for additional information.
According to the Alabama Power website, Macon County is expected to receive about $27 million in revenue from the project over 20 years, or an average of about $1.35 million a year. Bullock will get $56 million in revenue, an average of $2.8 million annually.
Data centers have emerged as a major election issue in Alabama amid concerns about their impacts on local communities, particularly the environment and infrastructure. Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville has embraced their construction, while Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones has called for a one-year moratorium.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska State Fair will host US Senate debate between Osborn, Ricketts
description: The Nebraska State Fair is hosting a debate between nonpartisan U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn and U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts next month.
text:
A Nebraska State Fair banner at the State Fair on Aug 29, 2025. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Nebraska State Fair is hosting a debate between registered nonpartisan U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn and incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts next month. 
This is the first debate at the state fair in recent years, with the last one being in 2018 when U.S. Sen. Deb Fischer, R-Neb., debated state Sen. Jane Raybould of Lincoln, a member of the Lincoln City Council at the time, and then-Gov. Ricketts debated state Sen. Bob Krist of Omaha for governor.
News Channel Nebraska will moderate the Sept. 1 debate at Big Iron Events Center. In addition to NCN, The Examiner, Flatwater Free Press, and the Omaha World-Herald will also be part of the debate, with reporters serving as a panel to ask the candidates questions.
Ricketts said in a statement that he is excited about the debate, and that as governor and in the U.S. Senate he has “delivered safer streets, a secure border, and put more money back in Nebraskans’ pockets,” and “worked to deliver common-sense solutions for Nebraska families.”
“I’m excited to share that record with Nebraskans while discussing my vision for continuing to fight for them in Washington,” Ricketts said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Osborn said he’s looking forward to “getting in front of Nebraska voters, and making it crystal clear that I’ll stand for the working class and take their concerns to Washington, D.C.” 
“At the State Fair, Nebraskans will get to see the clear contrast between me and … Pete Ricketts, and I’m excited to show them why my vision is right for this state,” Osborn said in his statement. 
The Senate race has been heated. Osborn is hoping to do better than his 7-percentage-point loss to Republican U.S. Sen. Deb Fischer in 2024. Ricketts, who was governor of Nebraska from 2015 to 2023 before being appointed to the U.S. Senate in 2023, is facing one of his toughest challenges yet, as Osborn could prove to be a more serious candidate than Ricketts has faced in the past as an incumbent.
Legal Marijuana NOW Party’s U.S. Senate nominee Mike Marvin is still in the race, but he hasn’t qualified for the debate. 
This is likely the only debate in the race. The election is Nov. 3.
