title: Opponents ask New Mexico utility regulators to review whether PNM waived multimillion payout
description: An Albuquerque anti-poverty nonprofit is asking state utility regulators to order a hearing over whether the parent company of New Mexico’s largest electric provider forfeited a $350 million payment from the private equity firm looking to acquire it.
text:
Regional bulk transmission lines crisscross the area between Golden and Madrid along New Mexico Highway 14. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)An Albuquerque anti-poverty nonprofit is asking state utility regulators to order a hearing over whether the parent company of New Mexico’s largest electric provider forfeited a $350 million payment from the private equity firm looking to acquire it.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a filing with the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission Monday, attorneys for Prosperity Works argue that TXNM Energy Inc., which owns PNM, could have collected $350 million from private equity firm Blackstone Infrastructure in July when regulators shot down a controversial stock sale between the two companies.
Commissioners last month voted 2-1 that a $400 million stock sale between TXNM and a Blackstone subsidiary violated state law because the parties did not first obtain PRC approval. After the vote, the commission ordered both sides to unwind the deal. In the Monday filing, Prosperity Works’ attorneys argue that the merger agreement between TXNM and Blackstone includes a provision to let TXNM collect a $350 million merger termination fee if the stock purchase did not go through.
Prosperity Works attorney Steve Michel said that PNM’s share of that would be $240 million. He argued that it would translate to a yearlong 16% rate reduction for PNM customers.
Since PNM and Blackstone announced plans for the $11.5 billion acquisition in 2025, officials from both companies have often said it was the best way to inject cash into New Mexico’s outdated electric grid.
“You’re a company that’s perpetually complaining that you don’t have enough money, and you’re just walking away from this $350 million cash infusion?” Michel said.
New Mexico residents turn out to UNM campus to weigh in on proposed private equity takeover of PNM

A spokesperson for Blackstone declined to comment. A spokesperson for PNM in an email to Source NM called Michel’s arguments “incorrect.”
“We did not have a legal basis to collect a termination fee from Blackstone Infrastructure,” the statement said. “We will respond through the Commission process and look forward to demonstrating the long-term benefits of the transaction to New Mexico and the communities we serve.”
A hearing will only move forward if the PRC schedules one. Prosperity Works successfully pushed for one related to the controversial stock sale earlier this year.
Prosperity Works and New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez earlier this year raised questions about the $400 million stock sale’s legality, which prompted the commission’s hearing examiners to open an investigation into the matter in March and to hold a lengthy hearing in April.

title: Blanche nomination for attorney general advanced by US Senate panel on party-line vote
text: WASHINGTON — U.S. acting Attorney General Todd Blanche was one step closer to permanently leading the Justice Department Tuesday, after two skeptical Senate Judiciary Committee Republicans voted to advance his nomination given Blanche’s signed promise that President Donald Trump’s nearly $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund is dead.Republican Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, who had been withholding support for Blanche, voted with other members of the committee along party lines, 12-10, to send Blanche’s nomination to the full Senate. It is unclear how soon the Senate will vote on the confirmation.Blanche, Trump’s former criminal defense lawyer, issued a brief signed statement on social media Sunday night promising the fund is “rescinded,” and an attached unsigned memo stated the tax immunity deal for Trump, his sons and the Trump Organization only applies “retroactively.” Trump did not sign the documents, and the president has defended the fund in recent days.Cornyn said ahead of the vote Tuesday he and Tillis came to an agreement with Justice Department officials on an “agency interpretive guidance document that reaffirms what Mr. Blanche said in his sworn testimony” that the tax audit immunity is limited to the parties and subject matter in Trump’s $10 billion lawsuit against his administration’s own IRS.Trump voluntarily dropped the lawsuit in May in exchange for tax enforcement immunity for him, his sons Eric and Don Jr., and the Trump Organization, as well as the creation of a $1.776 billion “anti-weaponization” fund that could potentially pay out to violent, but now pardoned, Jan. 6 rioters who assaulted police.“Given this agreement with Mr. Blanche, I expect the department to live up to this in future litigation, and I will vote to advance him out of the committee today,” Cornyn said at the opening of Tuesday’s meeting.Tillis said the question over the “payout pot for punks” was settled.“I've never liked this 1776 fund. It made no sense to me, and I thought it was an insult to the police officers and the people that defended us on January the 6th. It's done, it's been rescinded, and I am satisfied,” Tillis said.Tillis argued “both (sides) have a problem” and he hopes Blanche will attempt “a bending of the curve of this absurdity.”“If you want to talk about weaponization, take a look at the Biden administration … Maybe it's a little bit more intense in this administration than the last one, and that a little bit more intense than the prior administration, and so on and so forth. But folks, we've got to end this stuff,” he said.He added the “bonehead” DOJ official in North Carolina who is prosecuting former FBI Director James Comey for a social media post of seashells on a beach spelling out “8647” — a nod to a restaurant kitchen term to get rid of something — “better damn sure have information to back it up because if all it is is a picture, that person should lose his or her job.” Dems united in oppositionAll committee Democrats followed ranking member Dick Durbin of Illinois in delivering remarks opposing Blanche’s nomination. The panel’s minority members hammered concerns about Blanche’s handling of the Epstein files and meeting with convicted sex trafficker Ghislaine Maxwell, federal lawsuits for states’ voter records and a promise to faith leaders that the DOJ will make the Supreme Court’s decision to overturn federal abortion protections “permanent in every single state.”The Department of Justice did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment about the criticisms.Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey chastised his Republican counterparts for comparing the Trump administration’s actions to the Biden administration, including President Joe Biden’s pardons of his son Hunter and other officials just hours before leaving office.“That is like being obsessed and using a magnifying glass to study the stain on the living room carpet when behind you is a mountain of excrement covering the living room couch and coffee table,” Booker said. He added that Trump’s recent financial disclosure revealed he made nearly $2 billion in crypto and foreign investments, and pointed to his sons’ Eric and Don Jr.’s backing of defense tech business ventures.“The lack of proportionality going on (by) my colleagues, it is laughable,” he said.Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse described Blanche’s two-paragraph signed statement and unsigned memo in response to Cornyn and Tillis’ concerns as “decorative.”The Rhode Island Democrat said the Trump administration could reverse course and create a similar fund.“Nothing in this document prevents anything like that from happening,” Whitehouse said.Durbin accused Blanche of lying under oath when he denied during his confirmation hearing a comment he made about the “anti-weaponization” fund during a pre-hearing meeting with Durbin.“Mr. Blanche told me he made, quote, ‘a mistake,’ end quote, by creating the January 6th slush fund. Where did he say it? In my office, with witnesses on my staff to what I'm about to say. When I asked him about this under oath, Mr. Blanche falsely claimed that he never made this statement,” Durbin said.Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., slammed Trump for suing the Internal Revenue Service in the first place. The contractor who leaked Trump and his sons’ and organization’s tax information to reporters in 2019 was sentenced for the crime in 2024.“He waits til he’s president. He sues the IRS for $10 billion. In a stunning act of self-dealing, he purports to settle with himself. He's represented by his personal lawyers on the one hand, and by his other lawyers at the Department of Justice on the other hand,” Schiff said, highlighting the Florida federal judge’s order that Trump used his presidency to “manipulate” the court for his benefit. “Now there was an effort, and I appreciate my colleagues from Texas and North Carolina making an effort to try to rein in this tax settlement. But what they attempted to achieve has not been achieved,” Schiff said.Epstein survivors disappointedBlanche’s nomination vote drew criticism from outside the committee as well.In an open letter Tuesday, 18 survivors of abuse by the now deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and convicted sex trafficker Maxwell called the vote “a profound disappointment.”Survivors have slammed Blanche’s handling of the Epstein files release, which unmasked several survivors' names and images in the process “while he concealed the identities of alleged abusers and others connected to Epstein's trafficking network,” the letter stated.“When we met with Blanche (after his confirmation hearing), he interrupted us. He told us to ‘get to the point.’ He told us to report what happened to us to the FBI. We already have. Some of us have been reporting these crimes for decades,” the survivors wrote.In another line of criticism, the legal advocacy organization Democracy Forward said in a letter to the Justice Department Monday that Blanche has refused to provide a sworn statement in federal court that the “anti-weaponization” fund will not accept and pay out claims.Democracy Forward is representing several plaintiffs in a lawsuit over the fund, including a former federal prosecutor who alleges he was fired in June 2025 for his involvement in Jan. 6 prosecutions.“The American people are not fooled by this latest move, and neither are we. The Trump-Vance administration cannot ask the public or our clients to accept a late-night social media post in place of legally binding action,” said Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward in a statement Monday.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Wiggins rallies around Hood Industries workers after mill closure
description: An aerial view shows Hood Industries' Wiggins, Miss., plywood mill, which is expected to permanently close at the end of August 2026 after Tropical Storm Arthur caused significant damage to the facility.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
STONE CCOUNTY — As Hood Industries prepares to permanently close its Wiggins plywood mill at the end of August, community organizations are working to help approximately 250 displaced employees find new jobs and connect them with financial, mental health and other support services. 
A two-day job fair for former Hood Industries employees will be held Aug. 14 from noon to 6 p.m. and Aug. 15 from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. at Mississippi Gulf Coast Community College’s Perkinston campus. The event is part of a coordinated rapid response effort following the company’s announcement that the mill would close after Tropical Storm Arthur caused significant damage to the facility. 
The mill has operated in Wiggins for 56 years. 
“We are part of the rapid response team,” said Rachael Kunz, associate vice president of workforce solutions at Mississippi Gulf Coast Community College. “Rapid response starts immediately after the announcement of the closing of an industry partner … as a community college, we want to serve our community.” 
Screenshot Credit: Courtesy of Rachael Kunz
Kunz said the job fair was organized within a week of Hood Industries announcing the closure July 7. 
The rapid response team includes Mississippi Gulf Coast Community College, the Mississippi Department of Employment Security, the Mississippi Department of Human Services and Stone County Economic Development. In collaboration with MGCCC, Stone County Economic Development has also launched a website connecting residents with job opportunities, school supply assistance, mental health resources, food assistance and other community services. 
Kunz said the effects of the closure will extend beyond the mill’s workforce. 
“It’s not just the employees,” she said. “Suppliers, restaurants and other small businesses throughout the community will also feel the impact.”
Hood Industries said approximately 250 employees are affected by the closure. Company President Jay Galloway called the decision difficult.  
“We are well aware of the impact this decision will have on the Wiggins employees, their families and community,” Galloway said in a statement. 
The company said affected employees will meet with Hood Industries representatives to discuss transition assistance and opportunities at other company facilities. Employees will continue receiving pay through Sept. 5 as part of the company’s transition plan. 
Former Hood Industries employee Joseph Fairley worked at the Wiggins, Miss., plywood mill for 25 years before being laid off July 24, 2026. Credit: Courtesy of Joseph Fairley
For longtime employees, the closure marks the end of decades of work. 
Joseph Fairley spent 25 years at the mill as a lift driver before being laid off July 24.
“It was sad because I just never thought that it would close,” Fairley said. “It’s been there so long. I didn’t see it coming. It didn’t hit me that day … but the next day it did.” 
Fairley said the facility needed repairs before Tropical Storm Arthur damaged the mill, including work on the roof, but he hoped the problems would eventually be addressed. 
Lew Douglas Schuit, who worked at the mill for 13 years as a machine and forklift operator before also being laid off July 24, described hearing the news as “a sinking feeling.” 
“I wasn’t necessarily expecting it,” Schuit said. “With what they had said was the cause, it’s something I knew would happen eventually. I figured it would be able to be reconciled.” 
Former Hood Industries employee Lew Douglas Schult worked at the Wiggins, Miss., plywood mill for 13 years before being laid off July 24, 2026. Credit: Courtesy Lew Douglas Schult
Hood Industries is also expanding operations elsewhere in Mississippi, with a new sawmill in Wayne County and a new plywood mill in Perry County expected to be completed later this year. Fairley believes those investments influenced the company’s decision not to repair the Wiggins facility.
“I don’t think the owner wanted to put a lot of money in here because he put a lot of money into the new mills,” Fairley said. 
As the community prepares for the mill’s final weeks, Fairley said he is focused on taking time to recover before deciding what comes next. 
“Right now, I’m going to take some time off, just for my mental health,” he said. “I’ve been working so long. I’ve raised my kids through that mill, so I’m going to take a couple of months off.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Legal Marijuana NOW candidate will stay on fall ballot for Nebraska US Senate
description: Mike Marvin, one of the candidates accused of being a “plant” for Dan Osborn, didn’t submit the paperwork to drop out of the Nebraska U.S. Senate race.
text:
Signs in the bowels of the Nebraska State Capitol advocate for legalization of marijuana. Aug. 2, 2024. (Aaron Sanderford/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Legal Marijuana NOW Party’s U.S. Senate nominee Mike Marvin will stay on the ballot after all. 
Marvin, one of the candidates accused of being a “plant” for nonpartisan U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn, didn’t submit the paperwork to drop out of the Senate race, the Secretary of State’s office confirmed Tuesday. The deadline for a candidate to drop out was Monday. 
U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., center, faces nonpartisan candidate Dan Osborn, left, and Legal Marijuana NOW nominee Mike Marvin in Nebraska’s Senate race this fall. (Candidate photos courtesy of respective campaigns | U.S. Capitol photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)
Marvin has denied being a plant for Osborn. On his website, Marvin said he would “work with other candidates to make sure” to have a “united front against Pete Ricketts.”
Former Democratic nominee Cindy Burbank paid Marvin’s $1,740 candidate filing fee earlier this year. Burbank dropped out of the race one day after Osborn’s signatures to be on the fall ballot were verified by the Secretary of State. 
While the race technically has three candidates, Osborn and incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts are considered the leading candidates. 
There could also be two new state political parties that could get candidates on the U.S. Senate ballot, depending on whether their signatures are verified. 
The race between incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts and Osborn, which has turned Nebraska politics upside down with allegations that candidates are “plants” for other candidates, multiple lawsuits and new political parties emerging.  
The race has drawn national attention for its nontraditional political dynamics. The election is Nov. 3.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Former Jackson mayor moves to surrender law license after pleading guilty in federal bribery case
description: Former Jackson Mayor Chokwe Antar Lumumba, left, exits the federal courthouse in downtown Jackson behind his sister, Rukia Lumumba, after he pleaded guilty in a public corruption case on Monday, July 6, 2026.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Shortly after Chokwe Antar Lumumba pleaded guilty to a federal conspiracy charge, his attorneys shepherded the former mayor of Jackson into a witness room on the fifth floor of the Thad Cochran United States Courthouse. 
As the door closed, Jaribu Hill, the founder of the Mississippi Workers’ Center for Human Rights, hugged the 43-year-old and reassured Lumumba that he was still a lawyer. 
Soon, that will no longer be the case in Mississippi. On Monday, Lumumba informed the Mississippi Supreme Court he would give up his law license after the state bar association filed a complaint against him. 
Lumumba pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit bribery – a federal felony charge – in early July. His pleading came one week before he was expected to go on trial in a case stemming from an FBI operation that rocked Mississippi’s capital city.
In Mississippi, those convicted of most felonies cannot practice law. Lumumba did not respond to a call and text from Mississippi Today seeking comment. 
In 2024, a sweeping federal indictment alleged that Lumumba participated in a conspiracy to commit bribery along with former Hinds County District Attorney Jody Owens and former Jackson City Council Member Aaron Banks. 
Prosecutors alleged that in exchange for $50,000 in campaign donations, Lumumba directed a city employee to shorten a bid deadline to benefit a pair of out-of-town developers that were working with Owens. Unknown to the local politicians, the developers were undercover FBI agents. 
Lumumba described this action as “ministerial at best,” according to court documents, thus not in line with how federal law and the courts have defined an official action a public official must take as part of a quid pro quo. 
Elected mayor in 2017, Lumumba had promised to make Jackson the “most radical city on the planet.” His overwhelming victory in the Democratic primary came after he unsuccessfully ran in a special election to succeed his late father, Chokwe Lumumba, who was elected in 2013 but died months into his term.
Mayor of Jackson was not the only vocation into which Lumumba followed his father. Chokwe Lumumba was a famed attorney who once successfully defended rapper Tupac Shakur from charges of shooting two off-duty police officers. 
Inspired by his father’s career, Lumumba decided to become a lawyer, according to a profile in the Oxford American. He was admitted to practice law in Mississippi in 2008.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Judge orders state GOP to certify Danny Ford II for US Senate primary
description: COLUMBIA — Danny Ford II will be on the Aug. 11 ballot for U.S. Senate following a judge’s ruling Tuesday requiring the state GOP to certify his candidacy in time for early voting. Judge Daniel Coble gave the state Republican Party 24 hours to officially qualify Ford and ordered the state Election Commission to include […]
text:
U.S. Senate candidate Danny Ford II speaks with his lawyers ahead of a Richland County court hearing Monday, Aug. 3, 2026, in which he asked the judge to put him on the ballot for the special Republican primary. The judge ruled Tuesday in his favor. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Danny Ford II will be on the Aug. 11 ballot for U.S. Senate following a judge’s ruling Tuesday requiring the state GOP to certify his candidacy in time for early voting.
Judge Daniel Coble gave the state Republican Party 24 hours to officially qualify Ford and ordered the state Election Commission to include his name on “all ballots feasible” for voting that starts Wednesday. The order rejected the party’s and election officials’ arguments that such late changes aren’t feasible for an election already underway.
Ford wasn’t asking for changes to the nearly 1,900 ballots that had already gone out to absentee voters and military members overseas.
“This means that the Court’s Order can be tailored to impose minimal impact on the election,” Coble wrote.
Ford’s addition means there will be 10 people competing in the special GOP primary to replace the late Lindsey Graham as the nominee on November general election ballots.
He was among three candidates decertified shortly after the filing deadline ended July 28. Ford and Darius Mitchell were deemed ineligible for failing to meet a new rule the party passed at the June convention requiring all candidates vote in two of the last three statewide GOP primaries.
Acknowledging that such a ruling requires extraordinary circumstances, Coble wrote, “Is this case not one of an extraordinary measure?”
The unexpected death of South Carolina’s senior senator, a recently passed GOP rule, a lack of clarity on its specifics, a fast-moving election, exceptions to federal law for military ballots that had to be made to accommodate a truncated timeline, and a candidate who was just on GOP primary ballots in June all combine to make the court’s mandatory intervention appropriate, he wrote.
The ruling applies only to Ford.
“Our constitution says everyone wo’s qualified should have a chance to vote and to run,” said Senate Minority Leader Brad Hutto, one of Ford’s attorneys. “This upholds Danny Ford’s right as a Republican to be on the ballot.”
A party spokesperson did not immediate return a request for comment.
Check back for details. This is a developing story.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island joins two more lawsuits against Trump administration
authors: Lilo H. Stainton, William J. Ford
description: The Trump administration’s demand for states to provide Social Security numbers, immigration status, and other private information on low-income residents who receive cash benefits is improper and unconstitutional, a group of mostly Democratic-led states alleges in a new lawsuit. Officials with 24 states, including Rhode Island, and the District of Columbia[...]
text:
A group of mostly Democratic-led states is challenging a Trump administration rule that would force them to provide data on people receiving antipoverty benefits. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)The Trump administration’s demand for states to provide Social Security numbers, immigration status, and other private information on low-income residents who receive cash benefits is improper and unconstitutional, a group of mostly Democratic-led states alleges in a new lawsuit.
Officials with 24 states, including Rhode Island, and the District of Columbia say in the complaint that a regulatory change proposed by the U.S. Administration for Children and Families and set to take effect Aug. 11 greatly exceeds the federal government’s assigned role in overseeing the antipoverty program called TANF, or Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, and violates multiple privacy laws.
The change, first announced in June, will also cost states extra time and money and chill participation in a program that benefits some 2.4 million people nationwide, according to the 60-page lawsuit filed Monday in federal court in D.C. The states are calling for the court to throw out the proposed rule and ensure the confidentiality of this information.
In a separate suit Monday, Rhode Island was one of 25 jurisdictions to sue the administration over the imposition of what it called “unlawful” tariffs. They are just the latest in the dozens of legal actions against the federal government by Rhode Island and by the other states.
“Once again, the President is attempting to unlawfully gain access to sensitive data including Social Security numbers, addresses, and more,” Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha said in a statement Monday. “Here, beneficiaries of TANF benefits are low-income families in need of emergency housing, victims of domestic abuse, and others, all of whom would potentially have their personal information shared across the federal government and possibly with private companies under this change. It is the responsibility of the states to determine eligibility for this program, not the federal government, and the Trump Administration will learn this the hard way when we see them in court.”
The TANF lawsuit alleges the change is part of the Trump administration’s ongoing effort to target immigrants by tightening the rules around various social service programs. Administration officials say they are trying to root out fraud and abuse, but critics say the new rules are designed to force out people who were born outside the U.S.
The Administration for Children and Families declined to comment on Monday. According to the lawsuit, the administration said it will share the data it obtains with other government agencies or private entities as part of its quest to verify that states are properly spending taxpayer dollars.
Nothing in the law supports the federal department’s “extravagant claims of authority and gross breach of personal privacy,” the lawsuit says.
“The sharing of such information runs afoul of a thicket of federal privacy protections,” it says.
When TANF was created as part of a federal welfare overhaul in 1996, it was purposely designed to limit the federal government’s role and give states wide control over the program’s design, operation, and information verification, according to the lawsuit. The Trump administration has insisted problems with the program require greater federal scrutiny.
The regulatory change announced in June would force states to provide additional details on participants, including Social Security numbers, country of origin, and immigration status, even though 95% of children and 85% of adults receiving benefits are U.S. citizens, according to the lawsuit.
Rhode Island receives about $95 million a year in federal TANF funding, distributed to eligible families through the Rhode Island Works program. As of December 2025, there were 2,572 adults and 5,932 children who received cash assistance or other supports through the Rhode Island Works program, according to Rhode Island KIDS Count. Nearly 4 in 10 of the children who receive program benefits are  under 6 years old.
The lawsuit also alleges that the Trump administration has not specified how they plan to keep program participants’ data safe, that the change would place a “direct and significant” cost on states, and that releasing data to the federal government would erode trust state agencies have developed with participants.
In addition to Rhode Island, the plaintiffs are New York, D.C., California, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, New Jersey, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, and Wisconsin.

Those same states were part of the lawsuit against the Trump administration for imposing 10% and 12.5% tariffs last month on the European Union and 59 other countries that trade with the U.S.
The president imposed those tariffs under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 that’s used to combat “unfair trade practices” by other countries. The tariffs imposed in July affect over ​99% of U.S. ⁠imports.
The states’ lawsuit, which also includes North Carolina, was filed in the U.S. Court of International Trade in New York. It follows a May ruling that said the president’s 10% global tariff was unlawful. The 2-1 decision in that case also noted the president’s decision exceeded his authority.
But Trump has continued to pursue new tariffs, which he has made part of his foreign policy initiative since his second term in office.
“Americans are sick and tired of an economy that isn’t working for them, and President Trump is exacerbating the situation with every chance he gets,” Neronha said in a statement. “The U.S. Supreme Court has already ruled that the President’s tariffs are unlawful, and in typical fashion, he thinks he found a loophole in this new strategy. And we will fight to ensure he is unsuccessful in this latest attempt.”
Neronha as the state’s top prosecutor has led or joined 68 lawsuits against the Trump administration this year, including 16 cases filed in Rhode Island federal court.
Rhode Island Current reporter Nancy Lavin contributed to this article.
This story was originally produced by New Jersey Monitor and Maryland Matters, which is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network which includes Rhode Island Current, and is supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Supreme Court approves alternative licensure program for lawyers
description: New Mexico's Supreme Court on Tuesday announced its approval of an alternative licensure program for lawyers intended to help address the "legal desert" in much of the state.
text:
The New Mexico Supreme Court on Aug. 4, 2026, announced it had approved an alternative licensure program for law school graduates. (Stock photo by Greenleaf123/Getty Images)The New Mexico Supreme Court on Tuesday announced its approval of a new skill-based pathway for law-school graduates to become licensed lawyers.
Justices previewed the program for state legislators in June, saying it could help address the state’s shortage of lawyers. A news release Tuesday noted that New Mexico officially qualifies as a “legal desert” under the American Bar Association’s definition, as two-thirds of its 33 counties have fewer than one lawyer for each 1,000 residents.
 “The skills-based pathway to licensure ensures that new attorneys possess the practical, on-the-job lawyering skills needed to help New Mexicans,” Chief Justice Julie J. Vargas said in a statement. “This new option for admission to the practice of law also has the potential to increase the number of attorneys in New Mexico to address unmet legal needs, particularly in rural areas where it is difficult to find a lawyer.”
The new approach will offer alternatives to the two-day bar state exam required for law-school graduates, and follows recommendations made by a Supreme Court-appointed committee of lawyers, judges, and law professors who studied the issue for more than a year.
Under an order issued last week, the court will work with the State Board of Bar Examiners to establish various requirements for alternative licensure and issue an additional order with the program’s start date, anticipated to occur in mid-2027.
The new licensure pathway will require participants to work with a supervising lawyer and submit a portfolio demonstrating their legal skills. Specifically, they will be required to finish at least 675 hours of legal work within a 12-month period under that supervision and submit portfolios that demonstrate abilities in a variety of areas, including legal writing, client meetings and various negotiations. The State Board of Bar Examiners will evaluate the portfolios.
A news release said New Mexico’s new program is akin to one Oregon launched in 2024. Approximately half a dozen other states also have alternative licensure programs, and at least seven are exploring them.
“New Mexicans will benefit from these reforms to the legal profession,” Justice C. Shannon Bacon, who served on the court’s study committee and as vice chair of a national group that issued a report last year on the issues of legal education and licensure. “Skills-based licensure will enhance the readiness of new attorneys to practice law and expand access to our justice system for people with legal issues, whether it is custody of children, housing problems, or consumer debt.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Recount decision timeline moved up in 3-vote margin Indiana Senate race
description: The timeline has been moved up for Indiana Recount Commission decisions on disputed ballots in the narrow Republican primary race between a state senator and his President Donald Trump-endorsed challenger.
text:
Sen. Spencer Deery, R-West Lafayette, and challenger Paula Copenhaver are candidates for the Republican nomination in Indiana Senate District 23. (Photos by Whitney Downard/Indiana Capital Chronicle, courtesy of Copenhaver campaign)The timeline has been moved up for the Indiana Recount Commission to weigh in on disputed ballots in the narrow Republican primary race between a state senator and his President Donald Trump-endorsed challenger.
The commission will meet Monday in the recount that has lasted more than three months since the May 5 primary from which certified results show Sen. Spencer Deery of West Lafayette with a three-vote lead over Paula Copenhaver.
An order issued by Recount Director Evan Norris to set next week’s meeting calls it the “final hearing” on the process. The commission had been scheduled to meet Aug. 18, just ahead of the Aug. 21 deadline set by state law for the Indiana Election Division to certify candidates for the November ballot.
Attorneys for the two sides said last week that possibly more than 300 ballots remained in dispute for various reasons.
Voter subpoenas denied in recount of narrow Indiana Senate Republican primary

That is despite a ballot review by State Board of Accounts auditors coming up with no changes from the certified results that show Deery leading by a 6,337 to 6,334 margin.
The Recount Commission last week rejected Copenhaver’s request to question 11 voters under oath about whether they properly took part in the Republican primary as they had disclosed in social media posts or to news reporters that they had cast GOP ballots to support Deery despite being Democrats or self-identified “progressives.”
Copenhaver, the Fountain County Republican chair and staffer to Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith, won Trump’s endorsement because of Deery’s opposition to the congressional redistricting plan pushed last year by the president. 
Once the Recount Commission makes a final decision on the primary’s outcome, either side could then appeal that ruling directly to the state Court of Appeals.
The Deery-Copenhaver race is the last one undecided from the Republican primary in which Trump-endorsed challengers defeated six of the seven other incumbent senators targeted by the president in retaliation for their votes against redistricting.
The Deery-Copenhaver winner will face Democratic West Lafayette City Councilman David Sanders and independent candidate Joshua Brant in the November election for the heavily Republican district, which spans all or parts of six counties in the area between Lafayette and Terre Haute.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Amendment 3 ballot title, summary language, don’t pass muster, judge rules
description: A Florida circuit court judge has ordered Attorney General James Uthmeier to rewrite significant portions of the ballot and summary title of Amendment 3, ruling the words “Save our Homes from Excessive Property Taxes” are “akin to a political slogan” in violation of state law. “Simply put, the proposed ballot title does not state the […]
text:
New home under construction. (Dan Reynolds Photography/Getty Images)A Florida circuit court judge has ordered Attorney General James Uthmeier to rewrite significant portions of the ballot and summary title of Amendment 3, ruling the words “Save our Homes from Excessive Property Taxes” are “akin to a political slogan” in violation of state law.
“Simply put, the proposed ballot title does not state the basic legal purpose of the amendment; it endorses it and diverts voters from its actual effect,” Judge David Frank wrote in an 18-page ruling that affirmed the plaintiffs’ complaints about the proposal.
Frank found that Amendment 3’s ballot summary language — telling voters the amendment “benefits” taxpayers by “ensuring funding for core services,” “protecting small businesses,” and “ensuring fairness for Florida residents” — is misleading, in violation of basic legal requirements.
“Whether the amendment would “benefit” taxpayers is the central policy question voters are being asked to decide,” Frank wrote.
“The court drew a line”
Former Sen. Jeff Brandes addresses reporters ahead of a hearing on the property tax amendment in the Leon County Courthouse on July 29, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)
Former Republican state Sen. Jeff Brandes, one of the named plaintiffs, called the ruling a victory for Florida voters.
“Today, the court drew a line. The ballot box is not a place for political advertising,” he said in a text to the Phoenix. “This case was never about whether property taxes should be lower. It was about whether government can market a constitutional amendment instead of honestly explaining it to voters. The court said ‘no.'”
If passed, Amendment 3 would constitute one of the most significant changes to property taxes in the state in more than a generation. Its projected financial impact would reach up to $12 billion annually beginning in 2031. It has drawn widespread opposition from groups that represent firefighters, sheriffs, and police.
Brandes and other former state and local officials filed lawsuits challenging the wording of Amendment 3. The measure cannot be knocked off the ballot but state law allows for the summary to be rewritten.
The lawsuits named Uthmeier and Secretary of State Cord Byrd. Frank consolidated the cases and heard oral arguments in the challenge last week.
It’s not clear they will comply with the order or appeal.
Department of State spokesperson Gretl Plessinger said the department doesn’t comment on pending litigation. Meanwhile, Uthmeier’s office didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
If there’s no appeal, Uthmeier has until Aug. 14 to make the necessary corrections. That’s four days before the Aug. 18 primary, after which election supervisors around the state will start assembling the November ballots.
Frank’s ruling also rapped the ballot summary language as deficient for the lack of information provided to voters.
It “defectively omits at least one material fact. The amendment purports to change the constitutional baseline of city and county power by placing in the Constitution for the first time the Legislature’s right to control ad valorem tax spending,” he wrote.
The ruling was quickly praised by those who oppose Amendment 3.        
“The people of our state need real relief from Florida’s affordability crisis, but Amendment 3 is a handout to the owners of multimillion-dollar homes while working families and seniors are left to pay more through other taxes or face major cuts to local services we all rely on,” Jackson Peel, with the group Save our Services No on Amendment 3, said in a prepared statement.
‘Monumental cost shift’
The Florida Policy Institute also released a statement.
“Today’s ruling affirms our stated concerns since the idea of property tax elimination was first floated by Gov. DeSantis in February 2025: that presenting this as a ‘savings’ for Floridians fundamentally misrepresents the true consequences of this amendment,” the institute said.
“Eliminating homestead property taxes would be a monumental cost shift. It would result in reduced or eliminated public services — longer emergency response times, rural hospitals shuttered, libraries closing, and more expensive childcare and summer camps, to name just a few ways Amendment 3 would erode Floridians’ quality of life and make Florida more unaffordable. Floridians deserve accurate information on what is at stake and we urge Attorney General Uthmeier to respond to the judge’s order and strip out the extreme bias in Amendment 3’s ballot language.”
The Florida Legislature passed Amendment 3 in the form of HJR 1F in early June. The ballot title and summary language the Frank found deficient were drafted initially by the DeSantis administration, although the final amendment was significantly altered by legislative leaders. So much so that DeSantis has said he won’t campaign to help pass the proposal.
Amendment 3 maintains the existing homestead property exemption through this year for resident homeowners. But it increases the homestead exemption for longstanding property owners to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028.
House Democratic Leader Fentrice Driskell, who voted against the proposal in June, issued a written statement reiterating her opposition to the plan.
“The idea that this amendment would save our homes from excessive property taxes was always a scam and misleading to voters,” Driskell, a Tampa Democrat, said.
“This amendment to eliminate property taxes will hand massive tax breaks to billionaires and large corporations, leaving hard working families, seniors, and small businesses to pay for it.  This is not a tax break but a tax shift that will cause new fees, higher taxes, and cuts to essential local services.  I believe Floridians can and will stop this deception from seeing the light of day in November.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Trump administration approves disaster assistance for Upshur, Lewis counties
description: The federal government has signed off on disaster assistance to two West Virginia counties hit hard by last month’s deadly storms and flooding. The Trump administration approved $4.5 million in individual assistance for Lewis and Upshur counties, according to a news release from Gov. Patrick Morrisey.
text:
Members of the West Virginia National Guard continue flood recovery and debris removal operations in Lewis and Upshur counties, July 30, 2026. (Photo by Edwin L. Wriston/U.S. Army National Guard)The federal government has signed off on disaster assistance to two West Virginia counties hit hard by last month’s deadly storms and flooding. The Trump administration approved $4.5 million in individual assistance for Lewis and Upshur counties, according to a news release from Gov. Patrick Morrisey. 
“I spoke to President Trump this afternoon and thanked him for acting quickly to approve this request and deliver help to the people of West Virginia,” Morrisey said in the news release Monday afternoon. “Families in our hardest-hit communities have endured tremendous hardship, and this expedited approval will provide critical assistance as they begin the difficult process of rebuilding their lives. This is an important first step. Approximately $4.5 million is available now, and we expect that amount to grow as additional damage information is reviewed.”
Storms on July 21 and 22 brought 9 tornadoes and up to about 7 inches of rain in some areas of the state, leading to flash flooding. Central West Virginia was among the hardest hit. Flooding killed two people in Upshur County. 
Morrisey requested an expedited major disaster declaration for Lewis and Upshur counties along with Barbour, Doddridge, Harrison, Pleasants and Ritchie counties. The state’s congressional delegation also sent a letter requesting the Trump administration approve the request. The Federal Emergency Management Agency is still reviewing damage in other counties, Morrisey’s office said in a news release.
President Donald Trump reportedly announced his approval for assistance to Upshur and Lewis counties on his social media platform Truth Social. 
“I just spoke with Patrick Morrisey, the GREAT Governor of West Virginia, a State I love and WON BIG, with Record Setting Votes, three times, and told him I am approving 4.5 Million Dollars for severe storms, winds, tornadoes, flooding, landslides, and mudslides they experienced, and are still recovering from,” he wrote. “West Virginia is represented strongly by the Governor, Senators Jim Justice and Shelley Moore Capito, along with Members of Congress, Riley Moore and Carol Miller. I LOVE WEST VIRGINIA! President DONALD J. TRUMP.”
The governor’s office said FEMA is still working with state and local officials conducting damage assessments, and said additional assistance may become available as those assessments continue and more information is submitted for consideration.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Lynn Fitch announces run for governor
description: Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch speaks during the Mississippi Economic Council's annual Hobnob at the Mississippi Coliseum in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 30, 2025.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch on Tuesday announced that she will seek the Republican nomination for governor in 2027, calling herself a “Trump conservative who doesn’t back down from a fight.”
Fitch opted to announce her gubernatorial candidacy a day before Wednesday’s start of a statewide tour where her campaign had said she would make an announcement about her future. 
Fitch joins a Republican primary field to replace term-limited incumbent Gov. Tate Reeves that includes Agriculture Commissioner Andy Gipson, former House Speaker Philip Gunn. Several other candidates will likely enter the race in the weeks and months ahead. In a news release and accompanying video, Fitch highlighted her work fighting the spread of illegal drugs, human trafficking, and the harms of technology on children — experience she said equips her to lead the state.
“Mississippi is on the verge of moving from the nation’s best-kept secret to the nation’s leader in conservative governance,” Fitch said. “We need the right leader to make this moment count. I have the experience, the record and the proven leadership to take Mississippi to the top.”
Fitch also cited her role in overturning what had been a nationwide right to abortion, an issue that earned her national attention in 2022.
Attorneys from her office argued the landmark Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization decision, and now abortion is almost entirely banned in Mississippi and in several other states. Fitch’s role in that case has made her a lightning rod for supporters of abortion rights, as Mississippi has some of the worst maternal health outcomes in the nation.  
It also led to support from some elements of Mississippi’s conservative base, which remains loyal to President Donald Trump. Fitch made several overtures to the Trump supporters in her announcement, saying she backed him “from the beginning” and that she has “battled the radical left and won.” She also said she was elected after “insiders” spent millions trying to defeat her.
“I am a Trump conservative with Mississippi values,” Fitch said. “Together, we will make bold and sustaining change for Mississippi. That is how we make the most of this moment in time. That is how we make Mississippi the nation’s leader. That is how we give you and your family your best future.”  
Fitch will likely have to contend with a crowded field of Republicans who will be vying for support from the president’s base, if not support from the president himself. Other Republicans considering entering the race for governor in bright-red Mississippi include Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann, state Auditor Shad White, former U.S. Rep. Gregg Harper, and billionaire businessman Tommy Duff.
Fitch had over $3.5 million in cash on hand last year, second only to White. 
Fitch, a Holly Springs native, served two terms as state treasurer before being elected attorney general in 2019. She began her legal career in the attorney general’s office as a special assistant attorney general. She has also served as executive director of the Mississippi State Personnel Board, worked in private practice and was deputy executive director of the Mississippi Department of Employment Security.
Fitch is the first woman to serve as attorney general in the state, and would also be the first woman to serve as Mississippi’s governor, if elected.
Fitch’s “announcement tour” begins Wednesday, with stops planned in Jackson, Hattiesburg and Gulfport, Meridian, Columbus, Tupelo, Cleveland and Southaven.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Broken pipes reveal more than aging infrastructure
description: Like many Waterbury residents, I've watched aging infrastructure become an increasingly familiar part of life.
text:
When my husband leaned over last Tuesday morning and told me there had been another water main break and we had no water, my response surprised even me.
“Okay.”
Not because I didn’t care. But because I wasn’t surprised.
Unfortunately, this wasn’t the first time. Like many Waterbury residents, I’ve watched aging infrastructure become an increasingly familiar part of life. The inconvenience wasn’t unexpected.

Maybeth Morales-Davis

Like many families, we adapted. My parents live just down the road in Watertown, so we packed up laundry, filled water jugs for flushing toilets, and borrowed a shower. I checked in on my neighbor and reached out to friends nearby to see how they were managing and whether they needed anything.
Those conversations changed the way I thought about what had happened.
Almost immediately, I saw neighbors doing the same.
The local YMCA opened its doors and offered showers to residents who had nowhere else to go. Community organizations shared updates through social media. A former boss called to offer us his home to shower, do laundry, and even volunteered to drop off bottled water if we needed it.
Whether in Waterbury or at our family’s small casita in Puerto Rico, I’ve seen the same truth emerge: when public systems are strained, people become the safety net. Neighbors check on neighbors. Community organizations fill gaps. Families open their homes. That generosity is inspiring, but it should never be mistaken for a substitute for long-term investment.
The broken pipes exposed something else entirely: how much we rely on one another when everyday systems stop working. I’ve spent years talking about the importance of community partnerships. During those few days, I didn’t have to talk about them. I watched them in action.
When the water eventually came back, the questions remained.
What about residents without transportation to stay with family? Older adults living alone? Families already struggling to make ends meet? People who missed the latest update or didn’t know where to turn?
Those questions matter because they reveal something larger than a water main break.
When systems are under strain, trusted relationships become essential.
Nonprofits, faith communities, schools, neighborhood organizations, and local businesses often reach residents that government and traditional media cannot. They know who may need extra support and already have trusted ways to communicate. During a crisis, those relationships become lifelines, connecting people with reliable information and critical resources.
That’s why community resilience doesn’t begin when an emergency occurs. It begins years earlier by investing in relationships, strengthening partnerships, and building trust before they’re needed.
The recent water main breaks also exposed a deeper concern.
Many residents weren’t simply frustrated about being without water. They were frustrated because they didn’t know what was happening, how long it would last, or why this problem seems to keep happening.
One neighbor told me she felt left in the dark. She couldn’t understand why these breaks continue throughout the city or whether anyone was addressing the root cause. I don’t think she was alone. By then, the conversation wasn’t about when the water would come back. It was about whether people believed this cycle was ever going to change.
Strong communities don’t rely on Band-Aids to solve foundational problems. Whether we’re talking about aging water systems, neighborhood investment, or public confidence, lasting trust is built when people see problems addressed at their foundation and leaders communicate honestly about both the challenges and the path forward.
Every city with aging infrastructure will face moments like this. Waterbury is not alone. The question isn’t whether another emergency will happen. It almost certainly will.
The real question is whether we’ll use moments like this to strengthen not only the infrastructure beneath our streets, but also the partnerships and trust above them.
Because when the next crisis comes, and it will, our strongest infrastructure won’t be the pipes beneath our feet.
It will be the people who check on a neighbor. The parents who open their homes. The nonprofits that extend their services. The businesses that step up. The community leaders who bring people together.
Waterbury deserves infrastructure that is as dependable as its people. We’ve already proven that our neighbors will show up for one another when systems fail. Imagine what our community could accomplish if we invested in both with the same level of commitment.
Maybeth Morales-Davis of Waterbury was a member of the CT Mirror Community Editorial Board in 2022.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Attorneys general tell justices to let state court decide Boulder’s climate change lawsuit
description: Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser urged the U.S. Supreme Court to let state courts resolve a lawsuit between local governments and energy companies they sued for damages over the companies’ contributions to climate change. A 2018 lawsuit filed by the city of Boulder and Boulder and San Miguel counties against Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil […]
text:
The Suncor Energy oil refinery in Commerce City is pictured on June 16, 2023. (Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser urged the U.S. Supreme Court to let state courts resolve a lawsuit between local governments and energy companies they sued for damages over the companies’ contributions to climate change.
A 2018 lawsuit filed by the city of Boulder and Boulder and San Miguel counties against Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil seeks to hold the fossil fuel companies accountable through Colorado law. The local governments allege the companies knowingly contributed to climate change, which the governments say has harmed residents. 
The Colorado Supreme Court ruled last year that local governments can file such a claim in state court, but the companies appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, which decided in February to take the case. The companies argued in their appeal that federal environmental law shields them from claims related to in-state harms. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The case has the potential to broadly influence how local governments around the country hold oil and gas companies accountable for their role in climate change. 
Weiser and attorneys general from other Democratic-led states filed a brief Monday that says the Supreme Court should determine if it has the authority to hear the case at this stage before agreeing to hear the energy companies’ appeal. 
“Our federal system depends on state and federal courts each fulfilling their proper role,” Weiser, a Democrat who is running to be Colorado governor, said in a statement. “This case involves the basic question whether Colorado courts can consider common law claims that fossil fuel companies engaged in wrongful behavior that contributed to climate change. At this stage of the case, it would be an overreach and improper for the Supreme Court to prevent Colorado courts from considering the merits of this litigation.” 
The attorneys general say the Supreme Court’s involvement before the state proceedings are complete could affect a range of other cases across the country beyond climate litigation.
The local governments sued the companies because of the rising costs climate change created for them, arguing the cost should not fall solely on taxpayers. San Miguel’s suit is now separate from the Boulder case. 
Boulder’s case is one of dozens across the country seeking a legal remedy for the role the fossil fuel industry has played in climate change. 
Rising levels of greenhouse gases in the Earth’s atmosphere, mostly the result of fossil-fuel combustion, have caused average global temperatures to rise. Global warming is the driving factor in the “megadrought” that has depleted the Colorado River Basin in the last 25 years, the worst dry spell the region has experienced in more than a millennium.
Hotter, drier conditions in Colorado have stressed water supplies, made the state’s forests more vulnerable to insects and diseases, and greatly increased wildfire risk. This past winter was the warmest on record in Colorado, accompanied by low levels of precipitation. 
Suncor’s Commerce City oil refinery has repeatedly been penalized for violating clean air and water standards.

title: Minnesota’s most aggressive drug prosecutor keeps getting overruled. He’s running unopposed (again).
description: An alleged fentanyl dealer in East Grand Forks is getting a new trial after prosecutors botched their instructions to the jury that convicted him. Polk County Attorney Greg Widseth “plainly erred by misstating the law” governing drug conspiracies, the Minnesota Supreme Court ruled last month. To obtain the first-degree conspiracy conviction he sought, he nee[...]
text:
Polk County Government Center in Crookston, where the Drug War is still going strong thanks to County Attorney Greg Widseth. (Courtesy photo)An alleged fentanyl dealer in East Grand Forks is getting a new trial after prosecutors botched their instructions to the jury that convicted him.
Polk County Attorney Greg Widseth “plainly erred by misstating the law” governing drug conspiracies, the Minnesota Supreme Court ruled last month. To obtain the first-degree conspiracy conviction he sought, he needed to demonstrate that the alleged dealer knew that the amount of drugs sold by the dealer’s co-conspirators crossed a statutory weight threshold. 
Instead, Widseth’s team told jurors that the defendant’s knowledge of the quantity of drugs didn’t matter at all, a factual error severe enough that it prompted the Supreme Court to vacate the most serious convictions and order a new trial.
It’s the latest embarrassment for a county attorney who has spent decades pushing the law to its limits in pursuit of severe penalties for drug users.
‘Non-standard and punitive’: Aggressive drug charges in rural county raise civil liberties concerns

Widseth has previously made headlines for obtaining nearly the entirety of the state’s convictions under an archaic “drug tax stamp law,” a drug war relic that prompted ridicule from the lawmakers who eventually repealed it. In 2024, a Reformer investigation revealed Widseth was exploiting a different legal loophole to charge a woman for possession of bong water, again prompting swift action from the Legislature.
A subsequent Reformer investigation found that Widseth was going to unusual lengths to obtain enhanced penalties under a “drug-free zone” law, including requests to the East Grand Forks City Council to designate more public lands as “park” areas where the enhancements apply. It’s “virtually impossible for any person to traverse the city without finding themselves within a school or park zone,” as a county public defender put it several years ago.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Thanks in large part to Widseth’s aggressive approach, Polk County’s incarceration rate is three times higher than the Minnesota average. But beyond arrest and imprisonment numbers it’s unclear from the available data whether life in the county is any better as a result: The county’s drug overdose death rate is similar to demographically equivalent counties in northwestern Minnesota. Overall crime rates show a similar pattern.
Widseth has held the county attorney’s office for more than 20 years, and one obvious rejoinder to his critics is that if voters are unhappy with his approach they can simply kick him out of office. “If voters disagree with the decisions made by [the county attorney’s] office, they can voice that opinion at the ballot box,” as a local judge put it in a 2022 ruling upholding one of Widseth’s charging decisions.
But Polk County voters have been offered no alternatives, as Widseth has run unopposed in every election since 2002. That’s not unusual: All of Minnesota’s 87 counties are electing prosecutors this year, and as of this writing there are multiple candidates filed in just 10 of those contests.
Fargo woman facing 30 years in prison for bong water

Local prosecutors hold a tremendous amount of discretionary power, deciding who gets charged, what they get charged with, and whether to seek justice via a trial or a plea deal. Elections are the primary check on that power, but in Minnesota and elsewhere that check is largely theoretical. 
In the absence of electoral competition, accountability for rogue prosecutors is slow and often expensive, arriving well after the damage has been done. It can come in the form of a legislative push to close an obscure loophole, or a critical news story shining light on an abusive practice, or a Supreme Court ruling on a prosecutorial error after years of litigation.
But for every conviction that gets that scrutiny, countless charging decisions never will.

text:
Gov. Beshear said he would restore some budget cuts he announced last week.
(Screenshot)Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear joined a coalition of Democratic state officials in suing to block the Trump administration from getting access to sensitive data of families receiving Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) benefits. 
Filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., the lawsuit said that the Administration for Children and Families had issued a notice to authorizing disclosing records of millions of Americans to “ any public or private entity that ACF chooses, at any time, for the purpose of scrutinizing States’ compliance with any provision of the TANF statute.” The ACF may disclose Social Security numbers, marital status, parentage, immigration status and more. 
According to a press release from the Beshear administration, more than 28,000 Kentuckians receive money through the federal program, which is administered by the Kentucky Transitional Assistance Program (KTAP) in the state. 
“I joined this lawsuit because no Kentuckian – and no American – should have to worry about their confidential and personal information being shared unlawfully,” Beshear said in a statement. “Social Security numbers, addresses and more are private – and we’re fighting back against the Trump administration’s unlawful actions to ensure they stay that way.”
Other states represented in the case are Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin, as well as the District of Columbia.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: President Donald Trump is denouncing mail-in voting. Alaska Republicans are doing it anyway.
description: Since 1994, the Alaska Republican Party has sent absentee ballot applications to registered voters across the state, urging voters to cast their ballot by mail.  The party continued the process this year, despite denunciations of mail-in voting by President Donald Trump, who has called voting by mail “cheating.” In a mailer sent to some voters […]
text:
The front page of Alaska's 2026 primary election ballot is seen on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026, the first day of early voting in person. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)Since 1994, the Alaska Republican Party has sent absentee ballot applications to registered voters across the state, urging voters to cast their ballot by mail. 
The party continued the process this year, despite denunciations of mail-in voting by President Donald Trump, who has called voting by mail “cheating.”
In a mailer sent to some voters last month, the party included a partially complete absentee ballot request form and a notice urging the recipient to “advance Republicans to the general election ballot.”
Through July 31, the Alaska Division of Elections reported that 9,981 Alaskans had requested absentee ballots for the Aug. 18 statewide primary.
Of the requests, 28.5% had come from Republicans. Among the state’s 602,131 registered voters, 23.6% are Republicans. 
That indicates Republicans are seeking absentee ballots at a disproportionately higher rate than registered voters overall.
The same disproportionate pattern is true with Democrats, who generally support mail-in voting. The Alaska Democratic Party also sent out an absentee ballot request form to voters statewide. 
Of absentee requests received through July 31, 19.7% were from registered Democrats. Members of that party make up 11.6% of the state’s registered voters.
The trend across Republicans and Democrats is likely due to the fact that registering with a party means that person is at least somewhat engaged with politics and thus more likely to vote overall.
Undeclared voters — those who haven’t chosen a party affiliation — represent 49.5% of the state’s registered voters, but only 32.1% of absentee ballot requesters.
Nonpartisan voters — Alaskans who specifically chose to be separate from any political party — make up 13.6% of voters and 18.8% of all absentee ballot requesters.
Voters from the state’s minor political groups make up the remaining balance of requesters.
The deadline for an Alaskan to request a paper absentee ballot be mailed to them is Aug. 8. The deadline for requesting a blank absentee ballot be sent by email is Aug. 17. 
All absentee ballots must be postmarked — or faxed — no later than election day, Aug. 18.
