name: Washington State Standard
title: It’s primary election day in WA. Here’s what you need to know
description: Washington voters on Tuesday will start to winnow the competition in hundreds of local, state and federal races in this busy election cycle. All 98 seats in the state House and 24 in the Senate are up for grabs, as Democrats seek to widen their majorities in each chamber and Republicans hope to claw back […]
text:
A ballot dropbox in Olympia on March 12, 2024. (Photo by Bill Lucia/Washington State Stadard)Washington voters on Tuesday will start to winnow the competition in hundreds of local, state and federal races in this busy election cycle.
All 98 seats in the state House and 24 in the Senate are up for grabs, as Democrats seek to widen their majorities in each chamber and Republicans hope to claw back seats. There are numerous open seats as members have left the Legislature, so there will be new lawmakers in Olympia for the next legislative session beginning in January. 
And a number of incumbents are trying to fend off challengers, including from their own party. 
For instance, state Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, faces activist Hannah Sabio-Howell running to his left. Pedersen has been the target of mailers ahead of the primary funded by rich conservatives stoking frustration with the legislative leader after he shepherded the state’s new income tax on high earners. Republicans don’t have a chance of flipping the seat representing ultra-liberal Seattle neighborhoods.
Meanwhile, in central Washington, Rep. Mike Steele, R-Chelan, faces Republican pastor Adam James, among the most prolific campaign fundraisers of this election season. 
All 10 of Washington’s seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are on the ballot, as well. Most of the incumbents are expected to sail to reelection, but a few races are notable. 
Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez’s reelection bid could factor into the balance of power in Congress. The Democrat in southwest Washington’s 3rd Congressional District is vying for a third term. She will have to hold off a big field of candidates, namely state Senate Minority Leader John Braun, who is a Republican, and fellow Democrat Brent Hennrich, who is running to her left. 

 Voter guide

	Check out the Standard’s voter guide to key legislative races, the state Supreme Court contests and two of the most closely-watched battles for seats in the U.S. House. We surveyed over 100 candidates to see where they stand on a range of issues. You can find the voter guide here.

Rep. Dan Newhouse’s retirement in central Washington’s 4th Congressional District has drawn nearly a dozen hopefuls for the safely Republican seat, including his 2024 opponent, Jerrod Sessler, Yakima County Commissioner Amanda McKinney and state Sen. Matt Boehnke.
And Tuesday’s primary will reveal if far-left former Seattle City Councilmember Kshama Sawant’s insurgent bid to unseat longtime Rep. Adam Smith has a shot in the 9th Congressional District, which extends south from Seattle.
Every voter will weigh in on four state Supreme Court races, as the high court faces heavy turnover. Two will serve as the first electoral tests for Gov. Bob Ferguson appointees, Colleen Melody and Theo Angelis. Another will fill a vacant seat for a departing justice. And Chief Justice Debra Stephens faces multiple challengers. A fifth position will be on the November ballot, with only two candidates running.
Supreme Court elections often pass by without much attention, but this year is expected to be different. All eyes are on the court ahead of an expected legal fight over the “millionaires’ tax” that’s sure to end up before the justices.
The top two candidates in each race advance to the Nov. 3 general election.
As of Monday night, just over 1 million of Washington’s 5.1 million registered voters had returned their ballots, for a 19.9% turnout. King County has among the lowest turnout so far, while Garfield, Jefferson and Wahkiakum counties, which have far fewer residents, are leading the way. When it’s all said and done, participation could sit around 40%, if past midterm primaries are an indicator. 
Mailed ballots must be postmarked by Tuesday, or turned into one of the state’s numerous ballot drop boxes or election centers by 8 p.m., to count. A map of drop boxes and voting centers can be found here. 
Procrastinating? Information on candidates running for all levels of office can be found in the official online voters’ pamphlets for the state and counties. In all, 688 elected offices and 80 local measures are on the ballot in the 2026 primary. There are 1,334 candidates running.
If mailing in, given less frequent pickups from the U.S. Postal Service, election officials recommended sending ballots in at least a week before Election Day to ensure they’d be tabulated. 
Voters can track their ballots online at VoteWA.gov, and can get text alerts about the status of their ballots there or by texting “VOTE” to 868392.
Initial results are expected to drop just after 8 p.m. County election offices and the secretary of state will post early tallies online. Results can shift as more votes are counted in the coming days in Washington’s mail-ballot system. The secretary of state has to certify results by Aug. 21.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi foster care system fails to meet dozens of safety requirements, new report says
description: Andrea Sanders, commissioner of the Mississippi Department of Child Protection Services, speaks after Gov. Tate Reeves signed House Bill 1671, House Bill 510 and Senate Bill 2696 into law at the Walter Sillers Building in Jackson, Miss., Wednesday, April 19, 2023.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Mississippi’s foster care system continues to endanger children under its care at higher rates than a federal court order permits, according to a new report for a federal lawsuit the state seeks to dismiss. 
The Mississippi Department of Child Protection Services met 22 of 107 applicable safety measures related to the agency’s care of foster children throughout most of 2025, a court monitor found. The measures are agreed upon by the department and plaintiff lawyers in the Olivia Y. v. Barbour federal lawsuit, a decades-old case that alleged Mississippi frequently endangers those in the state’s child welfare system. 
The report, published on July 29, says that children in the state’s care experienced abuse or neglect at more than twice an acceptable rate, were frequently placed in unlicensed facilities or with relatives before the department finished background checks and often went without required visits from caseworkers.
The department also undercounted how many foster children experienced abuse and didn’t provide enough information for the monitor to determine whether some requirements were being met, according to the report. The monitor did find that caseworkers more frequently had appropriate caseloads and foster children were less often placed in overcrowded homes compared to previous years. 

The latest assessment is the first full court monitor report published since 2021, when lawyers for both sides agreed that Mississippi’s child protection department doesn’t “have the capacity to comply” with the settlement.
In an affidavit filed in May, Department Commissioner Andrea Sanders said through policy and organizational efforts, the state has since made positive changes to its foster care system that “have been far reaching, covering the work of the Agency across many areas” like staffing improvements and technology upgrades.
Sanders is the fourth commissioner of Mississippi’s child protection department, an agency created in 2015 as a result of the Olivia Y. lawsuit. 
Gov. Tate Reeves and the Mississippi Department of Child Protection Services, represented by Attorney General Lynn Fitch’s office and the national law firm Baker Donelson, are trying to dismiss the lawsuit. Their lawyers said earlier this year that Mississippi has made sufficient progress in keeping children safe. 
Reeves and the state’s child welfare department did not respond to emails from Mississippi Today. MaryAsa Lee, a spokesperson for Fitch’s office, said the office does not comment on active litigation and would speak through its court responses.
Chief U.S. District Judge Sul Ozerden, who’s overseeing the lawsuit, said lawyers representing Mississippi foster children could wait until the court monitor submitted its 2025 report to file a response to the state’s motion to dismiss. Marcia Lowry, the lead lawyer for the foster children, told Mississippi Today the report contradicts the state’s position on the case. 
“It’s one thing to make grand statements,” Lowry said. “‘We’re going to keep all children safe. We’re going to give all children whatever they need.’ But then you have to find out whether you’re really doing that, and they’re not doing it in Mississippi.” 
Lawyers for Reeves and Mississippi’s child welfare agency asked Ozerden to require a response from Lowry about their motion to dismiss the case before the report was published, saying it “has no bearing” on their argument. Lowry disagreed in a filing, saying that the report would contain core elements related to the motion. 
Underreported abuse and insufficient investigations
Many of the dozens of required safety measures Mississippi’s child welfare agency didn’t meet have direct implications on foster children’s wellbeing. 
For example, lawyers for both sides agreed that except in certain circumstances, no foster child under the age of 10 should be placed in group housing — where abuse and mistreatment can be a high risk. But the monitor found 22 children under the age of 10 living in these facilities who shouldn’t have been placed there. Additionally, the department only completed reports on mistreatment in a timely manner about half the time, far below the court’s 90% standard. 
Case workers make in-person visits to assess the physical and mental wellbeing of foster children, but the report says they are doing so at much lower rates than the standard. It found that the child welfare agency self-reported its workers attending less than half of their required meetings with children, foster parents and biological families.
The report also highlighted specific examples of alleged abuse from last year that Mississippi’s child welfare department may have mishandled. In one investigation the monitoring team reviewed, three teenage children alleged a range of abuse from their foster parent, from encouraging fights between the children to leaving one child so traumatized that the teenager needed acute care for suicidal thoughts. The state’s investigation found insufficient evidence for the allegations, but the monitor report says the state did not look into several of them.
In another, different children had reported a foster mother of being physically and verbally abusive four times within a year and a half, including restricting how frequently they could use the bathroom. Mississippi’s child protection department said all the allegations were unsubstantiated, but the report says caseworkers documented enough evidence at least once to suggest that professionals should address the concerns. It was unclear to the monitor if the department ever provided that intervention. 
Marcia Lowry, founder and executive director of A Better Childhood.  Credit: Courtesy of A Better Childhood
Lowry blamed Sanders, who has led the agency since 2020, for many of the issues the report identified. She said the changes Sanders cited in her May affidavit haven’t resulted in tangible results for Mississippi foster children. 
“She’s gotten the overall number of workers to be within a reasonable limit, but I don’t know what else she’s been doing,” Lowry said. “Because there are so many issues here that are so important to kids and to their safety.”
Lack of data makes some measures unknown
Data collection and reporting issues made it difficult for the monitor to determine whether the state’s child welfare agency was meeting certain lawsuit safety standards, according to the report. For a dozen measures, the monitor said the Mississippi agency didn’t provide enough information to make a reliable assessment. 
The report also says the child protection services department miscalculated some safety measures. The agency identified 25 to 30 incidents of foster child maltreatment during the monitoring period, but the monitor found at least 18 more that should’ve been included. Out of a random sample of mistreatment investigations, the report found that only 82% of the department’s conclusions were backed by available evidence.
While certain measures, including the rates of foster child mistreatment, have improved since the last full report in 2020, the number of measures Mississippi’s child welfare agency met decreased in 2025. Many of the safety measures that have improved still do not meet agreed-upon safety standards.
Lowry said she plans to incorporate this report into her team’s response to Mississippi’s motion to dismiss the Olivia Y. lawsuit, which it has to file by late August. Whether the lack of data or actual violations led to Mississippi not meeting the agreed-upon safety measures, she said, the number of unfulfilled requirements is unacceptable. 
“That’s ridiculous,” she said. “The differences are not one or two kids. The differences are significant.”

Agriculture Commissioner Andy Gipson, a Republican candidate for governor next year, says he’s concerned the proliferation of data centers in Mississippi puts the state at risk and that he’s hearing major concerns about data centers and AI from Mississippians as he campaigns across the state. Gipson said data centers and the AI boom are being funded by debt and “circular financing,” similar to what happened with other tech before the dot-com bubble burst in the early 2000s. name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri Primary Election Day FAQ: What you need to know to make sure your vote counts
description: Voters will head to the polls Tuesday to choose nominees for state auditor, Congress and a host of state legislative seats, as well as decide the fate of four proposed constitutional amendments. The Independent tried to answer some of the questions you may have about voting in Missouri’s primary.  Polls across the state open at […]
text:
(Jim Neuger/Maine Morning Star)Voters will head to the polls Tuesday to choose nominees for state auditor, Congress and a host of state legislative seats, as well as decide the fate of four proposed constitutional amendments.
The Independent tried to answer some of the questions you may have about voting in Missouri’s primary. 
 What time do polls open?

Polls across the state open at 6 a.m. and close at 7 p.m. Voters in line by 7 p.m. are entitled to cast a ballot.
Where do I vote?
Before you head out the door, check your voter registration and polling location at GoVoteMissouri.com. 
Some local election officials said the state’s website has the most up-to-date information on the new polling sites. Others recommended going directly to the county’s website or calling local officials instead. The GoVoteMissouri.com website will also provide the information you need to contact your local election authority.
 How do I find out what’s on the ballot?

Local election authorities provide sample ballots, which voters can study, fill out and bring with them on Election Day to use as a guide. They are typically posted on your county’s website. Researching your ballot ahead of time will help cut down on the time you spend at the polls, and local election officials are encouraging voters to do this.
 What are acceptable forms of ID to vote?

To cast a regular ballot, registered Missouri voters must present photo identification issued by Missouri or the federal government.
Voters without acceptable identification may cast a provisional ballot. The ballot will count if the voter returns to the polling place on Election Day with acceptable photo identification or if the local election authority determines that the signature on the provisional-ballot envelope matches the signature in the voter’s registration record.
Accepted forms of photo identification include:

A Missouri driver’s license or nondriver identification card that is unexpired or expired after Nov. 5, 2024;
An unexpired military identification card, including a veteran identification card
An unexpired U.S. passport;
Another photo identification issued by Missouri or the federal government that is unexpired or expired after Nov. 5, 2024.

If you cast a provisional ballot, you will receive a stub from your provisional ballot envelope with instructions on how to verify that your provisional ballot is counted.
 Can I wear a T-shirt with my candidate’s name on it?

Missouri prohibits campaign apparel advocating for a candidate or ballot issue inside a polling place. Electioneering is also prohibited within at least 25 feet of the building’s closest outside door, although some local election authorities may establish a 50-foot boundary.
Voters should not photograph or share a marked ballot. Missouri law prohibits intentionally revealing a ballot to show how a person voted or intends to vote.
 Who can I call if I need help?

Voters may call the Secretary of State hotline at 1-800-669-8683 with any questions or to file a complaint with the the agency’s elections division.
A nonpartisan election protection hotline (866-OUR-VOTE) will also have trained lawyers ready to answer questions on election day.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Preakness, Pimlico left out of new race series by Churchill Downs, Belmont
description: Just days after state officials announced they had finalized an $85 million deal to acquire the rights to the Preakness Stakes, they learned that Pimlico had been excluded from a new championship racing series organized by the other two Triple Crown tracks.
text:
Gov. Wes Moore with the Woodlawn Vase trophy, part of the Preakness holdings the state has acquired, after the 151st running of the Preakness at Laurel Park this year. (Photo by Joe Andrucyk/Patrick Siebert/Office of the Governor)Just days after state officials announced they had finalized an $85 million deal to acquire the rights to the Preakness Stakes, they learned that Pimlico had been excluded from a new championship racing series organized by the other two Triple Crown tracks.
Churchill Downs Inc. and the New York Racing Association Inc. announced Monday that they are launching a six-race, five-month Thoroughbred Championship Series to be run at Churchill Downs, Belmont Park and Saratoga Race Course. Three-year-old thoroughbreds that compete in the series will get points across the season, with a $5 million prize pool for the series, in addition to individual race purses.
Officials with the two organizations said the championship series, which is scheduled to start in 2027, is designed to create a season-long competition that will encourage the best horses in the field to compete against each other repeatedly. Races at Churchill Downs will be broadcast nationally on NBC while races at NYRA tracks, Belmont and Saratoga, will be broadcast on Fox.
“The Thoroughbred Championship Series will extend the excitement of the sport across a five-month season,” said Bill Carstanjen, CEO of Churchill Downs Inc., in the announcement of the series. “This series gives … fans a reason to stay engaged with the sport’s biggest stars throughout the season. By connecting these premier events through one championship, we’re creating a season-long storyline that benefits the future of thoroughbred racing.”
The series will run from May through September, with the first two races at the Kentucky Derby in May and the Belmont Stakes in June, the first and third races of Triple Crown. The Preakness, the second race in the Triple Crown, was skipped over for the championship series.
State finalizes deal to buy rights to Preakness for $85 million

Other races in the series would be the Matt Winn Stakes at Churchill Downs in July, the Jim Dandy Stakes at Saratoga in late July or early August, the Travers Stakes at Saratoga in late August and the final Championship Race at Churchill Downs in September.
“This series is designed to showcase the sport’s best 3-year-olds across a season-long championship, elevating our biggest events and creating the next generation of fans,” David O’Rourke, NYRA president and CEO, said in the announcement.
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore’s office declined comment on Monday’s announcement and the Maryland Jockey Club, which will operate races in the state under the state’s new ownership, did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment.
But state Republicans were quick to jump on the news, saying that the state’s decision to buy the rights to the Preakness and the Black-Eyed Susan Stakes will leave taxpayers “with the financial responsibility while others continue shaping the future of racing.”
“For months, the governor claimed he had ‘saved the Preakness.’ But this announcement makes clear that owning the trademark isn’t the same as owning the future of the sport,” said Senate Minority Leader Steve Hershey (R-Upper Shore).
I warned that Maryland wasn’t buying certainty, we were buying risk. The Governor chose to own the liability rather than secure a long-term partnership with the industry’s most influential organizations. Today, Churchill Downs and NYRA have shown exactly where they believe the future of Thoroughbred racing lies, and Maryland was on the outside looking in,” Hershey said.
Hershey said that the new series gives owners and trainers an incentive to build their schedules around the Preakness, putting it at a disadvantage in the fight for the sport’s best horses.
“The long-term financial implications remain to be seen, but any development that diminishes the prestige or commercial value of the Preakness should concern those responsible for repaying the bonds issued to acquire these rights,” he said.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Carstanjen shook Maryland officials this spring when he announced that Churchill Downs Inc. had agreed to purchase intellectual property rights to the Preakness and Black-Eyed Susan Stakes from 1/ST Maryland LLC, the company that owned and operated both. But the state’s deal with 1/ST gave it a right to match that offer, which it did.
Moore announced Friday that the state had finalized the purchase, with not tax dollars involved but with funds from notes issued by the Maryland Economic Development Corp. Those notes are supposed to be repaid with revenues from the two races.
Rights to the Preakness were just the latest investment in racing by the state, which bought and is investing $400 million in the renovation of Pimlico Race Course in Baltimore.
The state also bought Shamrock Farms in Carroll County in the last year, with plans to turn it into a training center. Those plans were abandoned when the state encountered financial and logistical problems with the site, and the state is now in the process of buying Laurel Park for $48.5 million to make it the state training center.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Data privacy bill must have real teeth
description: We can end Big Tech’s abuses — but only if we have the courage to stand up to the tech oligarchs and maintain the strong standards of our consumer protection law when it comes to enforcing our data privacy law.
text:
RIGHT NOW, lawmakers in Massachusetts are hashing out the differences between House and Senate data privacy bills. Both bills completely ban the sale of our precise geolocation data, a huge win for residents and visitors. 
Elsewhere, there are some important differences to be resolved. The Senate bill would ban the sale of other sensitive data, such as biometrics and information about health, sexual orientation, gender identity, and minors’ activities online. These are critical provisions that should be included in the final law. 
Another key point revolves around enforcement.  
Today, Massachusetts consumer protection law enables individuals to seek redress in court when companies violate their rights. Such accountability gives state law teeth and encourages compliance.  
The House bill maintains this enforcement standard in the data privacy bill, giving individuals — as well as the attorney general — the right to take Big Tech companies to court over privacy violations.  
If we want strong privacy protections in fact, and not just on paper, the conference committee should include the House’s enforcement language in the final bill. 
Big Tech is lobbying fiercely to strip individuals of this “private right of action.” That’s no surprise: Their entire (very lucrative) business model is built around collecting, manipulating, trading, and selling extremely sensitive information about you, your family, and your neighbors. 
This surveillance economy puts everyday people at risk. Anyone with a credit card can buy location data showing the travel patterns of health care providers and patients who seek abortion or gender-affirming care. In today’s political environment, that’s terrifying. 
A strong data privacy bill would block these and other dangerous practices in Massachusetts. 
The key word is “strong.” A law without a strong enforcement mechanism is more like a suggestion. 
If the private right of action is stripped from the bill and enforcement is left to the attorney general alone, companies like Meta and Google won’t face meaningful accountability. Our AG is fantastic — but given her limited staff and the broad range of issues her office is responsible for, she simply does not have the resources to police every major privacy violation impacting Massachusetts residents.  
Time and again, Meta has been caught egregiously violating consumer privacy. It has been slapped with significant fines and judgments. None of that has changed the company’s behavior. The threat of an occasional lawsuit from the Massachusetts AG likely won’t, either. 
On the other hand, if the data privacy law empowers individuals to hold them accountable in court, tech billionaires like Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, and Elon Musk will be forced to take the law seriously.  
Consumers will hold them accountable in court. By making repeat violations of the law highly visible, those suits would also give courts incentive to go beyond imposing monetary judgments and start ordering Big Tech companies to change their behavior and abide by the law protecting Massachusetts residents. 
Importantly, the House language permits consumer lawsuits against only the biggest data holders, companies that collect personal information on millions of Massachusetts residents. That provision ensures that we can hold the worst abusers responsible for violations, while shielding small- and medium-sized businesses from lawsuits if they make mistakes while handling consumer data.  
There are a lot of important nuances for lawmakers to consider as they draft the final bill.  
But the bottom line is that lawmakers have the power to stop Big Tech abuses — and they must seize the moment. 
As things now stand, each of us is treated more like a product than a consumer. Meta, Google, and scores of data brokers you’ve never heard of stalk us across the digital and physical worlds, scraping tens of thousands of data points about every intimate facet of our lives. They then sell that data to advertisers, political campaigns, government agencies, scammers, stalkers — anyone with a credit card. 
The harms from this surveillance economy are staggering: political manipulation, domestic abuse and stalking, the targeting of protesters and legal immigrants, the harassment of political foes, health care providers, and patients. When companies can gobble up data showing every place we go, 24/7, and sell it on the open market, it enables extremists to interfere with our basic rights and makes us all unsafe.  
The Massachusetts consumer data privacy bill aims to put an end to Big Tech’s arrogance and abuse by returning power to the individual. It insists that companies respect our fundamental privacy rights, which are essential for our autonomy and even our democracy.  
Voters have flooded the State House all year with calls, letters, and emails demanding a privacy law with real teeth. The only way to achieve that is to empower ordinary people to hold companies like Meta accountable if and when they violate our rights. 
 We can end Big Tech’s abuses — but only if we have the courage to stand up to the tech oligarchs and maintain the strong standards of our consumer protection law when it comes to enforcing our data privacy law. 
Kade Crockford is the director of technology and justice programs at the ACLU of Massachusetts.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Negative, false and misleading political ads pollute and undermine the election process
description: What is your reaction when viewing TV, listening to the radio or surfing digital platforms and there is a political ad filled with false and misleading information that you can neither verify nor confirm? Billions of dollars are spent in a national election cycle. Millions of those dollars are spent by candidates and ballot-measure campaigns […]
text:
(mcdustleroy/iStock Images)What is your reaction when viewing TV, listening to the radio or surfing digital platforms and there is a political ad filled with false and misleading information that you can neither verify nor confirm?
Billions of dollars are spent in a national election cycle. Millions of those dollars are spent by candidates and ballot-measure campaigns to saturate traditional and social media with a barrage of negative, false and misleading ads.
How much better and more beneficial it would be if those dollars were spent on messages that help educate voters about the issues, what is at stake and specific actions needed for a remedy — instead of the perennial platitudes and often what turns out to be empty promises.
In Missouri during this midterm election cycle, two hotly contested amendments are on the ballot, and campaigns have raised nearly $40 million for ads to persuade voters. Millions are also being spent in candidate campaigns for state legislative and congressional seats.
As you are bombarded with these ads, are you able to distinguish fact from fiction; truth from distortions, deceptions or lies; vacuous promises from attainable goals?
A mixed bag of campaign ads is airing in city, county and state elections across the country.
What a gross disservice to a public seeking accurate information to make an informed decision about who can best represent them or how best to vote on a proposed ballot measure.
It is little wonder that the average citizen thinks our election process has become a misleading contrivance, a necessary performative evil. Sadly, many, not knowing where the truth lies, choose to dismiss, ignore or do nothing.
This perception and resignation are doing more harm than good.
The body politic affects our lives in all its aspects — from where our children go to school, to what money is left from our paycheck to improve our standard of living, to the quality and bacteria-free food we put on our tables for our loved ones to eat.
If one just stops to think, it becomes abundantly clear that approved ballot measures and decisions made by politicians every day, at every level of government, are eventually felt in our daily lives. There are few, if any, exceptions.
Too often, we as citizens do not want to have anything to do with it. What is allowed in terms of false, distorted and negative advertising during campaigns is a travesty, an insult to democracy and the fullness of its meaning and our intelligence.
More and more in the current political environment, it seems that anything goes.
Unfortunately, with the behavior of our elected officials — and now candidates on the campaign trail in this midterm election year — whenever we hear the word politics, any one of a number of things comes to mind: the grandiose promises candidates make to get elected or reelected to office, only to forget or ignore those same promises once in office; or the leveraged influence that gets concessions and benefits from governmental entities at the average citizen’s expense.
Look at the political action committees (PACs) and their ability to put millions of dollars into a campaign to influence the outcome, often using negative and false political ads — all to promote or preserve a special interest or agenda.
These practices are further confounded by the constant parade of elected officials lured by the temptation to line their own pockets and those of their friends and family, or who insist on indulging in unethical and unsavory behavior.
Whatever impressions the average citizen holds, many are negative because of the behavior of elected officials at all levels of government, exemplified first by the campaigns that got them there.
The bad or evil deeds of the few, too often, overshadow the silence and tolerance of the majority.
When the great Greek philosopher Plato wrote the seminal book “The Republic” on government and the role of citizens in governing, politics was not only an honorable and patriotic process, but it also represented the heart and soul of a healthy society.
Politics meant those active deliberations, sometimes vigorous and lively discussions, among citizens who diligently searched to determine and promote the greatest good for the greatest number with each policy decision made.
The United States is a republic. What say we?
Two things are fundamentally different in our country today and are mirrored at all levels of government.
First, as the population increases, citizens’ interest and participation in the welfare of their government decrease. Fewer people bother to vote. Many of us cannot tell who our city, state or national elected officials are.
Second, consistently low voter turnout represents the feeling of powerlessness and unconcern on the part of many of us. Somehow, too many citizens feel that their involvement or vote will not make much of a difference anyway.
This deep-seated feeling of impotence, if not helplessness, is the most insidious and potentially harmful trend of all — particularly for those who are already at a disadvantage economically, socially and educationally.
The consequences of nonparticipation in politics and the political process are grave and lasting.
Many elected officials do not feel obliged to represent, protect or fight for the interests of those who bother to cast a vote, let alone those who do not.
The critical question in the upcoming elections is: Can we afford to continue to be spectators rather than participants, irrespective of how disgusting some aspects of the process have become?
Our political process is increasingly sliding to a place where negativity and incivility reign.
We can’t cut it out.
Our apathy or disenchantment with it will not make it go away.
Then isn’t our only viable alternative to get involved and influence it?
Not succumb to the negativity, but rise above and defeat it.

name: WyoFile
title: On Wind River Reservation, artist Sarah Ortegon finds healing via visual expression
description:
Through beadwork, painting and jingle dress dance, the Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho artist transforms personal healing and cultural reconnection into work that offers hope.
The post On Wind River Reservation, artist Sarah Ortegon finds healing via visual expression appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
FORT WASHAKIE—Sarah Ortegon’s home studio sits high on the Wind River Reservation, where sweeping views of the mountains meet the constant Wyoming wind. What looks at first glance like a dedicated creative space is simply her living room. Canvases, beadwork supplies and the subdued glow of natural light fill the space where she raises her 4-year-old son, two rescue cats and a French Bulldog with her husband. 
“I don’t have a studio,” Ortegon says with a soft laugh. “I just make art in my home.”
Growing up, Ortegon always turned to art — particularly beadwork — as a form of quiet expression. 
A ‘quiet’ expression
Born in Denver to an Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho mother and white father, she spent summers on the reservation with family, where she learned beadwork from her mother in what she describes as small, stolen moments. In a bustling family where she was the 10th of 12 children, art offered a way to express herself without “taking up too much space.”

Sarah Ortegon taps into beadwork skills she learned from her mother to make regalia for her 4-year-old son. (Rebecca Huntington/WyoFile)

“My dad was a preacher, and so I had to, a lot of the time, be quiet because he was studying,” she recalls. “It was hard to be an actual kid, and so one of the ways in which I expressed myself was quietly, which is basically what art is.”
Making art is also freeing. “You can use as many colors as you want,” she says. “You are not limited in what you create.”
For Ortegon, that early sense of restraint shaped the beginning of a lifelong creative path. While in college at Metropolitan State University in Denver, she began exploring the “tension” between the identities she carried. Art became a bridge — a place where she could reconcile social expectations in a predominantly white community in Denver with the freedom she experienced when embracing her Native heritage.
Coming home to create
In 2025, after three decades of splitting her time and life between Colorado and Wyoming, Ortegon made the decision to move permanently to the one place that always felt like home — the Wind River Reservation. 
Finding suitable housing, however, has been a significant challenge, Ortegon says. Her family spent several years on a waiting list for housing and still rents a home today. 
But, despite the hurdles, Ortegon says that returning felt right.
“My mom said it fairly well the other day,” she says. “She said: ‘You know, no matter where you go as an Indigenous person, there’s always a certain connection that you feel going back to a certain area.’” For Ortegon, that certain area is the Wind River Reservation, landscapes heavily featured throughout her art.  
“The pace of life out here is less stressful,” she says. The slower rhythm, combined with the landscape she adores, has given Ortegon more space and time to create. The Wind River Range appears in her artwork, not just as backdrop but as a living connection to place and memory.
“This place always felt like home to me growing up, because my aunt and uncle, George and Shirley Enos, gave me the freedom to play outside — to go swim in the Bull Lake and to go play in the ditch, and to play on bikes and run away from rez dogs … I wouldn’t trade [those] summers for anything,” she says.
Ortegon observed that her mother was happiest on the reservation.That, combined with the presence of her uncle and aunt, made her feel deeply connected to the place. 
With more “room to breathe,” she has returned to meditation, movement and the canvas with clearer intentions. “Now I have the ability to create things that I feel like make the world a better place,” she says.
Healing through art and motherhood
When Ortegon and her husband welcomed their newborn son, becoming a mother shifted her perspective as an artist even further. Watching her growing son explore the world with unrestrained energy has become part of her healing from intergenerational trauma.
“I don’t want him to feel the way I felt,” she explains. Where she once had to suppress emotions, she now makes space for her son’s feelings — toddler tantrums and all — offering hugs when he’s ready. “I want to provide [to him] what I would have wanted as a child.”
This intentional parenting is part of breaking cycles, Ortegon says. Her mother, who learned beadwork in boarding school at St. Mary’s Episcopal School for Indian Girls in Springfield, South Dakota, shared that skill with Ortegon and her other daughters in brief moments of respite from her everyday responsibilities as a wife to a man whom she had met when she was only 17. 
Because Ortegon and her five sisters often crowded into their basement in Denver while her brothers stayed elsewhere, beadwork became a medium not just to pass time, but also a road to learning who she was.
“[The basement] was underground — not a whole lot of light — not a whole lot of things to do,” Ortegon says. “I think that that’s one way that my mom felt like she was helping us pass the time by giving us this gift of beadwork.
“It felt like it kept us afloat. My dad was a preacher, but as a teenager — at least for me — my whole life wasn’t revolving around reading the Bible. It was around wanting to learn who I was, and so [beadwork] helped me learn who I was.”
Today, Ortegon sees her own motherhood as continuing that thread of resilience that her mother bequeathed to her. Art, too, plays a similar role. 
“I want the world to be a more beautiful place because I know how hard it can be, and I see how devastating different aspects of different people’s lives can be, and how lonely it can be,” she explains. Her work often blends painting and beadwork, carrying forward traditions while creating new expressions of resilience and joy. 
“Maybe if I create an image, someone could look at it, and they could receive just a little bit of joy. And I think that sometimes just one word, one image, one thought can change somebody’s life.”
A platform for Native American culture
Recent artistic opportunities have affirmed the power of personal voice and cultural connection for Ortegon. In 2024, she was part of multidisciplinary Indigenous artist Jeffrey Gibson’s project for the Venice Biennale, a global art and culture festival often described as the “Olympics of the art world.” 
Dancing, like Ortegon’s visual art, offers her healing and connection, but through the medium of movement. At the Venice Biennale, she was to perform a jingle dress dance — a Native American and First Nations women’s ritual — which was conceived around 1920, at a time when traditional Indigenous dances and ceremonies were still banned in the United States via federal policies like the Religious Crimes Code of 1833.
As one of 26 dancers featured at the Venice Biennale — where Gibson was the first Native American to represent the United States — Ortegon faced a unique challenge. Due to travel complications, her regalia — the sacred traditional clothing and accessories — got lost with her luggage. Because of the weight of the dress embellished with rows of metal cones, or jingles, transporting it in her carry-on bag had not been a possibility. 
Unlike outfits associated with many other non-sacred dance forms, tribal regalia are culturally and religiously significant items, which is why Ortegon recalls feeling “naked” without hers. 
“It showed me the power that our stories hold,” she says. “I could have gone up there and danced in my regular skirt or dress, but it wouldn’t have been as impactful as having the story behind the jingle dress.”
To Ortegon’s relief, the dress eventually arrived the midnight before her performance. 
Following the dance, Ortegon remembers feeling an all-encompassing sense of gratitude. 
“I was appreciative of the chance to represent my tribe and our nations, but I was also appreciative that Jeffrey Gibson — as also a Native artist — felt called to include other Natives with him … That is one example of how someone with that stature can help others. He did that on an international level, and it was just awesome to be a part of.” 
Painting solutions and hope
As a Native American artist, Ortegon often paints solutions before they arrive. For a mural on the side of a Patagonia store in Denver, she crossed out the words “Mount Evans,” the official name for the highest peak in the Mount Evans Wilderness in Colorado. The summit had been christened after John Evans, the second territorial governor of Colorado, who was behind the 1864 Sand Creek Massacre — where the U.S. Army carried out a surprise attack on a peaceful village of Cheyenne and Arapaho people — killing over 230 women, men, children and elders. 

Sarah Ortegon stands in front of a mural of Mount Blue Sky that she painted on the outside of the Patagonia store in Denver. (Courtesy photo)

On her mural, Ortegon replaced the peak’s then-official name with “Mount Blue Sky,” a title chosen and recommended by the Colorado Geographic Naming Advisory Board to the U.S. Board on Geographic Names, based on the recommendations of tribal leaders and communities. The new suggested name was rooted in cultural significance for both tribes affected by the 1864 tragedy; while the Arapaho are also known as the “Blue Sky People,” the Cheyenne hold annual life-renewal ceremonies using the same term. 
Two years after Ortegon painted her mural supporting the initiative, the name “Mount Blue Sky” was officially adopted. 
“I wasn’t [officially] part of the name change. It’s just what I wanted to see happen, and it happened,” Ortegon says. The day the Colorado peak was officially renamed in September 2023, Ortegon says it snowed on the mountain, which she saw as a sign of purification.
The Wind River Reservation, like many Indigenous communities across the country, faces significant challenges. Missing and Murdered Indigenous Relatives (MMIR) remain a persistent crisis, with Indigenous people in Wyoming experiencing homicide rates several times higher than the state average for White people, alongside facing ongoing gaps in law enforcement and justice system responses. Families continue to seek answers and accountability in cases that have stretched for years.
“There’s no way for me to make things happen,” Ortegon reflects. “But if I paint it, maybe it’ll come true someday.”
Looking forward
As someone who discovered her passion for art as a child, Ortegon encourages young Native artists to follow their intuition. “In order to express yourself, you don’t need a degree. Don’t let anyone put you down for what you’re doing. Life will reveal itself to you as an artist,” she says.
“Your main focus as an artist is expressing yourself and sharing what you feel you need, whether it be trauma that you need to get out of yourself, or whether it be wanting to make the world a better place.”
As an artist, Ortegon also lives by the same hope she encourages in other Native American creatives: “Maybe in just some small little drop in a bucket, I am hopefully making the world a little bit better than when I came into it.”

name: WyoFile
title: Ann and Al Simpson were each other’s ‘greatest champions’
description:
Their 70 years of marriage were defined by appreciating what each brought to the table, writes columnist Kerry Drake.
The post Ann and Al Simpson were each other’s ‘greatest champions’ appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Several photographs accompanied articles about the death of Ann Simpson last week that aptly illustrated the love between her and her husband of 70 years, the late U.S. Sen. Al Simpson. 

Opinion

That includes one of them smooching in their later years, with the senator looking like he still couldn’t believe how lucky he was.
I realize that’s probably the sentimental favorite of everyone who knew the couple. But there’s an image of Ann highlighted by WyoFile that’s even more emblematic of her courage and the devotion and love she had for him. Ann was at the senator’s funeral last year, looking elegant as always and beaming with pride that so many people in their lives honored him as he was laid to rest.
I hope Ann realized that she was being honored too, because having each other gave them their best chance at happiness in all their endeavors, including her love of the arts and advocacy for mental health. They were a team that rooted for each other, even in politically taxing times.
I didn’t know Ann well, even after covering Al’s political career for many years. But I do know how much he loved her, because it was evident every time he spoke her name or talked about what she was doing.
In 2011, Al’s press secretary and then chief of staff, Donald Hardy, wrote the appropriately titled “Shooting From the Lip” about his former boss, who could be cranky about the political scene in Washington as being too polarizing and at odds with his life in Wyoming.
Hardy’s book is a great read about a politician who frequently got into trouble for expressing views that were often unflinchingly honest but unpopular. To me, it’s a much better look at the man than the book Simpson wrote about his often combative relationship with the media, “Right in the Old Gazoo.”
But I hadn’t re-read Hardy’s book, even after Al died at age 93 last year. When I wrote a column about my relationship with the politician I admired but also shared some combative times with, I relied on the recollections and articles I’d written. My conclusion was Simpson is a “prime example of precisely what American politics are missing today.”
When I read about Ann’s death at age 94, though, I knew I had to look at Hardy’s book in a new light, because I had forgotten some great anecdotes the author recounted about her influence on Al. I offer a sample with the hope that anyone curious about the life and times of the Simpsons will check it out.
Ann Schroll entered the picture when she and Al were in high school; he in Cody and his future wife in Greybull. She was a tall cheerleader who, like her twin sister Nan, was on the lookout for tall boys.
“Back in high school, we had been on the lookout for the Simpson boys [Al and his brother Pete] at the next basketball tournament,” she told Hardy. “We spotted them, and they spotted us. Unfortunately, they didn’t know how to dance. 
“Right away we ruled them completely off our list,” Ann added.
Al copped to his failure, and listed a few more of them. “We were the ‘zit kings’ of the world,” he recalled. “I was knock-kneed and heavy. I had good hair, though — like Tony Curtis! Ann didn’t mind that, but was unimpressed once she found out I couldn’t dance.”
So Ann knew exactly what she wanted, but she didn’t realize until they started dating at the University of Wyoming that Al would endear himself in ways that earned him a second chance. 
I forgot about this entry, but once I saw “port-a-potty incident” in the index, I had to check it out. It involved the 1986 wedding of their eldest son Bill, in the far reaches of the Cody countryside, hence the need for rented portable toilets.
In the book, Al notes with laughter that Ann discovered the toilets lacked chemical deodorants, prompting behavior that didn’t match her refined image. 
“Ann, in a magnificent pink silk dress, was galloping around the outdoor toilets in her slippers, with this rich, blue deodorant elixir, which, if you spilled it, would probably eat through your epidermis,” Al said. “Quite a sight it was.”
One of the things that endeared me most to what Ann represented in Al’s life was the heavy criticism he received in 1991 for badgering law professor Anita Hill when she told a Senate panel and national TV audience that Supreme Court nominee Clarence Thomas had allegedly sexually harassed her.
Al was unrelenting in his hostile questioning of Hill. During the hearings, Al referred to Ann as “the most important person and the brightest guiding light” of his life.
But while it might have been easier to “stand by her man,” Ann couldn’t sit back and watch the damage without telling him what she thought.
“He was so defensive during the hearings that I finally said to him, ‘You’ve had such a great reputation here, and now you are destroying it by the way you are behaving. Why don’t you just shut up?’”
Al, Hardy wrote, was stunned: “That’s the first time you’ve ever told me to shut up.”
Ann responded, “Well, you need it.”
Al came to the same realization, but probably only because of Ann’s stinging rebuke. “I have been riding high, a bit too cocky, arrogant, yeah, too smart by half sometimes,” he later admitted at a GOP fundraiser in Cheyenne.
Except for that incident, though, I couldn’t find a single reference where Ann did not stick up for her husband, no matter how much he was getting beaten up by the press. But she knew where to draw the line.
In Ann’s obituary, she was deservedly praised for her work to promote the arts in Wyoming. She founded the Artmobile more than 30 years ago, bringing some of the art objects in the University of Wyoming’s collections to people statewide. It was named in her honor, and the Ann Simpson Artmobile was an enormous gift to Wyomingites; it won’t stop traveling with her passing.
A mental health advocate, Ann was said to be passionately involved in the Congressional Wives Mental Health Group. She was co-chair of the group and focused on legislative support for mental health issues.
The Simpsons were both highly quotable, and each one said poignant things about the longevity of their marriage and gave advice to couples, especially when they were playing matchmakers. But their daughter, Sue Simpson Gallagher, has a special insight into her parents that she expressed on June 21, 2024, on their 70th wedding anniversary.
“My parents recognize each other’s gifts,” she said. “They are appreciative of what they each bring to the table. They don’t try and be everything to each other either. They know how important it is to have friends but to have each other as their greatest champions.”
The post Ann and Al Simpson were each other’s ‘greatest champions’ appeared first on WyoFile .

title: Idaho governor’s race: Pickens, Stegner say they are in it to win it
description: Democrat Terri Pickens and independent John Stegner said they each will run active, statewide campaigns in their efforts to unseat incumbent Republican Gov. Brad Little, who is seeking a third term.  Little, Pickens, Stegner, a Constitution Party candidate who legally changed his name from Marvin Richardson to Pro-Life and Libertarian Paul Sand are all runni[...]
text:
Voters cast their ballots for the May 19, 2026, primary election at Fox Hollow Elementary School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Democrat Terri Pickens and independent John Stegner said they each will run active, statewide campaigns in their efforts to unseat incumbent Republican Gov. Brad Little, who is seeking a third term. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Little, Pickens, Stegner, a Constitution Party candidate who legally changed his name from Marvin Richardson to Pro-Life and Libertarian Paul Sand are all running for governor in Idaho’s Nov. 3 general election. 
“I got into this race because I think Idaho is worth fighting for, and I didn’t see anybody else willing to take up the mantle in the way that I thought it needed to be taken up,” Stegner said in a July 10 interview. 
Pickens, an attorney who owns her own business, is also optimistic about winning. Pickens described Little as an unpopular incumbent governor who has tied himself fully to President Donald Trump just as what Pickens described as a “Trump slump” is playing out across the country.
“We have built momentum, both face-to-face and also with our social media,” Pickens said July 15. “I can’t go anywhere in the state of Idaho without people recognizing me, and that is really huge for a candidate going in. We also have a wildly unpopular governor (in Little).”
Efforts to reach Little and Sand were unsuccessful. 
“It’s a hard job. It’s a thankless job in many respects,” Stegner said, of running for governor. “But I’ve also had any number of people come up to me and tell me that I’ve given them hope. And if that’s all I get to do, I would consider this candidacy a success. But I aspire to more. I aspire to be governor, and I think there’s a path to victory in the way that the team that we’ve built and the campaign that we’ve constructed is working.”
Former Idaho Supreme Court Justice John Stegner is running for governor as an independent candidate. (Photo courtesy of John Stegner)
While Stegner served as a judge for 25 years in Idaho, including as a member of the Idaho Supreme Court, this would be the first statewide elected political office. 
“Running for governor as the first political office out of the blocks is a little aspirational,” Stegener said. “I shouldn’t say a little; it’s quite aspirational to start at the top. But I think having been on the Supreme Court and having seen how government works, I have a solid understanding of how things work. And I think being governor at this juncture is an important office and an important place for somebody with my background because I sincerely believe that neither the Democrats nor the Republicans have a lock on good ideas. And as a governor, I would aspire to implement good ideas irrespective of their source.”
To do that, Stegner said he will launch a series of campaign events this summer and fall. 
“Our goal is to reach every one of the 44 counties,” Stegner said.
 Pickens says contested primary election and her unsuccessful 2022 campaign made her a stronger candidate

Pickens knows that any Democrat running for statewide office faces an uphill challenge. No Democrat has been elected governor in Idaho since 1990, when the late former Gov. Cecil Andrus won his fourth and final term. 
In 2022, Pickens ran unsuccessfully for lieutenant governor – losing to incumbent Republican Lt. Gov. Scott Bedke. 
Pickens said her experience as a candidate has helped her grow. She said her unsuccessful 2022 campaign for lieutenant governor helped her gain name recognition. And she said this spring’s contested Democratic primary for governor, which Pickens won, helped her improve as a candidate. 
Pickens said she has already campaigned across Idaho three times, held events in 30 counties and has plans to have visited all 44 counties before Election Day. 
Terri Pickens is a Democrat running for Idaho governor. (Photo courtesy of Terri Pickens)
“I will tell you that having to have an active, healthy primary was not just good for the party, but it was good for me,” Pickens said in a July 15 interview. “It taught me to be a better candidate. I got the opportunity to have three forum town hall debates with the candidates, and it allowed me to kind of fine-tune my message and get ready for what I perceive is going to be an uphill battle in the general election.”
Pickens said she doesn’t think Stegner’s independent campaign hurts her chances as the Democrat.
“I’m actually looking at this as a good thing for my campaign,” Pickens said in a July 15 interview.
Pickens said she thinks Stegner will pull Republican voters away from Little, drawing down Little’s support and making it easier for Pickens to win as a Democrat in the minority party. 
“We are jumping after different demographics,” Pickens said. “I’m going for the 18- to 30-year olds. I’m going for all of the women who are going to show up to vote for their bodily autonomy, and I’m going for every Democrat in the room.”
“I think (Stegner) is really going to pull those Republicans who would never vote for a Democrat anyway,” Pickens said. “But they’re so disappointed in Brad Little that they want 2018 Brad Little, and I think that’s what John Stegner offers them.”
 At least one Idaho candidate for governor does not plan an active political campaign

In contrast to Stegner and Pickens, the Constitution Party candidate who changed his name to Pro-Life does not plan to run an active campaign and does not think anyone will beat Little. 
“We already know who’s going to win,” Pro-Life said July 16. “We know that Brad Little’s going to be our governor and everybody else is maybe dreaming or faking that they might be able to somehow pull off a win, but it’s not going to happen.”
Pro-Life said he would agree to a debate or a town hall event with gubernatorial candidates, but he does not anticipate mounting an active campaign of his own. 
“Probably not,” said Pro-Life, who has not reported raising any campaign money this year. “I’m old and I have to work on my farm and I can’t hire labor, so I don’t think I am going to do anything.”
Instead Pro-Life said he is running to bring public accountability to political candidates and to encourage Christian morality. 
 



 Campaign finance: Who has raised the most campaign money in 2026?

Republican Gov. Brad Little: $2,130,522
Independent John Stegner: $410,332
Democrat Terri Pickens: $161,787
Libertarian Paul Sand: $310
Pro-Life: $0

text:
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador participates in a May 2026 National Police Week roundtable at the Eisenhower Executive Office Building in Washington, D.C., alongside Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel and other officials. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Attorney General's Office)Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador has released a list of 39 hazardous products subject to a federal recall from the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission for the month of July.
The recalled products include household appliances, electronics, and furniture, and 10 items specifically designed for infants and toddlers.
“Idahoans need to know when everyday products put their families at risk,” Labrador said in a July 30 press release. “This month’s 39 recalls include ten products made for infants and toddlers, from baby loungers to dressers to pool drain covers. Check this list, check your home, and take action.”
The Consumer Product Safety Commission reports the following products were recalled in July:

Heated Sherpa Throws and Blankets Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Fire and Burn Hazards: The electrical cord on the recalled throws and blankets can detach and ignite, posing a risk of serious injury or death from fire, burn and shock hazards.
Galanz Americas Recalls Retro Refrigerators Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Fire and Burn Hazards; One Death Reported: The recalled refrigerators’ internal electrical components can short circuit and ignite, posing a risk of serious injury or death from fire and burn hazards.
Jake’s Fireworks Recalls World Class Fireworks “Skull Strobe” Rockets Due to Risk of Serious Injury from Explosion and Burn Hazards: The recalled fireworks rockets can explode prematurely before reaching their intended height, posing explosion and burn hazards.
Trsmima Zipline Kits and Zipline Spring Brakes Recalled Due to Fall and Collision Hazards: The zipline kit’s steel cable, turnbuckle and seat can detach or break during use, posing a fall hazard. The zipline spring brakes are not stiff enough to safely slow a rider down and the kit design does not include an emergency brake, posing collision and fall hazards.
HARPPA Recalls Nordi Toddler Tower Stools Due to Risk of Serious Injury and Death from Entrapment and Fall Hazards: The recalled tower stools can collapse or tip over while in use, and a child’s torso can fit through the openings on the front and back sides, posing a risk of serious injury and death due to tip over, fall and entrapment hazards.
Mangohood Direct Kids Kitchen Standing Towers Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury and Death from Entrapment and Fall Hazards: The recalled tower stools can collapse or tip over while in use, and a child’s torso can fit through the openings on the front and back sides, posing a risk of serious injury and death due to tip over, fall and entrapment hazards.
Recall of Cpzzkq Baby Loungers Expanded Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Suffocation Hazard: The recalled baby loungers violate the mandatory safety standard for infant support cushions because the padding can obstruct an infant’s breathing, posing a serious risk of injury or deadly suffocation hazard.
Golden Link Recalls Fantastic Four Cups and Captain America Popcorn Helmet Containers with LED Lights Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Battery Ingestion Hazard: The cups and containers violate the mandatory standard for consumer products with button cell and coin batteries because they contain button cell batteries that can be accessed easily by children.
BenQ America Recalls GV31 Portable Projectors Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Fire and Burn Hazards: The recalled projectors’ lithium-ion battery can overheat, posing a risk of serious injury or death from fire and burn hazards.
15-Drawer Dressers Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Tip-Over and Entrapment Hazards: The recalled dressers are unstable if they are not anchored to the wall, posing tip-over and entrapment hazards that can result in risks of serious injuries or death to children. The dressers violate the mandatory safety standards as required by the STURDY Act.
OCOOPA Direct Recalls 1.5 Million Rechargeable Hand Warmers Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Fire and Burn Hazards; One Death Reported: The lithium-ion battery in the recalled hand warmers can overheat and ignite, posing a risk of serious injury or death from fire and burn hazards.
Woodure Toddler Kitchen Step Stools Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury and Death from Entrapment and Fall Hazards: The recalled tower stools can collapse or tip over while in use, and a child’s torso can fit through the openings on the front and back sides, posing a risk of serious injury and death due to tip over, fall and entrapment hazards.
Mommy’s Baby Lovely Deluxe Baby Doll Playsets Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Choking Hazard; Violate Small Parts Ban: The recalled doll playsets violate the small parts ban because the toys are for children under three years old and some of the accessories are small parts, posing a deadly choking hazard.
5-Drawer Dressers Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Tip-Over and Entrapment Hazards: The recalled dressers are unstable if they are not anchored to the wall, posing tip-over and entrapment hazards that can result in risks of serious injuries or death to children. The dressers violate the mandatory safety standards as required by the STURDY Act.
Peony Design Recalls Personalized Baby Bibs and Stroller Bags Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Choking Hazard: The snap can detach from the recalled bibs and stroller bags, posing a risk of serious injury or death from a choking hazard to young children.
12-Drawer Fabric Dressers Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Tip-Over and Entrapment Hazards: The recalled dressers are unstable if they are not anchored to the wall, posing tip-over and entrapment hazards that can result in risks of serious injuries or death to children. The dressers violate the mandatory safety standards as required by the STURDY Act.
CuddleCubs Creations Teething Toy Sets Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Choking: The recalled teething toy sets contain a pull string teething toy that violates the mandatory standard for toys because the silicone strings are smaller and longer than permitted. The strings can reach the back of a child’s throat and become lodged, posing a risk of respiratory distress and a deadly choking hazard.
Sviyatp Pool Drain Covers Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Entrapment and Drowning Hazards: The recalled drain covers violate the entrapment protection standards of the Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act (VGBA), posing deadly entrapment and drowning hazards to consumers.
OeyUoc Pool Drain Covers Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Entrapment and Drowning Hazards: The recalled drain covers violate the entrapment protection standards of the Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act (VGBA), posing deadly entrapment and drowning hazards to consumers.
Noerishia Adult Portable Bed Rails Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Entrapment and Asphyxiation: The recalled bed rails violate the mandatory standard for adult portable bed rails because users can become entrapped within the bed rail or between the bed rail and the side of the mattress, posing a serious entrapment hazard and risk of death by asphyxiation. In addition, the bed rails do not bear the required hazard warning labels.
Conair Recalls Cuisinart Propel+ Four Burner 3-In-1 Gas Grills Due to Risk of Serious Injury from Laceration Hazard: The tempered glass window in the pizza oven can shatter during use, posing a risk of serious injury from laceration hazard.
Greenworks Tools Recalls 24V and 48V Kobalt Yard Power Tools with USB-C Batteries Due to Risk of Serious Injury from Fire Hazard: Charging the lithium-ion batteries through the USB-C port while the batteries are inserted in the yard power tools can cause the batteries to short-circuit, posing a risk of serious injury from fire hazard.
WonderStone Infant Walkers Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Fall Hazard; Violate Mandatory Standard for Infant Walkers: The recalled infant walkers violate the mandatory standard for infant walkers because they can fit through a standard doorway and fail to stop at the edge of a step, posing a risk of serious injury or death due to a fall hazard.
Best Buy Recalls Insignia® Gas Ranges Due to Risk of Serious Injury from a Fire Hazard: The recalled ranges’ front-mounted knobs can be activated accidentally by humans or pets, posing a risk of serious injury from a fire hazard.
Moodooy Bed Rails Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Entrapment and Asphyxiation: The recalled bed rails violate the mandatory standard for adult portable bed rails because users can become entrapped within the bed rail or between the bed rail and the side of the mattress, posing a serious entrapment hazard and risk of death by asphyxiation. In addition, the bed rails do not bear the required hazard warning labels.
Flaunt Recalls Magsafe Battery Chargers Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Fire and Burn Hazards: The lithium-ion battery in the recalled power banks (chargers) can overheat and ignite, posing a risk of serious injury or death from fire and burn hazards.
Biometric Gun Safes Recalled Due to Serious Injury Hazard and Risk of Death: The biometric lock on the gun safes can be opened by unauthorized users, posing a serious injury hazard and risk of death.
Rowenta Recalls Cordless Vacuum Cleaners Due to Risk of Serious Injury from Fire and Burn Hazards: The recalled lithium-ion battery in the vacuum cleaner can overheat and ignite, posing a risk of serious injury from fire and burn hazards.
Vevor Recalls Baby Loungers Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Entrapment and Fall Hazards: The recalled baby loungers violate the mandatory safety standard for infant sleep products. The sides are too low to contain an infant and the enclosed openings at the foot of the loungers are wider than allowed, posing serious risks of fall and entrapment hazards to infants. In addition, the baby loungers do not have a stand, posing a fall hazard if used on elevated surfaces. These violations create an unsafe sleeping environment and can cause death or serious injury.
Conair Recalls Over One Million Cuisinart Grill Brushes Due to Ingestion Hazard: Small metal wire bristles can detach from the brushes and stick to the grill or food, posing an ingestion hazard and risk of serious internal injuries that could require surgery.
Winco Fireworks International Recalls Unity 7 Shot 200 Gram Aerial Cake Fireworks Due to Risk of Serious Injury from Explosion and Burn Hazards: The recalled fireworks can tip over, posing a risk of serious injury from explosion and burn hazards.
Junpower CR2032 Lithium Coin Batteries Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Battery Ingestion Hazard: The lithium coin batteries are not sold in child-resistant packaging and do not bear the warning labels as required under Reese’s Law. When button cell or coin batteries are swallowed, the ingested batteries can cause serious injuries, including internal chemical burns and death.
AMASKY Nursing Pillows Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Suffocation: The recalled nursing pillows advertised for infant feeding and tummy time violate the mandatory safety standards for nursing pillows and infant support cushions because they can obstruct an infant’s breathing, posing a serious risk of injury or death from suffocation.
Winco Fireworks International Recalls Roman Candles 8 Shot Fireworks Due to Risk of Serious Injury from Explosion and Burn Hazards: The recalled fireworks can malfunction, and shots can blow out the side of the tube, posing a risk of serious injury from explosion and burn hazards.
Projecting LED Finger Light Toys Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Battery Ingestion: The recalled LED finger lights violate the mandatory safety standard for toys because they contain button cell batteries that can be easily accessed by children. If button cell or coin batteries are swallowed, the ingested batteries can cause serious injuries, including internal chemical burns, and death.
Cooper Lighting Recalls Metalux Optimized High Bay LED Light Fixtures Due to Fire Hazard: The LED’s board can overheat or come into contact with the lens or nearby combustible materials, posing a fire hazard.
Topyond Pool Drain Ports with Covers Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Entrapment and Drowning Hazards: The recalled drain ports with covers violate the entrapment protection standards of the Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act (VGBA), posing deadly entrapment and drowning hazards to consumers.
Target Recalls Gigglescape Under the Sea Popping Toy Due to Choking Hazard: The clear plastic dome can detach from the blue plastic base, making the small plastic balls inside the toy accessible to children, posing a choking hazard.
Diamond Wipes International Recalls CVS Health Medicated Hemorrhoidal Wipes Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Child Poisoning: The recalled medicated wipes contain lidocaine, which must be in child-resistant packaging, as required by the Poison Prevention Packaging Act. The packaging of the wipes is not child-resistant, posing a risk of serious injury or death from poisoning if the contents of the wipes are ingested by young children.

“If you believe you recently purchased a recalled product, stop using it, and check its recall notice,” the AG’s press release said. “Follow the notice’s instructions, including where to return the product, how to get the product fixed, how to dispose of the product, how to receive a refund for the product, or what steps must be taken to receive a replacement product.”
To file a complaint about a defective product, go to the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission website.

text:
The Aug. 6, 2026 Republican primary for Tennessee governor includes U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, left; U.S. Rep. John Rose, top right; and state Rep. Monty Fritts, bottom right. (Photos: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Cookeville U.S. Rep. John Rose loaned his gubernatorial campaign an additional $4 million in the final days of the Republican primary, bringing his total in self-funding to $13 million. 
For U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn the Tennessee Freedom Fund and Team Tennessee political action committees, PACs, backing her bid have consolidated under one entity after raising a total of $12 million this cycle so far. This includes a recent donation of $250,000 from San Francisco-based artificial intelligence company Anthropic.
Anthropic’s primary product is the AI agent Claude, and with its contribution, it’s one of the top spenders backing Blackburn. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Candidates filed their final campaign finance reports to the Tennessee Registry of Election Finance on Friday, detailing their contributions and spending one week before the August 6 primary. 
Blackburn, Rose and Kingston state Rep. Monty Fritts are running for the Republican nomination to replace term-limited Gov. Bill Lee. The winner of the Republican primary is widely considered to be the favorite to become the state’s next governor, as Tennessee voters haven’t elected a Democratic candidate to a statewide office since 2006 and has never elected an independent one.
For much of the last year, Blackburn held a significant polling advantage over Rose. But in the last few weeks, Rose’s campaign released polling showing the race tightening, which Blackburn disputed. There has only been one non-campaign-funded independent poll conducted, which shows a close race. 
Blackburn has raised $10.8 million for the election, and Rose has raised $15 million, including his self-funding. Fritts has raised close to $300,000.
Blackburn has raised money from more individuals, and Tennesseans specifically. But the largest checks supporting her have gone to the independent expenditure PACs backing her. 
The top donor to the two PACs is the pro-private school voucher group affiliated with Club For Growth called the School Freedom Fund. The group donated $4.81 million to a PAC backing Blackburn a month after her federal Senate campaign donated a nearly identical amount to the organization’s primary PAC.
Blackburn moves $4.8M from US Senate campaign account in apparent legal ‘workaround’

Other top donors to Blackburn’s PACs are Club for Growth funder Jeff Yass ($1 million), payday lender Advance Financial ($800,000), Tamara Stephens ($279,000) and logistics entrepreneur Spencer Patton ($250,000)
Rose doesn’t have a PAC, and has used his used his personal wealth, estimated at $55 million, to counter the disadvantage.
But a dark-money group called the American Exceptionalism Institute has been running advertisements attacking Blackburn. The group has not registered with the state under its legal requirement to disclose its spending, leaving its donors unknown. A Blackburn campaign surrogate filed a complaint with the state agency in charge of overseeing campaign finance.
