title: Democratic state officials urge US Supreme Court to affirm pause on Trump vote-by-mail order
text: WASHINGTON — States do not have time before November’s midterm elections to comply with President Donald Trump’s executive order mandating overhauls of their mail-in-voting systems, two dozen Democratic state officials told the U.S. Supreme Court on Monday.Justices should keep a stay pausing the order in place through Election Day, the Democrats, led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta, wrote. The court is compelled to keep voting rules in place this close to an election, but the executive order would force massive changes on state administrators, they wrote.Neither the president nor the U.S. Postal Service has authority to administer elections under the U.S. Constitution, which assigns that responsibility to state governments, the Democrats wrote. Trump’s March 31 order directs USPS to collect lists of registered voters from each state and only mail ballots to registered voters, and the Department of Homeland Security to compile lists of voting-age citizens in each state. That would insert the executive branch directly into elections administration and the administration has not defended the legality of that move, the Democrats wrote.Worse, the officials said, the order would create mass confusion at this point in the election cycle, meaning that the court should delay considering whether it is legal until after the midterms.“Because of the high risk of errors and the limited window for correcting mistakes, many of the millions of voters who rely on mail voting—especially voters with disabilities and those in rural areas—would likely be denied mail ballots and, as a result, disenfranchised,” the state officials said. “Many more voters would be confused—either because they wouldn’t receive their mail ballots or would fear that USPS would fail to deliver their voted ballots to state officials for tabulation.”Bonta signed the brief along with the attorneys general of Massachusetts, Washington, Nevada, Arizona, Connecticut, Colorado, the District of Columbia, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia and Wisconsin. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro also signed on.Their filing was the Democrats’ response to the Justice Department request that the Supreme Court overturn an appeals court decision against lifting a district court stay of the executive order. The court is considering the issue on its emergency docket that allows for speedy decisions.Spokespeople for the Justice Department did not return a message seeking comment Monday.No final rule The administration argued that the states’ challenge was premature because the Postal Service and DHS had not yet written the rules the executive order directed.While a three-judge panel of the U.S. 1st Circuit Court of Appeals sided with the Democratic states, a separate case at the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals agreed with the administration that the states could not yet challenge the policy because there was no final rule. The case under consideration at the Supreme Court is from the 1st Circuit.In an amicus brief supporting the federal government, a coalition of conservative groups led by attorney William Olson said Monday that the district court stay was possibly the first time a judge has blocked a notice of proposed rulemaking, which “is the very definition of an agency action which is not a final agency action.”Sowing voter confusionThe states said Monday the order itself, even without final rules from the affected agencies, would impose significant burdens on their election administrators. And the administration has detailed in court the steps the agencies must take to finalize the order’s mandates.Forcing the states to wait until there is an actual rule in place, especially when the steps agencies have taken “do not materially differ” from the order, would mean state election officials could face an untenable situation of needing to prepare for the new requirements.“If litigation challenging final implementation of the EO does not even begin for several more weeks, it would be extremely difficult—if not impossible—to obtain a definitive judicial resolution with enough time remaining for States to redesign and reorder their ballot mail, train elections officials, and adequately educate the public before the November midterms,” the state officials wrote.That would drain significant resources from overworked election offices at a busy campaign time, and leave voters “confused about which rules govern,” they added.Support for statesSeveral friend-of-the-court briefs weighed in on the states’ side. Scores of state and local election officials and the nonprofit voting rights group Center for Election Innovation wrote in one amicus brief that if the executive order is allowed to proceed, it would put them in the “untenable position” of updating their mail-voting procedures in the midst of primaries and just weeks before a general election.And Democratic campaign groups said the order was plainly unconstitutional and rejected the administration’s argument, saying it “makes little sense.” In part, the administration argued the district court injunction caused irreparable harm because the administration was running out of time to implement the policy before the midterms, attorney Marc Elias wrote for the Democratic National Committee, three campaign groups and the Democratic leaders of each chamber of Congress.“When the President launches an unconstitutional seizure of sensitive election powers during an election year, he may not avoid an injunction by insisting he is in a rush,” Elias wrote.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Hinds County DA gains additional prosecutor to ease caseload and jail crowding
description: A Hinds County Sheriff's Office van passes by the entrance to the Hinds County Detention Facility in Raymond, Miss., Monday, Aug. 1, 2022. On Friday, July 29, 2022, U.S. District Judge Carlton Reeves, placed the center into receivership after citing "severely deficient" conditions at the facility.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Following a request from temporary Hinds District Attorney Brad McCullouch, the Hinds County Board of Supervisors on Monday agreed to pay for a prosecutor to resolve cases that haven’t gone to trial. 
McCullouch told the board that the new prosecutor would work to quell crowding in the Hinds County Detention Center in Raymond – a proposal that delighted some of the county’s five supervisors.
The new DA was appointed by Gov. Tate Reeves in July after former Hinds County District Attorney Jody Owens pleaded guilty to federal charges of conspiracy to commit bribery and resigned.
“All I can say is, ‘outstanding idea,’” said District 2 Supervisor Tony Smith, who represents the county’s rural, westernmost district from Bolton to Utica.
One cause of overpopulation at the jail is that cases trickle through the county’s justice system, with some people sitting in jail for over a year before trial. As of Sunday, the jail, which has 594 beds, is overcapacity by more than 300 people, according to the county’s daily inmate count. 
McCullouch argued that an additional prosecutor would allow the office to indict cases faster or offer defendants an alternative resolution more quickly. 
Brad McCullouch, a Madison attorney who Gov. Tate Reeves appointed Hinds County District Attorney in July, discusses proposals he believes could reduce overcrowding at the jail. Credit: Molly Minta/Mississippi Today
The county pays for salary supplements to each of the 15 state-funded prosecutors in the district attorney’s office, which prosecutes felony cases in the state’s Seventh Circuit Court District. The money for the additional prosecutor will come from the county’s “unappropriated surplus,” said Lynn Seals, the county administrator. 
Seals said the county’s comptroller would know the total dollar amount of the county’s unallocated surplus, but the comptroller did not return an email from Mississippi Today by press time. 
The boost to the DA’s budget comes after supervisors heard pleas from the Hinds County Public Defender’s Office earlier this year to increase the salaries of the county’s 23 public defenders. 
For years, Gail Wright Lowery, the head public defender, has told the board that her office experiences persistent turnover because public defenders are not paid enough in Hinds County. Lowery has also argued that this turnover leads to jail crowding because indigent defendants lack an attorney who could seek their release. 
At the time, the board told Lowery the county didn’t have the funds for a $350,000 across-the-board pay raise she had requested. 
“If we can get these people out, then we can have extra money to give you guys a raise,” Smith said earlier this year. “So the problem is, I understand you need more money. I wish we had (it) to give it.”
Seals then found about $261,000 in leftover pandemic relief money the county had previously allocated to construction of a water tower at the new jail. 
But the stopgap funding didn’t stop the turnover in Lowery’s office. On Monday, McCullouch attended the board meeting with a new prosecutor who recently left the public defender’s office, virtually doubling his salary overnight. 
In addition to resolving cases of people who haven’t been indicted, McCullouch told the board the new prosecutor would work to reduce the number of people in Raymond on nonviolent charges or who need “expedited medical services.” 
“We think it’s going to be dramatic savings to the county,” he said. 
District 5 Supervisor Bobby “Bobcat” McGowan was the lone voice opposing the new prosecutor. He asked McCullouch: “My question is, do we got to pay for it? Is it in your budget, what you’re trying to do?”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Klobuchar gives low-dose THC industry some hope for a reprieve from coming prohibition
description: The low-dose THC industry that makes the popular beverages and edibles you see at liquor and convenience stores and breweries got a sliver of hope Sunday in the face of a looming federal prohibition of the key ingredient they need for their products.   Sen. Amy Klobuchar, who is a candidate for governor of Minnesota, said […]
text:
The Hemp Planning Predictability Act would delay the ban on THC products derived from hemp plants, which is set to take effect Nov. 11, for one month.  (Photo by Nicole Neri/The Minnesota Reformer)The low-dose THC industry that makes the popular beverages and edibles you see at liquor and convenience stores and breweries got a sliver of hope Sunday in the face of a looming federal prohibition of the key ingredient they need for their products.  
Sen. Amy Klobuchar, who is a candidate for governor of Minnesota, said her bill — known as the Hemp Planning Predictability Act — made it into a bipartisan Senate budget deal that would keep the government open until December. It still needs to pass the House and Senate and win the signature of President Trump. 
The Klobuchar provision would delay the ban on THC products derived from hemp plants, which is set to take effect Nov. 11, for one month. 
“Brewers, farmers, small businesses, and customers in Minnesota have made clear that the federal ban on hemp products will be devastating,” Klobuchar said in a press release. 
Low-dose THC retailers told the Reformer last fall that a hemp ban would effectively shut down Minnesota’s low-dose THC industry because they’d have to enter the more expensive conventional cannabis industry, with its higher taxes, severe banking regulations and more expensive product. 
The low-dose industry arose out of 2018 federal Farm Bill, which took took hemp off the controlled-substance list in an effort to encourage industrial hemp for commercial use. The bill defined hemp to be any cannabis plant or product with 0.3% or less of tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, which is the psychoactive drug from the plant.
That’s enough for most people to get high, however.
The bill created ambiguity that Minnesota Democrats in the Legislature exploited with a 2022 law that allowed for the manufacture, distribution and sale of THC products from “legally certified hemp” — creating a booming THC beverage and edibles industry that, paired with sales of adult-use marijuana, brought in more than $27 million in tax revenue last year. 
The Legislature went on to fully legalize cannabis in 2023. 
But Sen. Mitch McConnell attached a provision banning intoxicating hemp to a budget bill last year, effective November 2026.  
(That ban will have no effect on the legal status of cannabis in Minnesota, which allows adults 21 and older to enter a licensed dispensary and buy all manner of THC intoxicants or grow small amounts of their own cannabis.)
But the federal law caps THC derived from hemp plants at 0.4mg per container, effectively banning intoxicating THC drinks and edibles, which, even at the lowest doses, have at least 2mg of THC.
McConnell, who is said to be in poor health after being hospitalized in June, sought to close the loophole he helped pass in 2018 — which allowed for the hemp-derived THC industry to thrive — as part of his departing agricultural policy legacy, Politico reported last year.
Klobuchar introduced the reprieve provision with U.S. Sens. Rand Paul, R-KY, and Jeff Merkley, D-OR, in efforts to pursue a long-term solution.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Judge: Operators of rural, unlicensed care facility are ‘a danger to the public’
description: Six years after it first opened, a care facility in rural Iowa that has allegedly been operating without the required licensure has been temporarily shut down by a court order. District Court Judge Crystal S. Cronk issued a temporary injunction last week barring the owners and affiliates of Centerville’s Old Cabin Retreat from continuing to […]
text:
Old Cabin Retreat, which is alleged to have operated as an unlicensed hospital, in Centerville, Iowa, and its owner, Eddie Gingerich. (Main photo and inset photo courtesy of Appanoose County)Six years after it first opened, a care facility in rural Iowa that has allegedly been operating without the required licensure has been temporarily shut down by a court order.
District Court Judge Crystal S. Cronk issued a temporary injunction last week barring the owners and affiliates of Centerville’s Old Cabin Retreat from continuing to engage in the unlicensed practice of medicine, dentistry and dietetics, ruling that they “are a danger to the public.”
The order was issued in response to a new lawsuit initiated by three of Iowa’s health-related licensing boards. The Old Cabin Retreat has been in business since 2020, according to state records, and is alleged to have promoted treatments for cancer and other ailments despite the fact that none of the staff are licensed medical professionals.
The retreat, which has been the subject of at least one death investigation in recent years, has allegedly advertised a “100% success rate with hiatal hernias” and seizures, as well as proven success with “many cancers, Lyme Disease, heart disease, stomach issues, prostate issues (and) autoimmune disorders.”
In April 2026, Appanoose County prosecutors criminally charged 36-year-old Eddie Gingerich of Moravia, the owner of Old Cabin Retreat, with ongoing criminal conduct; money laundering; engaging in the practice of medicine, dietetics or dentistry without a license, and violating medical licensure laws and state laws regulating hospitals. He has pleaded not guilty to all of the charges.
In court filings, Gingerich has indicated he never progressed in school past the eighth grade but, according to Appanoose County law enforcement, he also claims to have treated more than 70 cancer patients at the Old Cabin Retreat.
In June, Gingerich’s attorney, Alfredo Parrish and his co-counsel, filed motions to withdraw as Gingerich’s legal counsel in the case, citing Gingerich’s desire to act as his own attorney in the matter. The court agreed to the request, but days later both attorneys filed new appearances in the case on behalf of Gingerich, indicating they are again representing Gingerich. A jury trial is scheduled for Sept. 15, 2026.
On July 27, 2026, the Iowa Board of Medicine, Iowa Dental Board and Iowa Board of Dietetics launched new civil proceedings against Gingerich, asking the court to permanently bar him and two of his alleged business partners — Jake Gingerich and Dan Helmuth — from engaging in the practice of medicine, dentistry and dietetics.
“Eddie Gingerich, with assistance from defendants Jake Gingerich and Dan Helmuth, is practicing medicine without any license,” the three licensing boards told the court.
The boards allege that while Old Cabin Retreat is a sole proprietorship owned, operated, and managed by Eddie Gingerich, Jake Gingerich is running Kingdom Health Source, and Helmuth has run Solutions by Nature, with all three businesses having operated out of the same building at one time or another.
Solutions by Nature has allegedly offered a wide variety of herbs, supplements and other natural “remedies” sold by Helmuth and which correspond to the products Eddie Gingerich has prescribed to patients. Jake Gingerich is alleged to have purchased Solutions by Nature and now operates the business in largely the same manner as Helmuth but under the name Kingdom Health Source, the boards allege.
Parrish did not immediately return messages seeking comment Monday and there was no answer at the retreat. Iowa Capital Dispatch was unable to locate the three defendants in the civil case for comment.
Deputy describes one patient death
Court records show that in the spring of 2021, less than a year after the Old Cabin Retreat opened for business, Appanoose County Deputy Jonathan Printy filed a search warrant application with the court as part of an investigation he was conducting into the facility.
Printy told the court his investigation began when an Amish man complained that he had taken his wife to the facility to be treated for some unspecified type of illness, but his wife was later discharged in worse condition than ever, barely able to speak or walk.
On Nov. 5, 2021, Printy went to the Old Cabin Retreat where, he reported, a large banner hung outside saying, “Members Only. Private Organization.”



Quotation







A young Amish man was laying on a hospital-type bed and had some wires or tubes coming from his body and going into a laptop computer … I asked, ‘What does that do?’ Gingerich then stated, ‘It goes through and gets the (microorganisms) of, you know, what’s in people – and that’s kind of what we use to go by what herbs they need.' 


– Appanoose County deputy describing a discussion with Eddie Gingerich


According to Printy’s warrant application, Eddie Gingerich met him at the door and told him, “It’s all-natural therapy, is what we do, like whole-body balancing is what we specialize in … We’re all into herbs, it’s all herbs we’re using.”
When Printy asked about the “quantum feedback scanner” the business was promoting, Gingerich allegedly showed him into a room where, Printy told the court, “a young Amish man was laying on a hospital-type bed and had some wires or tubes coming from his body and going into a laptop computer or a machine that was hooked up to a laptop computer … I asked, ‘What does that do?’ Gingerich then stated, ‘It goes through and gets the (microorganisms) of, you know, what’s in people – and that’s kind of what we use to go by what herbs they need. If, you know, they got any health issues, it’ll pop up, you know, kind of (indicate) what’s going on, and that’s kind of how we go at it.’”
In his warrant application, Printy told the court Gingerich explained that no diagnoses are made at Old Cabin Retreat, telling the deputy, “Usually most people that come in, they got diagnosed from a doctor somewhere. They come in here, then we know what’s going on mostly. That’s our main thing. They come from a doctor and they don’t want to take medication … They want to go on herbs.”
Court records show that one month after that visit, Printy was dispatched to the Old Cabin Retreat, where a 53-year-old Wisconsin man named Dan Miller was reported to have died. When Printy arrived, Miller had no pulse but was still warm to the touch. In Miller’s room was a chart listing the supplements and food Miller was to be given.
The chart’s printed letterhead, later copied for the court, stated, “Old Cabin Retreat …  A Private Health Care Membership Association… THE HARDEST THING IN THE WORLD TO OPEN IS A CLOSED MIND!”
Printy grabbed the chart, EMTs arrived on the scene and notified the medical examiner, and Miller’s body was transported to a nearby funeral home, according to the court records.
The three licensing boards that are now suing Gingerich allege that Miller had been diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2018 and then, in August 2021, sought inpatient treatment at Old Cabin Retreat.
The state medical examiner later ruled Miller died from “untreated prostate cancer,” the licensing boards allege. At the time, Eddie Gingerich allegedly informed the sheriff’s office he anticipated future deaths at the facility, indicating the retreat was a place for patients to come and die.
Youth hospitalized after treatment
Court records show that a year and a half after Miller’s death, in July 2023, an 11-year-old Amish child traveled to Iowa from Indiana with his parents to receive inpatient care at Old Cabin Retreat for his Type 1 diabetes.
The youth’s healthcare plan indicated he received treatment designed to “re-train his pancreas to make insulin,” according to the licensing boards
The boards allege that on the advice of Eddie Gingerich, the child gradually stopped taking insulin, with his last dose administered at Old Cabin Retreat on Aug. 17, 2023. Eddie Gingerich then prescribed the child a whole-foods diet, plus various herbs and supplements, the boards allege.
Three days after stopping insulin, the child began feeling unwell and was vomiting, the boards allege. On Aug. 22, 2023, three weeks after his admission at the retreat, the child was taken to a nearby hospital emergency room due to complications from uncontrolled diabetes. According to the licensing boards, the child was then life-flighted to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit at a Des Moines hospital where he was admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis and treated for four days before his blood levels returned to normal.



Quotation







Cows eating the wrong salts will refleck in the numbers! Only in there milk. Any salt thats not pure salt will give you a low sugar for 6 days, its impossable to make a new cell when sugars are low, oxygen is not available, won’t be available for 6 days!


– Written dietary advice allegedly dispensed at the Old Cabin Retreat


In response to that incident, the Appanoose County Sheriff’s Office conducted another investigation, this time using an undercover operative to gather more information. Using the pseudonym “Rachel Miller,” a woman visited the retreat on Oct. 19, 2023, armed with a hidden camera.
After collecting urine and saliva specimens for testing, Gingerich allegedly told “Miller” there was “no doubt” she had cancer cells in her pancreas, liver, and large intestine, that her kidneys were functioning poorly, that she had high blood pressure, and that her liver was in “bad shape.”
According to the state licensing boards, Eddie Gingerich prescribed a comprehensive dietary regime and supplement plan and provided written dietary advice, with unusual spelling and punctuation, that included the admonition, “Your theory got you here, let someone change it for you! holding on to your logics won’t get your health BACK!!!!”
The written advice also is alleged to have stated, “Cows eating the wrong salts will refleck in the numbers! Only in there milk. Any salt thats not pure salt will give you a low sugar for 6 days, its impossable to make a new cell when sugars are low, oxygen is not available, won’t be available for 6 days!”
On Nov. 3, 2023, Appanoose County charged Eddie Gingerich with the felonies of practicing medicine and dietetics without licensure and operating a hospital without a license. Within two weeks, he and the Appanoose County Attorney’s Office reached a plea deal that resulted in Eddie Gingerich pleading guilty to one reduced misdemeanor charge of employing an unlicensed dentist.
Court records show Eddie Gingerich paid a fine of $1,500, and the Old Cabin Retreat remained open for business.
On Sept. 26, 2025, the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals, and Licensing conducted an on-site visit at Old Cabin Retreat. According to the licensing boards, DIAL allegedly collected photographic evidence showing all of the facility’s “medical, dental, and pseudoscientific equipment” remained on-site and available for use.
‘Bring us your worst case. Warning: There are no MDs here.’
Newly disclosed records related to a June 2026 search warrant for Eddie Gingerich’s phone indicate that police believe Gingerich bought the Appanoose County property and built the Old Cabin Retreat in 2020.
Shortly thereafter, police now allege, a bank account that appears to be have been used by Eddie Gingerich to deposit revenue from the business began to grow in size.
One search warrant application describes “yearly totals” for account “activity” — it’s not clear whether “activity” references deposits, withdrawals or both — grew from $58,909 in 2019 to $914,256 in 2022.
The warrant application indicates the “only year Eddie Gingerich filed taxes was in 2021,” when he allegedly stated his total annual income was $67,538 — although, deputies allege, bank records point to income of at least $792,548 in 2021.
Court records show the facility is outfitted with therapy and treatment rooms, patient rooms with hospital-style beds, an oxygen chamber, a heat bed, an office with laboratory equipment, on-site laundry facilities, a kitchen and a dining area.
According to the licensing boards, one room at the Old Cabin Retreat is outfitted with a dentist’s chair and “equine dental tools” — tools typically used by veterinarians in treating the teeth of horses. “Charts on the wall purport to map out how specific teeth in a person’s mouth are related to other parts of the body and/or vital organs,” the boards allege.
The boards’ lawsuit also claims all patients at Old Cabin Retreat sign a “Private Healthcare Membership Association” contract before treatment in which they acknowledge they are pursuing health care treatments using nontraditional methods, and that the care they receive is provided by people without any license to practice medicine.
The licensing boards’ lawsuit alleges that records seized from Old Cabin Retreat show that as part of their treatment, many patients received “Miracle Mineral Solution,” which is the trade name for chlorine dioxide gas, a toxic industrial disinfectant that is considered unsafe for human consumption but is promoted by some alternative practitioners as a cure for various ailments.
According to county deputies, the Old Cabin Retreat has advertised on social media by stating, “Helping the sick – spiritually, mentally and physically, by the Word of God and with God-given foods and herbs!! Bring us your worst case. Warning: There are no MDs here, only the wisdom God taught us, and to him be all the glory.”
In addition to seeking a permanent injunction barring the two Gingeriches and Helmuth from practicing medicine, dentistry or dietetics, the three state licensing boards sought, and were immediately granted, a temporary injunction, citing what the boards described as practices that “already resulted in the death of one man and the life-threatening hospitalization of a minor child.”
The defendants’ actions, the boards told the court last month, “pose a serious, ongoing threat” to the public health.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi lawmakers launch redistricting process after Supreme Court ruling
description: Committee members meet during the Mississippi Legislature's Joint Redistricting and Reapportionment Committee organizational meeting at the Capitol in Jackson on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Lawmakers on Monday took the first steps toward potentially redrawing Mississippi’s legislative, congressional and judicial districts in the wake of the U.S. Supreme Court’s landmark Louisiana v. Callais decision that weakened minority voting protections. 
The Joint Redistricting and Reapportionment Committee, comprised of House members and senators, met at the state Capitol for the first time since the Supreme Court ruling. The state legislative committee will solicit input from voters in eight different areas of the state over the next two months on how the districts should be redrawn in light of the Callais decision. 
The committee also voted to hire attorneys from Butler Snow to serve as general counsel. Republican Sen. Dean Kirby from Pearl was elected chairman of the committee, and Republican Rep. Noah Sanford of Collins was named vice chair.
Republican Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann declined to say which districts he thinks the committee should prioritize or even if it was certain the committee will redraw judicial, legislative and congressional districts. 
“I don’t want to pre-suppose anything,” Hosemann said. “The committee needs to do its work. They’re going to be going all over Mississippi hearing from people.” 
Though the committee has scheduled eight hearings, some voting rights activists worry the hearings are merely a facade, and lawmakers have already made up their mind to dismantle majority Black districts. 
Amir Badat is the Southern states director and senior adviser for Fair Fight Action, a voting rights advocacy organization. He told Mississippi Today in a statement that the committee’s redistricting process is “putting lipstick on a pig.” 
“At its core, this process is an effort to diminish Black political power,” Badat said. “No number of meetings or public hearings will change that fact. If the joint committee truly cared about what the public wants, it would end this sham process before it begins.” 
The joint hearing came after Scott Colom,  Mississippi’s Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate, organized a voting-rights town hall on Saturday evening with Democratic U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Democratic U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson of Mississippi and Mississippi NAACP Director Charles Taylor. 
The panel encouraged the roughly 100 attendees at Farish Street Baptist Church in Jackson to make sure they’re registered to vote, help register other people to vote and turn out to vote in record numbers.
Alsobrooks told Mississippi Today that she would encourage Mississippians to “stay the course and keep fighting” against efforts to weaken majority Black districts. 
“It was not all that long ago, we’re reminded, that John Lewis walked across the Edmund Pettus Bridge and was beaten within an inch of his life with a pole that was wrapped in barbed wire” as he marched for voting rights for Black people,  Alsobrooks said. “It was a sacrosanct right that we’re never going to give up.” 
If the committee decides to tackle congressional redistricting, Thompson, Mississippi’s lone Black and Democratic official in Washington, will almost certainly be targeted by the majority-Republican state Legislature. 
Some Republicans, such as state Auditor Shad White, have called on the Legislature to effectively dismantle Thompson’s district, which comprises portions of the Jackson metro area and the majority-Black Delta. 
Thompson told Mississippi Today on Saturday that his campaign team will be monitoring the hearings and hopes state lawmakers will truly be receptive to the comments they gather from the public hearings. 
“I hope their work will be done in public and not behind closed doors,” Thompson said. 
Here is the schedule of hearings that will take place at 6 p.m.: 

Aug. 18 at Itawamba Community College in Tupelo 
Aug. 27 at Northwest Mississippi Community College in Senatobia 
Sept. 1 at Delta State University in Cleveland 
Sept. 8 at Alcorn State University in Natchez 
Sept.10 at a venue to be determined in Meridian 
Sept. 17 at the University of Southern Mississippi in Hattiesburg 
Sept. 22 at Mississippi Gulf Coast Community College in Gulfport 
Sept. 24 at the state Capitol building in Jackson

title: As Alaska’s U.S. Senate campaign heats up, super PACs boost out-of-state candidates

text:
A super PAC listing this Wasilla office space as its address is boosting a Green Party and fringe Democratic Party candidate in Alaska's U.S. Senate race. (Amy Bushatz/Mat-Su Sentinel) This story was originally published in the Anchorage Press. Subscribe here.
Richard Grayson lives in Arizona and has been a fringe candidate in a number of federal elections. That includes in New York, where records show he’s established campaign committees named “The Leopards Eating People’s Faces Party Supports NY-21 Write-In Candidate Richard Grayson,” and “Write In Richard Grayson New York’s Cutest Communist.”
This year, Grayson is on the ballot in Alaska’s U.S. Senate race, where two heavyweights, Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola, are running in a contest that could help decide control of the chamber.
And now, two weeks before the primary election determines which four candidates advance to  the general, Grayson, who’s running under the Green Party label, is getting an unexpected boost: A new super PAC has spent more than $100,000 on his behalf.
Fair Deal Alaska registered with federal campaign finance regulators a few days ago and lists as an address a suite in a Wasilla office building that offers “virtual office and mail services.”
In multiple filings with the Federal Election Commission, it has since reported spending some $180,000 on mailers, phone calls and other media supporting Grayson — as well as roughly the same amount on behalf of another Democrat in the race, Carol Hafner, who lists a South Dakota campaign address and uses a New York City phone number.
Neither Grayson nor Hafner responded to requests for comment Saturday. (Grayson did write a letter to the Fairbanks Daily News-Miner in June saying that the temperature in August in his Arizona town rises to 114 F, and that “just as our town is filled with seasonal residents from Alaska and other northern climes, I now have a good excuse to visit my snowbird neighbors and mooch off them for a while.”)
The apparent purpose of the spending on the two fringe candidates is boosting Hafner or Grayson onto the general election ballot, where either of them could pull a small number of votes from Peltola and potentially tip the race toward Sullivan. Fair Deal Alaska is also spending more than $65,000 on mailers opposing Peltola, according to its disclosures.
A similar group, Right for Alaska, has taken a similar strategy to boost candidates who could pull votes from Sullivan — supported by a six-figure contribution from a retired surgeon in Massachusetts, William Harris.
The group last week spent more than $250,000 on print ads opposing Sullivan, the incumbent Republican, and the same amount boosting lesser known candidates who, if they advance to the general election, could pull votes from him.
“They’re just trying to get some people in there to dilute either the Democratic vote that Mary’s going to get, or dilute the Republican vote that Daniel S. Sullivan is going to get,” said Jim Lottsfeldt, a longtime Alaska strategist who’s worked with candidates of both parties. “It’s just a tactic.”
The political operative who filed Right for Alaska’s paperwork with the Federal Election Commission, Thomas Datwyler, did not respond to requests for comment. Harris, the surgeon who contributed $100,000 to the group, declined to comment.
Fair Deal Alaska, the group opposing Peltola, did not respond to an email sent to the address it registered with the commission. Its listed address in Wasilla also hosts a gun shop, Arctic Ammo and Reloading Supplies; signs advertising two Republican politicians — incumbent U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III and gubernatorial candidate Bernadette Wilson — stood outside when a reporter visited Friday.
The group has not yet reported any of its fundraising information, though it will have to in a subsequent filing with campaign finance regulators.
A spokesperson for Sullivan’s campaign declined to comment on both Right for Alaska and Fair Deal Alaska. An from Peltola’s campaign said it was not familiar with either group.
There’s a long history of groups boosting third-party and fringe politicians to try to engineer the success of major candidates in Alaska elections. In 2014, incumbent Democratic U.S. Sen. Mark Begich’s campaign promoted libertarian Mark Fish in an effort to pull votes away from Sullivan, who nonetheless won the election.
In 2024, a group run by Lottsfeldt and aligned with Peltola, who was then running for re-election to the U.S. House of Representatives, spent significant sums running adswith the apparent aim of boosting less-competitive Republicans onto the general election ballot to pull votes from Nick Begich III, the leading GOP candidate.
In theory, Alaska’s ranked choice voting system should minimize the risk that the third- or fourth-placed candidates in the general election will pull significant numbers of votes from the top two — because their supporters’ votes are supposed to be redistributed to the candidates ranked next on each voter’s ballot.
But not everyone ranks all four candidates. In the 2024 U.S. House race, more than 7,000 voters only ranked the third- and fourth-placed candidates, John Wayne Howe of the Alaska Independence Party and Democrat Eric Hafner — and ultimately didn’t express a preference between Begich and Peltola, the top two finishers.
Begich ultimately won by some 8,000 votes.
“People on the far left and the far right don’t rank,” Lottsfeldt said. “They just vote for their favorite, and then they quit.”
Similar types of spending are happening elsewhere around the country, according to Lottsfeldt.
In Wisconsin, a Republican group is spending millions to boost a democratic socialist gubernatorial hopeful, Francesca Hong, who’s viewed as a more vulnerable candidate in the general election.
Amy Bushatz with Mat-Su Sentinel contributed reporting.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa now meets federal nursing home inspection requirements, audit finds
description: An audit released Monday shows the state has made “substantial improvements” in efforts to inspect nursing homes and now meets federal requirements, state Auditor Rob Sand said. In 2024, the state auditor’s office found certified nursing homes in Iowa were inspected by the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing on average every 17.1 months […]
text:
Iowa's nursing homes are now being inspected on average every 12 months, bringing the state into compliance with federal requirements, state Auditor Rob Sand said. (Photo by Jose Miguel Sanchez/Getty Images)An audit released Monday shows the state has made “substantial improvements” in efforts to inspect nursing homes and now meets federal requirements, state Auditor Rob Sand said.
In 2024, the state auditor’s office found certified nursing homes in Iowa were inspected by the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing on average every 17.1 months — four months beyond the federal mandate requiring homes to be inspected on a 12.9 month average. This requirement was set by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), the federal entity that pays for states to inspect nursing homes for compliance with federal regulations.
But according to data released June 1, 2026, Sand said Iowa’s nursing homes are now being inspected on average every 12 months, bringing the state into compliance with CMS requirements.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I believe it demonstrates what happens when government agencies are held accountable and have proper oversight — always good to have a little bit of encouragement to make sure that improvements are getting made.” Sand told reporters Monday.
Additionally, Iowa has made progress in meeting the requirement for each individual care facility to be inspected at least once every 15.9 months. In 2024, 85.4% of Iowa’s 403 nursing homes had not been inspected within this deadline at least once during the past three inspection cycles, the auditor’s report found. But the new report found as of 2026, only 2.8% of Iowa’s 389 certified nursing homes had missed the 15.9 month deadline in the past three inspection cycles, representing a nearly 83-percentage point decrease in overdue inspections.
Sand, the only Democrat to hold statewide elected office in Iowa and the Democratic nominee for Iowa governor in 2026, credited the GOP-led state Legislature and current Republican administration for investing in the issue, and for increasing the number of DIAL staff dedicated to nursing home inspections.
“Because there’s more people doing it, because they’ve made that investment, that means that we are increasing the number of inspections that are getting done, and we’re increasing how frequently they’re getting done,” Sand said. “Obviously, any parent who has told their kids or expected to have a clean room, and is able to take a look every now and then, can understand why that level of inspections and that level of oversight is important. Because as the number of staff go up, then nursing homes themselves can count on someone coming in to actually check their work, and make sure they’re doing what they’re supposed to do, at least as frequently as they are supposed to be looking into it.”
Sand said he believed the major improvements in these inspection rates should “largely be credited to staffing improvements — the number of individuals who are inspectors as state employees, has been increased.” While inspection staffing has improved, he said other workforce shortages remain.
Sand: Care facilities still struggle with nursing staff levels
“More people can get more inspections done. Pretty simple,” Sand said. “We also still face some challenges when it comes to staffing levels, and this is important to note, we do rank 47th nationally in the number of nursing staff per resident in nursing homes.”
In addition to having a low number of licensed nursing staff per resident in compared to other states, Iowa has also seen a high annual turnover rate, at 44% for nursing home staff. Though the report found this rate is an improvement from the previous report, when the state had a turnover rate of 54%, the report stated this still means “more than 9 out of 20 nurses who worked at a certified nursing home in the previous year are no longer employed by the facility.”
An Iowa Capital Dispatch review of 2025 federal data found 15% of Iowa nursing homes were cited for insufficient staffing.
There are also 17 fewer nursing homes in the state as well as roughly 2,000 fewer beds available for residents in Iowa compared to 2024. Sand said this reduction especially impacts Iowans in rural areas.
“They’re typically closing in rural areas where the population density is even lower to begin with,” he said. “That can make it harder for folks in rural areas who need to be in a nursing home to have access to one in their community or close to their family.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Former Nebraska Democratic Party employee sues, alleging sexual harassment, retaliation
description: A former employee of the Nebraska Democratic Party is suing the party, alleging sex discrimination and retaliation.
text:
Cutouts at an Omaha office of the Nebraska Democratic Party on April 3, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/ Nebraska Examiner) LINCOLN — A former employee of the Nebraska Democratic Party is suing the party, alleging sex discrimination and retaliation. 
The complaint was filed in the U.S. District Court of Nebraska by Larissa Schultz, the party’s former young Democrats organizer who is currently chair of the Saunders County Democratic Party. The lawsuit alleges that NDP Communications Director Jose Flores Jr., started “directing unwanted personal and sexual attention toward Schultz” in 2023 and state party leaders didn’t properly investigate it. 
The lawsuit alleges Flores repeatedly sent Schultz inappropriate text messages about her appearance, calling her “cute” and a “fox,” and also used terms of endearment such as “dear” and “mama.” He told her he was looking forward to seeing Schultz and asked whether her partner would accompany her on work trips, according to the lawsuit. 
He also twice invited Schultz to his hotel room for a drink after a work event in 2024, the lawsuit states. Schultz declined. Later, the lawsuit alleges, Flores put his arms around her and kissed her on the cheek during a work event in Kansas City in 2024.
Schultz reported the behavior to NDP Executive Director Precious McKesson on Aug. 30 of that year and filed a formal written complaint. Then, according to the lawsuit, the party didn’t “communicate with Schultz about any formal investigation or corrective action for more than two months.” 
After she filed a complaint, Schultz alleges that her “treatment within NDP changed” and that “Flores continued engaging in unwanted conduct toward” her.
In November 2024, Schultz reached out to Nebraska Democratic Party Chair Jane Kleeb for an update on the investigation and, according to the lawsuit, Kleeb responded that she wasn’t aware of the complaint. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
After affirming her intent to file a formal complaint, the lawsuit states that the NDP’s ad hoc ethics committee interviewed Flores in January of 2025.
Schultz was removed from the party’s public staff website by Jan. 24, 2025, the lawsuit says. 
Democratic Party responds
Kleeb said in a statement that the Nebraska Democratic Party “takes all complaints of harassment seriously.” 
“We stand by our internal process and decisions regarding the allegations and that there was no harassment,” Kleeb said. “This was also reviewed by the EEOC, and no further action was taken by that body. As this matter is now in litigation, we will only address the claims through the legal process.” 
The lawsuit states that the EEOC (Equal Employment Opportunity Commission) issued a “notice of right to sue” in April of this year.
Neither Schultz nor her attorney, Jennifer Turco Meyer, responded to requests for comment.
The Nebraska Republican Party released a statement Monday asking Nebraska’s 2nd Congressional District Democratic candidate Denise Powell and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Lynne Walz to speak on the lawsuit. 
“Lynne Walz and Denise Powell can’t have it both ways, they can’t accept the Nebraska Democratic Party’s money and organizing muscle while staying silent about how that same party allegedly treated an employee who came forward with a harassment complaint,” Nebraska Republican Party Chair Mary Jane Truemper said partly in a statement. 
Walz told the Examiner that “sexual harassment is very serious.”
“All allegations should be investigated. Those who commit sexual misconduct or cover it up should be held accountable,” Walz said. 
Powell told the Examiner, “These allegations are very troubling and should be fully investigated.”
“Everyone deserves to feel safe and supported at work and there should be no tolerance for this type of behavior in politics or in any other work environment,” Powell said. 
Schultz is asking the court to award lost wages and benefits, as well as compensation for “emotional pain, suffering, inconvenience, mental anguish, loss of enjoyment of life, and other nonpecuniary losses.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Governor and attorney general appeal to defend South Dakota’s ban on abortion-pill advertising
description: South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden and Attorney General Marty Jackley, both Republicans, filed an appeal Monday in defense of a new law that criminalizes abortion-pill advertising in the state. They’re also seeking to set aside a lower court’s order blocking enforcement of the law while the litigation plays out. Nancy Turbak Berry, who formerly served […]
text:
South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden, left, delivers his annual budget address on Dec. 2, 2025, at the Capitol in Pierre while state Attorney General Marty Jackley, right, listens from the floor of the House of Representatives. (Photos by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden and Attorney General Marty Jackley, both Republicans, filed an appeal Monday in defense of a new law that criminalizes abortion-pill advertising in the state.
They’re also seeking to set aside a lower court’s order blocking enforcement of the law while the litigation plays out.
Nancy Turbak Berry, who formerly served as a Democratic state legislator from Watertown, and New York-based nonprofit Mayday Health filed a lawsuit in May against Rhoden and Jackley. Rhoden signed the legislation into law in March after lawmakers approved it, but it wasn’t scheduled to take effect until July 1.
In mid-July, a federal judge in Rapid City ruled the state could not enforce the new law while the lawsuit played out. On Monday, Jackley and Rhoden appealed that decision to the U.S. Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals.
South Dakota already had a near-total ban on abortion, except when it’s necessary “to preserve the life of the pregnant female.”
Judge temporarily blocks South Dakota’s abortion-pill advertising ban as lawsuit continues

The new law prohibits the dispensing, distribution and advertising of abortion pills and other abortion-related items, and makes violations punishable by felony prosecutions and fines.
Mayday Health and Turbak Berry say the law illegally restricts Turbak Berry’s free speech. As an example, the lawsuit says the prohibition on advertising would prevent her from wearing a sweatshirt sold by Mayday. The sweatshirt says abortion pills can be obtained in all 50 states and encourages people to learn more on Mayday’s website.
“Unless this court grants relief, Turbak will be deterred from wearing the sweatshirt,” and thereby deterred from engaging in First Amendment-protected speech, the lawsuit says.
U.S. District Judge Camela Theeler wrote in her July ruling that the state’s lawyers have “not shown that Mayday advertises with the specific intent that another person engage in specific criminal conduct and thus have not shown that Mayday’s advertising is integral to criminal conduct.”
In court documents filed Monday, Jackley and Rhoden criticized Theeler’s ruling and Mayday’s advertising, which formerly included placards at gas station pumps in the state.
“The Court has legalized the solicitation and aiding and abetting of an illegal drug and erroneously broadened the scope of the term advertising,” the state said in its court filing, adding that the ruling “could just as easily protect the solicitation and aiding and abetting of online methamphetamine sales by groups who claim to simply ‘provide information’ about methamphetamine and offer consumers the ‘choice’ to commit an illegal act.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Johnson emphasizes funding strength for general election, while James shifts focus to Democrats
description: Just before an event with supporters in downtown Lansing Monday, Perry Johnson said he isn’t considering the possibility that he’ll lose Tuesday’s Republican gubernatorial primary. As for why Republican voters should put him on the general election ballot in November, he emphasized his financial resources — Johnson, an independently wealthy businessman, has[...]
text:
Republican gubernatorial candidate Perry Johnson speaks to supporters at Kelly's in Lansing the day before the primary election. Aug. 3, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Just before an event with supporters in downtown Lansing Monday, Perry Johnson said he isn’t considering the possibility that he’ll lose Tuesday’s Republican gubernatorial primary.
As for why Republican voters should put him on the general election ballot in November, he emphasized his financial resources — Johnson, an independently wealthy businessman, has put nearly $30 million of his own money into his campaign and says he has reserved $5 million of general election ads to start immediately following the primary. 
His primary opponent, U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Twp.), reported about $1.4 million cash on hand, according to campaign finance filings from late July. Mission Michigan, the PAC backing James, has an additional $1.9 million cash on hand. 
“The number one issue is, I’m really the one person that could defeat Jocelyn Benson,” he told Michigan Advance. “Jocelyn Benson just put up a $10 million buy. John James is broke and everybody knows it. I’m obviously not.”
Republican gubernatorial candidate Perry Johnson speaks to supporters at Kelly’s in Lansing the day before the primary election. Aug. 3, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
James is considered the front-runner in the race and is leading in most recent polls, especially after snagging the endorsement from President Donald Trump — which Johnson called “the weakest endorsement in the history of endorsements” — but Johnson said he believes people will be shocked by the results of the primary.
“I’ve got to win. I don’t even want to think about that. I’m the kind of guy that plans to win,” he said. “When you have momentum like we have, it’s more than momentum. It’s almost a movement, and it is in the air where we go because people feel it.”
Johnson’s event was one in a series of campaign stops that both candidates are making in the days leading up to the primary election — he will hold a major campaign rally in Novi on Monday night, while James is hosting a “Primary Eve Party” in Harrison Township alongside U.S. Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Bruce Township) and other supporters. 
Speaking at that event Monday afternoon, James did not discuss his primary competition or mention Johnson at all, focusing instead on the Democratic ticket and what he called a race that is “common sense versus crazy.”


 
“If you can’t get fired up about this state and what this means for our kids, what this means for the rest of the nation, then you don’t have a heart in your chest,” James said to a crowd of supporters. “Michigan has always been called to stand up in defense of what’s right, but because of your help and because of your effort, we are going to win. But it will not happen if we don’t spread the news.”
Other speakers at the event, including James’ former primary competitor Mike Cox, similarly focused on the need to win in November, with McClain saying, “this election is going to be a turnout election.”
“It starts right now, because we cannot allow the socialists to take our nation in the wrong direction with the next president,” James continued. “It starts right here with who runs our state and who runs our future.”
Despite Johnson’s desire not to consider a scenario where James takes the Republican nomination in the primary, he said that he would still support down-ballot Republicans financially if he were not on the general election ballot himself.
Johnson also said he would not seek the lieutenant governor position, which will be chosen by nominations at the party’s late August convention.
Signs for Republican gubernatorial candidate Perry Johnson at an event in Lansing the day before the primary election. Aug. 3, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
“Of course not,” he said when asked. “Come on. I have companies around the world. I mean, I’m sitting over here donating my time, and I’m running because I can change the state.”
If he does pull out a victory on Tuesday, Johnson said he believes that he will be able to unite a conservative coalition in November that includes independents, Republicans and even Libertarian Party members. 
“If I’m at the top of the ticket, we know I will work harder, I will spend more. I’m not broke, and we will win,” he said.
He added that he believes Trump will back him in a general election if he is the nominee, though Trump’s campaign team has called him a “Never Trumper” on social media during the primary election. 
“I think President Trump likes me,” Johnson said. “I even helped the president run. So it’s not like we have a bad relationship.”
The video of the James event is in partnership with C-SPAN.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico plugs record number of abandoned oil and gas wells, thanks to Biden-era funding
description: New Mexico environmental officials plugged a record number of abandoned and orphaned oil and gas wells last year, thanks in large part to funding from Biden-era grants, they told a panel of state lawmakers Monday.
text:
A pumpjack between Hobbs and Lovington in the Permian Basin as seen on Aug. 7, 2025. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)New Mexico environmental officials plugged a record number of abandoned and orphaned oil and gas wells last year, thanks in large part to funding from Biden-era grants, they told a panel of state lawmakers Monday.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Nonetheless, across the state, approximately 1,600 wells remain that are designated for cleanup but have yet to be plugged or fully remediated, EMNRD Deputy Secretary Ben Shelton told lawmakers on the interim Economic and Rural Development and Policy Committee.
In the most recent fiscal year, which concluded in June, EMNRD’s Oil Conservation Division plugged a record 114 wells — a significant increase from its previous annual average of 25-50, Shelton said, largely crediting multimillion-dollar grants from the federal Bipartisan Infrastructure Law.
That improved funding stream should help to plug more wells in the coming years, he added.
“They should probably break that record just about every single year for the next few years with the way that the funding is going,” Shelton said.
A 2025 Legislative Finance Committee report found that plugging and cleaning up abandoned wells could cost the state between $700 million and $1.6 billion. Currently authorized clean-up sites will cost the state about $200 million, Shelton said Monday.
Plugging 114 wells last year cost $28.4 million, Shelton said. Going forward, environmental leaders like Shelton hope that a newly approved measure will keep taxpayers from footing as much of the bill as they have in recent years.
The Oil Conservation Commission — a three-member governing body that oversees rulemaking — recently passed new bonding requirements, a term that refers to the minimum amount of money oil and gas operators have to post upfront for cleanup costs.
Historically, the state has only plugged about 5% of abandoned wells that end up plugged and private industry operators have handled the rest. That still costs taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars, though. The goal of raising those bonding requirements, Shelton said, is to shield taxpayers from the multimillion-dollar burden of cleaning up these sites.
While conservationists praised the decision to raise the bonding requirement at the time of the vote, some Republican lawmakers Monday scrutinized it.
State Sen. Crystal Brantley (R-Elephant Butte) told Shelton she was concerned the new rules could unnecessarily penalize responsible oil and gas operators.
“I understand that there are bad apples in oil and gas,” she said. “When we raise those bonding minimums so high, who we seem to hurt are New Mexico businesses and New Mexico families…the bigs who are based out of Midland or Dallas or Houston can afford to pay those minimums.”
Shelton told her that the newly approved rules took that concern into account. In particular, oil and gas operators that do not own a high number of non-productive wells can get discounted “blanket bonds,” he said.
“We are talking about a minority of the wells in the state. Mostly the industry is plugging its own wells as it’s supposed to,” he said. “Why does the state tackle orphaned wells? It’s because they are, by definition, wells that do not have a responsible party who you can pursue to get them to clean up. At the end of the day, if you just leave a well, the community is the one that’s going to suffer.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: States sue Trump administration over plan to share antipoverty program data
description: A group of mostly Democratic-led states is challenging a Trump administration rule that would force them to provide data on people receiving antipoverty benefits.
text:
A group of mostly Democratic-led states is challenging a Trump administration rule that would force them to provide data on people receiving antipoverty benefits. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)The Trump administration’s demand for states to provide Social Security numbers, immigration status, and other private information on low-income residents who receive cash benefits is improper and unconstitutional, a group of mostly Democratic-led states alleges in a new lawsuit.
Officials with 24 states and the District of Columbia say in the complaint that a regulatory change proposed by the U.S. Administration for Children and Families and set to take effect Aug. 11 greatly exceeds the federal government’s assigned role in overseeing the antipoverty program called TANF, or Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, and violates multiple privacy laws.
The change, first announced in June, will also cost states extra time and money and chill participation in a program that benefits some 2.4 million people nationwide, according to the 60-page lawsuit filed Monday in federal court in D.C. The states are calling for the court to throw out the proposed rule and ensure the confidentiality of this information.
New Jersey Attorney General Jen Davenport said in a statement that the regulatory change would “obliterate” existing guardrails on sensitive data and “violate the privacy of families that are just trying to make ends meet.”
“The Trump Administration has tried time and again to weaponize every aspect of government as part of their reckless immigration enforcement efforts. Now, they want to misuse a program intended to help vulnerable families and children as a tool for harassing immigrants,” Davenport said.
States have the right to “protect critically needed services for families in their time of greatest need,” Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield said in a statement.
“Families turn to these programs because they’re doing everything they can to keep a roof over their heads and food on the table — these programs are a literal lifeline for struggling parents and their kids,” Rayfield said. “But the Trump Administration is trying to weaponize these emergency assistance programs, taking families’ private, personal data and using it to advance a partisan political agenda that is tearing communities apart.”
The lawsuit alleges the change is part of the Trump administration’s ongoing effort to target immigrants by tightening the rules around various social service programs. Administration officials say they are trying to root out fraud and abuse, but critics say the new rules are designed to force out people who were born outside the U.S.
The Administration for Children and Families did not respond to a request for comment on Monday. According to the lawsuit, the administration said it will share the data it obtains with other government agencies or private entities as part of its quest to verify that states are properly spending taxpayer dollars.
Nothing in the law supports the federal department’s “extravagant claims of authority and gross breach of personal privacy,” the lawsuit says.
“The sharing of such information runs afoul of a thicket of federal privacy protections,” it says.
When TANF was created as part of a federal welfare overhaul in 1996, it was purposely designed to limit the federal government’s role and give states wide control over the program’s design, operation, and information verification, according to the lawsuit. The Trump administration has insisted problems with the program require greater federal scrutiny.
The regulatory change announced in June would force states to provide additional details on participants, including Social Security numbers, country of origin, and immigration status, even though 95% of children and 85% of adults receiving benefits are U.S. citizens, according to the lawsuit.
The lawsuit also alleges that the Trump administration has not specified how they plan to keep program participants’ data safe, that the change would place a “direct and significant” cost on states, and that releasing data to the federal government would erode trust state agencies have developed with participants.
The plaintiffs are New York, D.C., California, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, and Wisconsin.
