name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Signature cases add fuel to calls for ballot access reform
authors: Katie Castellani | State House News Service
description: Legislative negotiators are finalizing the details of a bill requiring more frequent financial disclosures for statewide ballot question campaigns and implementing guardrails around the use of paid signature gatherers.
text:
IN THE WAKE OF alleged signature fraud, rifts within the Republican Party have emerged. Republicans and Democrats have also found common ground: a desire to reform the process for getting on the ballot.
During a Sunday appearance on WCVB’s “On the Record,” MassGOP Chair Amy Carnevale said the allegations of signature fraud that disrupted or derailed three statewide Republican campaigns speak to a public policy question.
“So, I think what this calls out is really a reform of the process by which candidates can qualify for the ballots,” Carnevale said while responding to a question on if she’d be empathetic to Democratic candidates who faced similar allegations. “It’s become commonplace for not only statewide candidates, but also ballot questions, to hire signature gathering firms. So really, it’s become a process of who has the most money to hire these firms to collect signatures.”
Top Beacon Hill Democrats frustrated with an influx of ballot questions backed by special interest groups have delivered a similar message. Legislative negotiators are finalizing the details of a bill requiring more frequent financial disclosures for statewide ballot question campaigns and implementing guardrails around the use of paid signature gatherers. The House’s bill, which representatives passed unanimously, would also create a legislative commission to review the whole initiative petition process, with recommendations for statutory and constitutional amendments due by the end of 2027.
Asked if she thinks candidates need too many signatures to get on the ballot, Carnevale said “I do. I do. I think our process needs reform here in Massachusetts for them to get on the ballot, and I think that’s what this calls out.” She did not specify reforms she’d like to see and a MassGOP spokesperson did not immediately respond to the News Service’s questions about how the party is seeking to change the process.
“Absolutely. So, I think we’ll have to do that in the wake of this election, obviously, we’re mid-cycle in an election, but I think after this election, it’s appropriate to take a step back and work collectively with the Democratic Party,” Carnevale said when asked if she’s pushing for serious change. “I’d be willing to work with them and with Independents to try to reform our system.”
The alleged signature fraud issues have exposed fissures within the GOP.
Last week, Republican gubernatorial candidate Brian Shortsleeve launched his first television campaign ad titled “Voter ID.” In the 30-second spot, Shortsleeve attacks his primary opponent Mike Minogue’s response to the alleged signature fraud. 
“When Mike Minogue’s preferred running mate committed election fraud, he endorsed it,” Shortsleeve said in the ad that’s airing statewide. “Defending the political insiders. Attacking those who exposed it. And now he wants you to trust him to lead Massachusetts? Give me a break.”
Two GOP lieutenant governor hopefuls were knocked off the ballot as a result of the allegedly fraudulent signatures: Anne Manning Martin and Anne Brensley, who Minogue backed. Brensley accused her signature gatherer, Joe Bronske, of collecting fraudulent signatures and causing her to fall short of the required 10,000 certified signatures. Michael Walsh, a GOP candidate for attorney general, faced similar allegations and was able to restore his ballot access. 
Hours after Shortsleeve’s ad went live, Carnevale came to Minogue’s defense.
“As Chair of the Party, it is my responsibility to stand up for and support Republican candidates, particularly when they are being unfairly attacked, misrepresented, or wronged,” Carnevale said in a statement. “In this case, fraud was perpetrated against our candidates. Brian Shortsleeve’s attempt to exploit that fraud for political advantage, while portraying himself as a champion of election integrity and disparaging fellow Republicans, is both misleading and deeply disappointing.”
Carnevale expanded on those comments while appearing on “On the Record,” saying the candidates who faced fraud allegations did “nothing wrong” and it was their signature gatherer who allegedly committed signature fraud. 
“They were called out by Brian Shortsleeve in this effort. So I thought, as party chair, I do owe a service to these candidates to defend them and their integrity in qualifying for the ballot.”
Asked on “On the Record” about a path to a more unified Republican Party in wake of Shortsleeve’s ad, Carnevale said she wouldn’t characterize the dynamic as fighting and that it is “an isolated case of really calling out an ad that was disingenuous and misleading” towards some candidates. 
“I think we have come a long way in the Republican Party over the last three years of coming together. I think Mike Minogue and the team that we have running for office here in Massachusetts has done a great job in terms of bringing Republicans together, really kind of closing some of those divisions we have had in the past,” Carnevale said. “And I think we’re really a united party going forward.”
Shawn Oliver, a Republican candidate for lieutenant governor who is aligned with Shortsleeve, filed the complaint that knocked Manning Martin off the ballot. Oliver’s complaint was consolidated with a similar one Democratic Party Executive Director Adam Roof filed. More than 20 Republican State Committee members condemned the move saying in an email that it showed “willing coordination and collusion” between the Democratic Party and Oliver’s campaign, along with Shortsleeve’s camp by extension.
Minogue also condemned Oliver.
“It is shameful that anyone would oppose unifying to win, but unfathomable that anyone would join arms with bad actors to block the democratic process,” Minogue said in a statement to the Boston Herald.
Oliver and Shortsleeve have stood by the complaint and criticized both Minogue’s and MassGOP’s response to the allegations of fraud. Shortsleeve said MassGOP is asking Republicans to “ignore election fraud because it’s one of their own” and that he would not. Shortsleeve also said Minogue’s response to the issue raises “serious questions” about how he would handle potential election fraud and corruption if elected governor and called on him to “rethink the consequences of his defense of election fraud.”
In July, MassGOP passed a resolution saying it is “committed to upholding the highest standards of integrity, transparency, and fairness in all aspects of the electoral process.” The resolution also calls for a “thorough and timely” investigation into alleged fraud or “irregularities” with the signature collection process and says the party supports “fair and transparent” resolution of the matters in court and appropriate administrative processes. It also calls on the auditor to conduct a “comprehensive review” of the state’s signature verification and certification processes to ensure “uniformity, accuracy, and adherence to best practices.”
Minogue spokesperson Elizabeth Hopkins said in a statement to the News Service that the candidate believes in “safe and fair elections” and that as governor, he would audit the system to “ensure it is one of the best in the country.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Moral Monday leader, activists arrested in U.S. Senate Office Building
description: Bishop William Barber and a group of faith leaders were arrested in Washington, D.C., Monday following a demonstration inside the Hart Senate Office Building. Barber and the activists were attempting to meet with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota, to voice their opposition to voter suppression and the SAVE America Act. Earlier in the […]
text:
Bishop William Barber, president of Repairers of the Breach and founder of the Moral Monday movement (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)Bishop William Barber and a group of faith leaders were arrested in Washington, D.C., Monday following a demonstration inside the Hart Senate Office Building. Barber and the activists were attempting to meet with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota, to voice their opposition to voter suppression and the SAVE America Act.
Earlier in the day, Barber, president of Repairers of the Breach and founder of the Moral Monday movement, held a press conference at the steps of the U.S. Supreme Court to explain why faith leaders from across the nation are laser-focused on voting rights.
With less than 100 days until the 2026 midterm elections, Barber said Christian, Jewish and Muslim faith leaders will use that time to mobilize 1,000 marches to the polls to encourage early voting and participation in the Nov. 3 elections.
Bishop William Barber is led by officers out of the Senate Office Building on August 3, 2026. (Photo: screenshot from Repairers of the Breach video)
“We will cast a vision for a hundred days of mobilization,” Barber said. “In this moment, we do not need to have a march on Washington. We need a march in the states to change Washington.”
Repairers of the Breach held a series of “public pulpit” events in the nation’s capital this summer, but Barber said faith leaders must now return home to get occasional voters engaged in what is occurring in state legislatures.
“The power is in the states. States can block your living wages. States can make [voter] suppression laws that we’ve already passed over 87 of them, particularly in southern states,” said Barber.
NC Republicans look to add new restrictions
Barber’s focus on the states comes just days after the North Carolina Senate passed a controversial elections bill that will reduce early voting periods during primaries, primary runoffs and special elections from 17 days to 10 days.
House Bill 958 will also require the state auditor to conduct post-election audits of county election systems. The number of audits to be conducted is at the sole discretion of the auditor.
Democrats voiced concerns about another provision in H958 that would use federal databases and information from other states to identify people who have died but remain on the voter rolls. Sen. Mujtaba Mohammed, D-Mecklenburg, argued last week that provision could lead to living voters being wrongfully removed, especially amid confusion over similar names.
As the bill heads back to the state House on Tuesday, Republicans have argued that the legislation improves election administration and further enhances security.
NC Senate approves controversial elections bill along party lines

Gov. Josh Stein criticized the measure, saying the bill erodes trust by injecting more politics into the State Board of Elections.
Awakening disengaged voters
Repairers of the Breach and partner organizations are developing a plan to reach five million infrequent, low-wage voters and one million Black male voters through texting by their peers and knocking on doors in the coming weeks.
“We’re here because the ballot is sacred,” Rev. Dr. Hanna R. Broome told reporters on Monday.
With the U.S. spending an estimated $1.5 billion per day on the war in Iran, Barber said even infrequent voters know that money could be addressing real issues “rather than being poured down a dark hole in the immoral and illegal war.”
Barber said voters must also be made aware of changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, under President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Nationwide, more than 4.5 million people are no longer receiving SNAP benefits. According to a new report by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, SNAP participation in North Carolina has dropped more than 12% between July 2025 and April 2026.
Starting this October, states will be required to pay a portion of the benefits for the first time in program history. That payment is based on the state’s error rate for SNAP payments.
“How damnable is it to say we got money for war, but we don’t have money for children?” Barber said.

name: VTDigger
title: Burlington is facing a public safety emergency
description:
Open-air drug use and dealing have become impossible to ignore in downtown Burlington, and it's time for a dedicated task force to restore order.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Burlington is facing a public safety emergency.
text:
Dear Editor,
As a father of two young daughters, aged 4 and 5, I never imagined that a simple walk to get ice cream would become a lesson in open-air drug use and public disorder in the heart of our city.
Recently, while walking to Ben & Jerry’s on Church Street in Burlington, we passed a park where multiple individuals were openly using drugs. Moments later, we were followed by another person who appeared to be under the influence, yelling at people trying to eat dinner on Church Street. We then saw a white Mercedes pull to the curb. An individual stepped out, appeared to exchange something with someone in the park, lingered briefly in conversation and then drove away. What appears to be open-air drug activity has become increasingly visible in downtown Burlington, and it is deeply concerning. It feels like no one is truly in control. We are ticketed for parking violations, yet open drug use and suspected dealing unfold in plain sight in our public spaces. On behalf of parents, business owners and every law-abiding resident who expects basic order in their city, we deserve far better from our leadership.
No parent should have to walk their children through this on the way to get ice cream. No business owner should have to wonder how many customers are choosing to stay away because they don’t want to walk through this spectacle just to support local businesses. Burlington’s economy depends on people feeling safe enough to visit our downtown. How many families are quietly deciding it simply isn’t worth it anymore? Tourism is down here in “mini San Francisco.” Perhaps the flash mob thefts will come next.
This is not a letter about homelessness. It is a letter about open-air drug use, public disorder and the failure of leadership. We should continue helping people who are homeless, struggling with addiction or facing mental illness. But compassion does not require surrendering our parks, sidewalks and downtown streets to illegal drug activity and suspected dealing.
The U.S. Department of Justice and other federal research have consistently found that open-air drug markets attract far more than drug activity. They are associated with increased violence, robberies, illegal weapons, intimidation of residents and neighborhood disorder. They also expose children to criminal behavior that no child should ever have to witness. Cities across the country have recognized this reality and created specialized drug market enforcement initiatives because traditional policing alone was not enough.
Burlington has reached that point.
This problem has grown beyond the capacity of our current approach. Our elected leaders have shown us that what we are doing is not working. It is time for Vermont to recognize this as both a public safety and public health emergency and provide emergency funding to establish a dedicated public safety and drug market task force.
This task force should bring together the Burlington Police Department, the Vermont State Police, prosecutors, addiction specialists, mental health professionals and outreach organizations with one clear mission: dismantle open-air drug markets, restore public spaces, hold dealers accountable and connect those who want help with treatment.
In addition, Burlington needs a dedicated, visible downtown public safety presence: an appropriately staffed and trained police unit whose sole responsibility is maintaining order downtown. Other cities, including several on the West Coast that faced similar breakdowns in downtown public order, have implemented specialized downtown policing teams with consistent foot and bike patrols. These units are not about over-policing; they are about restoring baseline safety, deterring open-air drug activity and ensuring that public spaces are actually governed by law. Burlington should adopt a similar model so that residents, families and visitors can once again walk downtown without fear or disruption.
Other cities have demonstrated that focused, coordinated efforts can reclaim neighborhoods without abandoning compassion. Burlington should expect nothing less.
I love this city. That is exactly why I am writing this letter. My daughters deserve better. Every child in Burlington deserves better. Our businesses deserve better. Our residents deserve better.

READ MORE

And to those who are turning our parks and sidewalks into open-air drug scenes: enough is enough. This is not your place to destroy. This is a city where families live, where children walk and where decent people are trying to build a life. That basic truth must be respected again.
The question is no longer whether Burlington has a problem. The question is: What more do we need to see before we decide enough is enough?
August Letendre, 
Shelburne, Vt.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Attorneys and advocates cheer Michigan Supreme Court decision demanding new Line 5 permit review
description: Following the Michigan Supreme Court’s Friday ruling striking down state energy regulators’ decision to permit the Line 5 tunnel project, pipeline opponents convened to celebrate the decision and talk about the next steps.  The controversial pipeline runs from Superior, Wisconsin to Sarnia, Ontario, with a 4.5-mile segment of dual pipelines running through t[...]
text:
Ceremonial rock in Mackinac Straits prior to Anishinaabek water ceremony at McGulpin Point, Mackinaw City. May 2021 | Laina G. StebbinsFollowing the Michigan Supreme Court’s Friday ruling striking down state energy regulators’ decision to permit the Line 5 tunnel project, pipeline opponents convened to celebrate the decision and talk about the next steps. 
The controversial pipeline runs from Superior, Wisconsin to Sarnia, Ontario, with a 4.5-mile segment of dual pipelines running through the Straits of Mackinac, where Lake Michigan and Lake Huron meet. 
Bay Mills Indian Community President Whitney Gravelle, Michigan Climate Action Network Executive Director Denise Keele and several attorneys who challenged with Michigan Public Service Commission’s permitting decision told reporters the courts’ ruling marked a victory for the tribal nations, environmental advocates and attorneys who advocated for a broader review of the environmental harms that could come from the project.
This map shows the proposed tunnel and the existing dual pipelines crossing the Straits of Mackinac. | Screenshot from the MPSC Line 5 Issue Brief
The Commission, which oversees natural gas and pipelines within the state, granted Line 5’s owner, Enbridge, a permit to move forward with its plans to replace its dual pipelines operating within the Great Lakes with a new segment placed in a utility tunnel beneath the lakebed.
Enbridge has championed the tunnel as a solution to concerns that the pipeline could rupture, spilling oil and natural gas liquids into the ecologically sensitive Straits of Mackinac, where Lake Michigan and Lake Huron meet. However, pipeline opponents say the tunnel project would still harm environmental and cultural resources.
In their decision Friday, the Michigan Supreme Court determined the Public Service Commission had failed to consider alternatives to the Line 5 tunnel project, and had improperly limited the scope of the environmental review by preventing intervenors from submitting information detailing the project’s environmental impacts and examining the public need for the petroleum products Line 5 transports.
“The court rejected the commission’s framework of analysis and sent this back to the drawing board,” said Adam Ratchenski, a senior attorney for Earthjustice who argued on behalf of  the Bay Mills Indian Community, the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians, Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians, and Nottawaseppi Huron Band of the Potawatomi. 
“It didn’t say go back and do a little more,” Ratchenski continued, “It said go back and do it right this time, and we’ll be fighting every step of the way to make sure that happens. The case sets a precedent that will result in better protection for Michigan’s air, water, and natural resources, and critically for the communities and creatures that rely upon them. That’s a great thing for everybody, and we should celebrate it.”
Moving forward, Gravelle said the commission can now review the full 641-mile scope of Line 5, as opposed to the four-mile segment located in the Straits, noting that the pipeline has spilled more than a million gallons of oil along its route.
In a statement to Michigan Advance, Enbridge Spokesperson Ryan Duffy said the company is reviewing the court’s legal opinion and assessing its legal options.
“The Court’s decision is unfortunate in that it adds an additional delay to the permitting process for the Great Lakes Tunnel, which is designed to protect the Great Lakes and ensure the ongoing safe, reliable and efficient delivery of energy to our region,” Duffy said.
While Enbridge could appeal the decision to the U.S. Supreme Court, Riyaz Kanji, who represented Flow Water Advocates in their appeal of the permit, argued the company lacks the legal basis, given that the case deals with state law like the Michigan Environmental Protection Act.
“These are quintessential Michigan legal issues, and the Michigan Supreme Court has the final word,” Kanji said, noting that this leaves the Public Service Commission as the next step. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ratchenski anticipated that the commission could hold a new hearing on the permit sometime in 2027. 
Alongside the permit from the commission, Enbridge needs to secure permits from the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers in order to move forward with construction of the tunnel project.
However, as Michigan moves to meet a 100% clean energy standard by 2040, Keele questioned the logic of investing further resources into the more than 70 year old pipe line.
“It just defies common sense to invest in a fossil fuel pipeline that endangers our greatest freshwater resource amid rising global temperatures,” Keele said. “We are in this fight to ensure that we at least recognize the reality of climate change and fully consider the likely impacts from increased greenhouse gas emissions.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Fact check: Kansas organization’s mailer on constitutional amendment ignores details of cases
description: Group championing constitutional amendment requiring election of Kansas Supreme Court justices sidelines murder case details to make a point.
text:
Kansans for Democracy, a advocate for a proposed state constitutional amendment requiring election of Kansas Supreme Court justices, is attempting to influence voters with mailers offering an incomplete picture of decisions the state's highest court made in two murder cases. (Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — An organization seeking to convince Kansans to support a proposed amendment to the Kansas Constitution took liberties when crafting two-sided cards mailed to potential voters.
The amendment on Tuesday’s ballot would require Kansas Supreme Court justices to be elected rather than appointed.
Dark money, misleading claims flood Kansas ahead of judicial selection referendum

Kansans for Democracy, which backs the amendment, used the flier to portray members of the Supreme Court as “liberal justices” who put “Kansans in danger” by overturning murder convictions. Adjacent to the claim, the organization pointed to the case of Devonte Wash, who was charged in the 2018 death of Ashley Harlan and her unborn child in Olathe.
Wash was found guilty of capital murder in 2022 and sentenced by Johnson County District Judge James Droege to serve life in prison without the possibility of parole.
In June 2025, the Supreme Court unanimously vacated the conviction and remanded the case for possible retrial because of multiple instances of prosecutorial error that deprived Wash of a fair trial. The decision was affirmed by justices appointed by Republican and Democratic governors, including Justice Caleb Stegall, the court’s most conservative member who was appointed by GOP Gov. Sam Brownback.
“I concur with the result because I agree the state failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the identified prosecutorial errors were harmless,” Stegall wrote at the time.
The Supreme Court found that assistant district attorney Jacob Gontesky, who prosecuted Wash at trial and argued for preservation of his conviction on appeal, stood before the jury and referenced firearm forensic evidence the district judge had excluded. In addition, the court found Gontesky improperly suggested during closing argument that certain disputed information was undisputed.
The Supreme Court concluded the prosecution sought to fill gaps in a largely circumstantial case against Wash by relying on flawed tactics.
“Once identified, prosecutorial error is harmless only if the state shows there is no reasonable possibility the error contributed to the verdict,” Justice Dan Biles said in a written opinion. “Here, the state fails to carry that burden because its circumstantial evidence contained meaningful gaps the prosecutor attempted to close with unfair tactics that cannot be dismissed as minor aberrations in a prolonged trial.”
Biles said the prosecution made mistakes that violated an obligation to safeguard Wash’s right to a fair trail while vigorously seeking a conviction.
Wash remains in custody while awaiting retrial for capitol murder.
Meanwhile, Kansans for Democracy contended on the mailer to voters that passage of the constitutional amendment Tuesday would “keep murderers off the street.” The claim was accompanied by photographs of Jonathan and Reginald Carr and a 2014 TV news headline noting the Supreme Court overturned a portion of the brothers’ death sentences.
The brothers were charged with multiple counts of murder, robbery, kidnapping and rape in the 2000 deaths of five people and wounding of two others in Wichita. In 2002, they were convicted of dozens of offenses and each received four death sentences.
A majority of the Supreme Court in 2016 overturned three death sentences because jury instructions on sex-crimes tied to capital murder were “fatally erroneous” and three capital murder charges duplicated the first. In addition, the Supreme Court said the trial judge failed to adequately separate the penalty proceedings for each defendant so the jury could show mercy to one defendant while refusing to show mercy to the other.
The U.S. Supreme Court reinstated the death sentences for the Carr brothers by concluding the jury instructions and combined proceedings didn’t violate the Constitution.
The state Supreme Court affirmed the death penalty for the brothers in 2022. At no point in the appellate process were the brothers released from state prison.

name: VTDigger
title: Scott’s veto reasoning doesn’t hold up
description:
The bill the governor killed protected ratepayers and cut pollution more strongly than the version he says he preferred.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Scott’s veto reasoning doesn’t hold up.
text:
This commentary is by Ben Edgerly Walsh, the climate and energy program director of the Vermont Public Interest Research Group.
Let’s start with what isn’t in dispute. The data center bill Gov. Phil Scott vetoed, H.727, was among the strongest such laws written in any state. AI data centers are driving up electricity bills across the country, and having major impacts on air, water and climate pollution in the process. And here in Vermont, that now-dead bill that would have addressed each of those issues passed both the House and Senate with overwhelming support from both Democrats and Republicans, before being killed by Gov. Phil Scott and the 52 Republican representatives who voted to sustain his veto.
You may hear that the final bill was somehow worse than the earlier House version — a fumble, a bill that “shape-shifted” into something that demanded a veto, as one commentary in these pages put it recently.
The truth of the matter is that the final bill built on what the House started, and protected Vermonters more effectively in almost every way than that initial version.
Let’s take a look at what actually changed.
On your electricity bill, the earlier version the governor preferred directed utilities to “mitigate the risk” that other ratepayers would cover “unwarranted” data center costs. To mitigate means to reduce impacts, not eliminate them, meaning the governor’s preferred bill inherently allowed data centers to pass on even some unwarranted costs to Vermonters.
The legislature rewrote that to require other ratepayers be “insulated from all costs” tied to data center deployment.
On pollution, the legislature turned vague language into hard requirements. It required data centers to maximize on-site renewable energy. It required them to fund energy-saving projects in surrounding communities, to offset their inherent environmental impact. And it barred them from running on-site fossil-fuel generators except in a genuine emergency, preventing the kind of practices that have spiked air pollution in communities across the country.
So put the question plainly to every representative who voted to sustain the veto, every organization like Vermonters for a Clean Environment that has since complained about this stronger version of the bill and Gov. Scott: Which of those provisions made the bill worse? Was it the one that shields your power bill? The one that cuts pollution? The one that delivers benefits directly to any communities hosting data centers?
The only way the “it got worse” math works is if weaker protection for Vermonters is the goal.
The governor also offered another reason for his veto. In his veto letter, he wrote that the bill imposed “new and unnecessary regulatory systems” that were only “seemingly aimed at data centers” and would drive other businesses away.
The reality is that the bill was narrowly targeted at data centers alone, at a time when state after state is tightening regulations on large loads across the board, sweeping in any business that draws a lot of power. Vermont’s legislature deliberately chose not to go that route. H.727 applied to data centers, and only data centers, a single and uniquely power-hungry class of user. It answered the governor’s stated concern before he ever raised it.
Lastly, the governor argued, “existing Vermont law already provides substantial regulatory authority to prevent harmful impacts.” In essence, “we’re fine, I’m not worried.”
That question, whether Act 250 and other Vermont laws already have us covered, was one of the very first things the legislature dug into when they took this bill up. The answer? Perhaps on paper, but there were clearly gaps.
In the context of an industry with numerous players that count their market value well into the hundreds of billions or even trillions of dollars, that can hire armies of lawyers unlike an Act 250 district commission or even the Vermont Public Utility Commission has ever seen, that is steeped in a move fast and break things mentality, the legislature chose to do everything it could to fill those potential gaps.
In essence, seeing massive costs and pollution from AI data centers around the country, the legislature took a better-safe-than-sorry approach. The legislature handed the governor the strongest data center protections in the country: narrowly written, hard on costs and pollution, leaving every other Vermont business or potential business untouched.

READ MORE

Simply put, the governor’s veto of a bill to protect Vermonters from AI data center costs and pollution is baffling. Vermont needs these protections before we suffer the harms people are already experiencing in other states. Data centers aren’t going away, so we’ll be back next session to fight for Vermonters again. 
In the meantime, if a representative or governor tells you the bill they helped kill was actually too strong, ask them the one question they still haven’t answered: Which protection, exactly, were Vermonters better off without?

name: Rhode Island Current
title: West Nile risk level rises in Rhode Island as virus found in more mosquitoes
description: Five mosquito pools collected in Providence County tested positive for West Nile virus last week, bringing Rhode Island’s total to seven positive samples this summer. The latest findings in East Providence, North Providence and Providence led state officials to bump up the statewide West Nile risk level to “high,” according to a joint announcement issued […]
text:
A close-up view of the wings and abdomen of a Culex quinquefasciatus, or southern house mosquito. (Photo by Lauren Bishop/U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)Five mosquito pools collected in Providence County tested positive for West Nile virus last week, bringing Rhode Island’s total to seven positive samples this summer.
The latest findings in East Providence, North Providence and Providence led state officials to bump up the statewide West Nile risk level to “high,” according to a joint announcement issued by the Rhode Island departments of Environmental Management and Health.
No people have tested positive for West Nile in Rhode Island this year.
Last week’s positive samples all contained mosquitoes from the Culex genus, also known as typical mosquitoes, of which several species are known to transmit West Nile virus. This is the largest batch of positive samples tested in Rhode Island this mosquito season, which runs from May to October. 
Three of the positive samples came from East Providence. North Providence and Providence accounted for one positive sample each. The five positives were gathered on July 20 as part of Environmental Management’s weekly testing. Mosquitoes are trapped at various locations statewide, then sorted into “pools” based on species. Each pool is then tested at the State Health Laboratory. 
For the week of July 19 through July 25, 155 mosquito pools — 2,021 mosquitoes in all — were collected and tested.
The first positive sample of 2026 came from a Culex pool in Providence the week of June 28 to July 4. The second positive sample came from a pool containing a different kind of mosquito, Coquillettidia perturbans, that was collected in Cranston the week of July 12 to July 18.
So far, there haven’t been positive tests of any other mosquito-borne illnesses like Eastern Equine Encephalitis or Jamestown Canyon virus.
West Nile is the most common of mosquito-borne illnesses in the United States, and most infected people do not develop symptoms. About 1 in 5 who contract the virus may have fever, headaches or body aches. Rarely, the virus can cause neuroinvasive illnesses like encephalitis or meningitis. 
There have been 113 cases of West Nile virus in people across 23 states so far in 2026, according to preliminary data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Of those cases, 76 involved neuroinvasive illness.
State health officials advise residents to guard against mosquitoes by applying bug repellant, wearing long sleeves and pants when the mosquitoes are active around dawn and dusk, emptying standing water where mosquitoes can breed and fixing holes in windows or door screens so mosquitoes can’t enter homes.
The Department of Health maintains and uploads its weekly testing data online.

title: Brown University President Christina Paxson to step down before her contract ends
description: Brown University President Christina H. Paxson announced Monday she will step down at the end of the 2026-27 academic year — a full year before the end of her current contract, which was extended last year. Paxson, who became Brown’s 19th president in July 2012, wrote in a letter to the university community Monday that […]
text:
Brown University President Christina H. Paxson, who announced Monday that she will step down at the end of the 2026-27 academic year. (Photo by Nick Dentamaro/Brown University)Brown University President Christina H. Paxson announced Monday she will step down at the end of the 2026-27 academic year — a full year before the end of her current contract, which was extended last year.
Paxson, who became Brown’s 19th president in July 2012, wrote in a letter to the university community Monday that she had “mixed emotions” when she told the school’s ruling body, the Corporation of Brown University, earlier Monday about the early end to her tenure.
But Paxson, 66, maintained in her letter that this is “the right decision for me and my family. And I firmly believe that it is the best path for Brown.”
“Fifteen years is a significant tenure for any president, and in that time, this amazing community of faculty, staff, students, alumni, parents and friends showed up in so many ways to achieve the bold aspirations in the strategic plan we developed together near the beginning of my presidency,” Paxson wrote, adding that the campus “worked vigilantly to demonstrate the value of Brown to the world.”
She wrote that Brown should have a change in leadership so that “the vision for the next phase is set by Brown’s next leader and stewarded by them from the beginning.”
In his own letter to the school community Monday, University Chancellor Brian T. Moynihan said the Corporation will launch a national search for Brown’s next president with participation from the campus community, although there’s no timeline yet for choosing Paxson’s successor. 
In May 2025, the Corporation of Brown University unanimously approved an extension of Paxson’s term through June 30, 2028. Her presidency would have expired in June 2026 without the extension. At the time of the extension, Paxson said her decision to stay on was influenced by a federal freeze on certain research funding and broader uncertainty in academia amid changes introduced by President Donald Trump’s administration. 
Brown University extends Paxson’s presidential term through June 2028

Paxson — a Columbia University-educated economist whose own research focused on poverty, health, education and inequality — reiterated in her Monday letter that she remained president to “help Brown navigate a federal funding freeze that imperiled our mission of research and education.” 
Brown and the Trump administration later struck a deal that reimbursed the university for more than $50 million in unpaid federal grant costs, and also melted a deeper freeze that could have tied up about $510 million in grants for health and life sciences research at the university. 
As part of the bargain, Brown was required to provide $50 million over 10 years to local workforce development initiatives. The settlement also concluded three federal probes: one involving race-conscious admissions, another involving alleged Title VI violations and a third regarding the school’s response to antisemitism on campus. Brown was not required to make payments to the federal government or admit wrongdoing. 
“I am proud that we came to an agreement with the federal government that restored our funding while staying true to Brown’s values,” Paxson wrote.
Brown also agreed to adhere to revised federal definitions of gender when it came to university athletics and housing. Paxson’s decision to accept the compromise that offered only binary definitions of gender drew criticism from some students, faculty and LGBTQ+ advocates who saw it as a capitulation to the Trump administration. 
Other high-profile incidents which transpired during Paxson’s tenure included the campus shooting in December 2025, which killed two students and injured nine people, as well as on-campus conflicts over the Gaza war. In April 2024, Paxson reached an agreement with pro-Palestinian students to end their weeklong encampment on Brown’s College Green. A student-led initiative to have the Corporation divest from companies connected to Israel was rejected later that year. 
Moynihan attached to his letter a list of “major highlights” from Paxson’s presidency.
“Chris has steered the University through very challenging times, including a pandemic, dramatic policy changes for higher education, and a tragic shooting,” Moynihan wrote. “She has done so with that balance of commitment to academic excellence, operational excellence and a collaborative philosophy.”
Among those accomplishments credited to Paxson are more than $2 billion in campus investments, including about $700 million in Providence’s Jewelry District. The BrownTogether fundraising campaign saw more than 76,800 donors contribute over $4.4 billion during Paxson’s tenure. 
The creation or expansion of institutions including the School of Public Health, Brown Arts Institute and Jonathan M. Nelson Center for Entrepreneurship occurred during Paxson’s presidency, as did the elimination of loans from undergraduate financial aid packages and tuition for families making under $125,000 a year. 
“I will look back on my time as Brown’s president as the most rewarding job I could possibly have had,” Paxson wrote in her letter. “Truly, it has been the opportunity of a lifetime.”
Paxson said she will soon outline priorities and goals for her final year in the president’s office.
“This is not a time to put ambitious plans on pause,” she wrote. “I look forward to working with all of you as we continue to move Brown forward.”

text:
New statewide initiative will coordinate business resources, while questions remain about grant selection, oversight and measurable returns
By George D. Rotsch, Editor Delaware LIVE
WILMINGTON, Del. — Gov. Matt Meyer on Monday launched Innovate Delaware, a statewide initiative intended to help startups find capital, connect with established companies and research institutions, and expand Delaware’s ability to attract emerging businesses.
The program will be housed within the Delaware Prosperity Partnership, the state’s public-private economic development organization, and will focus on financial technology, advanced materials, biopharma manufacturing, clean energy and next-generation chemical products.
Meyer said Delaware has many of the assets needed to compete for innovative companies but has lacked a coordinated system to connect entrepreneurs with investors, universities, corporations and business-support organizations.
“Delaware has all the ingredients to lead in innovation,” Meyer said. “We have world-class research institutions, talented entrepreneurs, and a prime, central location. Now we have the infrastructure to turn great ideas into great companies.”
Innovate Delaware will operate around four areas: developing a stronger pipeline of startups, attracting investment capital, connecting new companies with corporations and helping international companies establish operations in Delaware.
The initiative also will create a digital “front door” intended to provide entrepreneurs with a central place to seek assistance and receive referrals to existing organizations.
Supporters say the approach could make it easier for business owners to navigate Delaware’s economic development system without creating a replacement for organizations already serving entrepreneurs.
The administration said Innovate Delaware will track startups, investors, referrals and program outcomes. That focus on data and measurable results could help address concerns that economic development programs sometimes measure activity — such as meetings, events and applications — without demonstrating whether they produce lasting jobs or private investment.
The state will provide $1.36 million over two years from the Delaware Strategic Fund to pay for personnel, technology, marketing and events associated with Innovate Delaware.
DPP separately operates on a $3.1 million budget supported by the state Bond Bill and private-sector investments.
Noah Olson, DPP’s vice president of innovation, said the program is designed to improve Delaware’s ability to attract and retain high-growth companies, venture capital and skilled workers.
“The four-pillars approach will systematically improve Delaware’s competitiveness in the attraction, development and retention of high-growth companies, venture capital and innovation talent,” Olson said.
Rural health challenge will be first major project
Innovate Delaware’s first major undertaking will be the Delaware Rural Health Challenge, a multistage health technology accelerator that could provide as much as $25 million in grants over five years.
The program is intended to identify problems affecting rural and medically underserved communities and select technology companies to test new approaches to delivering care.
Potential areas could include telehealth, medical workforce shortages, transportation barriers, remote diagnostics and access to specialists, although the press release did not identify the specific technologies or companies that may receive funding.
The Rural Health Challenge will be supported through a federal Rural Health Transformation Program award funded by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.
The administration said the broader federal financial assistance award totals approximately $157.4 million and is fully funded by the federal government.
The health initiative could provide meaningful support to rural Delaware communities, where residents may have fewer providers and longer travel times for medical care. However, the announcement did not answer several questions about how grant recipients will be selected or how taxpayers will know whether the projects succeed.
Measuring results
DPP said the Delaware Strategic Fund is intended to support investments that generate measurable returns, including companies created, jobs produced, capital deployed and tax revenue generated.
That standard could provide a useful framework for evaluating Innovate Delaware.
The strongest case for the program would be evidence that it leads to sustainable businesses, private investment, permanent Delaware jobs and improved access to rural health care.
The program could face greater criticism if its results are measured primarily by conferences held, referrals completed, websites launched, or grant money distributed.
The announcement did not provide specific performance targets for the first two years of Innovate Delaware or explain what would happen if the program fails to meet its goals.
It also did not state whether an independent auditor or outside evaluator will review the program’s economic impact.
Who will select the winners?
The Governor did not identify the individuals or organizations that will evaluate applications and select companies for Rural Health Challenge grants.
It also did not specify whether selections will be made by DPP staff, state officials, outside health care experts, independent reviewers or a combination of those groups.
Other unanswered questions include whether the names and qualifications of the reviewers will be disclosed, whether companies will be scored using publicly available criteria and whether applications, rankings and award decisions will be subject to public review.
The administration also did not say whether grant recipients will be required to contribute private capital, create jobs in Delaware or maintain operations in the state after receiving public support.
Those details will be important because the program could distribute millions of dollars to private companies. Clear selection standards and public reporting could help protect the process from favoritism and ensure awards are based on the strength of the proposals rather than political relationships or preferred industries.
Questions also remain about how the state will evaluate whether a health technology is financially sustainable after grant funding expires.
Pilot programs often generate promising short-term results but end when government support runs out. A successful project would likely need a long-term customer, such as a hospital, insurer, medical provider or private investor, to continue operating without permanent taxpayer support.
Business and university leaders support initiative
Leaders from the University of Delaware, Delaware State University, the Delaware Small Business Development Center, the Center for Accelerating Financial Equity and several entrepreneurship organizations praised the announcement.
University of Delaware President Laura Carlson said the university is prepared to support the state’s effort to move research into commercial applications.
Stephanie Johnnie, executive director of the Pete du Pont Freedom Foundation, said Delaware entrepreneurs could benefit from a more coordinated system.
“Our opportunity is to build a more connected system that helps them move from idea to execution and from early traction to sustainable growth,” Johnnie said.
The initiative’s focus on connecting existing organizations rather than replacing them may appeal to business leaders who want the state to reduce barriers and improve coordination without building another large government bureaucracy.
The ultimate test, however, will be whether Innovate Delaware becomes a practical entry point for entrepreneurs or another layer in an already complex economic development system.
For now, the announcement represents a potentially pro-growth investment with bipartisan appeal: help businesses find capital, connect research to the marketplace and attract companies to Delaware.
But the program’s long-term credibility will depend on transparency, private-sector participation and measurable returns — particularly as officials begin selecting companies to receive funding through the Rural Health Challenge.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Two Georgia universities scratch extra essay from admissions process
description: High school seniors applying this year to two of Georgia’s most selective colleges may have it a little easier than their older brothers and sisters after the University of Georgia and Georgia Tech have both announced they will no longer require supplemental essays for applicants. “The ultimate goal is really to simplify the application for […]
text:
Future Georgia Tech students will have a little bit less work to do filling out their applications after the school along with the University of Georgia announced they are doing away with supplemental essays. John McCosh/Georgia Recorder (file photo)High school seniors applying this year to two of Georgia’s most selective colleges may have it a little easier than their older brothers and sisters after the University of Georgia and Georgia Tech have both announced they will no longer require supplemental essays for applicants.
“The ultimate goal is really to simplify the application for students, to take one layer out of the process,” said Mary Tipton Woolley, the executive director of Georgia Tech’s Office of Undergraduate Admission. “We know the application process takes time. It takes a lot of thought from students. It requires students to be thoughtful and introspective, and if we determine that something that is part of the application is no longer useful, then we want to remove that to make it more simple for students.”
Prospective students will still need to turn in a personal essay as part of the Common App, which is an online platform students use to apply for multiple colleges. That essay will be read by each school they apply for, but the change means students will no longer have to write separate essays assigned by the schools.
For Tech, the essay was typically about why the student wanted to study there or why they wanted to pursue their particular major, and UGA previously asked students to write about a book that had a strong impact on them.
College applicants sometimes find themselves writing over a dozen separate essays in an expensive and highly competitive process while balancing a full high school course load and other responsibilities.
A 2023 report from the National Association for College Admission Counseling found that nearly three quarters of counselors listed simplifying the application process as one of the top three proposed changes to help student mental health.
Woolley said part of the change comes down to the increasing use of artificial intelligence, but that’s not the whole story. The internet is full of advice on writing the type of college essay admissions officers supposedly want to read, she said, and with 68,000 essays to read from applicants last year, they start to sound the same.
“I think some of that is due to the fact that they’re just more well-known,” she said. “They’ve been around for a long time. There’s a lot available to students to guide them to write a certain way.”
Impact on students and colleges
Charles Mendels and Elaine Rosenblum, cofounders of Access Test Prep and Tutoring in Buckhead, work every day with students who dream of going to UGA, Georgia Tech or other top schools.
The two said the change will be a help for students like theirs, but Rosenblum lamented what she characterized as a shift away from emphasizing writing skills.
“I think there’s a cost to this in terms of the students and their critical and analytical thinking and having to talk about themselves or think about themselves in a critical and analytical way,” she said. “I think you can send people to college and give them technical skills, but without the critical and analytical skills, it could be an issue. I’m already seeing it with graduating students who aren’t being forced to write and really analyze.”
The SAT has discontinued its optional essay section, and students often skip the optional ACT essay because very few colleges require it as part of the admissions process.
Mendels said a move away from supplemental essays will mean more students will decide there’s no harm in applying to additional schools.
And having more applicants benefits institutions by making them seem more exclusive.
“If you get more people applying, you look like a more selective school,” he said.
Part of a trend?
Woolley said it’s too early to say whether the change will be part of a trend in Georgia, but other selective schools across the country have dropped their supplemental essays, including Tulane University, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, and the University of Virginia.
According to the UVA Alumni Association’s Virginia Magazine, the number of first-year applicants to that university increased by more than 27% the year after that school dropped its supplemental essay requirement. The school’s previous record application increase was 17% in 2021, though the university noted it could not speculate on a cause behind the increase.
In a response to a comment on a blog post announcing the change, UGA’s executive director of undergraduate admissions David Graves said he’s expecting an increase in applications, but not at the same level UVA saw.
“UVA is also test optional as opposed to UGA being test required, so we do not expect as much of a jump,” he wrote. “I also feel that if one 250-300 word essay is the difference between applying or not, then a number of additional applications might not be as strong. But this was more of a focus on both the applicants themselves and my team. We could have added hurdles for students to apply, but is that really for the best for our future applicants who are already stressed and overworked?”

title: Legal services contract expires, and unaccompanied immigrant children face deportation
text: WASHINGTON — More than 20,000 unaccompanied immigrant children Monday lost their legal representation because the Trump administration has not entered into a new agreement to take over their legal services after it let a longstanding contract with a nonprofit expire.Without legal representation, fewer than 10% of immigrant children win the right to remain in the United States while their case goes through immigration court. Immigration attorneys and advocates worry the loss in legal aid will put children on a fast track to deportations.“Right now we're all in the dark, and the secrecy is a big part of the problem,” said Shaina Aber, the executive director of the Acacia Center for Justice, which previously held the contract that expired July 31.The Department of Health and Human Services, which issues the contract, did not respond to several emails from States Newsroom asking which new organization will take over legal services in immigration courts for unaccompanied kids. HHS has also not submitted any request for new contractors to provide legal services to unaccompanied minors, according to a States Newsroom review of the federal government’s website for contracts.Additionally, Scott Ehlers, the director of the Texas Indigent Defense Commission, an organization that the Trump administration was initially eyeing to take over legal services for unaccompanied minors, told States Newsroom it had not been awarded a contract from HHS and had not been contacted by the department regarding one. Aber said that HHS has not informed Acacia who the new contractor will be, implemented a transition of children’s cases to new attorneys, or paid the organization for completed legal work since December. HHS has not reimbursed $65 million to Acacia, which distributes the federal funding to roughly 100 organizations across the country who provide legal representation to unaccompanied children in immigration cases. Struggle over sensitive informationThe Trump administration let the contract with Acacia expire after attorneys refused to hand over sensitive case information about their clients, such as whether a child has a pending visa. Aber said since January, immigration attorneys have seen government attorneys try to use visa information in order to place children in deportation proceedings. “The government has come up with this novel idea that they're using in the immigration court proceedings that if a visa is pending for a child, that means it's purely speculative that the child would ever have status, and therefore they are ordering deportations for kids who actually have pending T visas, that's a trafficking visa, kids who have pending special immigrant juvenile status, kids with U visas,” she said. “All of those kids are being ordered removed by the courts, even as their visas are awaiting them.”U nonimmigrant status, or U visas, are set aside for immigrants 21 and younger who were the victim of a crime, or helped provide information to prosecutors about criminal activity. Separately, a special immigrant juvenile status is extended to immigrant children who have been “abandoned, abused, or neglected” by a parent, and that visa provides a pathway for a green card. A nonprofit in Pennsylvania, the Jewish Family and Community Services of Pittsburgh, recently filed a lawsuit on behalf of several immigrant children against the Trump administration’s practice of targeting children with pending visas for deportation.Aber said she is worried that the next organization to obtain the contract will hand over that sensitive information to the Trump administration.  “We are very concerned about any agreement that the government has entered into with a new contractor about sharing confidential details or privileged information contrary to children's interests,” she said.Confusion about legal servicesAber said HHS is still working on accepting a transition proposal, meaning that Acacia and providers in its network cannot even begin having conversations with children to inform them that someone else will be representing them in immigration court. “To have those really sensitive conversations with the child, where you're saying, ‘Hey, I'm not going to be able to represent you anymore, or like these are your options in terms of representation’ …. we can't start having those conversations with kids without that information,” she said. She added that officials at the Office of Refugee and Resettlement, the agency within HHS that houses some unaccompanied immigrant children, are still reaching out to Acacia and its legal services providers even after the contract expired, asking for legal services for newly arrived children. Almost 1,800 children are in ORR’s care, according to agency data from June. “They keep on reaching out to our legal service services network, asking if someone could please go over on their own dime to talk to new arriving children,” Aber said. Some of the organizations that partner with Acacia have been able to dip into reserves to continue providing services to kids, but others have had to stop providing the services altogether, Aber said.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: US Senate candidate asks judge to put him on special GOP primary ballot
description: A decertified candidate for U.S. Senate is asking a South Carolina judge to order his name be included on special primary election ballots.
text:
Decertified U.S. Senate candidate Danny Ford II speaks with his lawyers ahead of a Richland County court hearing Monday, Aug. 3, 2026, in which he asked the judge to put him on the ballot for the special Republican primary. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — A decertified candidate for U.S. Senate is asking a judge to order his name be included on special GOP primary ballots going forward.
But with absentee and overseas military ballots already in the mail, the South Carolina Republican Party argues altering ballots now would interrupt an election already in progress.
Danny Ford II of Clemson, one of a dozen people who filed to run in the Aug. 11 primary, sued the Republican Party last week for disqualifying him as a candidate. The winner of the primary will replace U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham on the ballot in November following his unexpected death July 11.

Circuit Court Judge Daniel Coble heard the case of decertified U.S. Senate candidate Danny Ford II on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026, at the Richland County Courthouse. Ford sued the state Republican Party and asked the judge to put him on the ballot for the special GOP primary. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)

Meanwhile, some 1,870 absentee and overseas military ballots have gone out since July 29 and nearly 60 have already been cast and returned.
“These are ballots that are in play,” said Thomas Nicholson, an attorney for the state Election Commission. “How do you un-ring that bell?
“I’m not sure how you do it without ordering a new election,” Nicholson added.
But Ford, son of Clemson’s first national football championship coach, is not asking the court to take it that far.
His lawyers said he respects that absentee and military voters won’t see his name on the ballot. Should the judge rule in Ford’s favor, they said, Ford’s name should be included on “all ballots practical” between the time of the judge’s order and election day Aug. 11.
Attorneys for the state GOP also urged Circuit Court Judge Daniel Coble not to make any changes. In the past, they said, courts have shied away from cases after voting is already underway.
“It would gut this election,” the party’s attorney, Rob Tyson, told reporters following the Monday court hearing.
Ford, who in June lost his bid to be South Carolina’s next agriculture commissioner, was one of three U.S. Senate candidates the GOP party decertified, citing party rules.
One candidate, Clark Neilson, was disqualified for living in North Carolina. The other two, Ford and self-named “hip-hop Republican” Darius Mitchell, were deemed ineligible for failing to meet a new rule requiring all candidates vote in two of the last three statewide GOP primaries.
Ford’s lawyers argued the rule, which the party added in June, violates the state constitution’s requirement that the Legislature set how and when an election takes place. Political parties, acting as an extension of the state Election Commission, certify that a candidate meets qualifications for office under state law, his lawyers said.
Because the party is essentially “inhabiting the role of the state,” said Ford’s attorney Skyler Hutto, state law doesn’t allow the party to enact rules that are in conflict with state or federal requirements. Because the rule disqualifies an otherwise qualified candidate, it goes too far, he said.

Democratic Senate Minority Leader Brad Hutto, left, and his son Skyler Hutto, right, served as attorneys for decertified U.S. Senate candidate Danny Ford II during a Richland County court hearing Monday, Aug. 3, 2026, in which Ford asked the judge to put him on the ballot for the special Republican primary. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)

“This is where the rubber begins to meet the road,” Hutto added.
The party countered that the First Amendment gives political parties leeway to decide who they affiliate with, and by extension, who can run in their primaries.
As long as party rules don’t run in direct contrast to the constitutional requirements to run for Senate — 30 years of age, a U.S. citizen for at least nine years, and residency in the state at the time of election — it has the ability to include additional requirements, the party’s lawyer said.
Tyson also said the party isn’t violating Ford’s right to seek office because he could run as a write-in candidate.
“But he doesn’t have a right to be on the Republican primary ballot,” he added.
Ford’s legal team also said the GOP’s new rule is arbitrary because it doesn’t define what counts as a separate election and leaves it up to party discretion on when to waive it.
Ford said he asked the party for a waiver. But the party’s waiver process does not allow candidates to apply for one themselves, spokeswoman Grace Short told the SC Daily Gazette. Party staff instead told decertified candidates they would need a voting member of the party to make a motion on their behalf.

South Carolina Republican Party Chairman sits in the audience for a Richland County court hearing Monday, Aug. 3, 2026, in which decertified U.S. Senate candidate Danny Ford II sued the party and asked the judge to put him on the ballot for the special Republican primary. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)

Of the 48 voting members from 44 counties present during the certification meeting, none spoke up for Ford or any of the other candidates, Short said.
Ford also contends his votes in the June 9 GOP primary and the June 23 runoff, in which he lost to Republican Cody Simpson to become the party’s nominee for state agriculture chief, should count as separate statewide elections, allowing him to run.
The party counted those as a single election cycle. Tyson said the state Election Commission did the same when it barred anyone who cast a Democratic ballot in June from voting in the special primary.
By that argument, Hutto countered, the party already granted Ford his GOP bona fides for this election cycle when it certified him to run for commissioner of agriculture.
Coble told lawyers to file paperwork by 5 p.m. Monday and said he’d make a decision soon after.
Depending on how quickly the judge rules, that could leave the state Election Commission with less than 40 hours to reprint ballots and reset voting machines in time for the start of early voting at 8 a.m. Wednesday.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Green FC men are undefeated national champions — again
description:
“I'm feeling a ton of pride,” said club co-founder Patrick Infurna in an interview Monday. “They always find a way to win.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Green FC men are undefeated national champions — again.
text:
The Vermont Green FC men’s team defeated Flint City Bucks on Aug. 1, 2026, to win the USL2 championship. Courtesy Vermont Green FC
Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
Mike Popovitch, a dyed-in-the-wool Vermont Green FC fan, spent a rainy Saturday evening in Flint, Michigan, leading over 150 traveling fans in song through a megaphone.
The Green won 2-1 against the Flint City Bucks that night in the national final of the United Soccer League’s second men’s tier. The win earned the club its second consecutive championship, making Vermont Green the first team to achieve that feat in over two decades. Head coach Chris Taylor’s team has not lost in the nationwide summer league, which is composed mainly of college players, since July 2024 — a 42-match unbeaten streak.
“It was an amazing experience,” Popovitch said of his journey to Michigan over the weekend. Having followed the Green “since day one,” he serves as a capo — a sort of informal chant conductor — for the club’s most dedicated supporters.
“It just really shows what this team has done for this community,” he said of the final’s atmosphere.
Saturday’s win comes in a triumphant period for soccer in Burlington. The University of Vermont men’s soccer team’s improbable championship win in 2024 was followed by the Green’s first national title last year. And after the club’s women’s side reached the national final in its inaugural year last month, the men’s team swept to yet another undefeated championship season.
Despite controlling large swaths of a cagey match Saturday, the Green were kept unusually quiet until breaking the deadlock by way of a second-half own goal. After conceding almost immediately, Vermont pulled ahead again in the 75th minute through a penalty kick from standout midfielder Ryan Zellefrow.
“I’m feeling a ton of pride,” said club co-founder Patrick Infurna in an interview Monday. “They always find a way to win.”
“It’s probably the most emotional I’ve been at the final whistle,” agreed Taylor in a club statement after the game. “To do it a second year in a row … last year was magical, this is incredible.”
For Infurna, it was painful to play the final away from the Green’s home support, which has seen Virtue Field’s 2,500-seat bleachers sold out nearly every match this season for both the men and women. Based on the team’s record, he feels this year’s playoff run should rightfully have been set in Burlington.
But nonetheless, he said, the traveling Green fans rivaled the much larger home crowd in rowdiness, creating an atmosphere “worthy of a final.” Watch parties across the state also tuned in from afar, from the Mad Rose in Rutland to the Zero Gravity Beer Hall in Burlington.

READ MORE

Over the last few years, Popovitch said, he’s been “growing to love the team — growing to love the sport — in a way that I didn’t know that I could.” In addition to his membership in the Green Mountain Bhoys, the club’s primary supporters’ group, he also co-hosts and produces the podcast “United in Green.” 
“You’re able to experience something that’s just joyful and positive,” he said of the team. “It’s kind of an escape for people from their hectic normal lives.”
The UVM Medical Center X-ray technician has seen his kids grow up around the club too, with both now holding season passes. He credits Vermont Green with creating a welcoming culture for its youngest fans, and “giving them the ability to dream, you know, that maybe they can play for this team someday,” he said.
Infurna said he has outlined the long-term aspirations of his club with this next generation of fans in mind. In the background of on-the-field successes, he said, the club is hoping to build lasting cultural infrastructure and find even more ways to connect with the growing community of fans.
“We want this to sit in people’s lives,” he said. By the time the kids watching today are adults, he added, “They get to remember it as it was, and they get to build on it themselves.”
Both the Green men’s and women’s teams will be back in regular season action next May.
In the meantime, Infurna hopes to celebrate Saturday’s win at a UVM sporting event soon, though many players have already dispersed across the country for their fall seasons. In any event, he said, “We’ll find ways to make sure that trophy gets around, and the people who really deserve to be a part of those celebrations get to be a part of it.”
