name: Washington State Standard
title: Rising tension in central WA as farmland is eyed for energy and data center projects
description: The Facebook post shows an AI-generated image of two farmers staring into the distance at golden hour, overlaid with the text “local landowners deserve a say.” It’s a reference to where energy projects should be allowed in south-central Washington. These sponsored posts from “Make Energy Right Klickitat” have been appearing in the social media feeds […]
text:
Windmills are seen on the horizon, above fields, in south-central, Washington. Known for agriculture, the area has become a hotbed for clean energy projects and interest in building data centers is also rising. (Photo by Emma Renly)The Facebook post shows an AI-generated image of two farmers staring into the distance at golden hour, overlaid with the text “local landowners deserve a say.”
It’s a reference to where energy projects should be allowed in south-central Washington. These sponsored posts from “Make Energy Right Klickitat” have been appearing in the social media feeds of residents in the area. 
Klickitat County is covered by rolling hills of hay production, vineyards and grazing livestock. But the county, which is roughly the size of Delaware and has about 24,300 residents, is also an epicenter in the region’s battles over clean energy facilities and more recently, data centers. 
County officials have been working on a policy to guide development of solar and large-scale battery storage projects and specifically how those are balanced against agriculture. 
“If the proposal is on what’s considered prime agricultural land that is highly productive, then it’ll be encouraged not to use those lands,” said Planning Director Scott Edelman.
There is a preference to support agrivoltaics projects, which means land would host solar panels and simultaneously be used for farming. The cost is generally higher for developers. Additionally, the policy would set guidelines for how close these projects could be to neighboring residents’ land and the allowed noise level.
River Turn and Make Energy Right
As the county irons out its policy, a proposed power facility now in the queue is the River Turn Energy Center. It was initially proposed as an 800-megawatt solar facility and 800-megawatt battery energy storage system on Klickitat’s eastern border, where the cropland is considered exceptionally poor.  
A new website for the project shows it could involve up to 1,050 megawatts of solar generation accompanied by an 800-megawatt battery storage facility. 
Savion Renewable Energy, a subsidiary of Shell Energy, is developing River Turn. If built, it would be one of the larger solar facilities in the Pacific Northwest. Documents show the company secured 4,700 acres for the project via a long-term lease with five separate landowners.
Previously, Savion has been at odds with the county over its solar ordinance, calling the draft one of the most restrictive policies of its kind in the country. 
The company argued it would push developers to seek approval from Washington’s Energy Facility Site Evaluation Council, instead of at the local level. Since then, local officials have revised the policy to be less restrictive. 
It’s against this backdrop that the Facebook posts have begun popping up.
A Facebook post that’s been appearing in feeds in south-central Washington is backed by a group that is aligned with energy project developers. It suggests landowners “deserve a say” in local land use policy. (Image via Facebook)
Records and information on social media reveal that Make Energy Right Klickitat is working with Savion to lobby landowners to submit comments in support of land use policies favored by developers. The goal is to build solar facilities on agricultural land. 
Views on this are mixed locally, as above-market lease payments can provide a financial lifeline for farmers.
“Farm owners who lease to solar are likely to retire on the solar rent check,” said Matt Chiles, a large landowner in Centerville, a small town in Klickitat. He has been approached by solar companies willing to buy his land outright for $10,000 an acre.
“Given that only about half of my land might be suitable for solar, they are essentially willing to pay $20,000 per acre for good solar production land,” Chiles added. In comparison, an acre of wheat crop on productive soil is worth around $50.
Questions about data center plans
There’s speculation that electricity generated from the River Turn Energy Center will be used for a data center. Shell Energy’s director of regulatory affairs, Greg Macdonald, declined to answer questions on whether that is the case. “I’m sure you understand,” Macdonald added.
A California-based company called AMAUTA Public Affairs is behind the Make Energy Right Klickitat campaign. It’s part of a broader Make Energy Right initiative the firm is overseeing. “We Don’t Just Understand Energy Projects. We Know How to Get Them Approved,” AMAUTA says on its website. 
Ignacio Barragan, the firm’s founder, said in an email that AMAUTA is a member of Renewable Northwest — an energy advocacy organization based in Portland. He said Make Energy Right began because “friends and colleagues across the country shared frustration about the lack of platforms in the energy sector that championed an all-of-the-above strategy in support of America’s energy independence.”
Renewable Northwest presses for clean energy projects in Washington, Oregon, Idaho, and Montana. Asked about those projects supplying power to data centers, Emily Butterfield, communications manager for the group, said: “We can’t and don’t want to direct how energy is used.” 
Cropland in south-central Washington, near the Columbia River. (Photo by Emma Renly)
Jeff Watson, senior development manager with Savion, said the company has worked with Barragan on “early-stage projects across multiple markets.” In a 2025 public comment to Klickitat County, Watson also listed himself as a “landowner advocate” with both Savion and AMAUTA. 
When asked questions about the River Turn solar facility, both Watson and Mitchell Taylor, Savion’s vice president of development, were hesitant to provide details, even walking back statements made in a public meeting early 2025, which Taylor said was only an “early threshold discussion with community leaders.”
He added that the size and scope of the proposed facility has not been finalized and “rather than share information that could ultimately prove inaccurate, we believe it is best to wait until those details are more clearly established.”
Watson added that Savion “remains committed to being transparent” and that the company “has not changed our long-term interest in responsibly exploring this project.”
In the meantime, the county’s planning department is awaiting legal review from an outside consulting attorney on the ordinance. It may be ready for a public hearing in September. An exact approval date is unknown.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Our children are telling us something. Are we listening?
description: Brainerd lost two of its children this summer. Ava Starr was 11 years old. Alexis Thornton was 13. Both were students at Forestview Middle School. They died three weeks apart. Brainerd is grieving. But Brainerd is not alone. Across Minnesota — in small towns and lake communities, on farms and in cities — families are […]
text:
(Photo by Quentin Young/Colorado Newsline)Brainerd lost two of its children this summer. Ava Starr was 11 years old. Alexis Thornton was 13. Both were students at Forestview Middle School. They died three weeks apart.
Brainerd is grieving. But Brainerd is not alone. Across Minnesota — in small towns and lake communities, on farms and in cities — families are facing the same unbearable loss. As Minnesotans, and as people who work every day on mental health, we owe it to Ava, to Alexis, and to every family living with this kind of grief to say plainly what is happening and what we must do about it. Minnesota is losing young people to suicide, according to deeply concerning recent data.
Preliminary data from the Minnesota Department of Health shows that in 2025, Minnesota’s statewide suicide rate increased by 4%  — more than 800 deaths in a single year. Rates are higher in rural counties than in the metro. And while suicide rates for older teens and young adults appear to have stabilized or declined, rates among children ages 10 to 14 are moving in the wrong direction. Ten to fourteen. Kids in middle school. Kids like Ava and Alexis.
This is not an abstraction. This is happening in communities across our state — places where neighbors know each other by name, where kids ride the same buses, where grief travels fast and lingers long.
And yet the resources needed to respond — school counselors, community mental health providers, crisis services, prevention programs — are not equally available to every Minnesota family. In many parts of our state, particularly outside the Twin Cities metro, the gap between need and available care can be vast. Distance is its own barrier. Stigma is another. And the shortage of mental health professionals across Greater Minnesota is not a new problem — it has simply grown more urgent.
Bullying, which is recognized as an adverse childhood experience, is part of this picture, too. We have learned that both Ava and Alexis were being bullied before they died. While bullying does not cause suicide nor is it the sole reason for a suicide loss — a complex public health issue — we know that bullying can intensify the pain of a child who is already struggling. Schools, families and communities all have a role to play in creating trauma-informed and responsive environments where kids feel safe, seen and supported — not just academically, but as whole human beings.
So what do we do?
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
We start by talking. For too long, suicide has been treated as something too frightening or too shameful to name. That silence costs lives. Parents can ask their children directly and compassionately how they’re doing — not just about grades or activities, but about how they feel. Teachers and coaches can be trained to recognize warning signs, and to be trusting adults that kids feel safe talking to. Communities can hold space for these conversations without shame, and prioritize bringing awareness to available resources.
We invest in prevention. Minnesota has evidence-based programs that work — in schools, in communities, in healthcare settings. But they require funding and political will to reach every corner of the state, including the corners that tend to be overlooked. For example, one practical place to start is taking a QPR training. Question, Persuade, Refer is a free, evidence-based course offered by NAMI Minnesota that teaches everyday people how to recognize the warning signs of suicide and how to respond. In 90 minutes, a parent, a teacher, a coach, a neighbor can learn skills that may one day save a life. It’s available online, which means distance is no barrier — anyone in Minnesota can access it from wherever they are.
We address the rural mental health workforce crisis. Telehealth has helped close some of the gap, but it is not sufficient on its own. We need loan forgiveness, other incentive programs, and sustained investment to bring mental health professionals to communities that need them.
We ensure both kids and adults know that there is someone to talk to. The 988 Minnesota Lifeline provides connection to free and confidential support for anyone experiencing mental health or emotional distress. Trained specialists are available 24/7 by dialing or texting the three-digit number 988, or by chatting online at 988lifeline.org. Middle and high school students throughout Minnesota’s school districts and charter schools can find the 988 Lifeline information on their student ID card.
And we hold the losses of Ava Starr and Alexis Thornton, and every family who has walked this road, at the center of everything we do. Not as statistics. As children.
NAMI Minnesota stands ready to help. We offer free education programs — including QPR suicide prevention training — and free support groups for individuals and families living with mental health challenges. No one should have to navigate this alone, and no community should have to face it without support.
To bring a QPR training to your school, faith community, workplace, or community organization, or to find a support group near you, visit namimn.org or reach our HelpLine by calling 651-645-2948 or emailing namihelps@namimn.org. If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text the 988 Lifeline available 24/7/365.
Our children are telling us something. Let’s make sure we’re listening.

name: Nevada Current
title: Retention of 3rd graders is far too late
description: The countdown clock is ticking loudly. Mandatory retention of low-level readers at the end of 3rd grade in Nevada is set to begin in 2028. It is time to pull the plug on, not resuscitate, this piece of legislation that continues to miss the mark in other states. Nevada district superintendents are pushing back. Let’s […]
text:
Retaining 3rd grade students to raise 4th grade reading test scores is a political ruse. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The countdown clock is ticking loudly. Mandatory retention of low-level readers at the end of 3rd grade in Nevada is set to begin in 2028. It is time to pull the plug on, not resuscitate, this piece of legislation that continues to miss the mark in other states.
Nevada district superintendents are pushing back. Let’s hope it’s not too late.
Educational leaders know there are harmful effects of retention after grades K-2 and no proven beneficial ones. They also should admit that individual students have a unique potential for the rate and level to which they learn. 
Retaining 3rd grade students to raise 4th grade reading test scores is a political ruse. If retention policies were truly effective at improving test scores and other academic outcomes, there would be marked improvement in test scores in later grades and college entrance exam scores would soar.
The “Mississippi myth” is perpetuated in spite of the negative influence on high school drop-out and graduation rates. Retention policies have never meaningfully improved reading scores or closed academic achievement gaps. In Mississippi, 8th grade reading scores and ACT scores decreased after the adoption of 3rd grade retention policies.
This is reminiscent of the alleged “Texas miracle” in the 1990’s where statistics were heavily manipulated, student data was fudged and lower-achieving students were excluded from state testing. It created the false portrayal that instructional differences resulted in higher academic achievement, narrowing of achievement gaps and lower drop-out rates. A complete lie.
This helped solidfy the harmful misperception that curriculum and instruction have a weighty influence on standardized test scores. The Houston superintendent that led the district during this scam became the federal Secretary of Education and spearheaded the travesty known as “No Child Left Behind (NCLB)” in 2001.
NCLB established state and national standardized tests as the primary measure of school quality and student success. There has been no proven connection between differences in educational practice and differences in academic outcomes. Yet, educational leaders continue to let media critics and politicians belittle public education with unfounded rhetoric and expectations.
A recent editorial should not go unaddressed. It calls out Nevada education leaders, particularly in the Clark County School District (CCSD). Suggesting that holding back 3rd graders will improve academic outcomes is complete nonsense. There is no evidence that this practice has ever been effective in raising reading test scores.
The editorial rants about fear of accountability and the benefit of retaining low-level readers. This is a prime opportunity for educational leaders in Nevada, particularly superintendents, to step up.
There should be no fear of accountability when measurements of quality and effectiveness are directly linked to educational practice. Graduation and drop-out rates, student behavior along with the safety and well-being of students and staff can be improved. Academic achievement as measured by standardized test score averages cannot.
Stop pretending that curriculum revisions or alignments, improved instructional practices or changes in personnel have ever raised standardized test score averages. Stop smugly touting small random percentages of improvement that are not sustainable. Stop the professional validation of standardized test scores as appropriate measures of classroom learning.
Stop seeking additional funding based on the premise that it will help improve test scores. That too is a political ruse. Adequate funding provides personnel and resources to effectively educate students. Around 80% of a school’s budget is personnel. Test score outcomes are not contingent upon the amount of funding. Money cannot buy higher test scores.
Discontinue using any metric of standardized test scores in district improvement plans. The only proven method to substantially improve test score averages is cheating. Student demographics have always determined state and national testing outcomes.
CCSD’s latest strategic plan includes unattainable goals of raising percentages of proficiency on state tests. Goals similar to those of the two previous superintendents. Goals that resulted in unfulfilled promises. This only adds to the perception that public education is failing.
Students begin to develop feelings of inferiority when they are placed in the bottom reading group in 1st grade. With few exceptions, they will continue to be regarded as low-achievers for the duration of their educational career. It is not due to the lack of motivation or appropriate instruction.
Retention in 3rd grade is humiliating and further solidifies their low standing. Reminders of inferiority occur each year when standardized test results are released. Academic helplessness develops unless other measures of success are obtainable.
Standardized tests produce a normal distribution (bell curve) of raw and percentile scores. The bell curve never shifts. Year after year. Decade after decade. If state and national tests did not yield consistent results, they would have been dumped long ago.
Schools and districts with higher family income levels, better parent education levels and lower levels of English learners and special education students have higher state test score averages. Lower family income and parent education levels produce lower test score averages. EVERY TIME. A consistent pattern in the seventeen public school districts in Nevada.
The title of this column may suggest that retention before 3rd grade is acceptable. Retention should always be carefully considered by the parents, teacher, counselor and principal. It is not universally recommended for any grade level.
This is not a call for the elimination of standardized testing in education. Tests measure some types of academic ability. There should be consideration toward the frequency of testing and the validity of test score averages.
Prior to the testing frenzy of the last quarter century, testing for reading and intelligence levels was commonly administered twice before high school. Typically in 3rd and 7th grades. Then, as now, achievement levels of individual students remained consistent. Test scores were subtly used to rank and sort students.
This is a call for both the governor and state legislators to rescind this harmful mandate. We need to quit playing political games at the expense of children.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Orbin Mauricio Henriquez Serrano survived a violent arrest in St. Paul. It still haunts him.
description: The morning of Jan. 11 began for Orbin Mauricio Henriquez Serrano with an ominous warning: The gas light on his Jeep Cherokee was glowing yellow on the dashboard. He didn’t want to go to work at the restaurant that Sunday morning, but several of his fellow cooks had already called out, fearful of the immigration […]
text:
ST. PAUL, MINNESOTA - JANUARY 11: U.S. Border Patrol agents detain Orbin Mauricio Henriquez Serrano after he whofailed to present citizenship documentation at a gas station on January 11, 2026 in St. Paul, Minnesota. Then-Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino watches in the background. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)The morning of Jan. 11 began for Orbin Mauricio Henriquez Serrano with an ominous warning: The gas light on his Jeep Cherokee was glowing yellow on the dashboard.
He didn’t want to go to work at the restaurant that Sunday morning, but several of his fellow cooks had already called out, fearful of the immigration agents swarming the city. Just four days earlier, ICE agent Jonathan Ross shot Renee Good through her car window, the fatal bullet entering her left temple, as she and her wife protested the agents’ presence in their south Minneapolis neighborhood. Henriquez Serrano had seen the video; it made him feel sick to the stomach.
“I’m counting on you to come in,” Henriquez Serrano’s manager had texted. So he put on his work clothes — dark jeans, a black tee shirt and a faux leather jacket with grey lining — and drove to the gas station closest to his home, the Speedway at the intersection of Snelling and Portland Avenues in St. Paul. 
He pumped gas, bought a Red Bull inside, then got back in the car as a dozen armed, masked Border Patrol agents poured out of their vehicles and into the small parking lot, a handful of protesters and journalists close behind. 
The agents approached Henriquez Serrano’s car and asked him to roll down the window and show them his citizenship documents. 
“We’ve got a Honduran here, we’re trying to get status,” an agent said to someone outside the frame of a video recorded by Status Coup.
Henriquez Serrano refused to roll down the window or open the door.
“I was scared mostly because of the incident with the woman that they killed,” Henriquez Serrano said in Spanish in an interview with the Reformer. “I remember telling them not to kill me like they did to her.”
His words were inaudible behind the glass of the drivers-side window.
“I’m gonna break it, open the door. Open it! Last warning,” an agent shouted, smashing a glass-breaking tool into the bottom right corner of the window.
Henriquez Serrano panicked as the agents reached through the broken window and opened his car door, scrambling over the console into the passenger seat. Officers circled the car, opening the passenger door and attempting to pull him out. Others grabbed at his legs, still on the drivers’ side, yanking him in the opposite direction. The man who broke the window hit him repeatedly with the glass breaker, Henriquez Serrano said. He felt a sharp pain in his knee, which he’d had surgically repaired in 2022 after a car accident.
One of the agents wrapped his arm around Henriquez Serrano’s neck and pulled him to the ground at the base of the gas pump. Four officers kneeled on Henriquez Serrano’s back as they handcuffed him, groaning, his cheek pressed to the frozen concrete. His shirt and coat gathered above his chest, exposing his torso covered in cuts and grease.
ST. PAUL, MINNESOTA – JANUARY 11: U.S. Border Patrol agents drag Orbin Mauricio Henriquez Serrano from his car after breaking the window when he failed to present citizenship documentation at a gas station on January 11, 2026 in St. Paul, Minnesota. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)
A helmeted Gregory Bovino, then-Commander-at-large of the Border Patrol, watched his men swarm around Henriquez Serrano, while others pushed back protestors and reporters. Around this time, Bovino was leading the media on enforcement tours, stopping at gas stations across the Twin Cities to face off with protestors. 
“We’re going to pacify this place, we’re going to roll ‘em up,” Bovino told prosecutors in the U.S. Attorney’s Office shortly after Good’s killing, according to a recent CNN report. (The U.S. Border Patrol did not respond to the Reformer‘s emailed questions for this story.)
The last sensation Henriquez Serrano remembers is the officers’ knees pressing into his back. He couldn’t breathe. The sounds of shouts, horns and whistles disappeared, and his vision faded to black. 
From Honduras to the United States
Henriquez Serrano is from the department of El Paraíso in Honduras, along the border with Nicaragua, where U.S.-backed Contra rebels staged their operations during their three-decades-long guerilla war against the Sandinistas.
The war ended eight years before Henriquez Serrano was born in 1998, but the conflict’s shadow lingered over his country — nearly two-thirds of Hondurans live below the poverty line, and crime is so prevalent, the U.S. State Department warns Americans not to travel to some parts of the country. Henriquez Serrano stayed in school until the age of 16, when his family needed him to start earning money. 
Then, gang members began recruiting him. He did his best to avoid them, he said — he wasn’t interested in their lifestyle. He saw a better future for himself in the Honduran army, but his mother wouldn’t let him join. 
Eventually the hunger, the insecurity and the fear became intolerable. He left Honduras in 2019 with $500, some important documents and the clothes on his back, planning to make the journey on his own — without a coyote, a person who smuggles immigrants across borders for a fee. 
Just half an hour after he arrived at the central bus terminal of the Mexican border city of Nuevo Laredo, two men approached him with machetes, asking questions about who he was and where his family lived, Henriquez Serrano said. They forced him into a van, then ordered him to call his relatives in the United States so they could demand a ransom. Henriquez Serrano complied: “If you don’t, they kill you,” he said. 
The family members paid up, and the kidnappers dumped him on the American bank of the Rio Grande, his phone broken and documents soaked in river water, he said. Immigration agents found him there, and he requested asylum.
He was given a court date and told he would have to wait in Mexico, he said, over his pleas to stay in the U.S. for fear of being kidnapped again. 
The authorities returned him to Nuevo Laredo.
Razor wire along the Rio Grande on the Texas side of the U.S.-Mexico border. Photo by Ariana Figueroa/States Newsroom.
While he was in a store buying a new phone, armed men again approached him, kidnapping him a second time. His family paid another ransom, and this time when the men took him across the river, he fled north as fast as he could. His papers were ruined, and he didn’t want to stick around for the court date.
“That’s why I couldn’t show my documents” to the agents in St. Paul, Henriquez Serrano said. “I didn’t know if I had an order out for my arrest or deportation — I didn’t know anything about that.”
He made it to San Antonio, and eventually Austin, where his sister was living. He found work in the construction industry in the booming metro area, but after four years there, he was ready for a change. 
His relatives in Minneapolis told him there were better job opportunities up north, and he had some friends in Minnesota who wanted him to live nearby. In September 2024, he moved to St. Paul and took a job at a restaurant. His life was simple, he said, mostly commuting between work and home, where he played video games in his spare time. Some weekends he would join friends for a carne asada — a cookout. But he never let his guard down. 
“In the United States, we can never relax,” he said. 
When ICE came to town in December, he figured he’d be alright — he’d only been stopped by the police once, in Texas, for speeding, he said. And he’d paid the ticket. He thought since he only left the house for work, he wasn’t a likely target.
Missing
When the agents finished handcuffing Henriquez Serrano and stood up, Henriquez Serrano lay motionless, face down on the ground. When an officer grabbed his shoulder to roll him onto his back, his head lolled. Agents dragged Henriquez Serrano’s limp body to a van, his left shoe gone, the toe of his sock trailing behind him. None of them checked for a pulse.
Henriquez Serrano woke up in the back of the van, sandwiched between two agents, with two others in the front seat. He asked for an attorney, for medical attention, and for the agents to loosen his handcuffs. The agents said he could talk to an attorney and see a doctor when they arrived at the Whipple Building, Henriquez Serrano said, but that never happened.
He spent the night on a concrete bench in a holding cell in the headquarters of ICE in Minnesota. In the morning, they loaded him onto a plane, chains wrapped around his hands, feet and stomach. 
ST. PAUL, MINNESOTA – JANUARY 11: U.S. Border Patrol agents detain Orbin Mauricio Henriquez Serrano after he failed to present citizenship documentation at a gas station on January 11, 2026 in St. Paul, Minnesota. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)
Video of his violent arrest quickly spread on social media, with commenters wondering who Henriquez Serrano was; whether his family knew what happened; and whether he was alive. 
A St. Paul car detailer looked up the registration information for the abandoned Jeep and posted Henriquez Serrano’s name and birthdate on Facebook, searching for his family.
“Everyone wants to know if he is alive he did not look alive at the end of the video,” the top comment on the post read. 
Reddit threads and TikTok videos about the violent arrest garnered hundreds of comments and tens of thousands of views, with many commenters assuming Henriquez Serrano was dead. Some noted that Henriquez Serrano’s breath — visible in the below-freezing air — appeared to stop while he was unconscious. 
The day after the arrest, the car detailer connected with some of Henriquez Serrano’s family members — but none of them knew where Henriquez Serrano was or what condition he was in.
By then, Henriquez Serrano was in Camp East Montana, the now-infamous, disease-ridden tent detention center in El Paso, where Japanese Americans were once incarcerated during World War II. ICE shipped more than 2,300 people arrested in Minnesota there during Operation Metro Surge. 
His body was sore and his knee throbbed. His repeated requests for medical care were denied for several days, he said. (In an unrelated case of a detainee being denied medical care, the Department of Homeland Security boasted, “This is the best health care that many individuals have received in their lives,” read a statement, a claim belied by the government’s own assessments.)
Camp East Montana at Fort Bliss in El Paso, Texas on Sept. 7, 2025. (Photo by Paul Ratje for The Texas Tribune)
He had none of his personal belongings, and didn’t have any of his family members’ phone numbers memorized. So he asked an acquaintance to ask their family member on the outside to Google the restaurant where his sister worked. The acquaintance copied it down for Henriquez Serrano, and through the restaurant he finally reached his sister, two days after the arrest.
Shortly after, Minnesota news organizations began reporting that Henriquez Serrano was alive. 
A friend of Henriquez Serrano’s sister set up a GoFundMe to help the family hire an attorney, quickly raising tens of thousands of dollars from the crowd of people who had been waiting for an update. 
But the day before Henriquez Serrano was set to meet with the attorney, a guard knocked on the door of his cell. It was time for him to go. 
Aftermath
Henriquez Serrano touched down in the Honduran city of San Pedro Sula with nothing but the filthy clothes he’d been arrested in and a little cash provided by the Honduran government to cover a bus ticket. 
He was scared; having been in the United States made him a target for robbery, he said. 
“I tried to get out of there as fast as I could,” Henriquez Serrano said of his time in the city. He hid out in a relative’s house in the country for a couple of days, until he could find a way to his father, who was living with a group of construction workers in another part of the country. 
After hiring an immigration attorney — who couldn’t help much after Henriquez Serrano was deported — the family still had tens of thousands of dollars from the GoFundMe. Henriquez bought a car and a small plot of land in the mountains, where he planted coffee, which he expects will begin producing in a few years. He sent a chunk to his pregnant sister, and some to his friends in Minnesota. Another chunk he set aside to cover a potential surgery on his knee. 
He retained an attorney in Minnesota to sue the federal government under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which provides for the compensation of people harmed by federal workers. 
Then, he made his way to his father and the tin-roofed building where he and the other construction workers live. 
Someday he wants to come back to the United States, where he didn’t live in so much fear of murder, robbery and kidnapping.
But in his nightmares, he sees the agents of the American government lunging towards him, over and over. This time, they kill him.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Family of woman who died after contracting cancer in prison settles lawsuit with VitalCore
description: Susie Balfour, who emerged from prison with advanced cancer, died Friday, Aug. 1, 2025, in hospice care. She had filed a lawsuit alleging poor medical care by prison health contractors.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
The family of a woman who died of cancer has reached a legal settlement with a Mississippi prison system healthcare provider she sued in federal court claiming it failed to diagnose and treat her disease until it spread.
Susie Balfour died of breast cancer last year at the age of 64. Her lawsuit said exposure to cleaning chemicals in prison might have led to her cancer, and that prison health providers delayed or failed to schedule follow-up cancer screenings for Balfour even though they had been recommended by prison physicians. She only learned about the disease two weeks before her 2021 release from prison after serving more than 30 years. 
Balfour sued three companies contracted to provide health care to prisoners at the facility over the course of her sentence — Wexford Health Sources, Centurion Health and VitalCore, the current prison medical provider. In an order handed down last week, U.S. Southern District Judge Kristi H. Johnson wrote that Balfour’s family had reached a settlement with VitalCore.
“This is one step in the fight to get justice for Susie, and for everyone who continues to be incarcerated and denied life saving care,” Balfour’s sister said in a statement to Mississippi Today. “We will not stop until those responsible are held accountable. These corporations choose profits over patients, and we intend to make sure those responsible for such inhumane greed answer for it.”
Balfour’s attorneys said they could not reveal specific terms of the settlement.
Wexford was dismissed as a defendant, while Balfour’s family intends to continue its lawsuit against Centurion. The companies have argued they followed laws with respect to the provision of health care to prisoners. A trial could begin in September or October. Balfour died in Shelby County, Tennessee, so a probate court needs to approve the settlement with VitalCore, Johnson wrote in her order.
Kansas-based VitalCore has settled other litigation from former prisoners alleging inadequate care, and some lawmakers have attempted to pass laws that could lead to its replacement as the prison medical contractor. It has recieved hundreds of millions in taxpayer funds for its work as Mississippi’s prison health contractor. 
A spokesperson for VitalCore did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the settlement.
During more than 30 years of incarceration, Balfour used cleaning chemicals without protective gear, which likely contributed to her cancer, she argued in the federal lawsuit she filed in 2024.  
She placed blame on the prison health system’s current and former healthcare providers for failing to diagnose and treat the cancer for years, including not taking her for recommended mammograms and waiting until 2021 to take a biopsy, which ultimately confirmed the diagnosis. 
“I just want everybody to be held accountable,” Balfour told Mississippi Today in 2024. “… and I just want justice for myself and other ladies and men in there who are dealing with the same situation I am dealing with.”
Similar cancer diagnoses and delayed care might not have been isolated to Balfour. An earlier version of her lawsuit alleged at least 15 other incarcerated women contracted cancer after using cleaning materials at the Mississippi women’s prison, the Central Mississippi Correctional Facility, and similarly had their diagnoses and care withheld, but some of those women were not plaintiffs in the lawsuit. 
Balfour’s family continued her lawsuit after her death. The court allowed her to give a deposition months before her passing to preserve her testimony for the case. Shirley Balfour, who is the executor of her late sister’s estate, took over as the plaintiff in the suit. Balfour’s son, Duwan, also joined the lawsuit as the wrongful death beneficiary. 
Balfour’s story also led to legislative reform that could protect future Mississippi prisoners from suffering a similar fate.
When Rep. Justis Gibbs, a Democrat from Jackson, caught wind of her story, he drafted legislation during the 2025 session to require protective equipment for prisoners. The bill died in the Senate, but he tried again this year, and the first-term Democrat ultimately advanced the only prison health care reform to survive legislative negotiations this session. Republican Gov. Tate Reeves signed the bill into law this April.
The Senate this year again blocked most of the proposals to improve healthcare in Mississippi’s prisons, which were driven in part by findings from an ongoing Mississippi Today investigation.
Rep. Becky Currie, the House Corrections chairwoman driving the push for reforms, said she will try again next session. 
Balfour was convicted of capital murder in 1989 for shooting Southaven Police Lt. Billy Lance, who stopped her and her boyfriend after a convenience store robbery. She received a death sentence, but it was overturned years later because the Mississippi Supreme Court found her constitutional rights were violated during trial.
She accepted a plea agreement for a lesser charge and was resentenced, her attorney said.
Instead of getting the chance to rebuild her life, Balfour was released with a death sentence, said Pauline Rogers, executive director of the RECH Foundation, who has highlighed Balfour’s case. 
“Susie didn’t just survive prison, she came out fighting,” Rogers said in an earlier statement. “She spent her final years demanding justice, not just for herself, but for the women still inside. She knew her time was limited, but her courage was limitless.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri turnout could hit 1.4 million as ballot measures drive primary interest
description: Missouri election officials expect as many as 1.4 million voters will cast ballots by the time polls close Tuesday, continuing the historic trend of high turnout in primary elections featuring major ballot questions. Secretary of State Denny Hoskins last week forecast turnout will be about 32% of registered voters, which if correct would be the […]
text:
Missouri could have a near-record primary turnout Tuesday as voters decide two major ballot questions and congressional primaries in three districts (Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight).Missouri election officials expect as many as 1.4 million voters will cast ballots by the time polls close Tuesday, continuing the historic trend of high turnout in primary elections featuring major ballot questions.
Secretary of State Denny Hoskins last week forecast turnout will be about 32% of registered voters, which if correct would be the highest primary total vote since 2004. That election involved a proposed constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage and an historic Democratic primary where Gov. Bob Holden became the only Missouri governor ever defeated by his own party for re-election.
This year, there is no headline-grabbing statewide candidate primary. Instead, two ballot measures — Amendments 4 and 5 — have drawn more spending than in any candidate race.
Local election authority estimates show turnout will vary widely across the state, Hoskins’ office said in a statement to The Independent. Intense congressional primaries are underway in the northern half of the state in the 1st, 5th and 6th districts, plus hard-fought state legislative and local races.
Campaign spending accelerates as Missouri primary election draws near

Turnout is expected to be as low as 20% in some counties and as high as 70% in others, Hoskins said.
Because his estimate is based on local projections, it is only as good as the guesses behind it, Hoskins said. In 2022, turnout was estimated at just under 32% and actual turnout, of about 1 million voters, came in at 24%. There was a crowded U.S. Senate primary in the Republican Party that year but no major ballot measure. 
In 2018, there were no high profile candidate primaries, but a right-to-work referendum drew 1.4 million voters.
Reports on early voting from some of the state’s larger counties show high voter interest. 
In Boone, Greene and St. Charles counties, the number of people who had voted by the end of last week exceeded early-voting numbers from the 2024 primary.
More than 4,000 people had voted in Boone County by the end of the day Thursday, said County Clerk Brianna Lennon. 
“The past two days have been over 500,” she said Friday morning. “I anticipate today will be similar.”
In Greene County, where as many as 55,000 people are likely to cast ballots, more than 4,600 had done so by Friday morning, County Clerk Shane Schoeller said. In 2024, the total absentee vote was just under 3,200.
Early voting ends Monday afternoon at local election offices and designated voting locations in larger counties.
In Missouri’s primary, a voter can request a ballot from the party they prefer — Democratic, Republican or Libertarian — or a nonpartisan ballot with only ballot issues. In Greene and St. Charles counties, a significant number of voters are skipping the candidate races and requesting a nonpartisan ballot.
Missouri Ethics Commission records show that almost $40 million has been spent on the two major ballot questions, Amendment 4, which would change the way majorities are tallied on constitutional amendments proposed by initiative; and Amendment 5, which would give lawmakers authority to increase and expand the sales tax to replace the personal income tax.
Of that amount, The Independent’s tracking of broadcast ad spending reports to the Federal Communications Commission shows almost $8.9 million for television and radio ads in the Amendment 5 debate, with proponents holding an edge of about 4-to-1. 
On Amendment 4, opponents have had the airwaves almost to themselves, with $3.9 million in spending.
Historic data shows that the voters who swell turnout for ballot-measure primaries lean heavily Democratic.
Greene and St. Charles counties are rich in Republican primary voters. In the past four primaries, an average of 33,403 Republicans have voted in Greene County primaries. In St. Charles County, the average of the past four primaries is 47,666 Republican votes. The highest primary vote in each was in the 2016 primary for governor, when there was no major ballot measure.
Democrats average 11,737 and 20,371 votes in non-ballot measure years in Greene and St. Charles, respectively. That jumps to 19,740 and 35,742 Democratic votes in years with major ballot measures.
Schoeller said almost 7.5% of the ballots cast so far this year have been non-partisan, compared with 0.8% in the 2024 primary. 
Missouri congressional incumbents flush with cash heading into primary election

Along with the statewide ballot measure campaigns, congressional and legislative candidates are using airwaves, social media and mail boxes to bombard voters.
More than $6.5 million has been spent on broadcast ads to influence congressional primaries, mainly in the 1st, 5th and 6th Districts. 
Almost $2.5 million has been spent on television and radio in the 1st District Democratic primary in St. Louis, with an equal amount spent in the 5th District Republican primary.
In the 1st District, incumbent U.S. Rep. Wesley Bell has outspent former U.S. Rep. Cori Bush by a 12-1 margin. Both have been outspent by the United Democracy Project, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee-backed group that has spent $1.5 million on Bell’s behalf.
In the 5th District, where six candidates are vying to take on U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver in the gerrymandered district, outside spending is also eclipsing candidate spending. Win It Back PAC, supporting state Sen. Rick Brattin, has spent $1.4 million on broadcast ads, while Brattin himself has spent $100,000.
Conservatives for American Excellence, backing Taylor Burks of Boone County, has spent $512,000, while Burks has spent $300,000 on television and radio. Another PAC, Show Me Valor, has spent $133,000 to blanket the district with radio ads promoting Burks.
The broadcast spending tally for state Senate races so far is $2.8 million. The largest amount is in the 18th District in northeast Missouri, where more than $720,000 has been spent on television and radio ads for state Reps. Ed Lewis of Moberly, Greg Sharpe of Ewing and business owner Dusty Blue of Mexico, Missouri.
Large amounts from NEMO Leadership PAC, set up to promote the political interests of the outgoing incumbent, Senate President Pro Tem Cindy O’Laughlin of Shelbina, have been funneled into other PACs, named Protect NEMO Values and Let’s Go Brandon PAC, for ads attacking Blue. 
The second highest amount of broadcast ads are playing in the 20th District of southwest Missouri, where incumbent Republican state Sen. Curtis Trent is trying to fend off a challenge from Springfield attorney Lori Rook. 
So far, $574,000 has been spent on broadcast ads, and Trent has a 2-to-1 advantage in on-air advertising.
St. Charles County is holding one of the most significant local Republican primaries, with former state Sen. Bill Eigel and Lake Saint Louis Mayor Jason Law challenging long-time incumbent County Executive Steve Ehlmann. An Eigel victory is viewed by many as setting him up for a 2028 primary rematch with incumbent Gov. Mike Kehoe.
Kurt Bahr, St. Charles County director of elections, said his office had received more than 14,000 ballots by Thursday afternoon.
“We have already surpassed our 2024 primary absentee numbers,” Bahr said.
Of that number, 8.5% of voters are opting for the non-partisan ballot. That could show a high level of interest in the ballot measures, he said.
“Or the dislike,” he said, “of political parties.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Nine Republican primaries, one question: what do GOP voters want from Jefferson City?
description: For weeks, The Independent has profiled 11 state Senate primaries on Tuesday’s ballot, including nine Republican contests. In most of these districts, the primary is the whole election. Read together, the GOP primaries look less like nine separate campaigns than nine versions of the same argument: What, exactly, do Republican voters want? Four things will […[...]
text:
Voters will head to the polls on Tuesday to vote in Missouri's statewide primary (Getty Images).For weeks, The Independent has profiled 11 state Senate primaries on Tuesday’s ballot, including nine Republican contests. In most of these districts, the primary is the whole election.
Read together, the GOP primaries look less like nine separate campaigns than nine versions of the same argument: What, exactly, do Republican voters want?
Four things will likely decide the outcome of those races.
The first is money.
No race has displayed its force more nakedly than the 16th District, where an Illinois gambling company seeking to legalize video lottery terminals has poured more than $400,000 into a PAC attacking former state Rep. Hannah Kelly while backing state Rep. Bill Hardwick, the House sponsor of the legislation the company wants.
Then there’s the 20th District in southwest Missouri, where incumbent state Sen. Curtis Trent and an aligned PAC have spent $1.3 million trying to fend off a challenge from elder law attorney Lori Rook.
In most of the races, at least one candidate is vastly outspending any rivals. Maybe the money carries them. Or maybe it becomes evidence for their opponents’ central claim: Jefferson City is run by candidates whose alliances are measured in PAC checks.
The second is Amendment 5.
The income-to-sales tax overhaul was expected to be a loyalty test — and a cudgel against Republicans who voted no. A PAC funded by the group promoting Amendment 5 has spent more than $137,000 attacking state Reps. Rudy Veit in central Missouri’s 6th District and Greg Sharpe in northeast Missouri’s 18th.
But the striking thing across these races is not Republican discipline. It is retreat.
Rook opposes Amendment 5. So does Kelly. In the 18th, Dusty Blue opposes it. In the 16th, state Rep. Don Mayhew voted to put it on the ballot but has since soured on it.
Four of the six candidates in the 6th oppose it or question its details. Veit highlights his opposition in ads. So does Sharpe. In the 28th, physician Sam Alexander opposes the current version, while state Rep. Brad Pollitt, who repeatedly voted for it in the House, won’t say how he’ll vote on the ballot.
Even 6th District candidate Jake Vogel, endorsed by Gov. Mike Kehoe, offers only: “It is a plan.”
The third is data centers.
In the 10th District, where projects are rising along Interstate 70, state Rep. Tricia Byrnes built much of her campaign around opposition to them, while Missouri Cattlemen’s Association executive Mike Deering moved toward calling for “massive” guardrails.
In the 16th, Kelly, Hardwick and Mayhew all oppose data centers in the district. In the 18th and 28th, concerns about farmland, water, electric bills and local control have intruded into races once expected to revolve around more familiar conservative issues.
In the 20th, Rook has tied Trent to the 2025 utility law he supported, which lets electric companies bill customers for power plants still under construction — the plants data centers are lining up to draw from.
Trent, in turn, is airing an ad saying he is “sponsoring a moratorium on new data centers,” though no such moratorium appears among the bills he sponsored this year.
Finally, there is anger.
Blue in the 18th, Rook in the 20th, Alexander in the 28th and former state Rep. Dan Stacy in the 8th aren’t simply running against their opponents. They are running against Jefferson City itself — the “swamp,” the consultants, the lobbyists, the legislative leaders and the expectation that newcomers should wait their turn.
Even the lack of video livestreaming in the Senate comes up repeatedly as proof that the Capitol prefers to conduct business beyond public view.
Four forces, and they cut against one another. The money says the establishment holds. The anger says it won’t. Amendment 5 was meant to sort Republicans into camps, but many are edging toward the door. Data centers began as a wedge, and now candidates compete to oppose them hardest.
Tuesday tells us which force was real.

title: Oklahoma Highway Patrol unveils new look for motorcycles patrolling urban areas
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — The Oklahoma Highway Patrol has unveiled a new look for some of its motorcycles. OHP introduced two new black-and-white BMW motorcycles earlier this month, a nod to the its historic color scheme. Lt. Mark Southall said the motorcycles were black and white until about 15 years ago, when the agency opted for […]
text:
The Oklahoma Highway Patrol unveiled two new motorcycles wrapped in black and white, a color scheme the patrol's vehicles were historically outfitted in. (Screenshot courtesy of the Oklahoma Highway Patrol)OKLAHOMA CITY — The Oklahoma Highway Patrol has unveiled a new look for some of its motorcycles.
OHP introduced two new black-and-white BMW motorcycles earlier this month, a nod to the its historic color scheme.
Lt. Mark Southall said the motorcycles were black and white until about 15 years ago, when the agency opted for the cheaper, all-black paint alternative. Now, Southall said the agency is able to get the bikes wrapped with the dual-color scheme for significantly less than years ago.
He said when a motorcycle needs to be replaced, troopers will be able to choose between all black or the white and black wrap. Southall said some bikes will stay entirely black but most will likely adopt the reintroduced color scheme.
“For generations, the black and white has symbolized professionalism, service, and a commitment to protecting the people of Oklahoma,” reads the post unveiling the new bikes on the Highway Patrol’s Facebook. “These new motorcycles honor that legacy while carrying it forward.”
Each motorcycle costs about $40,000 and is outfitted with the sirens, heated handlebars and the wrap.
A total of 10 troopers on motorcycles  — called the Flying Squadron — patrol the Oklahoma City and Tulsa metropolitan areas, where the small vehicles are safer to navigate through traffic than patrol cars, Southall said.
He said OHP has also wrapped about 35 cars with the new color scheme.
OHP first began using motorcycles in 1937, Southall said. After being phased out in the early 1940s, state troopers began using them again in January 1999.

name: WyoFile
title: Coal’s share of electricity-production in Wyoming at all time low despite peak demand
description:
Coal accounts for 47% of the state’s power production this year, down from 94% in 2008.
The post Coal’s share of electricity-production in Wyoming at all time low despite peak demand appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Amid a sweltering “heat dome” across much of the U.S. and Wyoming, electrical demand is spiking, prompting an all-hands-on-deck approach among utilities and an emergency order from the U.S. Department of Energy. The order, issued July 26, requires certain power producers in 17 states — including some in Wyoming — to keep available electrical generation facilities ready for backup.
It’s unclear to what degree the order applies to the coal-fired Laramie River Power Station near Wheatland, which serves both the western and eastern grids. However, Basin Electric Power Cooperative, which operates the plant, says Laramie River Station, as well as its other coal plants, are helping meet spiking demand.
“Recent hot temperatures and low wind conditions have put added emphasis on our coal generating stations like Laramie River Station, which is available for full production,” the company told WyoFile in a statement. 
Heat waves and cold snaps are typically good news for Wyoming coal, which goes almost entirely to fueling U.S. power plants. In fact, about 18% of the U.S. electricity supply during the heat wave is coming from coal-fired power plants, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. That’s more than the 15% that coal has supported on average so far this year.
This chart depicts Casper area temperatures so far in 2026. (National Weather Service)
Yet the overall share of the nation’s energy mix shouldered by coal continues to shrink — even in Wyoming. 
In fact, Wyoming, where coal has long dominated the in-state mix of electrical generation, is reporting the lowest percentage of coal-fueled power in decades. Among all power sources — including natural gas, hydroelectric and renewables — coal accounted for more than 94% of Wyoming’s electrical generation in 2008, according to the EIA. It had slipped to 60% by 2024 and continues to trend downward.
Coal now accounts for about 47% of power generation in the state, according to the University of Wyoming School of Energy Resources’ most recent Consolidated Review of Energy in Wyoming report. Federal sources suggest it might be lower. Meanwhile, renewables in Wyoming (solar and wind combined) are on the rise, accounting for about 39%, and natural gas continues to increase its share, now at about 16%, federal data shows.
Natural gas takeover
The primary factor for coal’s declining share of energy production in Wyoming has been the conversion of several coal-fired power generation units to natural gas in recent years.
The two remaining coal units at the Naughton power plant near Kemmerer were converted to natural gas this year. A third coal unit at the plant was switched in 2020. Two of four coal-burning units at the Jim Bridger power plant outside Rock Springs were switched to natural gas in 2024. A multiple-utility power outage last fall knocked out a coal-burning unit at Glenrock’s Dave Johnston Power Plant and it remains off line.
This graph depicts Wyoming’s net electrical generation by source. (University of Wyoming School of Energy Resources)
Rocky Mountain Power’s parent company PacifiCorp is the majority owner of all those power plants. The coal-to-gas conversions were necessary to provide “the least-cost, least-risk option for the company and its customers,” PacifiCorp has stated in documents filed with the state.
Politically driven swings in federal regulations have also resulted in shifting retirement dates for various coal units in Wyoming. Age is also an underlying factor. The Naughton, Jim Bridger and Dave Johnston power plants are all beyond 50 years old, approaching the end of their functional life. A University of Wyoming analysis suggests the average age of power plants served by Wyoming coal is 41 years.
Coal industry implications
Wyoming coal mines have recently seen a slight reprieve from a 20-year production decline. The industry notched a 10% increase in tonnage produced from 2024 to 2025, according to federal data. Still, the 211 million tons mined in 2025 were less than half what Wyoming scooped in 2008. The industry’s estimated 52.4 million tons for the first quarter of this year (the most recent data available) suggests it is maintaining the 2025 pace. 
Many coal proponents — including Gov. Mark Gordon — attribute the uptick to the Trump administration’s multi-pronged effort to save the industry via federal subsidies and relaxed human health and environmental regulations.
Still, climate and extreme weather may temper what might otherwise be a heat-wave-boon for the mining industry here.
The mild 2025-2026 winter left a glut of coal and natural gas supplies, driving down market pricing for both commodities. When natural gas is cheap and plentiful, utilities tend to favor it and dial back burning coal to make electricity.
Although it may seem counterintuitive in the midst of drought and historically low snowpack, hydroelectric generation may also temporarily displace coal-powered generation. 
Hydroelectric is up 20% so far this year, according to federal data. Part of the reason might be that federal water managers have increased releases from some reservoirs to meet water delivery demands downstream, a University of Wyoming energy industry watcher told WyoFile. Those extra releases flow through turbines to generate electricity.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: What’s an Oklahoma water board to do about a lake running dry? Let’s start with their job.
description: No resource is more critical to our state’s future than water. Our agricultural industry relies on it. So does our oil and gas industry. And all Oklahomans need it for drinking, cooking and bathing. Yet the state agency entrusted with ensuring that our water resources are being managed appropriately is dispatching a clear SOS that […]
text:
A dock sits above the water level at Cedar Lake near Hinton, Okla., Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)No resource is more critical to our state’s future than water.
Our agricultural industry relies on it. So does our oil and gas industry. And all Oklahomans need it for drinking, cooking and bathing.
Yet the state agency entrusted with ensuring that our water resources are being managed appropriately is dispatching a clear SOS that they’re in over their heads.
The Oklahoma Water Resources Board is giving the alarming impression that their employees are little more than glorified paper pushers and exceedingly shortsighted and fearful when it comes to making hard decisions that affect access to water. 
Instead, their lackadaisical approach shows they’d rather shirk their responsibilities and let our courts determine how water should be used.
Nothing has demonstrated their ineffectiveness more clearly than the fiasco playing out at Cedar Lake, approximately 45 miles west of Oklahoma City.
Over a year ago, residents of the area that shares a name with the lake began complaining to the Water Resources Board that something other than drought was drying up the body of water and draining water wells in the community of about 400 that has existed for over 75 years.
Turns out Oklahoma’s weak water laws emboldened a neighboring property owner to build not one, but two, dams on tributaries that have long fed the lake. An independent hydrologist’s analysis recently found that those tributaries have also helped recharge the Rush Springs aquifer. 
The aquifer, which dates back over 250 million years to the Permian Period, isn’t a minor underground water source. The Water Resources Board reports it covers over 2,400 square miles in the west-central portion of our state, providing water in counties where tens of thousands of Oklahomans live and work, including Grady, Caddo, Custer and Washita.
The drop in water levels is noticeable to pretty much anyone. For generations, residents have baptized children there. They’ve fished and boated.
Water levels have dropped so much that boat docks are sitting many feet above the water or landlocked. Private water wells have dried up and have started producing mud. And residents are rationing water, taking sponge baths because there’s not enough for a shower. Their property values are plummeting because nobody wants to buy lakefront property on a disappearing lake.
For anyone else, except our winsome Water Resources Board, this would be a clear warning that something is very, very wrong with the watershed and aquifer out there. 
Wouldn’t any regulator with an ounce of sense feel compelled to get out of their comfy chairs at their Oklahoma City headquarters and head out to Cedar Lake to get to the bottom of what’s going on?
Apparently not these Oklahoma regulators.
For Cedar Lake residents, there is no mystery. They’re convinced a politically well-connected family built an unpermitted dam, known as Dam No. 6, on a tributary. They believe that dam and another on the property, known as Dam No. 5, are the source of their woes. (It’s not clear who owned the property when dam No. 5 was built in 2005.)
The current manager of the neighboring property is one V. Glenn Coffee, an attorney who is paid $150,000 to advise the state Senate Republican Caucus. The Republican is also a former Senate president and served as Oklahoma’s secretary of state during former Gov. Mary Fallin’s administration.
It’s clear from emails Oklahoma Voice obtained through an open records request that the Water Resources Board did nothing substantive to address residents’ escalating complaints for over a year. That is, until last month when they suddenly and inexplicably decided to let the dams remain while the property owners went through the permitting process after the fact. After facing an angry group of residents, they decided to wait to take up the issue until September.
Their recommendation to let the dams remain is despite a report from Carol Becker, an independent hydrologist with Johnson-Becker LLC, who has about 35 years experience in water quality and resource management.
Becker found that the two dams alone are capturing runoff from almost 40% of the watershed. In layman’s terms, the dams are impounding water that’s supposed to be flowing to Cedar Lake. Becker found the lake, meanwhile, recharges the Rush Springs aquifer that sits beneath it. That aquifer in turn feeds Cedar Lake residents’ water wells.
So why is the Water Resources Board OK with all this? 
Our outlet asked.
Rather than do their job – which should include educating the public about water laws and explaining policy decisions – leaders at the Water Resources Board offered one of the flimsiest excuses I’ve heard.
They said that they had gotten so many questions about the situation that they weren’t going to bother to answer any.
That’s not how a state agency should function. Have they forgotten that the taxpayers pay their salaries and that’s who they’re accountable to?
One thing they did explain in a prepared statement is that state law apparently allows property owners to construct dams willy-nilly on their property without first obtaining permits. For the record, that’s a crazy way for any state to manage water.
It’s not clear why lawmakers continue to allow that. It’s also not clear if the Water Resources Board even has the power to order an unpermitted dam demolished.
The state agency also brazenly suggested that the Cedar Lake property owners establish a rural water district, incorporate the community to make it eligible for financial assistance, connect to a nearby rural water district, or obtain expanded surface or groundwater rights.
Why should these residents have to upend their way of life when there’s clearly an unpermitted dam that is impacting an entire watershed?
It’s past time that lawmakers take a closer look at our water laws because, if this isn’t clear, they’re very weak. 
Right now, it’s Cedar Lake residents that are suffering. Who’s next? Our growing economy? Farmers and ranchers and the growing number of people who call our state home?
It’s time for the Water Resources Board to do their job.
Because we don’t want the courts to shape our water laws for us.
