name: Alabama Reflector
title: Doug Jones’ agenda is a reminder: Alabama Democrats have to be bold
description: Conservatives play the music in Alabama politics. They set the tempo, call out the steps and judge the dancers. So the ball is always the same. The right-wingers waltz with large business; do a bit of liturgical dance and stomp and shout at anyone deemed an outsider. Non-conservatives stepping onto the floor might want to […]
text:
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones speaks in Birmingham, Alabama on July 27, 2026.  Jones outlined a policy agenda that called for Medicaid expansion, support for housing and childcare, protections for IVF and contraception and greater power for local governments. (Andi Rice for Alabama Reflector)Conservatives play the music in Alabama politics. They set the tempo, call out the steps and judge the dancers.
So the ball is always the same. The right-wingers waltz with large business; do a bit of liturgical dance and stomp and shout at anyone deemed an outsider.
Non-conservatives stepping onto the floor might want to try something different. But they have to follow the beat. Which often means stepping left and right in awkward, self-defeating ways.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
So Doug Jones’ policy agenda, unveiled last week, stood out for trying to change the tune.
Now, the Democratic gubernatorial nominee’s proposals will be hard to pass, even if he pulls off a longshot electoral victory. But they represent something we rarely see in Alabama politics: ambition.
Jones made the now-dutiful Democratic calls for Medicaid expansion, a lottery vote and abolition of the state grocery tax. Good ideas but familiar ones.
Yet the agenda went beyond those. The headline proposal was a one-year moratorium on data centers. It’s an obvious contrast with Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville, who has embraced the facilities to the point of accusing their opponents of being foreign agents.
But Jones also pledged to address childcare and use a recently passed federal bill to expand affordable housing in the state.
He also called for constitutional protections for in vitro fertilization and contraception. That would preserve key elements of women’s health. (It also reminds voters that the Republican-controlled Supreme Court tried to ban IVF.)
And while he didn’t use the term, Jones made a pitch for constitutional reform. He wants to give more power to local governments and create a citizen ballot initiative process to allow votes on popular issues the Legislature may block (like Medicaid expansion).
It’s bold series of ideas for the state. But one can’t forget that the Alabama Legislature, not the governor, has the last word on policy. Should Jones win, he will likely face two Republican-controlled chambers. Democrats have candidates in 53 of the state’s 105 House districts and 20 of the state’s 35 Senate seats. Many of them are newcomers or running against well-funded incumbents.
The Democrats running the table is about as likely as winning the lottery while getting struck by lightning. A best-case scenario — the odds of which are almost as long — would be Democrats breaking supermajority control in one of the chambers and getting some leverage over bills. But a GOP-controlled Legislature is not going to embrace a Democratic governor’s agenda. That’s politics.
But it’s hard to argue against the merits of Jones’ proposals. Alabama government is overly centralized and sub-democratic. Housing and childcare are major concerns in Alabama. I’m not a fan of lotteries. But I don’t like the grubby ways lawmakers have thwarted popular votes on the issue.
And Jones might as well try audacity. For one thing, he doesn’t have a chance unless he excites Democrats or the millions of Alabamians who choose not to vote. Apathy is not his ally.
But Jones’ proposals also draw a contrast with Tuberville. Yes, the U.S. senator is making nonsensical plans to prosecute people who haven’t committed crimes (Dr. Anthony Fauci; New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani). He’s spewed disgusting rhetoric about Muslims, immigrants and descendants of enslaved people. Tuberville makes a show of sounding tough and aggressive.
But he’s spitting acid from safe spaces. He limits appearances to Republican amusement parks. He speaks almost exclusively to conservative media, and he’s celebrating guns and wealth while attacking minorities and government. The standard choreography of a GOP frontrunner.
This has led to some odd developments. Tuberville late last month announced the formation of a transition team for an election he hasn’t won yet. His campaign manager, Jordan Doufexis, said the team would give Tuberville “a plan to clean up the place” — that place being the Montgomery state government Tuberville’s party has controlled for 16 years.
So the Republican gubernatorial nominee’s campaign says elected Republican officials are rotten. That’s where reflexive government bashing gets you.
But more important, Tuberville isn’t offering anything new to voters. It’s the bog-standard conservative approach in the state: Reward wealthy Alabamians, ignore real problems and pretend that minorities or outsiders cause all our struggles.
We’ve done this dance for decades now. And anyone trying to do something different has had to trim their message or suggest they’re the real conservatives as they try to keep in time with a hostile band.
But then we’ve seen people like Tuberville’s darling, Donald Trump, ignore the usual music, almost exclusively for worse. And whatever else can be said about the past few decades of Republican control, Alabama remains at the bottom of most measures of joy and happiness. The old politics aren’t keeping prices down or protecting our children from guns.
I don’t know that Doug Jones can win this contest. But he seems to know that he can’t dance to the old tunes. And that Alabama needs to try some new moves.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: At summer meeting, Alabama GOP votes for closed primaries, rejects lawsuit disqualifications
description: The Alabama Republican Party Saturday voted to add closed primaries to its official party platform but rejected a proposal to prevent those who bring “frivolous” litigation against the party from running for office for seven years.  The rule change would have denied ballot access to any individual who brought legal action against the Alabama Republican […]
text:
U.S. Sen. and Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville speaking at the Alabama Republican Party's Summer Dinner on July 31, 2026, at the Renaissance Hotel in Montgomery, Alabama. Tuberville and other speakers at the dinner praised the party and sharply criticized Democrats. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector) 


Key points

The Alabama Republican Party State Executive Committee rejected a proposal to prevent those who bring unsuccessful “frivolous” litigation against the party from running for office for seven years. A former gubernatorial candidate sued the party earlier this year, and was named the reason for the rule change.
The executive committee unanimously approved a measure to add mandatory party registration, or closed primaries, to its official party platform at its bi-annual meeting on Saturday.
During a celebratory Friday dinner, headliners U.S. Sens. Tommy Tuberville and Katie Britt, among some southern colleagues in the U.S. House, praised the party and sharply criticized Democrats and the Democratic Socialists of America.




The Alabama Republican Party Saturday voted to add closed primaries to its official party platform but rejected a proposal to prevent those who bring “frivolous” litigation against the party from running for office for seven years. 
The rule change would have denied ballot access to any individual who brought legal action against the Alabama Republican Party, the executive committee or any local committees unless the legal challenge is successful on all accounts. State Auditor Andrew Sorrell, the chair of the Bylaws Committee who proposed the rule, said the party spent nearly $50,000 on defending challenges to U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville’s eligibility to run for governor. 
“We have wasted tens of thousands of dollars in legal fees that should have been spent on important elections this fall, swing legislative districts in Madison County, swing districts in the Montgomery area, and winning back CD2,” Sorrell said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
About 58% of the Alabama Republican Executive Committee at the GOP Summer Meeting in Montgomery voted to indefinitely postpone the change. William Rayburn of Crenshaw County, who also sits on the Bylaws Committee, said the proposal would silence candidates.
“What this is doing, and what they’re not telling you, is this is an attempt to silence anyone that seeks to remove and try to do things against certain parts of this community and this party,” Rayburn said. 
Sen. Sam Givhan of Huntsville said it was too reactionary.
“The McFeeters lawsuit against Coach Tuberville in Covington County was probably the most frivolous lawsuit I’ve ever seen. It was absurd,” Givhan said. “We’ve got to be mindful that there may be times we disagree. The headline up there says ‘frivolous lawsuit.’ You can lose a legitimate lawsuit, just because you lose a lawsuit does not make you frivolous. We can have good disagreements, honest disagreements about things that sometimes require litigation.”
Former Republican candidate for governor Ken McFeeters sued Tuberville and ALGOP in Covington County Circuit Court in March, alleging that Tuberville did not meet the residency requirements to be governor. The case was dismissed the day before the primary election due to a lack of standing.
“In my opinion, anyone who wastes $50,000 of our money should be ineligible to run on our ballot for the next seven years,” Sorrell said.
Sorrell’s proposal got some support. Josh Dodd of Lauderdale County said that he could not see a legitimate reason to sue the party. 
“I don’t think that we need to be wasting a ton of money fighting lawsuits, and then allowing them to come in service, they should be sued,” he said. “I think we need to handle those matters internally.”
Suzelle Josie of Autauga County said that while she often agrees with Sorrell, she could not vote for this proposal.
“While we have great leadership now, there may come a time in our Republican Party when we really would like the opportunity to vote for and present our position,” Josie said. “We really need to think about this because this would allow a type of almost arbitration or harmful power that we will have a hard time taking back if we relinquish this at this time.”
McFeeters said in a statement Sunday morning that the majority of the Republican party are good people, but others seek total control.
“This is about control and power, not about what’s best for the people of Alabama,” he said. “We need to purge the party of these people.”
Closed primaries
Andrew Sorrell, chair of the ALGOP Bylaws Committee, reading a proposed change to the party’s bylaws at the Alabama Republican Party’s Summer Meeting on Aug. 1, 2026, at the Renaissance Hotel in Montgomery, Alabama. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)
The motion to support closing primaries passed on a voice vote with no discussion. 
Republican lawmakers attempted to pass a law this spring that would have required voters to register with a party in order to cast a ballot. The measure passed the House despite opposition from Democrats and Republicans in and around Madison County, expected to see competitive legislative races this fall. 
The bill did not receive a vote on the final day of the regular legislative session due in part to lack of support in the Senate and concerns for independent voters. 
Sorrell said the need for party registration is ever present because of recent social media posts from Tabitha Isner, vice chair of the Alabama Democratic Party, calling on Democrats to pull Republican ballots in the Aug. 11 special primary election. 
On final day of 2026 legislative session, Alabama Senate tensions doom several bills

“It is time to strengthen our resolve and send an even stronger message to our elected officials by adding this to our Alabama Republican Party platform, I believe this will illustrate how serious we are on this issue,” Sorrell said. 
The special primary was called following a U.S. Supreme Court order that allowed the state to use a 2023 Legislature-passed congressional map, instead of a court-ordered one, for the 1st, 2nd, 6th and 7th Congressional Districts. Because of the special primary, ballots cast in the affected districts on May 19 were voided.
Isner said in an interview Wednesday that her calls for “so-called crossover voting” are “a consequence of what the Republicans did by voiding our votes back in May.” 
“Tabitha makes the case for closing our primaries better than I’ve ever been able to make it myself. You know what? I give her credit for taking advantage of our own stupidity for allowing us to continue,” Sorrell said.
The ALGOP is hoping to flip the 2nd and 7th districts, currently represented by Democratic U.S. Reps. Shomari Figures of Mobile and Terri Sewell of Selma, respectively. 
“We’re fixing to take the state,” said Rep. Scott Stadthagen of Hartselle, the chair of the Alabama Republican Party. “We need to put the prize of beating the Democrats in November first on the list.”
Republicans hold a supermajority in the Alabama Legislature, both U.S. Senate seats, five of the seven U.S. House seats and all of the constitutional offices. 
Dinner and a show
Republican nominees on the statewide November ballot walking together into the Alabama Republican Party’s Summer Dinner on July 31, 2026, at the Renaissance Hotel in Montgomery, Alabama. (Left to right) Matt Gentry [Public Service Commission nominee Place 1]; Corey Hill [Commissioner of Agriculture and Industries nominee]; Caroleen Dobson [Secretary of State nominee]; John Wahl [Lieutenant Governor nominee]; U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville [Gubernatorial nominee]; Katherine Robertson [Attorney General nominee]; Andrew Sorrell [State Auditor nominee]; Young Boozer [State Treasurer nominee]; Jim “Zig” Ziegler [Public Service Commission nominee Place 2] (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)On Friday evening, the party hosted a dinner for its members and guests headlined by Tuberville; U.S. Sen. Katie Britt; U.S. Reps. Tim Burchett of Tennessee and Brandon Gill of Texas, and former Auburn men’s basketball coach Bruce Pearl. Each speaker praised the party and criticized Democrats over the three-hour event.
Tuberville entered with fanfare alongside all the Republican nominees for Alabama’s constitutional offices. He was the only member of the ticket to speak, and promised to give Alabamians a “better life” without specifying how. 
“We can do things that can make everybody’s lives better, and then we’ll go outside our borders of the state of Alabama,” he said. “This guy’s not going to beat me. There’s no way in the world.”
He criticized Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones for platforms Jones has not publicly supported. 
“I want to hear his commercials about transgenders in sports. I want to hear his commercials about open borders and letting 5,000 people a day come here that don’t deserve to be here. I want to hear those commercials. I want to hear him talk about how we’re not going to support law enforcement,” he said. “You really can’t make it up. I’m not running against Doug Jones. I mean, I beat his brains in the first time. I’m gonna do it again.”
Tuberville beat Jones in 2020 during Jones’ reelection campaign to the U.S. Senate with 60% of the votes. Jones won in a 2017 special election against for Alabama Supreme Court Chief Justice Roy Moore by 21,000 votes. 
Jones has some traditional Democratic policy priorities like expanding Medicaid and a vote on a lottery. In a policy address last week, Jones also called for a data center moratorium, a state ballot initiative process; more powers for local governments; constitutional protections for in-vitro fertilization and contraception and additional investments in housing and child care.
Doug Jones calls for affordability measures, government reforms in policy speech

Britt urged attendees to organize in order to get Tuberville and the other statewide Republican nominees “the biggest vote in the history of this state” to prevent the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) from taking control of Alabama and Congress.
“This November, we are fighting for the soul of our nation, and we need every single one of you to step up and answer the call,” she said. “There is too much at stake. The next generation is counting on us, and we absolutely need your help. I know that Alabama is worth fighting for. I know that America is worth fighting for, and I know together we can make sure that we preserve the incredible nation founded on faith, family, and freedom that our forefathers set forth 250 years ago for the next 250.”
The DSA’s platform includes many governmental and social reforms, most of which it says can be done under the current system but would ultimately require “building a new society from the ground up.”
The Alabama Republican Party launched “Project Future Generation” led by Alabama-native Brilyn Hollyhand, a 20-year-old who helped President Donald Trump with his social media strategy in the 2024 election. The initiative, Hollyhand said, aims to get high school and college students registered to vote for the 2026 midterm elections.
“The goal of this student strike course will be to make sure that Alabama isn’t just a red state with a few blue dots in the middle of it, but it will be a solid red state. These students are ready and determined to do just that,” Hollyhand said.
According to a 2025 estimate by the Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement, a nonpartisan research organization, about 42% of Alabamians aged 18-29 cast a ballot in 2024, down from 47% in 2020.
Burchett and Gill told attendees stories of their time on the hill, mostly of interactions with Democratic lawmakers. Burchett emphasized the importance of downballot races. Alabama has straight-ticket voting, where voters can fill in one ballot mark to vote for one party’s slate of candidates.
Gov. Kay Ivey standing on stage at the Alabama Republican Party’s Summer Dinner on July 31, 2026, at the Renaissance Hotel in Montgomery, Alabama, after receiving the Lifetime Achievement Award. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)
“It’s very important that we vote Republican down the ballot; local, state and federal. These local races are incredibly important. We kind of skim over them,” he said. “We talk about Washington. The best thing we could ever have to report to you is that we didn’t do a damn thing this year, because the state and local offices – that’s where it happens.”
Gill said the Democratic Party does not have a platform and only attacks Republicans’ character.
“They’re going to call us racist or whatever other sort of bigotry they want to come up with. We have to fight back and say, “’I don’t care what you call me anymore. I just want my kids to grow up in a country that they recognize,’” he said. “If the election is we the people versus the socialists, we are going to win.”
Stadthagen presented the Lifetime Achievement Award to Gov. Kay Ivey, who became governor in 2017 and won two subsequent elections. She touted the state’s school choice program and low taxes in a short speech.
“In my time as governor, I am proud we have protected our Alabama values and maintained a good old common sense. We cut taxes. We enacted the best school choice program in the country. We are protecting girls’ sports, just to name a few things. None of this would have been possible without all of you here tonight,” she said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Data centers need massive power. They’re eyeing Kentucky’s idle industrial sites to get it.
description: Paducah Mayor George Bray calls the former Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant in McCracken County the ideal site for a hyperscale data center.  When the plant was enriching uranium, initially for the nation’s stockpile of nuclear weapons and then for nuclear power plant fuel, it had the ability to use over 3 gigawatts of power and […]
text:
The former Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant in McCracken County. (U.S. Department of Energy)Paducah Mayor George Bray calls the former Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant in McCracken County the ideal site for a hyperscale data center. 
When the plant was enriching uranium, initially for the nation’s stockpile of nuclear weapons and then for nuclear power plant fuel, it had the ability to use over 3 gigawatts of power and used 26 million gallons of water a day. 
“When we enriched uranium there, all the infrastructure around that power is still available,” Bray said. “Plus, we’ve got you know tremendous water capacity out there.” 
A drone shot of the former Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant as seen in 2024. (U.S. Department of Energy)
The plant closed in 2013 under the control of the federal government, and local elected leaders debated for years what could become of the infrastructure there, an active Superfund site needing remediation for the legacy of hazardous and radioactive waste released into the environment. 
The U.S. Department of Energy provided an answer late last month, planning to transform a portion of the site into a hyperscale data center and nearby natural gas-fired power plants to “the AI race.” The 1.8 gigawatt data center, one of the largest so far planned in Kentucky, is a part of a larger strategy by the Trump administration to turn former Cold War-era federal sites into hubs for data centers and energy production. 
That electrical infrastructure — high-voltage transmission lines, substations, transformers — that allows a hyperscale data center to access massive amounts of electricity is something that’s in high demand and in short supply across the country as technology companies spend billions of dollars on data center construction. 
And these data center developers are increasingly looking to Kentucky’s idled industrial sites — former coal mines, a former aluminum smelter, a former steel mill, industrial parks — to find it. 
While local economic development directors see an opportunity for new life at languishing industrial sites, one environmental attorney warns there could be a cost for ratepayers down the line.
A smelter into a hyperscaler
Along the Ohio River, the Century Aluminum smelter in Hancock County had shuttered its operations after over 50 years of operation in 2022, citing unsustainably high electricity prices. 
It laid off more than 600 employees in the county of about 9,000 people. The infrastructure where 482 megawatts of electricity flowed through transmission lines to craft military-grade aluminum products remained on site. 
Mike Baker, the director of the Hancock County Industrial Foundation, a local economic development group, said the loss of those smelter jobs and tax revenue meant the loss of personal livelihoods and money for local schools and government. He had been in talks with Century Aluminum, which owned the site, to try to find a new use for it.  
“Manufacturing is what we were hoping for,” Baker said. “Had nothing to do with data centers at the time in 2022. I don’t think anybody even knew what a data center was.” 
A hyperscale data center developer arrived years later. Investor-owned TeraWulf bought the site from Century Aluminum earlier this year, planning to use that power capacity to turn it into a 482-megawatt hyperscale data center. The company is leasing the data center to artificial intelligence company Anthropic. 
“It was a former industrial site that had the power,” Baker said. “That’s the number one draw for a data center is, ‘Is their power available?’ And that makes that location much more attractive.” 
There are a number of other idled industrial sites across the state that have been eyed by hyperscale data centers looking for places to hook up. 

The hyperscale data center developer based in Spain is looking at the former AK Steel mill in Boyd and Greenup counties to build a 2-gigawatt data center campus. 
Before the Bell County Fiscal Court passed a temporary ban on data center construction, a developer was looking to use more than 300 megawatts of leftover electrical transmission infrastructure from inactive coal mines to power a data center. 
TeraWulf is also planning on taking over an Eastern Kentucky industrial park— the same park where the state tried and failed to locate an aluminum mill — for another hyperscale data center. 
The city of Pikeville is also in negotiations to put a smaller data center in a local industrial park that has existing electrical infrastructure. 

Baker said the jobs created by TeraWulf at the former aluminum smelter site — about 200 permanent jobs — won’t make up for the lost smelter employment. 
But he believes the site, and industrial sites similar to it, are a much better fit for a large data center. He said that’s compared to a situation where a data center uses hundreds of acres of prime farmland or locates next to a subdivision. He called that a situation “that could generate the kind of emotion and concern that communities have” with data centers. 
“The tax revenue can be significant,” Baker said. “That can be a worthy use of that property.” 
In Mason County, the local planning and zoning committee approved the rezoning of more than 2,000 acres of rural, agricultural land to industrial use for a planned hyperscale data center by an undisclosed technology company. Local pushback against the project over land use and environmental impacts has been ongoing since last year. 
Chasing power — but at what cost?
Yet late last month, residents in Hancock County voiced strong concerns about the project to the state utility regulator Kentucky Public Service Commission in a local public hearing. They expressed concerns over the data center’s water usage, what it could mean for their electricity bills and the impacts of backup electricity generators installed at the industrial site. 
Gary Elder, a resident of the city of Lewisport, spoke at the hearing about the high electricity bills he’s experienced in recent months. (Screenshot/Kentucky PSC YouTube)
Gary Elder, a resident of the Hancock County city of Lewisport, told the PSC during that hearing he has concerns over utility costs, potential pollution and the “loud racket” with having seen reporting about data centers in other states. 
“It’s already been there at these states,” Elder said. “If it happened there, why do we not think it’s going to happen here? So, think about that — what you’re going to do to us.” 
The PSC is considering whether to approve a special contract for power between TeraWulf and electric utility Big Rivers Electric Corporation. 
Byron Gary, an attorney for the environmental legal group Kentucky Resources Council, said putting data centers on former industrial sites “certainly makes sense” from a developer’s perspective given much of the transmission infrastructure is already there. He said developers might also avoid local pushback on projects if it’s already been an industrial site in the past. 
But he worries about potential longer-term costs for Kentucky ratepayers, assuming all the proposed massive data centers come to fruition.
In the case of the Hancock County data center, he said, the TeraWulf data center also has a tentative agreement with Big Rivers Electric Corporation to get its power from the wholesale electricity market through the regional energy grid operator MISO, given that the electric utility doesn’t have close to enough power on its own to power multiple data center projects. 
He said as more demand for electricity comes onto regional energy grids that are a part of Kentucky — such as MISO and PJM — more transmission upgrades to the overall grid are needed. 
Byron Gary, an attorney for the environmental legal group Kentucky Resources Council, talks about the potential utility infrastructure costs of data centers at a conference in 2025. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)
Even though a company like TeraWulf may pay for its own electrical infrastructure upgrades at an industrial site, he said the larger upgrades to the overall grid are paid for by all ratepayers. He imagines that would also include significant upgrades to serve the massive data center and natural gas-fired power plants planned at the former Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant. 
“If those transmission upgrades are not directly allocated to an individual data center or a set of individual data centers, they end up being socialized across all ratepayers,” Gary said. 
Utility Dive reported last month that data centers were responsible for $6.3 billion in electricity capacity charges during energy auctions held by the PJM grid operator, meaning ratepayers are paying for higher energy costs and transmission costs because of data centers. 
The costs of natural gas-fired turbines — which Kentucky utilities are seeking — has also spiked because of demand from data centers who want to use them for on-demand power. 
“Those costs, whether they are to serve data centers or not, still impact all of us, Gary said. “The cost of new generation, transmission, and all of that are things that would have been needed in some cases anyway. We’re just going to pay a lot more for them.” 
‘Speculative’ versus ‘real’
One economic development leader in Eastern Kentucky told the Lantern that data center inquiries are unabated. 
Colby Kirk, president and CEO of One East Kentucky, who works with several coalfield counties, said it’s hard to discern “what’s real and what’s speculative” with data center requests. 
He gets inquiries asking for sites with millions of gallons of water a day or 1000 acres of land, something that “just doesn’t exist” in his part of Kentucky. Even though he would prefer to land a manufacturing outfit, he does see some potential for tax revenue from data centers. 
He pointed to  an effort to build a 100-megawatt natural gas-fired power plant at a Letcher County industrial park for a potential data center, a park that’s “been sitting there for 20, 25 years.”
But he also doesn’t know what the future of data centers in Kentucky will hold. He’s seen waves of interest from solar developers looking at Eastern Kentucky. Then cryptocurrency miners came looking at the area. Now, it’s data centers.
He said he’s not an economist, but he’s read news of a “potential AI bubble.” 
“Who knows what this landscape will look like two years from now?” he said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: The Fauci-Paul battle shows real cracks in public health. One group has answers.
description: As politicians in Washington D.C. and Dr. Anthony Fauci butted heads over the latter’s handling of the COVID-19 pandemic, a nonpartisan commission — which includes a former Kentucky governor — is pushing for better relationships between elected and public health officials.  The “Good Health is Good Governance” toolkit, released in July, challenges leaders to[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., is shown on a monitor as Dr. Anthony Fauci, left, testifies before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on July 29, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)As politicians in Washington D.C. and Dr. Anthony Fauci butted heads over the latter’s handling of the COVID-19 pandemic, a nonpartisan commission — which includes a former Kentucky governor — is pushing for better relationships between elected and public health officials. 
The “Good Health is Good Governance” toolkit, released in July, challenges leaders to commit to bipartisan principles to both strengthen public health responses and increase the trust people have in their leaders. 
It asks leaders to commit publicly to working together and decide on priorities to tackle together. The toolkit suggests two priorities that have bipartisan support: Strengthening localized data and ensuring reliable access to personal protective equipment (PPE). 
Former Gov. Steve Beshear — Gov. Andy Beshear’s father who served as Kentucky governor from 2007-2015 — told the Kentucky Lantern that the relationships between elected officials and public health experts indeed “suffered some damage coming out of COVID.”  
During this time, there was “some loss of trust and confidence, not only between the two groups, but with the public at large,” Beshear said. 
Members of The National Commission on Local Public Health Leadership “came together, recognizing that fall off in that relationship, and think it’s imperative that we help rebuild and strengthen that relationship between elected officials and public health officials for the future of this country,” said the former governor.  
Beshear’s fellow commission members include former Virginian Republican Congressman Tom Davis, former U.S. Surgeon General Dr. Regina M. Benjamin, former Republican governor of Ohio John Kasich and others. 
Gov. Andy Beshear and his father, former Gov. Steve Beshear, left, celebrated last year on election night. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)
“Public health has always been the foundation of the United States’ success since its founding. It has extended life expectancy. It’s improved community health. It’s made everyday life much better for millions of people,” Beshear said. “And for us to remain strong and economically competitive, the relationship between elected officials and public health leaders has to stay strong, and they have to work together to continue to provide that foundation for our country as we move forward.” 
Beshear, whose legacy as governor includes expanding Medicaid, said more collaboration from leaders can also help dispel misinformation and mistrust, such as the rampant misinformation and conspiracy theories that were common during the COVID-19 pandemic. 
“There’s no question that political partisanship has caused a lot of this disconnection on the local level, and it’s come, basically, from the federal level,” Beshear said. “You’re not going to do away with it in today’s world, but I think there are ways you can work through it at the local level and bring elected officials and public health officials together at the local level, and by working together on some common issues that will bring everybody together, it will strengthen that trust, and it will strengthen the public’s confidence and trust that they’re in good hands and that their folks are on the same page and have their best interest at heart.” 
If leaders in every state decided to take a working relationship seriously, the commission believes responses to health emergencies and crises will go smoother. 
The toolkit includes sample conversation starters — and language to avoid — for more collaborative discussions. 
“There’s always going to be ideological differences on some issues, but I think for the most part, we find that people are looking for the same result, they just may differ on how we ought to get there, and so that requires communication,” Beshear said. “That requires sitting down in good faith and talking through things and recognizing the differences, and then coming to some kind of agreement that will get us to where we all want to go. It may not be everything I want, or may not be everything you want. But together, we’re going to end up at the place we need to be.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Renee Shaw has no regrets (and plenty of gas left in the tank)
description: Editor’s Note: One of Kentucky’s most familiar faces is leaving our television screens. Renee Shaw has announced she is retiring from Kentucky Educational Television, where for the past 29 years she has covered innumerable stories, anchored thousands of shows, interviewed hundreds of people, and overall, brought Kentucky’s public policy issues into our homes[...]
text:
KET journalist Renee Shaw (Photo courtesy of KET)Editor’s Note: One of Kentucky’s most familiar faces is leaving our television screens. Renee Shaw has announced she is retiring from Kentucky Educational Television, where for the past 29 years she has covered innumerable stories, anchored thousands of shows, interviewed hundreds of people, and overall, brought Kentucky’s public policy issues into our homes and consciousness. It seemed like a good time for a trip to her KET office for an interview looking back on her career, on journalism, on Kentucky itself. This has been lightly edited for space and clarity.
 
Linda Blackford: Okay. Renee Shaw, queen of Kentucky journalism. So you have big shoes here. You do most of the public policy journalism from the only public television station in the state. You cover the legislature. You cover politics. You are leaving big shoes. Why now? 
Renee Shaw: Well, it’s the right time. I’ve always thought you want to go out on top of your game, and I feel that I have, given not just the last 10 years that I’ve been the host of Kentucky Tonight, but the 20 years prior to that. I’ve done it all, from working with Al Smith to working with Bill Goodman, and I came up through the ranks as an associate producer and a field reporter and a producer and a writer and a researcher. And so I really felt like I’ve given it my absolute best. 
We have been able in the last four to five years since launching the weeknight public affairs show, Kentucky Edition, to bring in some enormously talented folks. So I feel, Linda, that my job is done, that I’ve gone as far as I think this position allows me to be in, and there’s some talent behind me that I want to create a path for. And if you stay in your job, and you’re at the top, and you just stay there and stay there, it squelches the growth pattern for others who really need to blossom, and I don’t want to be guilty of doing that. 
LB: You have said you’re going to take a break, a sabbatical, right? But you’re not retiring, retiring. 
RS: So I like to say I am rewiring, not retiring, right? I am. I consider 53 to be young. I have a lot of energy left. Maybe even more so than I did in my 30s, one because I’ve got my priorities right. I’m not looking for name recognition. I think sometimes when you’re starting off and you’re young, you want to be known, and then when you get there, you kind of realize, huh? I don’t know if it’s all cracked up to be. 
It’s more about the work, and so you know, I know there’s a lot of gas left in the tank, and I don’t know what it looks like on the other side of a sabbatical, but I’m excited to get to the next chapter. And I know, as a woman of strong faith, that God’s got it all laid out. It’s just waiting for me. 
Renee Shaw of KET interviews U.S. Rep. Hal Rogers (Photo courtesy Renee Shaw)
LB: I didn’t know you started here when you were 24. How did you get to Kentucky? 
RS: I’m from Tennessee. Went to Western Kentucky University and got a bachelor’s in government, and they now call it broadcast journalism, but broadcasting. And then I stayed and got a master’s in organizational communication, and while all of that time I was working for the public television and public radio station there, so I have always been a PBS brat. I grew up in a very rural area in Portland, Tennessee. It’s a bedroom community of Nashville now, but you know, 50 something years ago, Portland was kind of remote, and we didn’t have early childhood education centers. It was called Mom Stays Home, and you watch PBS. PBS and my mother and father were my early educators, and my mother spent a lot of time with me watching Mr. Rogers and Sesame Street and all those great programs, where I saw a  world and life a lot larger than what was outside my window, and I learned about appreciating differences in people. Even then I thought, gosh, I think I might want to work for a place like that, right? 
So I was at Western, and the general manager at what’s now called Western’s Public Broadcasting Service, talked to Ginni Fox (former KET director), and she said, we’re looking for somebody to cover Frankfort – and I just learned this last week – Chuck Anderson said, ‘I’ve got the pick of the litter.’ And you know the rest is history. 
I have been in this office since January 6, 1997. 
LB: So, you came as a Frankfort reporter. What was it like the first time you went to Frankfort? 
RS: Oh my gosh, Linda! I was so intimidated, right? I remember just feeling in awe of the privilege for this to be the place I would work. Like this is my first really big girl job, and I’m covering Frankfort, and I get to know who these people are, and I’ve got access to these places. And I also realized that I didn’t know jack. 
It was the higher education session of 1997. That was my first session, and I remember, you know, at the time Bill (Goodman) had Charles Wethington and Paul Patton on for that show, and I just remember, like, wow! I am watching. I didn’t understand the significance of how important it would be, really. But looking back on it, look at that bedrock legislation. I mean, it was like it was like the KERA of 1990, right? 
And so I remember being intimidated, but full of anticipation about what I could do and the mark I could leave because I didn’t see many people like me. 
LB: Well, I wanted to ask you about that. Frankfort is known as being full of conservative rural men who may not have ever seen an African American woman in this position. What was that like? 
RS: You know, I think it was very respectful because I have a certain way of presenting myself, like I’m about the business. I would find the common ground in the rural experience because you know, Black or white, meet people where they are, and don’t pass judgment. So even at 24 years old, I knew I needed to be open-minded and not assume that because I was in a predominantly white male environment that they were going to look down on me or think that I was incompetent or I was not worthy of being in that environment. I assumed that they assumed the best about me. That’s how I approached it, and over time, I’ve been able to prove them right. I don’t believe that everybody who is praising me now thought I could do it 20-something years ago. I’m not that naive, but I’ve proven myself, and if you had doubts, I’ve shown you what I could do, and if you believed in me from the beginning, I hope that I’ve affirmed that and gone beyond. 
Renee Shaw in the anchor’s seat at KET (Screenshot KET)
But I also had some good mentors. Charles Marie Maxberry, who worked in state government; Joan Taylor. And when I got to Frankfort, these women, along with the late wife of Sen. Reggie Thomas, Linda Thomas, who worked here in education, they kind of surrounded me. Former Sen. Georgia Davis Powers was like ‘you know you’re new here. Let me just give you some advice.’ And I had these aunties, you know, these tias who were so prevalent in my life, saying, ‘Here’s how you got to hold yourself, you know, and here’s your countenance, and here’s how you got to do things, and be strategic in your thinking and in your words when you’re with them.’ All the things, and so you know, I look back on that and think of those women whose names I want to say proudly because they helped shape my path, and I owe a lot to them for that. 
LB: Back in 1997, things were not so ugly between between the press and politicians, basically. So it was a better atmosphere altogether. But you have held on to a level of trust from all manner of people, to an extraordinary degree, I would say. How have you done that?
RS: It is a high tightrope. I’ve got to be better than prepared. If I don’t know it, I need to go ask somebody who does. I need to read. You know, if you’re covering the session and you get through Friday by Saturday, I am reading those bills and I am highlighting. I like to highlight and make notes and margins so that when I sat down to ask a question about, you know, what was called the sewer bill? I crafted questions that got at the heart of what the viewer needed to hear and understand. And when someone told me something off the record, it was off the record. 
LB: Do you recall a story or a time when your questions were worrisome to KET, like when there was a real tension between ‘we’ve got to get to the bottom of this, even though it’s going to annoy people in Frankfort who pay our bills’?
RS: You know, I think that I have been very blessed that I haven’t had to run anything by them, right? I will say that I’ve been blessed to have Shae Hopkins, who has been the KET CEO from all most of my tenure, has never questioned my determination to be accurate and factual and fact-based, and to be respectful and civil. Now we may have had conversations about my outside role in doing public appearances and that kind of thing, right? I never wanted to look like I was favoring any particular side of anything by being in an advocacy role. I’ve been very mindful that my role is not to editorialize and to provide commentary. I settled into the role that I signed up for, and that is to be fact-centered and people-centered, and to also, I think, to elevate. I mean, the greatest joy hasn’t always been being at 700 Capitol Avenue. It’s being able to go out after the session into Hawesville or Pikeville or Paducah, or Boyd County, and really talk to people who are affected by the policy, or who have actually, in their community-mindedness, come up with solutions to solve some of the problems that government can’t or won’t fix. 
LB: Have you ever thought about going into politics? 
RS: Oh, good lord! How many times will I be asked that question? You know, I thought about it but I just don’t know, Linda. I don’t know if a person like me is in vogue enough for the electorate. I mean, I think people are complimentary, but just because they’re complimentary of you doesn’t mean they’re going to vote for you, right? But I think people might be very surprised to know I’m an independent by registration, you know, and I consider myself someone who likes the middle, right, and who believes in reasonable, thoughtful approaches to large, seemingly intractable problems.
LB: What are the stories that you recall that you did that had the most impact, and or what are your favorites? 
RS: My favorite. Well, we did a six part series on youth mental health called ‘You Are Not Alone,’ and we did that work circa 2017- 2018. I mean, before it was even popular to talk about mental health. It’s a really good volume of programming. 
When you get to talk to people, that’s the ‘heart’ work. That’s the soul of what I’ve done. I’ve had the best job to go up to people I’ve admired and say, ‘Hey, I want to talk to you,’ and they let me do it.” I hope that they took away from that that it was not just a show for me, that I was invested in learning about them and who they were, and that’s been the greatest. 
LB: Any other big ones? 
RS: Stedman Graham was my first interview for Connections back in August of 2005, and that is Oprah Winfrey’s beau, and he was here for the Lexington Minority Business Expo. But here’s what really impressed me about him was he said, ‘Don’t make your work your life. Don’t look back and wish you had given more to your life than your work.’
LB: And did you did you heed that advice?
RS: I don’t know if I did or not. I mean, honestly, I put it all out for this job. But you know, now my life as I’m older, I’m reprioritizing some of that and thinking, as you do in midlife, you wonder what if I’d concentrated more on this, would I have that. But I don’t have any regrets – I mean life is how it was supposed to be and it’s been a pretty charmed life, and I’ve been able to hopefully encourage young women who either look like me or don’t, to think that’s the way to do it. 
LB: You’ve been doing this a long time. You probably know the state and its issues better than a lot of people. Things are very divided, and Kentucky is still sick and poor and uneducated. What do we do? What do you see moving forward? 
RS: That is such a large question, and I think that education is the key. I mean, for me, education was my passport to a larger life. I’m a first generation college student, and my parents worked so hard to get me through college without having mounds of student debt and being able to get a postgraduate degree. We have to reframe how we see the value of education for everybody, regardless of their backgrounds and their pedigrees, and make it accessible. You know my former pastor at Bracktown (Rev. Dr. C.B. Akins), and he would say ‘there’s two things somebody can’t take away from you: Salvation and education.’
Renee Shaw leading a panel discussion at KET (Screenshot KET)
LB: Let’s switch to journalism. Journalism is also not in great shape. Where do you see journalism going, and or what do you think needs to happen? 
RS: Well, I think that even though we’re in the midst of our greatest challenge and maybe even identity crisis, I always like to look at the silver lining – that this is a time for extreme and immense opportunity. We know that people still value community-driven and centered journalism; that they still want to see themselves. So I think what we need to do is we need to lead local, and our stories need to be focused on the local people, their concerns, and really get at the heart of how they feel. And if they don’t see themselves reflected in the content that we deliver, then why would they ever invest in our content? 
But it also requires the community to want to be news literate. It is incumbent upon people to take it on themselves to be able to decipher: Is this AI or am I getting all my news from one source that really just affirms what I believe, or am I willing to be challenged by listening to the complete opposite? People have to do their own brain work, and I think it’s incumbent upon our industry to really try to do more in terms of news literacy and civic engagement.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Two Narragansett neighbors live separate lives on policy
description: Editor’s note: This is the first in a six-part series on state legislative races, chosen based on expected competitiveness between candidates and relevant issues to the district. Of the 113 seats in the Rhode Island General Assembly, all of which are elected every two years, 22 have primaries in September. Sen. Alana DiMario and her […]
text:
Sen. Alana DiMario is a licensed mental health counselor who was first elected in 2020. Her Democratic primary challenger, Mark Mesrobian, is an entrepreneur and general manager of the Bonnet Shores Beach Club. (Contributed photos)
Editor’s note: This is the first in a six-part series on state legislative races, chosen based on expected competitiveness between candidates and relevant issues to the district. Of the 113 seats in the Rhode Island General Assembly, all of which are elected every two years, 22 have primaries in September.
Sen. Alana DiMario and her Democratic primary challenger, Mark Mesrobian, live less than a third of a mile apart on the same street in Narragansett.
But the Tupelo Trail neighbors are miles apart in ideology and policy priorities for Senate District 36.


About District 36 
Represented by Sen. Alana DiMario since 2020
Geography: Includes part of North Kingstown, Narragansett, New Shoreham
Population: 29,000, 22,513 registered voters
Partisan breakdown: 56% independent, 29% Democrat, 14% Republican
Demographics: Median age: 49.1; 92% white; $103,982 median household income (2024)


DiMario was first elected in 2020, part of a band of progressive candidates that arrived on Smith Hill that year. A licensed mental health counselor and former chair of the Senate Committee on Environment and Agriculture, DiMario, 47, has led the way on state laws to preserve farm and forestland while promoting solar development, increasing access to affordable mental health services and childcare, and securing state funding for a pilot public transit program for people with disabilities. She’s not done.
“I have unfinished work to do,” DiMario said, rattling off mental healthcare issues, coastal protections and infrastructure constraints that require water bans in Narragansett every summer as examples. “The range of issues I become involved with, that are brought to my attention by my constituents, and advocates, just keep adding to the to-do list.”



Quotation







I have unfinished work to do. 


– Sen. Alana DiMario


By contrast, Mesrobian sums up his platform in a single word: business. A serial entrepreneur whose current business involves wholesale and direct-to-consumer eyewear — he also serves as general manager of the Bonnet Shores Beach Club — Merobian sees an unmet need in the business community.
“As a small business owner and the person presenting the budget to the board here at Bonnet, things have been increasing,” Mesrobian, 58, said. “You have double digit healthcare costs, energy is going through the roof, the lack of affordable housing…. It makes it difficult for us to hire, to be competitive.”
Navigating beach club politics
A first-time candidate, Mesrobian acknowledged he did not want to go up against his state representative, Carol Hagan McEntee, who has represented the district since 2015, and also belongs to the members-only beach club. But against DiMario, he saw an opening.
“She and I live on the same street and I’ve never met her once,” he said. “I have more name recognition than she does.”
DiMario in response pointed to her public-facing schedule of community events and outreach. She said has met Mesrobian’s wife while canvassing in the neighborhood.
“I’m one of the most publicly available and accessible lawmakers,” she said. 
DiMario prides herself on robust engagement with her district, which stretches down the eastern side of North Kingstown through Narragansett, and also includes New Shoreham. 
“My record of effectiveness has to do with the good relationships I’ve built, not only with my colleagues and with advocates but with my constituents and the communities I represent,” DiMario said.



Quotation







She and I live on the same street and I’ve never met her once. I have more name recognition than she does. 


– Mark Mesrobian, Democratic challenger


DiMario has not faced a primary challenger since 2020, although she had a Republican opponent in the 2022 general election. In 2024, she ran unopposed.
A self-described moderate Democrat backed by the conservative-leaning League of RI Businesses, Mesrobian offers a different viewpoint than DiMario on many of the hot-button issues that have come before the General Assembly in recent years. He opposed the millionaire’s tax enacted in the fiscal 2027 budget. He also said he wanted to consider lowering or eliminating the estate tax and a surcharge on high-value second homes included in the fiscal 2026 budget, often referred to as the Taylor Swift tax, which took effect July 1.
DiMario supported increasing taxes on top earners and on high-value second homes.
Born out of a gun rights campaign, The League of RI Businesses has endorsed a slate of legislative candidates — Democrats, Republicans and a few independents — who prioritize more traditionally conservative talking points like cutting state spending, lowering taxes, and Second Amendment protections 
Mesrobian said gun rights is not one of his “hot-button issues,” but added he would have opposed the 2025 law banning the sale and manufacturing of assault-style weapons. DiMario approved the bill, initially advocating for an even broader ban on assault style weapons. 
DiMario did not comment specifically on their policy differences.
“I don’t really know what his policy positions are,” DiMario said of Mesrobian. “His campaign doesn’t seem to be very policy-focused. A Democratic voter can look at my record and my stances, and know where I stand.”
For Mesrobian, it all comes back to economic issues.
“I’ve been leading people in building budgets for 25 years,” he said. “ I live, eat, and sleep business.” 
The winner of the Sept. 9 primary will be the only candidate on the ballot in the Nov. 3 general election.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia votes Tuesday: Everything you need to know about the 2026 primary elections
description: Virginians will head to the polls Tuesday for the 2026 primary elections, nearly two months later than usual after this year’s congressional redistricting referendum and the uncertainty over which map would govern the races delayed the state’s traditional June nomination contest.  More than 30 candidates are competing in the GOP primary for U.S. Senate and [[...]
text:
Voters on Tuesday will choose nominees for U.S. Senate and congressional races across the commonwealth. (Photo by Parker Michels-Boyce for the Virginia Mercury)Virginians will head to the polls Tuesday for the 2026 primary elections, nearly two months later than usual after this year’s congressional redistricting referendum and the uncertainty over which map would govern the races delayed the state’s traditional June nomination contest. 
More than 30 candidates are competing in the GOP primary for U.S. Senate and in seven of Virginia’s 11 congressional districts.
Republican voters will choose a nominee to challenge Democratic U.S. Sen. Mark Warner, while contested congressional primaries will unfold in the 1st, 2nd, 5th, 7th, 8th, 9th and 10th districts. Several incumbents are also seeking renomination without opposition. 
Polls are open from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m., and anyone in line by the cutoff will be allowed to cast a ballot. Voters can verify their polling place and registration status through the Virginia Department of Elections voter portal. 
An acceptable form of identification is required to vote. That includes a driver’s license, passport, voter confirmation document, utility bill or bank statement. Voters without identification may sign an identity confirmation statement or cast a provisional ballot. 
Because Virginia does not register voters by party, voters in localities holding both Democratic and Republican primaries may choose either party’s ballot, but they cannot participate in both. 
Here’s a look at the contests and the candidates on the ballot across Virginia. 
 U.S. Senate

Three Republicans are seeking their party’s nomination to challenge Warner, the Democratic incumbent who is running for a fourth term. 
A Northern Virginia business owner and former public accountant for several federal agencies and the White House, Kim Farington has centered her campaign on inflation, government spending and border security. 
Retired U.S. Army Maj. Gen. Bert Mizusawa, a former Pentagon official, is highlighting his military and national security experience while focusing on defense readiness, energy and foreign policy. 
Running as a political outsider, David Williams — a businessman, U.S. Navy veteran and former federal employee — is promising to cut taxes and reduce the size of the federal government. 
Warner does not face a primary opponent. Virginia has not elected a Republican to the U.S. Senate since John Warner, no relation to the incumbent, won his final term in 2002. 
 1st District

Seven Democrats are competing for the chance to challenge Republican U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman of Westmoreland, who has represented the 1st Congressional District since 2007, making it Virginia’s largest congressional primary field. 
The district stretches around Richmond, taking in parts of Chesterfield, Hanover and Henrico counties before extending east through the Williamsburg area and the Northern Neck. 
On the ballot are U.S. Army veteran Elizabeth Dempsey Beggs, Virginia Poverty Law Center attorney Salaam Bhatti, environmental advocate Tim Cywinski, U.S. Navy veteran and energy lobbyist Jason Knapp, healthcare attorney Ericka Kopp, longtime Henrico County Commonwealth’s Attorney Shannon Taylor and U.S. Army veteran and business lawyer Mel Tull. 
While the candidates have largely focused on affordability, healthcare and opposition to the Trump administration, they have drawn distinctions over whether Democrats should nominate a progressive or a moderate candidate to take on Wittman. 
 2nd District

Four Democrats are competing for the chance to take on Republican U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans of Virginia Beach in one of Virginia’s most competitive congressional districts. Anchored in Hampton Roads, the district includes Virginia Beach, the Eastern Shore and parts of Chesapeake, Suffolk, Franklin, Southampton and Isle of Wight counties. 
Former U.S. Rep. Elaine Luria, a retired U.S. Navy commander who represented the district for two years before losing to Kiggans in 2022, is seeking a rematch. Also on the Democratic ballot are physician Nila Devanath, who has focused her campaign on healthcare and reproductive rights; Bill Fleming, a physicist, veteran and Virginia Beach director with the Soil and Water Conservation District; and Patrick Mosolf, a former U.S. Agency for International Development employee.
Kiggans, a former U.S. Navy helicopter pilot and state senator, faces no opposition for the Republican nomination. 
 5th District

Both parties have contested primaries in the sprawling 5th District, which spans from Charlottesville and the Richmond exurbs south through Lynchburg and Danville. 
U.S. Rep. John McGuire, R-Goochland, a former U.S. Navy SEAL and state lawmaker serving his first term, is being challenged by Marine veteran and business owner Melanie Lucero. 
On the Democratic side, three candidates are seeking the nomination. Tom Perriello represented the district from 2009 to 2011 before serving in the Obama and Biden administrations. Suzanne Krzyzanowski is a physician and cancer researcher, while Robert Tracinski is a political commentator and former Republican-turned-Democrat. 
Although the district leans Republican, Democrats argue concerns about affordability and dissatisfaction with McGuire have made the race more competitive. 
 7th District

Three Republicans are seeking the nomination to challenge first-term U.S. Rep. Eugene Vindman, D-Woodbridge, in the Democratic-leaning 7th District, which stretches from Prince William County through Fredericksburg and into Stafford, Sportsylvania and neighboring rural communities. 
Entrepreneur and business executive Philip Harding has emphasized his private-sector experience while calling for a smaller federal bureaucracy. Entrepreneur and educator Douglas Ollivant has focused on job creation, domestic manufacturing, energy production and election security. 
Pastor and construction company owner Rick Smithers has made affordability the centerpiece of his campaign, advocating lower federal spending, fewer regulations and a pause on new data center development until local infrastructure catches up.
Vindman, a retired U.S. Army officer, is unopposed for the Democratic nomination after winning the seat by 3 percentage points in 2024. 
 8th District

Six-term Democratic U.S. Rep. Don Beyer of Alexandria faces four primary contenders in the heavily Democratic 8th District, which includes Alexandria, Arlington, Falls Church and part of Fairfax County. 
Among them is Michael Duffin, a former U.S. State Department employee laid off during federal workforce cuts who has centered his campaign on restoring federal jobs. Former Alexandria City Councilman and U.S. Department of Labor attorney Mo Seifeldein is running as an anti-establishment candidate. 
Marine veteran and former CIA officer Adam Dunigan has emphasized government ethics and generational change, while Stafford County teacher Lorena Bruner has called for a more aggressive Democratic response to President Donald Trump. 
GOP candidate Tony Sabio faces no primary opponent. 
 9th District

Three Democrats are seeking the nomination to challenge longtime Republican U.S. Rep. Morgan Griffith of Salem in the deeply conservative 9th District. The seat covers much of Southwest Virginia, including Bristol, Abingdon, Blacksburg, Christiansburg, Wytheville and communities along the Kentucky, Tennessee and West Virginia lines. 
Retired United Methodist pastor and attorney Douglas Crockett, who has roots in Wythe County, is running as a progressive while calling for efforts to ease political divisions. Software developer Adam Murphy, whose background includes the insurance, finance, manufacturing and aerospace industries, has focused on working-class economic issues, corporate power and technology policy.
Bedford County farmer and small business owner Joy Powers brings a background in agricultural development, foster care advocacy and leadership of the Bedford County Fair.
Griffith, first elected in 2010, faces no opposition for the Republican nomination. 
 10th District

Republicans have a three-way primary to determine who will challenge first-term Democratic U.S. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam of Loudoun. The Northern Virginia district includes Loudoun, Fauquier and Rappahannock counties, the cities of Manassas and Manassas Park, and parts of Fairfax and Prince William counties. 
Retired U.S. Airforce Col. Dave Beckwith, a former deputy assistant secretary of defense, has built his campaign on national security and government management. Fairfax County teacher Julie Perry, who previously ran for the state Senate, is emphasizing education, federal spending and opposition to diversity programs in public schools. Anthony Suttles, whose background is in national security and economics, is the third Republican candidate in the race.
The district has leaned Democratic since the party flipped it in 2018 after former U.S. Rep. Barbara Comstock’s retirement. Subramanyam won the seat in 2024 and is unopposed for the Democratic nomination.

title: Anti-Slapp law plays role in backing Va. teacher and parent targeted by false online accusations
description: A Northern Virginia court in June rejected social media efforts to damage the reputation of a teacher and parent, awarding them more than $1 million in combined damages. Robert Rigby Jr., a longtime educator and advocate for LGBTQ+ students, said after the leader of conservative political action committee Virginia Project posted unfounded accusations that he[...]
text:
The Fairfax County courthouse. (Photo by Charlie Paullin/Virginia Mercury).A Northern Virginia court in June rejected social media efforts to damage the reputation of a teacher and parent, awarding them more than $1 million in combined damages.
Robert Rigby Jr., a longtime educator and advocate for LGBTQ+ students, said after the leader of conservative political action committee Virginia Project posted unfounded accusations that he was a child sex predator online, his students’ interest in the Latin course he teaches wavered. 
“When rumors started spreading that kids didn’t even take my class because these things were being said … that’s always every teacher’s fear,” Rigby said. “It’s always every gay teacher’s fear.” 
The students’ reaction emphasized that the remarks weren’t simply harsh opinions, Rigby said, but false statements that carry consequential weight.
Across the country, social media campaigns targeting educators have been on the rise, including in Roanoke County and South Carolina, amid contentious school board politics that test the legal boundaries of free speech and defamation.
Rigby and the other plaintiff, Vanessa Hall, who are both active in Fairfax County Public Schools committees and advocacy, alleged that defendant David Gordon, founder of the Virginia Project, used his X account to publish false and malicious statements that damaged their personal and professional reputations.
 The case

Virginia’s anti-SLAPP law was central to the case, highlighting the legal limits of false speech, the civil liability it can create, and the policy gaps it exposes for people — including teachers — when the legal requirements are met.
Jason Zellman, the attorney who represented Hall and Rigby, said that Virginia has laws that protect opinions and silence criticism with the anti-SLAPP defense. Still, he says, accusatory public statements must have a factual basis. 
“And in this case… we had very declarative, actual statements that these individuals were child sex predators. They were part of a ‘grooming gang.’ They were part of a ‘child abduction scheme,’” Zellman said, quoting Gordon’s claims. “There was no qualifying language, and more importantly, there was no evidence at all, zero, to back up any of these statements.” 
In their complaints, Rigby also alleged Gordon labeled him and Hall as “notorious child sex perverts” with “free run of FCPS.”
Hall said Gordon mischaracterized her as an “employed crazy person with zero qualifications” who was given inappropriate access to children. The claims that she was involved in sexual crimes against children disturbed her the most, she said. 
“As a parent, as a Girl Scout leader, as a Sunday school teacher, as an advocate for children’s safety, that is frankly the worst thing you could say about anyone,” Hall said.
A year after the complaints were filed, juries in both cases ruled in favor of Hall and Rigby, awarding $700,000 and $350,000, respectively. 
Zellman said he is preparing for an expected appeal by Gordon.
 Policy reform

Rigby and Hall’s case drew attention to the state’s policy gaps concerning defamation, especially around punitive damages and fee recovery.
Zellman and Hall argued that Virginia’s legal framework still tilts unfairly against defamed teachers because the state’s anti-SLAPP law can require plaintiffs to pay the other side’s legal bills if they lose. 
The state’s punitive damages cap was set at $350,000 in the late 1980s in such cases, and standards on jury award limits, even for egregious cases, haven’t been updated since then. 
“It just doesn’t seem appropriate,” Hall said.
Zellman added that if the court had instead found the statements made by Gordon and the Virginia Project were an expression of opinion, didn’t rise to the level of defamation, or were speech protected by the First Amendment, they could become liable for the defendant’s costs and attorneys’ fees.
“What I think is a shortcoming in the law is that … there’s not a similar reciprocal provision that if Robert and Vanessa prevail, as they did in this case, that they get their attorneys’ fees and costs reimbursed,” Zellman said. “And I do think it would provide both an incentive and caution for any party … that you have to be pretty sure about your position.”



 Tips for educators

Attorney Jason Zellman offered several practical points for teachers and parents who become targets of defamatory online attacks.
First, he said, preserve evidence immediately.
“When these statements are made about you, and especially in the world of social media that we live in now, capturing those statements before they’re gone is number one to preserve evidence,” Zellman said. “People can delete their tweets, remove Instagram posts, whatever it may be, and so having that evidence is important.”
He also recommended teachers understand their legal rights and what constitutes free speech. Educators should seek legal advice.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Argue all you want about the cause of climate change. The 911 calls still come.
description: No one dials 911 to report climate change. They call because the water is over the doorsill. They call because a neighbor on the third floor, in an apartment with no air conditioning, stopped answering the door. They call because the road they were told to evacuate on is already under two feet of water. […]
text:
Flooding is shown on Redmond Street at Market Street in Warren, R.I., in 2019. (Photo by Warren Fire Chief James Sousa.)No one dials 911 to report climate change. They call because the water is over the doorsill. They call because a neighbor on the third floor, in an apartment with no air conditioning, stopped answering the door. They call because the road they were told to evacuate on is already under two feet of water.
In my 20 years wearing a badge in East Providence, I learned that the public rarely argues with a police officer about causation. They want the problem handled now. That instinct is worth borrowing for a debate that has been stuck for a generation.
So set aside whatever you believe about carbon, computer models, and international accords. Look at it the way an investigator looks at a case. What does the evidence on the ground actually show, and what does it oblige us to do about it?
What it shows, first, is a workload changing under our feet. Ambulance dispatches nationally rise somewhere between 6% and 18% during heat waves. Boston EMS has measured call volume climbing roughly 14% once the temperature clears 90 degrees. A research letter published this year in the Journal of the American Medical Association found heat-related EMS activations rose 65% nationwide between 2019 and 2024, with the sharpest acceleration in lower-income ZIP codes, which is to say the same neighborhoods that already generate the heaviest call volume for everything else.
Rhode Island is not exempt from the arithmetic. Summers here now carry roughly three more weeks of health-threatening heat than they did in the 1950s, and researchers project hundreds of additional heat-related emergency room visits every year by mid-century.
Then there is the part cops know in their bones and criminologists have finally quantified. Violence tracks heat. A systematic review in Environmental Health Perspectives, national analyses out of Japan and South Korea, and a 28-city American study all point the same direction: as the thermometer climbs, so do assaults, robberies, and homicides. One widely cited estimate puts the cost of a single degree Celsius at about a 6% increase in violent crime in this country.
That is not an environmental statistic. That is a staffing statistic.
I live in Warren, in a converted luggage factory a short walk from water that is coming for the street. In September 2021, the remnants of Hurricane Ida dropped more than 66 inches of rain on this town in a matter of hours. Market Street went under. It goes under now on ordinary king tides, without a storm’s help at all.
Warren did something unusual and honest about it. The Market to Metacom plan, adopted in 2021, proposes a managed retreat: voluntary buyouts, phased over decades, of the 300 to 400 structures projected to sit below the tide line by 2100, with new housing built on higher ground along Metacom Avenue. Planners around the country hold the plan up as a model. State environmental officials point to it as the template for every other coastal community that will eventually face the same conversation.
Five years on, nobody has moved. An $18 million grant application to NOAA was denied. A Department of Agriculture application failed. Until this spring, the town had been without a planner since late 2024. The plan is sound. The money is not there.
And the money is getting scarcer. In May, the FEMA Review Council recommended raising the threshold for federal disaster declarations and holding the federal cost share to the statutory minimum. In plain English: FFewer disasters qualify, and states pay a larger share of what is left. The Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities program, which funded precisely the kind of work Warren needs, was canceled in 2025. Hazard Mitigation Grant Program allocations have been stalled since the spring of that year. Emergency Management Performance Grants were frozen last October. FEMA absorbed a 14% workforce reduction and a 76-day departmental shutdown before its 2026 appropriation finally cleared at the end of April.



Quotation







What does the evidence on the ground actually show, and what does it oblige us to do about it?


Reasonable people can argue FEMA needed reform. Having dealt with my share of federal bureaucracy, I will grant the premise without a fight. But reform that arrives as an invoice mailed to the smallest towns in the smallest state, in the middle of hurricane season, is not reform. It is a transfer of risk to the people least equipped to carry it.
There is a specific operational reason this ought to worry anyone who has ever run a shift. Emergency response in Rhode Island rests on mutual aid, the standing assumption that when Warren is overwhelmed, Bristol and Barrington can send apparatus. That assumption holds when emergencies are local and randomly distributed. It collapses when they are regional and simultaneous. The storm that floods Warren floods Bristol and Barrington the same afternoon. Every unit is committed. Nobody has anything left to send. We have built a system on the premise that our neighbors will not be having our emergency at the same moment, and that premise is quietly expiring.
Layer on the toll the responders themselves absorb. Firefighters working in turnout gear at a triple-digit heat index, in an occupation already carrying a disproportionate rate of sudden cardiac death. Shorter recovery windows between calls. A behavioral health burden that research already places well above the general population’s, and that does not improve when the summer never lets up.
Here is the point, and it does not require anyone to revise a single belief about causes.
You can be entirely unconvinced by the climate science and still read a tide gauge. You can doubt every model ever built and still count ambulance runs. You can think the whole business is overstated and still notice that Market Street floods on a cloudless afternoon. Preparedness does not require agreement about etiology. Emergency management, done well, was never ideological. It is actuarial.
So treat it that way. Fund resilience in the same budget conversation as police and fire staffing, because it is the same conversation. Give Warren, and the dozen other Rhode Island communities staring at identical math, a state-level buyout mechanism that does not depend on winning a competitive federal grant lottery. Build the surge capacity now, before we need it: cooling centers with real staffing, mutual aid compacts written for regional events instead of local ones, EMS deployment models built around the hot week rather than the average one.
We can keep arguing about why the water is rising. The water is not waiting for us to finish.
